records.title: Evolving the Homeowner Messaging on the ROI of Resilience
records.summary: A LinkedIn article arguing that homeowners' expectation that a resilient roof pays for itself through lower insurance premiums does not match how the return is experienced. Using a $10,000 code-built roof against a $13,000 FORTIFIED roof and a 20% premium discount, it shows that rising premiums mean a homeowner still pays more each year even while saving against the counterfactual. It concludes that resilience messaging should start from insurance discounts but extend to future insurability, avoided damage and safety.
insights: The worked example sets a standard roof at $10,000 and a FORTIFIED roof at $13,000, a $3,000 resilience premium.
A 20% discount on a $100 monthly premium saves $20 a month in year one.
If premiums in at-risk places rise 50% over three years, the resilient homeowner pays $128 a month instead of $160, but still sees costs rising.
Because the counterfactual $160 is invisible to the homeowner, lower insurance costs cannot be the main justification for resilience.
The author recommends messaging on future insurability, avoided damage and household safety alongside discounts.

records.title: Congressional Reauthorization for the National Flood Insurance Program
records.summary: This FEMA page states the status of the National Flood Insurance Program's statutory authorization, which Congress must renew periodically. It records that on 2 September 2026 the president signed legislation extending the NFIP's authorization to 11 December 2026, by which Congress must reauthorize it. It explains that in a lapse FEMA would still pay valid claims but would stop selling and renewing policies, and it calls for reauthorization to simplify the program and strengthen its financial framework.
insights: Legislation signed on 2 September 2026 extends NFIP authorization to 11:59 p.m. on 11 December 2026.
In a lapse FEMA would keep paying valid claims from available funds but would stop selling and renewing policies.
The National Association of Realtors estimates a lapse could affect about 1,300 property sales per day, roughly 40,000 closings per month.
FEMA calls for reauthorization to reduce the program's complexity and strengthen its financial framework, citing damage from recent catastrophic storms.

records.title: The Weekly: El Niño Is a Stress Test for America's Infrastructure. It Can Show Us Where to Invest Next.
records.summary: This weekly newsletter's feature treats a forecast very strong El Nino as a stress test for US infrastructure that can reveal where to invest. It summarises expected regional impacts across the US and describes short-term preventative maintenance under way in California, such as clearing debris basins and storm channels. It argues that failures exposed this winter should become a list for future capital projects, and that local officials should model storm-scenario costs against their budgets, pointing to the RiskReserves Tool from GFOA and The Resiliency Company. The roundup covers NFIP lapse risk to home sales and California wildfire smoke remediation rules.
insights: NOAA's Climate Prediction Center puts the odds above 90% that this winter's El Nino becomes very strong, and 75% that it exceeds every event since 1950 in October to December.
A very strong El Nino has occurred only three times since 1950.
USGS modeling found a 60% to 80% chance of intense-storm debris flows on the Palisades and Eaton burn scars.
San Diego says it has $3.3 billion of stormwater improvements to make, with four dams still needing safety repairs.
The NFIP carries nearly 4.5 million policies and $1.3 trillion in coverage, and past lapses delayed or canceled thousands of home closings.

records.title: The Weekly: States' Resilience Investments Are Easing Housing Costs and Steadying Insurance Markets
institutions: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety
records.summary: This edition summarises a new publication of case studies and a policy brief on how six states finance IBHS FORTIFIED Roof upgrades: Alabama, Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina, Oklahoma and one Midwest state yet to launch. It sets out five funding levers states use and five design features common to their programs. Its central lesson is that resilience investments are increasingly evaluated as financial interventions that reduce future liabilities rather than as construction upgrades.
insights: For every $1 invested in pre-disaster mitigation, communities save $4 to $17 in later recovery and repair costs.

The five levers are direct public appropriations, insurance-sector funding mechanisms, tax code incentives including the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, capital market structures such as bonds and insurance-linked securities, and blended capital capturing avoided losses.
Common design features are payment only after verified FORTIFIED completion, mandated insurance discounts, risk-based targeting, need-based access, and reinvestment of tracked avoided losses.
Regulators in Alabama, Louisiana and Oklahoma require insurers to discount the wind portion of premiums for FORTIFIED homes.
Verisk expects global insured catastrophe losses to average $171 billion a year, with the US accounting for 68% of modeled insured catastrophe risk.

records.title: The Emerging Success Story of States Treating Home Resilience as a Public Investment
institutions: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety
Center for Risk and Insurance Research
records.summary: This article summarizes a new set of case studies and a policy brief from Duke University's Nicholas Institute, produced with The Resiliency Company, on how six states finance property-level resilience upgrades built to the IBHS FORTIFIED Roof standard. It reports the loss evidence behind FORTIFIED from Alabama and North Carolina, then sets out five funding levers states use and five design features common to the programs. The researchers conclude that resilience investments are increasingly treated as financial interventions that reduce future liabilities, connecting verified risk reduction to insurance pricing, capital allocation and public investment.
insights: An Alabama study of Hurricane Sally in 2020 found FORTIFIED Roofs reduced claim frequency by 55%-74%, claim severity by 14%-40% and loss ratio by 51%-72%.
In North Carolina, homes with FORTIFIED Roofs had roughly 35% fewer claims and 23% lower damage severity after major storms.

The five funding levers are direct appropriations, insurance sector mechanisms (premium taxes, regulatory fees, underwriting surplus, assessments), tax code incentives, capital market structures such as bonds and insurance-linked securities, and blended capital that captures avoided losses.

Common design features include paying only after verified completion, mandated wind premium discounts (Alabama, Louisiana, Oklahoma), risk-based and need-based targeting, and recycling measured savings back into the programs.
The piece cites $4 to $17 saved in recovery and repair costs for every $1 invested in pre-disaster mitigation.

records.title: The Durability of Capital Post-Disaster Is Key
institutions: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety
records.summary: The post, responding to a New York Times Magazine article on perpetual climate disaster, argues that the US disaster recovery funding system, built when disasters were rare, wastes capital by rebuilding what was lost exactly as it was. For capital to be used efficiently it must flow into making homes and infrastructure more resilient during rebuilding, which needs a durable flow of funds disciplined to last long enough. It rejects the idea that speed and durability of capital must conflict. It reports that since the January 2025 Palisades and Eaton fires, one third of homes lost in the Los Angeles region have been enabled to rebuild to an evidence-based wildfire-resilient standard.
insights: The author reports that one third of homes lost across the Los Angeles region in the January 2025 fires have been enabled to rebuild to an evidence-based wildfire-resilient standard.
Two levers are named: bringing the IBHS fire-resilient standard into rebuilding plans, and the Resilient Delta Fund.
The post argues that treating resilience as an afterthought at the end of rebuilding leaves too little capital to fund it.
Post-disaster success is measured by speed of relief and rebuilding, and the author argues speed and durability of capital need not conflict.

records.title: Ensuring a Better Future: Innovative Financing for Resilient Communities
records.authors: Kanika Singh, Alexander Meeks, Caroline Teare
institutions: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety (IBHS)
records.summary: This Milken Institute Financial Innovations Lab report, produced in partnership with Marsh, examines barriers to community-level resilience financing and proposes five innovative frameworks: a stakeholder-driven Community Plan with insurer engagement, a private-sector-led revolving loan fund, a district-backed resilience bond, a resilience innovation technology investment fund, and a state policy playbook. Grounded in the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires ($76–$131B in losses), the report draws on 75 stakeholder interviews and a Los Angeles workshop to identify capital structures that align divergent investor risk/return requirements at scale.
insights: Global natural disaster economic losses have exceeded $200B annually since 2016, with insured losses topping $100B for six consecutive years through 2025, yet uninsured losses now account for more than half of total global losses, signaling a widening protection gap that transfers costs to government and community balance sheets.

The 2025 LA Eaton and Palisades fires caused $76–$131B in estimated losses; one year later, 7 in 10 survivors remained displaced and over half faced losses exceeding their annual income, with a $5B underinsurance gap documented at the household level.

Florida mangroves provided an estimated $1.54B in flood-risk-reduction benefits during Hurricane Irma (2017), averaging $7,500/hectare, with Lee County alone receiving $802.6M in benefits, a quantified unit-economics proof point for nature-based coastal protection.

A Marsh/Nature Conservancy study found that combining wildfire buffer zones with updated building codes would have reduced wildfire losses in Paradise, CA by up to 42%; IBHS FORTIFIED roof standards, if universally applied in Hurricane Sally's path, could have cut policyholder losses 65% and insurer losses 75%.

FM Global's Resilience Credit, a 5% premium discount launched at $300M, estimated $20B in client loss reductions; doubling the credit to 10% (costing $825M in foregone premiums) is projected to save clients an additional $35B/year, demonstrating a quantifiable insurer-client ROI from ex-ante resilience investment.

Seoul's Cheonggyecheon stream restoration yielded a 76% increase in foot traffic for local businesses, 30–40% land value appreciation, 15% increase in bus revenues, and a 45% reduction in urban heat island effect, illustrating how resilience ROI can be captured across economic, fiscal, and public health dimensions.

records.title: California's Disaster Recovery Financing Districts: New Tools for Local Recovery
institutions: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
records.summary: This Milken Institute report (September 2026) analyzes California's newly authorized Disaster Recovery Financing Districts (DRFDs), created by SB 782 in October 2025 in response to the January 2025 Eaton and Palisades wildfires. It traces the policy lineage from redevelopment agencies through Proposition 13 to today's constrained tax increment financing tools, quantifies projected TIF revenues for the Altadena ($734M) and Unincorporated Santa Monica Mountains ($245M) DRFDs against rebuilding budgets of $2B and $233M respectively, and outlines implementation principles for braiding TIF with grants, CRA lending, revolving loan funds, and innovative insurance arrangements.
insights: Altadena DRFD projects $734M in present-value TIF revenues over 50 years against a $2B rebuilding and resilience budget, TIF covers roughly 37% of estimated need, confirming it is one tool among many.
Unincorporated Santa Monica Mountains DRFD projects $245M in TIF revenues against a $233M rebuilding budget, making it the more revenue-adequate district, though grant dependence remains significant.
Pacific Palisades DRFD analysis shows a wide $325M–$1.9B TIF revenue range over the district period, reflecting deep uncertainty in rebuilding pace, property turnover, and densification assumptions.

Proposition 13 caps assessed value growth at 2% annually, meaning a home appreciating $100K in market value yields only $280/year in incremental TIF revenue, structural constraint that makes post-disaster TIF slow to ramp.

LA County estimates $18.3M/year in recurring general fund revenue reduction from the Altadena DRFD by 2035 and $751K/year from the Santa Monica Mountains DRFD by 2036, quantifying the fiscal cost to surrounding communities.

Property tax relief policies for fire survivors (Prop 19 transfers, disaster valuation freezes) directly suppress TIF revenue, creating a tension between protecting individual homeowners and generating community-wide recovery capital.

The Delta Region Geologic Hazard Abatement District in Isleton, CA piloted a parametric insurance product disbursing immediate liquidity to property owners upon a flood threshold trigger, cited as a replicable model for LA DRFDs.

CRA-eligible disaster-affected census tracts (within 3 years of declared disaster) open a pathway for private bank lending motivated by Community Reinvestment Act obligations, supplementing scarce TIF dollars for projects that can support low-cost debt.

records.title: What Is PACE?
records.summary: This PACENation fact sheet (data through August 2023) provides an overview of Property Assessed Clean Energy (PACE) financing, a tool enabling 100% fixed-rate, long-term (up to 30-year) funding for energy efficiency, renewables, water efficiency, resilience, and public health improvements secured by a voluntary property assessment. As of mid-2023, $8.6B has been deployed on 350,000+ residential properties and $6.3B on 3,200+ commercial properties across 30 active states plus D.C. Estimated lifetime community benefits include $3.9B in avoided natural disaster losses, $12B in utility bill savings, and 214,000 job-years created.
insights: PACE has deployed $14.9B+ cumulatively (through August 2023): $8.6B across 350,000+ residential properties and $6.3B across 3,200+ commercial properties, demonstrating proven deployment at scale across both market segments.

$3.9B in avoided losses from natural disasters is attributed to PACE-financed resilience improvements (estimated over useful lifetime of installed measures through June 2023), providing a concrete quantified benefit for capital allocators evaluating resilience ROI.

The addressable market for deep building retrofits and electrification of U.S. buildings is estimated at $2+ trillion, indicating substantial runway for PACE financing as a private-capital instrument that does not require public subsidy.

PACE assessments are non-recourse and non-accelerating, transferring automatically upon property sale, a structural feature that differentiates PACE from conventional debt and reduces lender risk while simplifying borrower exit.

38 states and D.C. have enacted PACE-enabling legislation, with active programs in 30 states plus D.C., demonstrating broad but still incomplete policy coverage; residential PACE remains limited to California, Florida, and Missouri.

Estimated lifetime community benefits include 53B kWh of energy saved, 14M metric tons of avoided carbon emissions, $12B in utility bill savings, and $29B in total economic impact, offering a multi-dimensional value case for ESG-oriented allocators.
Over 90 active C-PACE lenders are operating across 30+ states, indicating a competitive and liquid private lending market rather than a single-source or government-dependent structure.

PACE covers 100% of hard and soft costs with fixed-rate fully amortizing terms up to 30 years, enabling projects that may be capital-constrained under conventional lending, including retrofits at healthcare, industrial, multifamily, and mixed-use properties.

records.title: The Weekly: LA Has the Leadership and Capital to Rebuild with Resilience. It's Missing the System to Connect Them.
records.summary: Jonathan Dromgoole of Resilient LA, a program of The Resiliency Company, reports three lessons from the Rebuilding with Resilience Summit held in Los Angeles on August 17 and 18. The summit concluded that Los Angeles has the ideas, expertise and capital to rebuild resiliently after the Eaton and Palisades fires but lacks the coordinating systems to bring them together. The lessons are that resilient rebuilding needs coordinated hubs and caseworkers rather than new organizations, that grants alone cannot rebuild at scale so proven financial models should be replicated, and that collaboration is itself infrastructure.
insights: The summit was organized by The Resiliency Company and SoCal Grantmakers, with day one on philanthropy's role and day two on implementation.
Survivors are described as navigating insurance, permitting, financing and government processes largely alone.
Lendistry's Disaster Recovery Mortgage and Alabama's FORTIFIED roof program are cited as financial models that show what is possible beyond grants.
Resilient LA is running pilot projects with builders and nonprofits and publishing a Rebuilding with Resilience Manual.
The reading list cites a Climate Policy Initiative finding that less than 10% of climate-related losses in emerging and developing economies are insured.

records.title: The Missing Piece in LA's Wildfire Recovery Is Coordination
records.summary: The article reports on a Funders Forum and a Rebuilding with Resilience Summit held in Los Angeles on 17 and 18 August after the Eaton and Palisades fires. It concludes that Los Angeles lacks not ideas or expertise but the connections, systems and capacity to deliver resilient rebuilding at scale. It draws three lessons: coordination of existing actors, a shift from ideas to implementation including financial structures beyond grants, and survivor-centred collaboration as the infrastructure for recovery.
insights: Participants concluded that grants alone will not rebuild thousands of homes and asked what financial structures could make resilient rebuilding work at neighbourhood scale.

Named models include Lendistry's Disaster Recovery Mortgage, Paradise's $650 Gravel Grants for the 0-5 foot 'Zone Zero', and the Resiliency Company's Delta Fund backing resilience upgrades with loan guarantees.
Alabama's FORTIFIED roof program is cited as providing up to $10,000 per roof with insurers then reducing premiums.
The Eaton Fire Collaborative is highlighted as connective infrastructure linking nonprofits, community groups and government around case management.
Resilient LA's Rebuilding with Resilience Manual translates technical standards into guidance for homeowners and builders.

records.title: The Weekly: When a Spark Can Bankrupt a Utility, the Grid Is Now a Wildfire Defense System
institutions: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety
records.summary: This edition explains how utilities in the West are redesigning grids for wildfire resilience after single ignitions have caused billions in damage and utility bankruptcies. It describes undergrounding, microgrids, data-driven vegetation management and centralised wildfire risk management, and notes the spread of mandatory utility wildfire mitigation plans. It argues that grid hardening and home hardening are complementary layers that insurers, regulators and investors should evaluate together.
insights: California in 2018 became the first state to require utilities in high fire-risk areas to publish wildfire mitigation plans; 11 states now require them.
An Integral Consulting analysis of hypothetical microgrids at the Camp, Thomas and Witch fire sites found benefit-cost ratios of roughly 105 to 746.
Undergrounding chosen from observed asset behaviour and modeled risk, rather than territory-wide averages, is said to retire more risk per dollar.
FEMA lost more than 4,300 employees in fiscal year 2025, a 55% increase in departures over the prior year, per GAO.

records.title: Physical Risk Only Becomes a Credit Problem When Governments Can't Manage It
institutions: Los Angeles Department of Water and Power
records.summary: The piece argues that physical climate risk becomes municipal credit risk only through a government's fiscal capacity, infrastructure decisions and governance, not mechanically through exposure. It uses Corpus Christi, Texas, whose water-utility debt was downgraded by Moody's, S&P and Fitch amid drought, to show that summer rainfall improved the physical outlook faster than the credit outlook, which still turns on financing a long-term water supply. It explains why the municipal market has proved more resilient than expected (diverse revenues, legal frameworks such as statutory liens, active management) and why stress tends to concentrate in enterprise systems such as water and power utilities. It recommends treating physical risk as a financial-management issue, with reserves calibrated to probabilistic risk modeling.
insights: Moody's, S&P and Fitch all downgraded Corpus Christi debt within a year, citing acute drought, water supply, financial performance and execution of a long-term water strategy, including a nearly $1 billion desalination project the council is divided over.

Municipal credit deterioration after disasters has been targeted rather than systemic: the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power faced rating pressure after the 2025 wildfires without a parallel downgrade of the city.
Statutory liens give bondholders a secured claim on pledged revenues that survives municipal bankruptcy, one structural reason the municipal market holds steady.

Historical distress came from discrete financial decisions: Harrisburg's incinerator financing and Jefferson County, Alabama's sewer debt and interest-rate swaps, which made its November 2011 filing the largest municipal bankruptcy in US history.
A drought becomes a credit problem when water revenues fall, emergency spending rises, capital needs accelerate, reserves prove inadequate or politics blocks rate and investment changes.
GFOA argues reserves should be calibrated to risk; The Resiliency Company has built a RiskReserve Tool applying a probabilistic model to a reserve framework to quantify natural hazard liabilities.

records.title: Can Investors Price the Risk? Assessing Municipal Bond Climate Disclosure and Financial Resilience
records.authors: Jake Rascoff, Holly Li, Eunyoung Lee
records.summary: This August 2026 Ceres report analyzes climate risk disclosure quality across 60 municipal bond offerings from the 20 highest climate-risk U.S. metro areas (by Cotality Composite Risk Score). It finds that current disclosure practices are inadequate for investor pricing: one-third of bonds make no climate mention, only 15% disclose governance accountability, and just 12% provide quantifiable metrics. The $4.4 trillion municipal bond market finances over 70% of U.S. infrastructure, making disclosure quality a systemic credit risk issue. The report uses TCFD as the scoring framework and cross-references Kestrel Environmental Scores to identify a "Silent Achievers" gap where resilience investments go undisclosed.
insights: One-third (33%) of 60 sampled municipal bond offerings from the 20 highest-risk U.S. metros make no mention of climate or extreme weather risk, while only 12% provide the quantitative metrics investors need to assess and price risk.

TCFD alignment is highly uneven across pillars: Strategy is addressed in 55% of bonds, Risk Management in 33%, Governance in 15%, and Metrics & Targets in only 12%, the pillar most critical for investor comparison and capital pricing.

The U.S. experienced 23 separate billion-dollar disasters in 2025 totaling more than $115 billion in damages, nearly four times the annual average of the 1990s, directly threatening the tax bases and fiscal stability that underpin municipal bond repayment.

Miami-Dade County's 2025 GO bond exemplifies best practice: it quantifies that a National Flood Insurance Program rating improvement (from a5 to a3) saves residents and businesses an estimated $12 million annually via a 35% flood insurance premium discount, a direct, investor-legible benefit of resilience investment.

LADWP's 2025 Water System Revenue Bonds disclose a layered wildfire insurance program totaling $273.65 million (including a $100M CAT bond for 2025–2028), providing concrete financial metrics for wildfire risk management that are largely absent from peer disclosures.

A 'Silent Achievers' cohort, issuers with high Kestrel Environmental Scores but low TCFD alignment, cannot capture potential borrowing cost reductions because their resilience investments are invisible to the bond market; approximately 15% of the $3.2 trillion Kestrel-covered universe exhibits resilience features.

Bonds issued by different entities in the same county can have materially different disclosure quality (e.g., Birmingham metro), confirming that disclosure is not driven by underlying risk but by issuer practice, undermining market comparability.

records.title: IDB Strengthens Belize's Hurricane Resilience with First Catastrophe Swap
records.summary: The Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) executed its first-ever catastrophe swap for Belize, transferring a layer of hurricane risk to international reinsurance markets via Swiss Re, which provides the underlying parametric coverage. The instrument offers up to $20 million in coverage (maximum $10 million per policy year) running August 2026–May 2028, enabling rapid post-hurricane liquidity. The transaction complements $25 million in IDB contingent credit and $118 million in loans protected by Climate Resilient Debt Clauses, forming a layered disaster risk-financing strategy for Belize under the FIRRe and Ready and Resilient Americas frameworks.
insights: The catastrophe swap provides up to $20 million in hurricane risk coverage for Belize, capped at $10 million per policy year, spanning two hurricane seasons (August 2026–May 2028).

Belize's total layered disaster risk-finance package reaches at least $163 million when combining the $20M cat swap, $25M IDB Contingent Credit Facility, and $118M in Climate Resilient Debt Clause-protected loans.

The transaction is the IDB's first catastrophe swap, positioning it as a replicable blueprint for transferring sovereign disaster risk to international reinsurance markets across Latin America and the Caribbean.
Swiss Re provides the underlying parametric coverage, meaning payouts are triggered by pre-agreed hurricane parameters rather than assessed losses, enabling faster post-event liquidity access.

Funding for the premium drew on three sources, technical cooperation from the Ready and Resilient Americas Initiative, donor contributions from the French Climate Fund, and the Government of Belize's own contribution, illustrating a blended finance structure for instrument affordability.

Climate Resilient Debt Clauses on $118 million in IDB loans allow Belize to defer principal payments for two years following an eligible natural disaster, reducing post-shock fiscal stress without requiring new borrowing.

The FIRRe (Ready and Resilient Americas financial instruments) framework is the vehicle through which the IDB intends to scale this cat swap model to other LAC sovereigns, signaling a programmatic rather than one-off approach.

The structure demonstrates how a multilateral development bank can act as arranger, rather than risk-bearer, channeling sovereign disaster risk to private reinsurance capacity while using concessional resources to subsidize the premium.

records.title: United Policyholders Receives Grant from the American Red Cross to Expand Roadmap to Recovery® and Preparedness Services to Los Angeles Wildfire-Impacted Communities
records.summary: United Policyholders, a national 501(c)(3) consumer advocacy organization founded in 1991, announced on 13 August 2026 that it had received a $650,000 grant from the American Red Cross for the Roadmap to Resilience Project, a 17-month initiative expanding insurance recovery assistance to households hit by the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires and increasing disaster readiness and financial health in high-hazard regions across Southern California. The work covers Pacific Palisades, Altadena, Malibu and surrounding fire-impacted areas. United Policyholders will update the printed Disaster Recovery Handbook and launch a digital version in English and Spanish, removing the physical distribution barrier for displaced survivors and covering insurance processes, financial and re-housing decisions and casualty loss tax rules. It will deliver specialized technical training and direct support to Disaster Case Managers and Long-Term Recovery Groups operating on the ground. The organization's own multi-year post-wildfire surveys find that most disaster-impacted households face prolonged negotiations, disputes over restoration cost and insufficient coverage for temporary living expenses. The grant also expands the Roadmap to Preparedness programme, running workshops for homeowners and renters in impacted and high-risk areas to identify and fix coverage gaps before the next disaster and to build insurance literacy.
insights: The intervention is on the claims side rather than the coverage side: it funds help extracting value from policies households already hold, which is where United Policyholders' own surveys locate the loss, in prolonged negotiation, disputed restoration cost and insufficient additional living expense cover.
Underinsurance for temporary living expenses is named as a recurring finding across multiple post-wildfire surveys, which makes it a structural product defect rather than a feature of one event.
Philanthropic capital, from a disaster relief organization rather than an insurer or a regulator, is paying for the consumer-side capacity that closes the gap between a policy and a settlement.

The preparedness half, workshops on identifying and fixing coverage gaps before a loss, is an attempt to convert post-disaster demand for help into pre-disaster insurance literacy in the same high-hazard communities.

records.title: New Zealand’s Natural Hazards Commission Secures Record $7.2 bn Reinsurance Cover
institutions: Natural Hazards Commission Toka Tū Ake
records.summary: The article reports that New Zealand's public Natural Hazards Commission secured a record NZ$12.3 billion (US$7.2 billion) of reinsurance for 2026, 20% more than the NZ$10.3 billion placed in 2025 and on a more cost-effective basis. The programme includes NZ$225 million from the multi-year Totara Re Series 2023-1 catastrophe bond, in force until May 2027. It presents the placement as an example of a public catastrophe scheme combining traditional reinsurance and capital markets to protect the Crown's balance sheet.
insights: The 2026 reinsurance programme is NZ$12.3 billion (US$7.2 billion), 20% larger than the NZ$10.3 billion of 2025.
The programme includes NZ$225 million from the Totara Re Series 2023-1 catastrophe bond, which remains in force until May 2027.
NHC reports the larger cover was bought more cost-effectively than in 2025.
The CEO, Tina Mitchell, attributes reinsurer support to scheme design, hazard science and modelling, investment in resilience and transparency with reinsurers.
The cover responds to earthquakes, storms, floods and other large disasters affecting insured homeowners.

records.title: 2026 Proposed Changes to the Community Reinvestment Act
records.summary: This Opportunity Finance Network (OFN) policy brief analyzes a 2026 joint OCC-FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking that would significantly restructure Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. The proposal raises asset-size thresholds, exempting an estimated 800 banks from the Community Development test and removing 376 banks from large-bank treatment. OFN estimates $2 billion per year in community finance is at risk. The brief highlights threats to bank-CDFI partnerships, LIHTC and NMTC demand, operating grant eligibility, and data availability, while noting some positive provisions including explicit CRA credit for disaster preparedness and resilience activities.
insights: The proposed OCC/FDIC rulemaking would move ~800 banks from intermediate to small classification, exempting more than 75% of all U.S. banks from the Community Development (CD) test and putting an estimated $2 billion per year in community finance at risk.

376 banks would shift from large to intermediate classification, reducing their obligation to report small business, small farm, and CD loan data and weakening the standalone investment test that incentivizes LIHTC and NMTC equity investments.

LIHTC has financed ~3.7 million affordable homes since inception; NMTC has deployed $63 billion into low-income communities, supported 888,000+ jobs, and financed 268 million sq ft of commercial real estate, both programs face reduced bank demand if CRA incentives are diluted.

In FY 2024, OFN members received $6.2 billion in borrowed funds from CRA-motivated banks, representing ~46% of their total borrowed funds, illustrating the financial materiality of CRA regulatory structure for CDFI capitalization.
47% of the ~800 banks newly classified as small are headquartered in rural areas, making the impact particularly acute in markets with fewer financial institutions and less access to private capital.

The proposal explicitly grants CRA credit for 'disaster preparedness and resilience activities,' a notable positive provision that could unlock new bank investment flows toward community resilience infrastructure.

Restricting CRA credit for operating grants (including a 15% overhead cap for large banks) would reduce flexible capital to CDFIs, undermining their capacity to reach hard-to-serve borrowers and deploy CRA-eligible lending at scale.

records.title: Narratives to Inspire and Align Local Governments Around Resilience
records.summary: Written after the first Resilient America Summit, which gathered more than 100 leaders from government, public finance, insurance, investing and philanthropy, this article argues that resilience needs a fuller narrative than one tethered to disasters. It sets out three parts: making explicit the tacit climate assumptions built into infrastructure, translating physical risk into fiscal risk to budgets, reserves, capital plans and debt, and giving reasons to believe through concrete financing examples. It concludes that the response depends on dedicated, predictable funding mechanisms rather than improvisation after disasters.
insights: State and local governments finance, build and maintain around 70% of the country's shared physical infrastructure.

Most fiscal risk is said to come from chronic stresses such as heat, repeated fires, ponding and freeze-thaw cycles rather than headline disasters, through higher maintenance costs, eroded tax revenue and higher borrowing costs.
With the Government Finance Officers Association, the summit showed how to translate physical risk into fiscal risk for budgets, reserves, capital plans and debt.
Examples presented include a state tool transferring disaster risk to capital markets, an independent public resilience authority, and an insurance premium tax funding FORTIFIED home retrofits.

records.title: Once Cities Implement a Stormwater Utility, They Don't Stop
records.summary: A report on the spread of the stormwater utility as a municipal funding mechanism, drawing on Western Kentucky University researcher Warren Campbell's 2026 survey, which counted 2,202 stormwater utilities in the United States, a 22 per cent increase since 2020. A stormwater utility charges property owners according to how much runoff they send into the system and uses the revenue to fund stormwater infrastructure, which the article describes as a blueprint for pricing climate risk into the built environment by shifting the financial burden onto the physical footprint of development. The average monthly single-family residential fee was $6.33. The model scales in both directions: the smallest identified utility serves Indian Creek Village, Florida, population 84, and the largest covers Los Angeles County, population over 10 million. The context is that downpours have grown heavier by an average of 30 per cent across the continental United States and 60 per cent in the Northeast since 1958 while drainage systems have aged. The durability finding is the striking one: of all the utilities Campbell has tracked, only 13 have ever been repealed.
insights: The durability is the finding: only 13 stormwater utilities have ever been repealed out of more than 2,200, so once adopted the mechanism essentially never reverses, which is rare for a local charge and makes it an unusually reliable revenue base to borrow against.
The fee prices the physical footprint of development rather than assessed value, which is a direct mechanism for charging climate risk to the party creating the runoff.
Scale is not a constraint in either direction, from a village of 84 people to Los Angeles County, which removes the usual objection that a utility only works for large jurisdictions.
An average monthly residential fee of $6.33 is the political price of the mechanism, and it is low enough to explain the near-absence of repeals.
The hazard trend is quantified independently of the mechanism: downpours up an average 30 per cent nationally and 60 per cent in the Northeast since 1958.

records.title: Colombia Strengthens Climate Resilience with Parametric Insurance for 14,402 Smallholder Farmers
records.summary: The Colombian government, led by the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development (MARD) and FINAGRO, contracted five parametric agricultural insurance policies covering 14,402 smallholder farmers (and up to 41,600 household members), across five departments (Sucre, Córdoba, Cundinamarca, Meta, and Chocó). Policies provide up to US$20.14 million in coverage against drought and excess rainfall, triggered automatically via a satellite-derived Water Balance Index. Delivered through a public-private partnership under the Tripartite Agreement Programme (UNDP, IDF, BMZ/ISF), this marks the first use of parametric insurance by Colombia's departmental governments for agricultural risk management, with explicit intent to scale nationally.
insights: The five parametric policies provide up to US$20.14 million in coverage for 14,402 smallholder farmers and up to 41,600 household members across five Colombian departments, representing a first-of-its-kind deployment at the departmental government level in Colombia.

Payouts are triggered automatically by a satellite-derived Water Balance Index (rainfall minus evapotranspiration at the municipal level), eliminating post-disaster loss assessments and enabling faster capital disbursement to affected producers, a key basis risk reduction feature for capital allocators evaluating parametric structures.

Premium co-financing by the Government of Colombia and the InsuResilience Solutions Fund (ISF) in year one demonstrates a blended finance model designed to make parametric insurance affordable for sovereign/sub-sovereign agricultural programs and to catalyze private reinsurance capacity.

The initiative reduces smallholder dependence on uncertain or delayed emergency funding, substituting a pre-agreed parametric trigger mechanism for ad hoc disaster relief, a structural shift with implications for sovereign fiscal planning and donor grant programming.

The product was co-designed and co-financed by a consortium of IDF members (Guy Carpenter, Swiss Re, AXA Climate, Munich Re, Raincoat, La Previsora S.A.), illustrating a replicable public-private co-design model that embeds technical, legal, and financial groundwork for scaling across additional departments.

UNDP's role extended beyond product development to institutional capacity building within Colombia's agricultural risk management framework, positioning this as a scalable policy infrastructure investment rather than a one-off pilot.

records.title: Wildfire Exposed Catastrophe Bond Issuance Soars to $5.183bn Year-to-Date in 2026
records.summary: Artemis reports that wildfire-exposed catastrophe bond issuance reached $5.183 billion year-to-date in 2026 (through early July), across 20 individual cat bond series, already matching the full-year 2025 count and nearing the 2025 full-year record of $5.55 billion. The surge reflects growing investor familiarity with wildfire risk models, prudent ILS structuring, and iterative pricing refinements highlighted by reinsurance broker Acrisure Re. Three pure wildfire cat bonds in 144A format have been issued in 2026, one behind the all-time annual record of four set in 2025, signaling that wildfire is becoming a more meaningful standalone peril in capital markets.
insights: Wildfire-exposed cat bond issuance hit $5.183 billion year-to-date in 2026 (20 deals), already equaling the full-year 2025 deal count and approaching the 2025 full-year volume record of $5.55 billion.
Issuance has grown rapidly from $2.57 billion in 2023 to $2.84 billion in 2024 to $5.55 billion in 2025, more than doubling in two years, and 2026 is on pace to set a new annual record.

Three pure wildfire cat bonds in 144A format were issued in the first half of 2026, one fewer than the four issued across all of 2025, which was the most in market history; this signals the wildfire peril is maturing as a standalone capital markets risk transfer category.

The majority of wildfire-exposed cat bond volume comes from multi-peril transactions where wildfire is one covered peril, a structure that has helped investors build comfort with the risk incrementally.

Acrisure Re attributes investor appetite growth to two factors: iterative pricing and coverage refinements from each fire season, and what it calls a 'profound' effect from improved wildfire risk models on investor confidence.

Growing ILS market capacity for wildfire is providing direct reinsurance support to insurers and policyholders in high-risk areas such as California, where property and livelihood exposure to wildfire remains acute.

The acceleration since 2022 suggests a structural shift in capital market willingness to absorb wildfire risk, with implications for insurance availability and affordability in wildfire-prone regions.

records.title: The Role of Insurance in Funding and Financing Resilience
institutions: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety (IBHS)
records.summary: This white paper from Insurance for Good and California Forward examines how insurance and parametric risk-transfer instruments can fund and finance physical climate resilience. It evaluates four mechanisms: premium reductions tied to verified mitigation (FORTIFIED roofing, wildfire hardening), post-disaster "build-back-better" endorsements, insurer education and policy advocacy, and parametric cat-bond structures. Key proof points include 25–55% mandatory premium discounts for FORTIFIED homes in Alabama, a 22% average premium saving in Louisiana, and a first-of-its-kind catastrophe bond by the North Carolina Insurance Underwriting Association that routes up to $2M annually into FORTIFIED roof upgrades during low-loss years.
insights: FORTIFIED roof construction reduced insured losses by 51–72% following Hurricane Sally (Alabama, 2020), with 55–74% fewer claims and 14–40% lower average claim costs, among the strongest empirical validations of a building standard in the U.S. market.

Alabama mandates premium discounts of 25–55% (varying by county hurricane risk) for FORTIFIED homes; Louisiana targets 20–30% discounts with an observed average saving of 22%, demonstrating that actuarially-justified mitigation incentives are achievable at scale.

The North Carolina Insurance Underwriting Association embedded a resilience mechanism in a catastrophe bond: NCIUA contributes an extra 0.35% annually into a resilience account that pays out over $2M for FORTIFIED upgrades in years where losses stay below ~$1.68B, creating a pre-funded resilience reserve without new appropriations.

Upgrading to a FORTIFIED roof at time of rebuilding adds only 1–3% to new construction costs ($700–$1,700 per home by IBHS estimates), and wildfire-resistant rebuilding adds less than 10% to reconstruction cost, indicating that build-back-better endorsements of ≤10% of replacement cost could cover most necessary upgrades.

Premium reductions face a structural financing gap: discounts are annual and variable, making them insufficient as collateral for upfront retrofit loans. No premium-reduction-backed financing model has yet succeeded at scale, partly because insurers cannot lock in multi-year contracts and face free-rider risk if policyholders switch carriers after retrofits.

California's Safer from Wildfires regulation (2022) requires insurers to offer discounts for up to 12 wildfire risk-reduction measures but does not mandate discount magnitudes; Insurance for Good analysis finds wide variation, with single-measure discounts being minimal and meaningful reductions requiring bundled actions.

records.title: First-Half 2026 Insured Catastrophe Losses: Below Trend, Rising Risks
institutions: Global Facility for Disaster Reduction and Recovery
records.summary: This Swiss Re Institute sigma insights note estimates global insured natural catastrophe losses of USD 42 billion in the first half of 2026, the lowest first half since 2020 and below the USD 66 billion trend. Severe convective storms in the US drove most losses despite storm activity 20% above average, because few high-impact storms hit densely insured areas. The Venezuela earthquake sequence was the costliest event in economic terms but carried low insured losses, illustrating the protection gap. The note highlights Europe's rising heat and wildfire risk and warns that second-half hurricane tail risk remains despite a strengthening El Niño.
insights: Global insured nat cat losses were USD 42 billion in 1H 2026, against a trend estimate of USD 66 billion.
Insurance covered about 42% of USD 100 billion in economic losses, above the 30-year average of 33%.
Severe convective storms generated USD 28 billion of insured losses, below the USD 36 billion trend, ending four years of first-half SCS losses above USD 30 billion.
The 24 June Venezuela earthquake doublet (Mw7.2 and Mw7.5) killed more than 5,000 people and caused about USD 20 billion of damage, with low insured share.
Europe now averages 21-26 hot days a year (2016-2025) versus 10-17 in the 1950s, a 64% increase.
Structural drivers could push long-term insured loss growth to around 5-7% a year; 22% of US hurricane landfalls in 1950-2025 occurred under El Niño.

records.title: The Compound Effect: Heat, Water, and the New Risk Landscape
records.authors: Ehsan Najafi, Colin Gannon, Auguste Boissonnade, Shree Khare, Max Stephens
records.summary: This Moody's Insurance Solutions white paper (August 2026) analyzes the compound physical risk posed by heat stress and water stress, framed around Europe's 2026 heatwave sequence and US industrial exposure data. Using the ORBIS database (~159,000 US water-intensive facilities) and Moody's Climate on Demand (MCoD) models under RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5, it finds ~49,000 US facilities projected to transition into high or very high water stress by 2100, with Texas (~17,000) and California (~5,800) most exposed. CDP-reported corporate water risk exposure totals $225B (2022). The paper argues parametric insurance structures are better suited than indemnity products to price chronic, compounding perils, and calls on insurers, reinsurers, and investors to embed forward-looking heat and water projections into underwriting, valuation, and capital allocation.
insights: ~49,000 of 159,000 sampled US water-intensive facilities are projected to transition from low/moderate to high/very high water stress by 2100 under RCP 8.5, with Texas (~17,000) and California (~5,800) accounting for the largest concentrations, a material, currently underpriced shift in operational and credit risk for heavy manufacturing (61% of sample), food and beverage (25%), and mining (14%).

CDP-reporting companies disclosed $225B in self-assessed financial exposure to water risk (2022); CDP's 2020 Global Water Report found up to $301B in potential business value at risk if water risks go unaddressed, more than five times the estimated $55B cost of action, a 5:1 benefit-cost ratio for water risk mitigation investment.

Global water demand is projected to outstrip supply by 40% by 2030 (GCEW, 2023), and billions more people are expected to face water shortages by mid-century, framing water stress as a systemic, not idiosyncratic, risk that undermines conventional insurance diversification assumptions.

Europe's 2026 heatwave sequence (May–July) caused over 2,000 deaths in Spain and France combined, strained power grids (Italy peak demand 15% above May levels), forced nuclear output reductions in France due to high river temperatures, and reduced Po River delta flow by two-thirds in under two weeks, illustrating how acute heat events translate rapidly into water infrastructure and energy system stress.

Heat and water stress compound into a third hazard: wildfire. Modeling projects significant increases in fire-weather severity across 68–91% of fire-prone areas by 2100, with at least 55% affected by 2040; Europe's 2025 wildfire season was the worst on record (>1 million hectares burned since records began in 2006), directly linking heat-water stress to insured and economic loss escalation.

records.title: The Weekly: The Tools to Finance Resilience Already Exist. To Unlock Scale, We Need Coordination.
institutions: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety (IBHS)
records.summary: This issue carries an excerpt of Matt Posner's takeaways from the first Resilient America Summit, held by The Resiliency Company in Chicago on July 23 with nearly 100 leaders from government, public finance, insurance, philanthropy and investment. Its central claim is that financing resilience is a coordination problem rather than a cost-benefit problem, and that resilience has to enter the financial decisions governments already make, since physical risk ultimately becomes fiscal risk. It describes the RiskReserve Tool, developed with GFOA, which uses Monte Carlo simulation to translate risks into potential financial losses and test them against a government's reserves. It places state and local governments at the centre of a team that includes public finance, philanthropy, insurers and investors.
insights: The inaugural Resilient America Summit in Chicago on July 23 brought together nearly 100 leaders from government, public finance, insurance, philanthropy, infrastructure and investment.
The Summit's core diagnosis was that resilience is a coordination problem, not a cost-benefit problem.

The RiskReserve Tool, developed by The Resiliency Company and GFOA, uses Monte Carlo simulation to translate natural hazard and other risks into potential losses and tests them against a government's reserves.
State and local governments are positioned to convene the ecosystem because they own assets, set policy, allocate capital and bear the consequences when risks materialise.
The digest cites Brookings: commercial property insurance premiums for multifamily buildings more than doubled as a share of rental income between 2019 and 2024.
Over 134 million people, about a third of Americans, were under a heat warning or advisory on the Monday of that week.

records.title: The Verdict From The Resilient America Summit: Financing Resilience Is A Coordination Problem
records.summary: An article of 31 July 2026 in The Epicenter by Matt Posner, contributing author and Head of Public Finance for The Resiliency Company, reporting three takeaways from the first Resilient America Summit, held on 23 July in Chicago. The summit brought nearly 100 leaders from state and local government, public finance, insurance, philanthropy, infrastructure, investment and the wider resilience ecosystem together around one question: what will it take to move resilience from a recognised need to something communities can actually finance and deliver at scale. Resilient America is a new initiative of The Resiliency Company and this was its inaugural summit. The article's headline conclusion is that financing resilience is a coordination problem.
insights: The summit's central claim is that the binding constraint is coordination rather than capital or pricing: the money and the instruments exist, and what fails is agreement between the parties who would have to act together.

The convening list is the useful artifact. Public finance, insurance, philanthropy and infrastructure in one room is the set of parties a blended resilience structure needs, and the summit's premise is that they do not normally meet.

The author is Head of Public Finance for the company that convened the summit, so this is a participant's account of its own event. Recorded as provenance: the observation about coordination is worth keeping and the framing is not independent.

records.title: Resilient America Summit: Takeaways and Further Resources
institutions: Resilience Authority of Annapolis and Anne Arundel County
Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety
records.summary: This synthesis of the inaugural Resilient America Summit, held in Chicago on July 23, 2026 with 98 attendees and 25 speakers, sets out six takeaways on moving resilience from recognized need to something communities can finance and deliver. It argues physical risk is fiscal risk and the gap is translation into budget language, and that resilience is a coordination problem rather than a cost-benefit one. It names five structural hurdles, each with working mechanisms: resilience bonds, conditional insurance policies, multi-jurisdictional resilience authorities, reserves managed as self-insurance, parametric cover and embedded staff. It closes with a table of tools, including the RiskReserves Tool, which pilots with 10 communities in Q4 2026.
insights: Resilience solutions are cited as returning $6 to $13 for every $1 invested, but the returns spread across many actors and avoided losses appear on no balance sheet.

In North Carolina, modeling $50M of free fortified roof upgrades showed $5.8M a year in reduced reinsurance and up to $200M avoided in a major storm, supporting a catastrophe bond with a resilience kicker that targeted $350M and closed at $600M.
In Escondido, CA, the first IBHS-certified wildfire-prepared neighborhood turned a projected FAIR Plan cost of $10,000 a year into $1,200 a year, guaranteed for three years.
The Resilience Authority of Annapolis and Anne Arundel County, launched in 2021, raised $80M across 32 projects in about three years, with $0.94 of every dollar going to projects.
The Community Rating System offers up to a 45% flood insurance discount, but only about 7% of eligible communities participate, largely for lack of staff capacity.
Miami's Forever Bond passed at 57% as a $400M general obligation issue with $200M earmarked for resilience.

records.title: Paying for Resilience in New York State
records.summary: Rebuild by Design, with the New York State Adaptation Practitioners Network, published a first-of-its-kind statewide inventory of known public sector climate adaptation costs on 23 July 2026, finding that New York State and its municipalities will need to spend $519 billion of taxpayer money to build, upgrade or retrofit infrastructure through 2050. The statewide per capita cost is approximately $26,000; New York City's is $50,000, the highest of any region, driven by construction and labor costs, limited space for nature-based solutions and the complexity of protecting dense populations and interconnected underground systems. The most expensive categories are sewer and stormwater upgrades and coastal defense on Long Island and in New York City. The analysis compiled over 700 projects and plans through desktop research informed by practitioners statewide, covering storm surge and sea level rise, erosion, grid resilience, stormwater and green infrastructure, shoreline and habitat restoration, disaster preparedness and resilience hubs, heat mitigation, wind and storm damage protection, flood risk reduction and sewer upgrades. The report states the true cost is unknown because most communities lack capacity to conduct a comprehensive needs assessment. On the resource side, the 2022 $4.2 billion Environmental Bond Act has already allocated $2.2 billion, the 2024 Climate Change Superfund Law would assign fossil fuel companies an estimated $75 billion but faces lawsuits from 22 states and industry plus a federal executive order and proposed Congressional preemption, and federal resources continue to shrink. The report cites a U.S. Chamber of Commerce figure that every $1 not invested in disaster resilience can cost up to $33 in lost future economic activity, and notes that credit rating agencies increasingly incorporate climate risk into municipal bond ratings, so communities that fail to invest may face higher borrowing costs.
insights: A $519 billion need against $2 billion of remaining Environmental Bond Act capacity is the central arithmetic: the identified state funding source covers well under one per cent of the identified need, which is why the report is really about finding a revenue stream.
The per capita framing, $26,000 statewide and $50,000 in New York City, converts an infrastructure total into a household liability and is the number that makes the case politically legible.

The report is explicit that its total is a floor and biased downward in the places with least capacity, because the estimate counts only documented needs and small municipalities have not assessed their risk, so the gap is widest exactly where it is least visible.

The Climate Change Superfund Law is the one identified source at the scale of the problem, $75 billion, and it is under simultaneous attack from state litigation, industry litigation, an executive order and proposed federal preemption, so the largest line item in the funding plan is the least certain.
The credit rating channel is named as a cost of inaction: failing to invest raises the cost of borrowing for the investment, which is a feedback loop that makes delay progressively more expensive.

records.title: The Great Unlock
records.authors: Matt Posner; Xavier de Souza Briggs
records.summary: The essay argues that resilience funding is shifting from a government-paid, post-disaster model to one where measurable resilience value unlocks private capital, which it calls the Great Unlock. Because rising losses, insurer withdrawal and federal cutbacks push fiscal risk onto states and localities, grants alone cannot reduce future risk, and bond debt, home and commercial lending, and insurance innovation matter more. It casts state and local government as the organizing platform rather than sole payer, and lists the beneficiaries (insurers, developers, investors, utilities, health systems, philanthropy) who can be turned into active resilience partners. It names the scaling mechanisms states are using, from mitigation appropriations to catastrophe bonds and blended structures repaid through avoided insurance losses.
insights: The Great Unlock is defined as the point at which resilience value can be measured and demonstrated, making mortgages, home equity loans, infrastructure bonds and insurance savings available to finance resilience.

Five scaling mechanisms are named: direct public appropriations for hazard mitigation, insurance-sector funding that recycles industry revenue, tax incentives for stronger construction, catastrophe bonds linked to mitigation-driven savings, and blended capital repaid through documented reductions in insurance losses.
North Carolina's $600 million catastrophe bond is cited as letting investors price hurricane risk while creating a way to recognize the value of loss-reducing investment.
FORTIFIED Roof incentive programs in Alabama, North Carolina and other southeastern states are presented as an insurer-recognized success story.
Florida and other states use a federal tax credit program to incentivize developers to build affordable rental housing to resilient standards.
The Resilient Delta Fund in Los Angeles brings philanthropy, building companies and public partners together around home lending for resilient rebuilding after the 2025 wildfires.

records.title: Financing the Missing Asset: Why Municipal Bonds Have Struggled to Finance Climate Resilience
records.summary: Part one of a series on embedding resilience into public finance. Posner argues the municipal bond market should be the natural home of resilience finance, since municipal bonds already are the backbone of American infrastructure finance and infrastructure investment is fundamentally resilience investment, and that it has failed to become so in two opposite ways. On one side are transactions that are too narrow: bespoke, highly engineered deals, among them environmental impact bonds, blended capital structures and special purpose vehicles, each of which reinvents its own rules and therefore cannot scale, forfeiting the very scalability that makes securities useful. On the other side are transactions that are too wide: general obligation issuances in which resilience outcomes become impossible to track or measure. The result he names is fewer bankable projects, a higher cost of capital, and a market that cannot fund resilience at scale. His proposal is a middle route, standardised enough to scale and specific enough to measure, sized against a cited $1 trillion of needed infrastructure repairs across 2,000 US cities.
insights: The diagnosis is symmetrical and that is the argument: bespoke deals fail because they cannot scale, and general obligation issuance fails because the resilience outcome cannot be measured, so neither end of the existing market can carry adaptation.
Environmental impact bonds and blended capital structures are named as examples of the too-narrow failure, which is a direct challenge to the instruments the field most often celebrates.
The consequence is priced: fewer bankable projects and a higher cost of capital, so the structural problem shows up as an interest rate rather than as an absence of intent.

The proposed middle route is standardisation, which is the same move the community land trust lending certification and the FORTIFIED standard make in their own markets: a class of deal a lender can underwrite without bespoke diligence.

records.title: Road to Resilience: Town Highway Disaster Reserve Benchmarks
records.summary: The Vermont Bond Bank released the first Town Highway Disaster Reserve Benchmarks, a financial planning tool and online database giving every Vermont town, city and village a data-driven estimate of the annual contribution needed to build an adequate disaster reserve for local roads and bridges. The benchmarks combine 16 years of inflation-adjusted FEMA Public Assistance data with the Bond Bank's own database of municipal financial statements and VTrans' Transportation Resilience Planning Tool. The headline finding is encouraging and the caveat is the substance: a typical Vermont community needs to set aside less than 1 per cent of its annual budget to meet its benchmark, but that amount would quadruple without FEMA assistance, and more than 40 per cent of towns would need more than half their annual budget to cover losses from a large event. The release situates the tool in a track record that began after the July 2023 floods, when the Bond Bank helped create the Municipal Climate Recovery Fund, which has since lent more than $33 million to 27 municipalities for recovery, and it is the first of a planned series of Bond Bank disaster resilience tools.
insights: The federal dependency is quantified rather than asserted: the required municipal reserve quadruples without FEMA assistance, and more than 40 per cent of towns would need over half their annual budget to absorb a large event, which turns federal policy uncertainty into a municipal balance sheet number.
Under 1 per cent of annual budget as the typical benchmark contribution is a genuinely actionable figure, because it is small enough to be adopted by a town meeting.

The method joins FEMA Public Assistance history to the Bond Bank's own municipal financial statement database, which is a combination only a state bond bank could assemble and is what makes the benchmark specific to each town.

A state bond bank is acting as a risk analytics provider and a lender at once, having already deployed $33 million to 27 municipalities through the Municipal Climate Recovery Fund created after the July 2023 floods.

records.title: 2025 Joint Summary Report on Multilateral Development Banks' Climate Finance
records.authors: African Development Bank; Asian Development Bank; Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank; Council of Europe Development Bank; European Bank for Reconstruction and Development; European Investment Bank; Inter-American Development Bank Group; Islamic Development Bank; New Development Bank; World Bank Group
institutions: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development
records.summary: This joint summary from ten multilateral development banks reports their 2025 climate finance and confirms they exceeded their collective 2025 goals set in 2019 and are on track for the 2030 estimates announced at COP29. Climate finance in low- and middle-income countries grew 21% to almost $103 billion, and total MDB climate finance rose 19% to nearly $163 billion. Adaptation finance in low- and middle-income countries grew 31% to $35 billion, close to the $42 billion annual level estimated for 2030. It breaks commitments down by activity, region and instrument and notes a new MDB Climate Finance Dashboard.
insights: In 2025 MDBs committed $102.585 billion in climate finance to low- and middle-income economies and $59.934 billion to high-income economies.
Adaptation finance in low- and middle-income countries rose 31% to $35 billion, against an estimated $42 billion annual level for 2030.
Private sector mobilisation accounted for $116 billion of climate co-finance, $35 billion of it in low- and middle-income countries.

Investment loans dominate at $110,229 million, followed by policy-based lending at $17,586 million, guarantees at $11,059 million and results-based financing at $6,544 million, with green bonds at $1,376 million.
By 2030 MDBs estimate annual climate finance for low- and middle-income countries of USD 120 billion, including USD 42 billion for adaptation, with USD 65 billion mobilised from the private sector.

records.title: Multilateral Development Banks Increased Climate Financing to $163 Billion in 2025, Supporting Climate-Resilient and Sustainable Growth
institutions: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development
records.summary: Multilateral development banks reported record climate financing for 2025 in their joint annual report: $163 billion across all countries of operation, up 19 per cent, of which $103 billion went to low- and middle-income countries, up 21 per cent and double the level of five years earlier. Adaptation finance in those countries rose 31 per cent to $35 billion against mitigation at $68 billion, with private-sector mobilisation of $35 billion. In high-income economies MDBs provided $53 billion for mitigation and $7 billion for adaptation, mobilising $80 billion privately. The reporting is coordinated by the EIB with EBRD assistance and combines data from the major regional development banks.
insights: Adaptation finance grew faster than mitigation in low- and middle-income countries, 31 per cent against 16 per cent, though the levels remain far apart at $35 billion against $68 billion, so the crossover is in growth rate rather than in volume.

The high-income split is the sharper number: $53 billion for mitigation against $7 billion for adaptation, a ratio of more than seven to one, and MDBs report already meeting or exceeding their 2030 high-income targets five years early.
Private mobilisation is larger in high-income countries than in low- and middle-income ones, $80 billion against $35 billion, so the leverage the banks achieve is weakest where the need is greatest.

The COP29 Baku commitments give the benchmark: $120 billion a year for low- and middle-income countries by 2030 including $42 billion for adaptation, plus $65 billion a year mobilised privately, so the 2025 adaptation figure of $35 billion is within reach of the $42 billion target.

An MDB Climate Finance Dashboard was launched in pilot in April 2026, giving granular breakdowns and the harmonised methodologies behind the headline figures, which matters because MDB climate finance accounting has been contested.

records.title: The Right Tool at the Right Time: CRDs vs. DRDs, What Every California Community Should Know
institutions: Sonoma County Regional Climate Protection Authority
records.summary: California Forward and Resilient Cities Catalyst compare California's two local resilience financing districts. The Climate Resilience District (CRD, 2022) and the Disaster Recovery Financing District (DRD, SB 782 in 2025) share the Enhanced Infrastructure Financing District framework, a Public Financing Authority board and the same toolbox of tax increment, benefit assessments, special taxes, grants and bonds. They differ in trigger, timing and permitted uses: a CRD can be formed at any time for long-term resilience investment and operations, while a DRD can only be formed within two years of a declared emergency and funds three recovery purposes. The authors argue California needs both tools and should start using them.
insights: A CRD can be formed at any time by local decision and runs as long as resilience needs exist; a DRD needs a Governor-declared state of emergency and must be formed within two years of it.

Both are built on the Enhanced Infrastructure Financing District framework, governed by a Public Financing Authority, and can use tax increment financing, benefit assessments, special taxes, fees, grants, gifts and bonds.

A DRD may fund only repair or replacement of disaster-damaged property, mitigation of future risk from the declared disaster within the district, and economic recovery; a CRD can also fund ongoing operations and maintenance and hire staff.
CRD formation often takes one to two years; a DRD compresses the infrastructure financing plan into two public meetings so it can be stood up within months.
Tax increment is the DRD's main tool but builds only as property values recover, so a DRD creates no immediate cash and communities still need bridge funding for early recovery.
Los Angeles County enacted the Altadena and Santa Monica Mountains wildfire DRDs within 40 days of SB 782 being signed; Inglewood formed a CRD in late 2024 for its transit connector.

records.title: The Weekly: Extreme Heat Is Straining the Grid. Redesigning How We Build Can Ease the Pressure.
institutions: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety (IBHS)
Center for Climate and Energy Solutions (C2ES)
records.summary: This newsletter issue argues that redesigning the built environment is one lever for cutting the costs of extreme heat as heat waves strain the US power grid. It reports that PJM Interconnection set an all-time demand record and has already fallen short of its 20% reserve margin for the 2027/2028 delivery year, while power prices spiked to $2,000 per megawatt-hour. It sets out three interventions: reflective materials such as cool roofs and reflective pavement, passive-cooling building design, and more efficient cooling systems, and names grid fortification and blended public and private financing of cooling infrastructure as further tactics. A digest summarises outside reporting on climate due diligence in M&A, insurance weather-risk research, locally led adaptation, living shorelines and wildfire insurance in California.
insights: PJM must hold capacity 20% above expected peak demand, and for the 2027/2028 delivery year it has already fallen short of that cushion.

Power prices hit $2,000 per megawatt-hour during the heat wave, against a typical $40, and three million households in the heat wave's footprint lack air conditioning (citing a Washington Post analysis).

Cool roofs can stay more than 50°F cooler than conventional roofs; Los Angeles's Cool Streets initiative has covered 60 miles of pavement with reflective paint, lowering road temperatures by up to 15°F.
Barajeel wind towers can lower temperatures by up to 50°F, and Boston's Winthrop Center became the world's largest passive structure in 2023.
The US HVAC market is projected to grow at a CAGR of 7.4% between 2024 and 2030.
Residents of the 65 largest US cities experience an average of 8°F of extra heat due to the built environment.

records.title: New Jersey's Stormwater Utilities Are a Funding Source for Flood Infrastructure
institutions: New Jersey League of Conservation Voters
New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection
records.summary: The article describes how New Jersey towns are using stormwater utilities, enabled by the 2019 Clean Stormwater and Flood Reduction Act, to fund flood infrastructure. The fee is set by each parcel's impervious cover, so large paved properties pay more, and credits reward green infrastructure. Using Raritan Township and Maplewood as cases, it explains the parcel-mapping task, how the revenue is ring-fenced for stormwater projects, and why framing the fee around flood risk rather than a 'rain tax' matters for acceptance.
insights: Rising flood risk puts $277.7 billion in New Jersey property value and $3.2 billion in annual tax revenue at risk, according to Rebuild by Design.
There are over 2,000 stormwater utilities in 42 states; four New Jersey towns have set one up since 2019.
Maplewood, which adopted its utility in December 2024, collected more than $800,000 in fee income in its first year, and its parcel mapping was funded at no cost by the state DEP.
The fee also reaches properties outside the property tax base, such as churches, schools and government agencies.
Credits for rain gardens, green roofs and porous pavers, plus a one-time $20 rain barrel credit, reward reduced runoff.
keywords: Clean Stormwater and Flood Reduction Act

records.title: FEMA Delivers More than $584 Million to Support Community-Led Resilience and Recovery Across the U.S.
records.summary: FEMA announced $584 million in approved funding across four grant programs, Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities (BRIC, ~$24M), Public Assistance (~$520M), Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (~$33.7M), and Individual Assistance ($6.7M), disbursed to more than 30 states, territories, and Tribal Nations. Funding supports public infrastructure restoration, flood protection, building code upgrades, generator installations, debris removal, and disaster case management. The announcement signals continued federal commitment to pre-disaster mitigation alongside post-disaster recovery, with documented unit-level grants ranging from $140K to $46.7M.
insights: FEMA's $584M tranche spans four programs: Public Assistance dominates at ~$520M (89%), while pre-disaster mitigation (BRIC + HMGP) totals ~$57.7M (10%), revealing that recovery spending dwarfs prospective resilience investment in this award cycle.

BRIC allocated nearly $8.3M to Hawaii for a community backup generator, one of the largest single BRIC awards, underscoring that energy reliability during outages is a primary infrastructure resilience priority under current federal criteria.

Seventeen BRIC project-scoping grants totaling $3.2M were awarded across 15 states and Tribal Nations, providing early-stage capital to convert community vulnerability into bankable project applications, a pipeline-building function critical for later capital deployment.

Building code adoption and enforcement received discrete BRIC grants in five jurisdictions (NC ~$1.87M, VT ~$1.2M, MD ~$660K, MA ~$505K, Weber County UT ~$140K), demonstrating federal willingness to fund the regulatory infrastructure that raises minimum resilience standards for new construction.

The $46.7M Public Assistance grant to New York City Housing Authority for Hurricane Ida repairs is the single largest disclosed project, illustrating the concentrated fiscal exposure of large public housing portfolios to named storm events and the delayed cost recovery timeline (Ida struck 2021).

HMGP's $6.27M across 13 projects to harden utilities and install generators at water treatment plants, medical facilities, and emergency services in six jurisdictions links critical-facility continuity directly to federal mitigation grant eligibility, a transferable structuring model.

records.title: Uneven Adaptation: Insurance Pricing and Household Climate Resilience (Hutchins Center Working Paper 109)
records.authors: Shan Ge; Ankit Kalda; Varun Sharma; Vikas Soni
records.summary: Ge, Kalda, Sharma and Soni provide causal evidence on whether insurance pricing makes households harden their homes, using more than 18 million policy observations from Citizens Property Insurance Corporation, Florida's insurer of last resort, from 2002 to 2023. They track five categories of wind and water resilience upgrade: roof-to-wall attachments, roof covering materials, roof deck attachments, secondary water resistance, and opening protection such as shutters or impact windows. Florida is a clean setting because state law requires insurers to offer mitigation discounts calculated as a percentage of premium, so savings grow proportionally as premiums rise, reaching as much as 47 per cent. Identification comes from Citizens implementing rate changes at ZIP code level at different times, isolating premium changes driven by insurer pricing rather than by deteriorating property conditions. The average household shows no statistically significant response, and that average conceals a sharp divergence: wealthier households increase adaptation investment when premiums rise, while lower-income households reduce it, because the higher premium tightens an already binding budget constraint faster than the larger discount can pull.
insights: The headline is that the average effect is zero and the average is the wrong statistic: premium increases raise adaptation among wealthier households and lower it among poorer ones, so a pricing signal that works in aggregate can be regressive in practice.
The mechanism is a race between two effects of the same price rise, a larger proportional discount and a tighter budget constraint, and which wins depends on the household's financial cushion.

Florida's mandated percentage-of-premium discount structure, reaching up to 47 per cent, is what makes the incentive grow with the premium, so the finding is a property of that design and not of insurance pricing generally.

Identification exploits ZIP-code-level rate changes timed differently by a state insurer of last resort, which separates insurer pricing decisions from property deterioration, a distinction most studies of this question cannot make.
