Households in smaller homes, where the upfront cost is lower, are more responsive, which points at upfront cost rather than the discount as the binding constraint for the households that adapt least.

records.title: Catastrophe Bond Market Records That Were Broken in H1 2026
records.summary: Artemis reports that H1 2026 set multiple records in the catastrophe bond market, with total issuance across all tracked cat bond types exceeding the prior H1 2025 record of $17.56 billion. The outstanding cat bond market reached nearly $65.6 billion as of June 30, 2026. May 2026 alone set a single-month issuance record of nearly $6.93 billion. Twelve first-time sponsors debuted, 83 transactions closed in the half-year, and 81% of risk capital used indemnity triggers, all records. The findings signal deepening institutionalization of cat bonds as a core reinsurance and risk-transfer instrument.
insights: Total catastrophe bond issuance in H1 2026 exceeded $17.56 billion (the prior H1 2025 record), with Rule 144A property cat bonds alone reaching nearly $17.3 billion, demonstrating consistent double-digit billion-dollar growth in a single half-year period.

The outstanding catastrophe bond market reached nearly $65.6 billion as of June 30, 2026, up from approximately $63.9 billion at end of Q1 2026, reflecting net growth even against the highest maturities in market history.

May 2026 set a single-month issuance record of nearly $6.93 billion, roughly $1 billion above the prior record of $5.93 billion set in May 2025, illustrating the acceleration of deal pacing and investor appetite.

83 cat bond transactions closed in H1 2026 alone, matching or exceeding full-year totals for most years in market history except 2023 (95), 2024 (~93), and 2025 (122); the full-year 2026 total is on pace to set an all-time annual record.

12 first-time sponsors debuted in H1 2026 (vs. 11 in H1 2025), and the majority of debut sponsors become repeat issuers, a structural demand driver that will sustain issuance growth beyond current cycle dynamics.

81% of risk capital issued in H1 2026 used indemnity triggers (vs. 79% in H1 2025), reflecting growing participation by primary insurance carriers that prefer indemnity structures to integrate cat bonds tightly into their reinsurance programs.

The growth in sponsor count, transaction volume, and indemnity trigger use collectively signal that cat bonds are transitioning from a specialist instrument toward mainstream reinsurance infrastructure, with implications for insurance-linked securities fund managers and direct institutional investors.

records.title: The Weekly: Capital Doesn't Fund Resilience Projects Until Someone Proves Who Benefits
records.summary: This edition of The Weekly argues that resilience projects become finance-ready through predevelopment work that identifies who benefits and quantifies avoided losses, drawing on a CA FWD and Insurance for Good article by PRE Collective. Its case study is Blue Forest Conservation's Yuba Forest Resilience Bond, where economic and environmental modeling with WRI, UC Merced and Stanford convinced beneficiaries such as the Yuba Water Agency to repay investors. The rest summarizes outside news on insurance, wildfire and agriculture finance.
insights: The Forest Resilience Bond raises upfront capital from private and philanthropic investors, and beneficiaries such as utilities and public agencies reimburse them.
The Yuba project is a collaboration of nine organizations protecting 275,000 forested acres in the North Yuba River watershed.
The final project included $4 million in upfront commitments from four lenders and more than $4.3 million paid by beneficiaries to investors.
Private capital let the project finish six years earlier than under public funding alone.
Additional hydropower revenue meant the value to the Yuba Water Agency exceeded its cost-share contribution.
A Rockefeller Foundation Zero Gap Portfolio grant funded the early-stage work.

records.title: Paying for Preparedness: Why California Needs Sustained Investment in Climate Resilience
records.summary: A July 2026 report from California Forward and Insurance for Good arguing that California needs sustained rather than episodic investment in climate resilience, opening with what it calls the fiscal imperative. Its distinguishing feature is who produced it: the report draws on an Adaptation Finance Workgroup convened as a multi-sector collaboration spanning municipal finance, insurance, adaptation risk reduction and lending, assembled to advance actionable strategies for community and household climate resilience investment. Named contributors include Kayla Calkins of Megafire Action, Kyra Peyton of CSAA Insurance Group, Shalini Vajjhala of PRE Collective and Anuj Desai of Southern California Edison, so an insurer, a utility, a pre-development specialist and an advocacy organisation are in the same room as the municipal finance participants. California Forward describes itself as a multi-partisan non-profit building a sustainable, resilient and inclusive California economy through a regions-up approach, and Insurance for Good as a non-profit supporting communities and policymakers with insurance-related solutions aligned to social and environmental goals.
insights: The workgroup composition is the substance: municipal finance, insurance, risk reduction and lending in one body is the coalition any household-level resilience financing mechanism would need, and assembling it is the report's real output.
Framing the argument as a fiscal imperative rather than a climate one is a deliberate choice for a multi-partisan organisation, and it puts the case in terms a state budget process can act on.

The presence of both an insurer and an electric utility among the named contributors connects the two parties that bear California's wildfire loss, which is where the financing question actually sits.
Sustained investment is the explicit ask, against a status quo of post-disaster appropriation, which is the same critique of episodic federal grant funding that the Brookings work makes.
Insurance for Good is the organisation behind the proposal, which places the argument with a group working on insurance design for community resilience rather than with a carrier or a regulator.

records.title: Responding to Risk: Tracking Financial Institutions’ Progress on Adaptation and Resilience - CPI
records.authors: Lizzie Russler; Frederick Fabian; Valerio Micale
records.summary: A Climate Policy Initiative brief tracking how financial institutions are progressing on adaptation and resilience, built on the Net Zero Finance Tracker, a not-for-profit dashboard assessing how 1,500 of the world's largest financial institutions respond to climate risk and drive real-economy outcomes. The tracker draws on over 600 datasets from 58 sources and organises its assessment across Targets, Implementation and Impact, with the explicit purpose of distinguishing symbolic commitments from measurable action. That design is the brief's analytical spine: rather than asking whether institutions have made adaptation commitments, it asks whether those commitments have implementation and impact behind them. The work was externally reviewed by specialists from Arc, Cadlas, CDP, Earth Capital Nexus, GFANZ, MSCI and the NGFS, and funded by the Hewlett Foundation, the Laudes Foundation and Bloomberg Philanthropies.
insights: The Targets, Implementation and Impact structure is the contribution: it is built to separate a stated commitment from evidence of action, which is the distinction most adaptation pledge tracking cannot make.
Covering 1,500 institutions from over 600 datasets across 58 sources makes this a census rather than a sample, so the absence of adaptation activity in a category is itself evidence.
Adaptation and resilience are assessed within a tracking infrastructure originally built for net zero, so the metrics may carry mitigation assumptions that were not re-derived for adaptation.
The external reviewer list spans a rating agency, a central bank network and the sector's own alliance, which is unusual breadth and strengthens the methodology's standing.

records.title: How 3 States Value and Invest for a More Resilient Future
records.summary: This Pew Charitable Trusts article profiles how Massachusetts, Minnesota, and Rhode Island are building comprehensive resilience investment frameworks, quantifying future climate costs, prioritizing assets, measuring outcomes, and deploying innovative financing. Minnesota projects climate-driven costs of $17B–$57B annually by mid-to-late century without adaptation investment, with resilience costing 8–15x less. Massachusetts estimates $90B–$130B in climate investment needs through 2050 and is advancing a $2B+ bond bill and a Resilience Revolving Fund. Rhode Island's Resilient Rhody Infrastructure Fund offers a revolving loan model for green infrastructure, floodproofing, and wetland restoration.
insights: Minnesota's Climate Adaptation and Resilience Cost Study projects annual climate-driven costs rising from $17B at mid-century to as much as $57B by end of century without additional adaptation investment; resilience investment is estimated to cost 8–15x less than inaction.

Massachusetts estimates that addressing climate risks will require $90B–$130B in investment through 2050, but its Municipal Vulnerability Preparedness program in 2026 could only fund ~25% of community requests with $28.7M awarded.

Rhode Island's Resilient Rhody 2025 plan inventoried 130,000+ publicly owned assets, narrowed to ~40 critical assets for further analysis, and identified 79 resilience actions costing an estimated $112M–$304M to complete.

Rhode Island's Resilient Rhody Infrastructure Fund (approved June 2025) is a state-sponsored revolving loan program offering below-market-rate loans for green stormwater infrastructure, culvert upgrades, wetland/dune restoration, floodproofing, and structure elevation, demonstrating how revolving loan funds shift resilience financing from episodic to systematic.

Massachusetts' proposed Mass Ready Act (>$2B environmental bond bill) would create a Resilience Revolving Fund providing low-interest loans to municipalities, water/wastewater utilities, and Tribal governments for stormwater management, floodplain protection, and nature-based solutions.

All three states have developed indicator-linked metrics frameworks (e.g., ResilientMass Metrics Framework) to track whether resilience investments reduce risk and reach vulnerable communities, enabling adaptive management of capital allocation.

State practitioners emphasize that grants alone are insufficient for resilience at scale and that peer-to-peer learning across states, on financing mechanisms, resilience standards, and metrics, can prevent duplicative effort and stretch collective resources.

records.title: Resilience Finance Guidebook for Local Governments: From Resilience Goals to Financeable Projects
institutions: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety (IBHS)
Nicholas Institute for Energy Environment & Sustainability Duke University
records.summary: The Resilience Finance Guidebook for Local Governments, produced by Duke University's Nicholas Institute and ICLEI USA (July 2026), is a structured translation framework helping local governments convert resilience goals into financeable projects. It diagnoses why resilience investments stall between clear need and available capital and offers a six-step Resilience Finance Diagnostic. The guide introduces six financial value pathways (avoided loss, reliable infrastructure, operational continuity, workforce reliability, faster recovery, and co-benefits), and presents case studies from Hoboken NJ, Longmont CO, Denver Water, Philadelphia, Mount Vernon WA, San Antonio, Chicago, Harris County TX, Hampton VA, Tulsa, and Pasco WA, illustrating layered capital strategies across grants, bonds, utility rates, special districts, environmental impact bonds, and catalytic capital. Key figures include a $2.5B Harris County flood bond, a $25M DC Water environmental impact bond, a 45% NFIP premium discount for Tulsa's Class 1 CRS rating, and adaptation returns of $10+ per dollar invested.
insights: A World Resources Institute 2025 analysis of 320 adaptation investments across 12 countries found every dollar invested in adaptation generates more than $10 in benefits over 10 years, with average returns of 20%–27%.
Aon reports 2024 U.S. natural disaster economic losses of $218B, of which only $113B (52%) was insured, leaving households, businesses, and governments exposed to $105B in uninsured losses.

The National Institute of Building Sciences finds federal mitigation grants save ~$6 per $1 invested; adoption of modern building codes saves ~$11 per $1 invested; above-code design saves ~$4 per $1 spent across large building portfolios.

IBHS FORTIFIED homes in Alabama suffered 55%–74% fewer claims and 14%–40% less severe claims than non-certified homes after Hurricane Sally (2020); FORTIFIED designation also carries ~7% higher resale values in coastal Alabama and reduces expected multifamily insurance costs by an average of $1,533/year in windborne-debris-prone regions (payback under 7 years on a ~$10,000 retrofit).

Philadelphia's Green City, Clean Waters program ($2.4B over 25 years) was associated with a 10.3% increase in residential property values near green stormwater infrastructure, ~$1.3B in added property value, ~$18M in additional annual property tax revenue, and an estimated $4B total economic impact over 25 years.

Mount Vernon, WA's $31M floodwall removed 223 buildings from the regulatory floodplain, produced a 40% reduction in NFIP premiums for affected property owners (~$139,000 per building removed), and catalyzed $10M in private investment in a formerly derelict property.

A New York State study on the Rockville Centre community microgrid found that avoiding a one-day outage could produce ~$9.7M in social welfare benefits, including $5M in avoided lost sales and $3.1M in avoided regional GDP.

records.title: FEMA's Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities (BRIC): Recent Developments
records.summary: This Congressional Research Service Insight tracks developments in FEMA's Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities (BRIC) grant program through June 2026. BRIC is the largest U.S. competitively awarded pre-disaster mitigation funding source, with $5.795 billion available across FY2020–FY2025. The document details the Trump Administration's April 2025 attempt to terminate BRIC, subsequent litigation by 20 states, court injunctions, and a December 2025 permanent injunction ruling the termination unlawful. As of mid-2026, FEMA issued a combined FY2024–FY2025 NOFO for $1 billion under court order, while $882 million in IIJA-appropriated funds remained at risk of reversion to Treasury.
insights: BRIC is the largest U.S. competitively awarded pre-disaster mitigation program, with $5.795 billion available across FY2020–FY2025; total demand across those cycles reached $15.665 billion (325% oversubscribed), signaling massive unmet need relative to supply.

Only 21.6% ($1.013 billion) of the $4.622 billion selected for funding across FY2020–FY2023 had been obligated as of March 29, 2026, revealing a severe execution bottleneck that predates the 2025 termination attempt.

Oversubscription rates varied sharply by cycle: FY2020 was 620% oversubscribed ($3.1B requested vs. $500M available), FY2022 was 157% ($3.6B vs. $2.295B), and FY2023 was 540% ($5.4B vs. $1B), illustrating persistent and growing demand for federal pre-disaster mitigation capital.

The administration's April 2025 termination attempt put approximately $882 million in IIJA-appropriated BRIC funds at risk of reversion to Treasury, directly threatening project pipelines in all 50 states, territories, and tribes.

A federal court issued a permanent injunction on December 11, 2025, ruling the BRIC termination unlawful; a follow-up enforcement order on March 6, 2026, required FEMA to issue the FY2024 NOFO within 21 days, demonstrating that litigation can serve as a mechanism to preserve federal resilience funding commitments.

The court's ruling explicitly does not compel FEMA to award specific grants, nor does it prevent FEMA from replacing BRIC with a different mitigation program, leaving long-term program continuity uncertain and creating investability risk for project sponsors relying on BRIC funds.

Obligated projects that had not yet started construction were subject to cancellation under FEMA's April 2025 guidelines, while only projects with active construction could continue, a critical distinction for project finance timelines and shovel-readiness requirements.

records.title: IMF Finds Climate Disasters Threaten Sovereign Debt as Adaptation Becomes an Economic Necessity
records.summary: A Devdiscourse article of 29 June 2026 reporting an International Monetary Fund finding that climate disasters significantly increase sovereign default risk, with every 1 per cent rise in disaster-related losses as a share of GDP raising default odds by 2 to 3 per cent, and framing climate change as a growing fiscal challenge. The report it describes concludes that greater investment in climate adaptation, supported by concessional finance such as Official Development Assistance, can strengthen resilience, reduce disaster losses and improve long-term debt sustainability for vulnerable countries.
insights: The elasticity is the reason to hold this: a 1 per cent of GDP increase in disaster losses raising default odds by 2 to 3 per cent converts physical risk into sovereign credit risk with a coefficient, which is what a debt-for-resilience swap or a climate-resilient debt clause needs in order to be priced.
This is a third-party account of an IMF working paper rather than the paper itself, so the figures in it are reported at one remove and should be traced to the IMF publication before being relied on.
The publisher is a news aggregator and the body carries substantial site furniture, so the citable content is the elasticity and the policy conclusion rather than any analysis.

records.title: The Weekly: The Warning Signs of Uninsurability Are Visible Before the Tipping Point
records.summary: This weekly newsletter summarises The Epicenter's six-stage framework for how a property insurance market becomes uninsurable: market entry decisions, portfolio concentration limits, loss-driven reassessment, model revisions, repricing against regulatory limits, and exits that worsen the remaining book. It argues that uninsurability is a sequence that plays out over years or decades and that its warning signs are visible before the tipping point. It concludes that intervening upstream, at pre-development and through resilient construction and community-wide mitigation, is how markets stay insurable.
insights: A well-built, fire-resistant home can still be rejected because the insurer has no more room for that exposure type in its portfolio.
A loss in one market, such as a major wildfire in New Mexico, can trigger reassessment of similar risks in California.
Smaller insurers that rely on third-party catastrophe models can be the first to change course when model outputs are revised.
In heavily regulated states repricing can take years, leaving insurers to absorb losses, non-renew or exit.
Each exit leaves the highest-risk policies concentrated on the books of those who remain, so profitability deteriorates progressively rather than collapsing like a bank run.

records.title: Adapting to Adversity: Poverty and Climate Risks in Latin America and the Caribbean (Chapter 4, Improving Adaptation)
records.authors: Alejandro de la Fuente; Miki Khanh Doan; Samuel Freije-Rodriguez
institutions: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
records.summary: A World Bank International Development in Focus volume, Adapting to Adversity: Poverty and Climate Risks in Latin America and the Caribbean, by Alejandro de la Fuente, Miki Khanh Doan and Samuel Freije-Rodriguez. Its adaptation investment section gives the region's adaptation finance in figures. Funding comes from governments, the private sector, NGOs, philanthropies and community groups, but the biggest share is international public finance delivered as grants, loans and equity, and it is heavily concentrated in Brazil, Colombia, Costa Rica and Mexico. From 2003 to 2023 multilateral climate funds approved $5.7 billion for 614 projects in the region, with the Green Climate Fund, the Clean Technology Fund and Brazil's Amazon Fund making up 67 per cent of that total. The Green Climate Fund is the largest player, backing 37 projects in 13 countries with $2.42 billion over that period, including $43 million in Colombia and $33 million in Bolivia in 2023 alone; the Clean Technology Fund provided $718 million through the World Bank and the Amazon Fund $684 million in grants. Bilateral donors including Germany and the United Kingdom also feature. Since 2015 the GCF has mobilised more than $40 billion including co-financing across more than 100 countries, and per the UNFCCC the region obtained 22 per cent of climate financing from multilateral climate funds in 2015 to 2016.
insights: Three funds accounting for 67 per cent of twenty years of multilateral adaptation approvals in a whole region is a concentration finding, and it means the region's adaptation finance is effectively three credit committees rather than a market.

$5.7 billion across 614 projects is an average of about $9 million per project over two decades, which is the scale problem stated arithmetically: these are not sizes institutional capital can underwrite without aggregation.

Concentration in Brazil, Colombia, Costa Rica and Mexico is the allocation counterpart of the concentration by fund, and it is the pattern the WRI philanthropy record and the IFC disclosures both describe from the supply side.
The volume's frame is poverty rather than infrastructure, so it connects adaptation finance to household vulnerability rather than to asset exposure.

records.title: Insurance Markets Don't Collapse Overnight
institutions: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety
records.summary: The article sets out a six-stage sequence by which an insurance market becomes uninsurable: insurers' market entry choices, concentration limits, losses exceeding model predictions, model revisions and reinsurance repricing, regulated rates lagging costs, and exits that worsen the remaining book. It uses California wildfire as the worked example, drawing on Francis Bouchard of Marsh McLennan, and says the same pattern is emerging in severe convective storm markets. It lists warning signs for identifying the next vulnerable market.
insights: California's 2017 and 2018 wildfire losses of $20 billion wiped out more than two decades of accumulated underwriting profit, and the 2025 LA fires generated another $40+ billion.
A fire-resilient home built to IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home Plus can still be declined because the insurer has reached its concentration limit for that peril.
California rate approvals have historically taken up to two years, while reinsurers outside state rate regulation can reprice immediately.
431,000 California structures are in the FAIR Plan versus 361 in Washington's insurer of last resort.
Warning signs include loss history worsening faster than models, insurers near diversification ceilings, and a last-resort plan growing faster than the voluntary market.

records.title: The Green Guarantee Company Closed Its First Two Transactions Mobilising USD 70 Million to Support the Mission 300 Initiative in Africa
records.summary: The Green Guarantee Company (GGC), managed by the Development Guarantee Group and funded by the Green Climate Fund, KfW, FCDO, Nigerian Sovereign Investment Authority, and Norfund, closed its first two transactions in June 2026, mobilising USD 70 million to support the World Bank/African Development Bank Mission 300 energy access initiative. The first is a USD 20 million framework guarantee to Bank of Africa UK for mini-grid development in Nigeria (~340,000 people, 13 MW). The second is a USD 50 million guarantee backing a green bond listed on the London Stock Exchange, arranged by Standard Chartered for UK/US institutional investors, funding AFC's distributed solar PAYGO receivable securitisations across Sub-Saharan Africa (~4.3 million people).
insights: GGC mobilised USD 70 million across two inaugural transactions, demonstrating that a BBB-stable-rated, DFI-backed guarantor can unlock institutional private capital for Sub-Saharan African energy access at scale.

The USD 50 million green bond guarantee enables a private placement to institutional investors (Legal & General, Calvert Impact Capital, Ceniarth) by elevating credit quality of AFC's PAYGO solar receivables securitisation to investment grade, illustrating how guarantees can bridge the gap between emerging-market risk and developed-market investor appetite.

The USD 20 million Nigeria mini-grid facility is projected to reach ~340,000 people with new or improved energy access and install 13 MW of renewable capacity, avoiding ~250,000 tCO2e per year, providing concrete unit economics for energy access guarantees.

The USD 50 million AFC green bond is expected to expand clean energy access for ~4.3 million people across Sub-Saharan Africa, with the structure designed to be replicable and to recycle DFI/MDB capital into private financing channels.

GGC's guarantee capacity is USD 1 billion, suggesting these two inaugural deals represent only 7% of capacity, signalling a large pipeline; the chairman explicitly noted 'a very strong project pipeline in EMDEs.'

The transaction establishes a blueprint combining a bond private placement, a third-party investment-grade guarantee, and PAYGO receivables securitisation, a replicable structure for scaling distributed renewable energy finance in Africa.

Technical assistance from the Global Green Growth Institute (via the Global Trust Fund) and the FCDO MOBILIST programme, alongside a Second Party Opinion from Sustainable Fitch, underscores the role of blended finance support in making first-of-kind capital markets structures viable.
records.publisher: The Global Innovation Lab for Climate Finance

records.title: Advancing Nature-Based Insurance to Protect People and Nature
records.authors: Megan A. Kelso, Rae Taylor-Burns, Guillermo Franco, Jane Carter Ingram, Borja G. Reguero, Michael W. Beck
institutions: Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures
Center for Coastal Climate Resilience at UC Santa Cruz
records.summary: This 2026 perspective in Communications Earth & Environment advances the concept of "nature-based insurance", combining nature-based solutions (NBS) with risk-transfer instruments such as parametric and indemnity insurance. Authored by researchers at UC Santa Cruz, Guy Carpenter, and Pollination, it identifies five frontiers: modeling habitats in industry risk models, pricing nature's risk-reduction benefits into premiums, de-risking green investments via catastrophe wrappers and environmental impact bonds, insuring ecosystems directly through parametric policies, and partnering with innovative insurers. The paper quantifies relevant market sizes (global property insurance premiums ~$1.2 trillion/year; nature-related bond issuance ~$113 billion/year) and documents real case studies including the Mesoamerican Reef parametric insurance ($1.025M paid out), the Belize Blue Bond catastrophe wrapper (3-point credit rating jump, $180M for conservation), and a Sierra Nevada wildfire policy with 39% lower premiums due to ecological forest management.
insights: Global property insurance premiums are estimated at $1.2 trillion annually; redirecting even a small percentage toward nature-based risk reduction could unlock tens of billions of dollars per year for adaptation and conservation.

The Mesoamerican Reef parametric insurance program has paid out $1.025 million cumulatively across ~800 km² of reef; extrapolating to 80,000 km² of global coral reefs implies potential average annual funding of $22.6 million through this mechanism alone.

A 2025 Sierra Nevada wildfire insurance policy explicitly priced ecological forest management into premiums and deductibles, resulting in premiums 39% lower and deductibles 89% lower than standard, the first documented case of NBS risk reduction reflected in commercial wildfire insurance pricing.

The Belize Blue Bond catastrophe wrapper facilitated a sovereign debt restructuring that reduced annual debt payments by $12 million/year, committed $4.2 million/year to conservation for 20 years, and produced a 3-point jump in Belize's S&P sovereign credit rating.

Salt marshes reduced flood damages from Hurricane Sandy by 15% (quantified using Moody's RMS hurricane model); mangroves reduce storm damages by >25% in Florida across a wide range of storm intensities, figures directly usable in insurance underwriting.

Less than a quarter of annual global disaster losses are insured; in Asia the insured share is under 10%, leaving a coverage gap exceeding $120 billion on that continent alone, the adaptation finance gap in developing countries is $279–$334 billion/year.

Coral reefs in the US provide over $1.8 billion in flood risk reduction benefits annually; natural habitat buffers could have reduced damages from the 2018 Paradise Fire by 21%, both findings support actuarial crediting of intact ecosystems.

records.title: Carlyle Rethinks Portfolio Risk to Give Weather Insurance a Bigger Role
records.summary: Carlyle Group, working with the insurance broker Marsh, has built a framework for portfolio risk that makes asset values reflect the insurance consequences of severe weather, and unveiled it at London Climate Action Week in June 2026. Steve Hatfield, co-head of global sustainability at Carlyle, says there has been no consistent mechanism allowing insurers to recognise how asset hardening reduces risk, so climate risk is not priced into valuations until coverage becomes expensive or is withdrawn after a loss. The framework has four steps: estimate the probability an asset is hit by an extreme weather event, including gradual value erosion; assess the gap between the asset's current resilience and what would make it resistant; estimate how resilience upgrades reduce expected losses; and have insurers use those calculations to offer better underwriting terms, including premium credits, deductible reductions and broader coverage. Mubadala and the Danish pension manager Sampension are among the institutional backers, alongside contributions from engineers, insurers and climate risk experts. Marsh's Amy Barnes says underwriters recognised the issue but did not know how to address it, and that designing in resilience is far cheaper than retrofitting. The article notes the relevance to data centre construction in exposed locations and cites a 2025 World Resources Institute study indicating adaptation investment could yield a tenfold return over a decade.
insights: The framework's load-bearing step is the fourth: it only works if insurers convert a modelled loss reduction into premium credits, deductible reductions or broader coverage, which the document states as a design requirement rather than as an aspiration.

The stated defect is a missing mechanism, not missing information: insurers could not recognise asset hardening, so a resilience upgrade earned no pricing response and therefore no return the investment committee could see.

Hatfield names the specific failure that stalled adoption inside Carlyle, an inability to show investment teams a near-term cash flow return on resilience spending, which locates the barrier in payback period rather than in risk awareness.
Marsh's point that insurance resilience expertise sits in sustainability functions and does not reach underwriting is an organisational explanation for why the price signal has been absent.
The framework is pre-commercial: Hatfield says he has previewed it with carriers and expects them to road test it, so no premium credit has actually been paid at the time of publication.

records.title: The Weekly: Cities Are Cutting Billions in Sewer Compliance Costs by Letting Nature Do the Work
records.summary: This weekly newsletter's feature shows how Kansas City, Missouri renegotiated its 2010 EPA sewer consent decree to count green infrastructure as a formal compliance strategy, cutting the total cost of managing its combined sewer system through 2040 by over $2 billion. The amendment introduced an adaptive management process allowing alternative, lower-cost control measures. The EPA has since tracked 18 cities or counties using green infrastructure in consent decree compliance. A news roundup covers catastrophe modelling, federal wildfire budgets, adaptation stock performance and hedge fund catastrophe desks.
insights: About 700 US municipalities operate combined sewer systems, and the EPA has issued 91 consent decrees since 1998.
Kansas City's amended consent decree reduced combined sewer management costs through 2040 by over $2 billion.
Louisville, Kentucky projects initial savings of $40 million and South Bend, Indiana more than $400 million from green-for-gray substitution.
Green infrastructure in Hoboken has reduced flooding by 88%.
Bloomberg Intelligence estimates extreme weather has shifted more than $20 trillion across the global economy this century.

records.title: How to Sell Flood Infrastructure: Make It a Park
records.summary: The article reports how Hoboken, New Jersey and Kansas City, Missouri use multi-benefit green infrastructure, such as parks that double as stormwater storage, to cut urban flooding. Hoboken's sponge city approach has reduced flooding by 88%, and ResilienCity Park stores runoff in a two-million-gallon tank under a basketball court. Practitioners advise leading with everyday benefits to build support and with cost avoidance when pitching to ratepayers, combining green with gray infrastructure, and treating maintenance as a continuation of capital investment. Kansas City turned green infrastructure maintenance into a jobs program.
insights: Hoboken's sponge city infrastructure has reduced flooding by 88%.
ResilienCity Park holds a two-million-gallon storage tank beneath its basketball court.
A Kansas City green infrastructure project cost $1.0 per gallon of annual overflow captured over a 50-year life cycle, versus $8.6 per gallon for the relief sewer it replaced.
Hoboken splits maintenance: the city funds green infrastructure from its operating budget and state grants, and the North Hudson Sewerage Authority maintains pumps and tanks.
Practitioners stress that green infrastructure alone cannot handle a deluge, so a hybrid with gray storage is needed.

records.title: Turning Adaptation Ambition into Investment at Scale
records.authors: Yamide Dagnet, Doug Sims, Jorge Gastelumendi
records.summary: An account of the FINI initiative, Fostering Investable National Planning and Implementation for Adaptation and Resilience, developed by NRDC with the Atlantic Council's Climate Resilience Center. Its diagnosis is that National Adaptation Plans do not translate into investable opportunities: project pipelines lack the elements investors need, risk, returns and insurability are not clearly defined or communicated, data for resilience projects is limited so risks are hard to price, and because risk drives return, ambiguity inflates a project's cost of capital into a cycle of underinvestment and escalating damage. FINI's purpose is to fix the system connecting global and domestic investors to national and local priorities.
insights: The mechanism named for underinvestment is priced rather than moral: unquantified risk raises the cost of capital, which makes projects less viable, which reduces the evidence base, which keeps risk unquantified. Ambiguity itself is the cost driver.

Adaptation finance needs are put at 12 to 14 times current public flows, and private capital is described as moving largely toward mitigation rather than adaptation, with the conditions to attract investment weakest where adaptation is needed most.

The gap is specifically that NAPs do not distinguish projects that can generate cash flows or savings, and are therefore suitable for private investment, from those that cannot. That triage is the missing step between a plan and a pipeline.

Capital is nonetheless described as already moving, with named examples: TPG Rise Climate in climate-resilient agriculture and crop shock tolerance, Invesco's dedicated adaptation funds, and Lightsmith Group backing satellite monitoring and water systems, with spending expected to exceed $1 trillion a year.

The misalignment problem is stated from both sides: private deals are being done but are often not connected to existing NAPs and not reaching the most vulnerable, while finance ministries and central banks find the efforts fragmented and too slow.
The worked illustration is small and physical, cool roofs made with solar-reflective paint in Ahmedabad, which sets the scale of the interventions against the trillion-dollar framing.

records.title: Uganda Pioneers New Approach to Turn Climate Resilience Into Stronger Credit Ratings
institutions: Coalition of Finance Ministers for Climate Action
records.summary: Uganda's Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development has launched an approach to integrate the economic and fiscal benefits of adaptation and resilience investments into sovereign debt sustainability analysis, which the article describes as a global first. An interim report sets out how returns on resilience could be made visible in debt dynamics and credit profiles. Treasury head Dr Ramathan Ggoobi argues that sovereign risk assessments capture the upfront fiscal cost of resilience but not its long-term benefits, which raises borrowing costs for countries that invest in resilience.
insights: Uganda is described as the first country to integrate the benefits of resilience investments into sovereign debt sustainability analysis.
The ministry's interim report aims to make returns on resilience visible within sovereign debt dynamics and credit profiles.
Dr Ggoobi says current sovereign risk assessments capture only upfront fiscal costs of resilience and overlook long-term benefits.
Agriculture and agro-industrialisation, pillars of Uganda's Tenfold Growth Strategy, are highly exposed to climate and nature shocks.
Uganda co-chairs the Coalition of Finance Ministers for Climate Action and hopes other countries adopt the method.

records.title: Safeguarding Tomorrow Revolving Loan Fund Program
records.summary: FEMA's program page describes the Safeguarding Tomorrow Revolving Loan Fund, authorised under Section 205 of the Stafford Act by the STORM Act, which gives capitalization grants to states, territories, eligible tribes and DC to establish revolving loan funds for local hazard mitigation. The IIJA appropriated $500 million over five years through fiscal year 2026. Unlike other Hazard Mitigation Assistance programs, entities make lending decisions directly, project types are not restricted beyond statute, no benefit-cost analysis is required, and loans can serve as non-federal cost match for other HMA grants. FEMA announced selections for $150 million in fiscal year 2024.
insights: The IIJA, law on Nov. 15, 2021, appropriated $500 million over five years for the program, lasting through fiscal year 2026.
On Sept. 16, 2024, FEMA announced selections for the $150 million available in the program's second year.
In the inaugural year, applicants could apply for up to $50 million in capitalization grants.
Loans may be used as non-federal cost match for another HMA grant, and FEMA does not require a benefit-cost analysis.
Entities make funding decisions and award loans directly, rather than passing subapplications through to FEMA.

records.title: World Bank approves $400m Morocco program to expand finance for climate, disaster, and cyber risks
records.summary: A report that the World Bank's Board of Directors has approved the $400 million Morocco Climate and Risk Finance Program, aimed at strengthening Morocco's financial resilience to climate, disaster and cyber risks while helping unlock private capital for climate infrastructure. The programme will develop disaster and cyber insurance instruments to expand risk transfer capacity, strengthen institutional frameworks, reinforce digital payments infrastructure to accelerate the flow of finance following shocks, and build the capacity of financial regulators to oversee climate and cyber risks affecting banks and insurers. To facilitate climate infrastructure investment it establishes a Project Preparation Facility to build a pipeline of commercially viable projects across renewable energy, energy efficiency, sustainable transport and water infrastructure, and it aims to de-risk private investment through blended finance structures and capital market instruments. Over five years the stated targets are to mobilise up to $400 million in private capital, put in place $1 billion in pre-arranged disaster financing, and extend cyber risk coverage to at least 20 financial entities. The Board also approved a separate $250 million Morocco Digital Transformation Acceleration Program supporting the Digital Morocco 2030 strategy.
insights: Digital payments infrastructure is named as resilience finance. The speed at which money reaches a household after a shock is set by the payment rails rather than by the instrument, so a fast-paying parametric policy over slow rails is not fast.

A $1 billion pre-arranged disaster financing target against $400 million of programme money is a 2.5 times leverage claim on contingent capacity rather than on deployed capital, which is a different and cheaper kind of mobilisation than the private-capital target sitting beside it.

Cyber sits alongside climate as a peril throughout, including in the regulator capacity-building and the 20-entity coverage target, so the programme treats the two as one insurability problem rather than as separate portfolios.

A Project Preparation Facility appears again, as it does in Meridiam's Urban Resilience Fund and in the Massachusetts and Rhode Island planning grants. Four records across three continents identify the same binding constraint: not capital, but bankable projects.

records.title: Counties Regroup After FEMA’s Resiliency Grant Program Resumes
records.summary: FEMA's Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities programme was ended by the Trump Administration in April 2025, halting roughly 2,000 active infrastructure and disaster mitigation projects. A coalition of 22 states and the District of Columbia sued FEMA, the Department of Homeland Security and the United States; a federal judge ruled for the states in December, ordering FEMA to reinstate BRIC and restore over $3.6 billion in canceled funding, and the agency resumed the programme on 25 March. Counties are now reassessing projects left in limbo. Clatsop County, Oregon and Columbia Memorial Hospital had been set to receive $14 million to build a tsunami evacuation zone into a hospital on the Cascadia subduction zone; the county pushed construction forward in early 2026 with federal funds still unresolved, stretching its reserves. Roughly two dozen Washington state projects worth more than $150 million were paused. Pierce County's deputy emergency management director Luke Meyers says restarting has been slow and questions whether original project scopes still hold given cost increases. The reinstated programme now prioritises shovel-ready projects and eliminates phased initiatives, with FY2024-2025 applications due 23 July. Meyers notes that a setback levee funded by hazard mitigation grants limited damage in Orting during atmospheric river flooding that produced Washington's largest public infrastructure damage total in over four decades, and argues federal programmes should work more like block grants with longer performance periods. The article cites the 2019 National Institute of Building Sciences finding of a $6 return for every $1 of public mitigation funding.
insights: The reinstatement changed the product as well as restoring the money: BRIC now funds only shovel-ready projects and eliminates phased initiatives, which excludes exactly the long-lead work that needs a planning phase before construction.

Clatsop County's response, spending its own reserves to keep a $14 million tsunami project on schedule while federal funds were in limbo, shows a local balance sheet absorbing federal programme risk, and only a county with reserves can do that.

Cost escalation during the pause is the unmeasured cost of the cancellation: Meyers's question is whether the original scopes are still deliverable at the original grant amounts, which turns a restored dollar figure into a reduced project.

The Orting setback levee is a natural experiment that the county documented, limited damage in a watershed that would traditionally have flooded worse, which is avoided-loss evidence generated by the disaster rather than by a model.

The ask is for block-grant flexibility and longer periods of performance, which is a request to change the instrument rather than its size, and follows directly from the restart friction the article describes.

records.title: About $165b ASEAN Renewable Assets Face Climate Risk, Zurich Insurance Says
records.summary: The article reports a Zurich Insurance study finding that about $165 billion of renewable energy assets across ASEAN, assessed at 1,380 existing and planned sites, could be exposed to physical climate risk. Zurich estimates that about $13 billion of upfront resilience investment could cut projected financial exposure by 40% to 50%, a return of 6.5 times. The report treats resilience as a driver of bankability and insurability and recommends screening, stress-testing and quantifying resilience benefits for lenders and insurers.
insights: About $165 billion of ASEAN renewable assets across 1,380 sites (excluding Timor-Leste) could be exposed to climate risk.
75% of total generation capacity could face severe climate risk exposure by 2030, and about 80% of solar sites are projected to fall into higher-risk categories by 2030.
An upfront resilience investment of about $13 billion could reduce projected exposure by 40% to 50%, an estimated 6.5 times return.

A modelled severe hail event could cause up to 90% damage to an unprotected solar project, a loss of about $178.5 million with up to 21 months of recovery; automated hail stow systems reduce the exposure.
ASEAN targets 45% renewable share of installed capacity by 2030, up from 33%, requiring about $190 billion of clean energy investment by 2035.

records.title: The Weekly: U.S. Data Shows Resilience Investments Pay Back $1.86 Per Dollar
records.summary: This issue of The Weekly summarizes new Swiss Re research on the natural catastrophe protection gap and the returns on US resilience projects. It reports that the global gap reached $424 billion in 2025 while insurance coverage has broadly kept pace with growing exposure. Swiss Re's review of US projects found every one anticipated positive net returns, with a median benefit-cost ratio of 1.86. The issue argues this strengthens the case for directing capital to targeted adaptation that lowers expected losses and supports insurability.
insights: Swiss Re puts the global natural catastrophe protection gap at $424 billion in 2025, a 7% jump from 2024.
Swiss Re's resilience index, the share of global catastrophe exposure covered by insurance, rose from 25% to 27% over the past decade.

Swiss Re reviewed US resilience projects approved 2010 to 2022 that disclosed benefit-cost ratios, about $9 billion in project value, drawing on Army Corps feasibility reports and state and municipal analyses.
Every reviewed project anticipated positive net returns; the median BCR was 1.86 and the highest, a New Mexico flood-risk levee project, was 9.63.
Swiss Re notes these BCRs likely understate returns because appraisals usually omit life-safety, wider economic and ecosystem service benefits.
A linked study projects climate change could increase global hail-related damage by as much as 42% by the end of the century.

records.title: Bonn Climate Conference 2026: Veredas Dialogue Targets Climate Finance Flows, Adaptation Funding and Investment Barriers
records.summary: Down To Earth reports on the first Veredas Dialogue at the SB64 Bonn climate talks on 9-10 June 2026, the successor to the Sharm el-Sheikh Dialogue on Paris Agreement Article 2.1(c). Sessions covered national policy tools, financial systems for climate resilience and international barriers to aligned finance. Adaptation discussion centred on the underpricing of climate costs, climate-risk insurance including subsidised and parametric products, disaster risk financing and fiscal integration. Participants also raised high capital costs and biased credit ratings for vulnerable countries, debt-for-nature and debt-for-climate swaps, and MDB guarantees and first-loss capital.
insights: The Veredas Dialogue was launched under the COP30 Brazilian Presidency as successor to the Sharm el-Sheikh Dialogue (2023 to 2025) on Article 2.1(c).
Subsidising insurance was identified as critical to scaling adaptation finance, with parametric insurance providing immediate liquidity.
Norway prices 85 per cent of its emissions and uses the revenue to reduce income taxes for lower-income households.
Uganda's Climate Finance Unit is tracking a $26.5 billion commitment gap to be filled by 2030.
Barbados uses debt-for-nature and debt-for-climate swaps under the Bridgetown Initiative to fund its Environmental Sustainability Fund.
Participants said prudential frameworks and credit ratings penalise vulnerable nations, with perceived risk far exceeding actual default rates.

records.title: Mexico Doubles Parametric Catastrophe Insurance to About $575m at 2026 Renewal
records.summary: An Artemis report by Steve Evans of 10 June 2026 on Mexico doubling its parametric catastrophe insurance for 2026 into 2027. The Ministry of Finance and Public Credit secured 10.4 billion pesos of catastrophe insurance protection in total, a doubling from the prior year, of which the main component is 10 billion pesos, around US$575 million, of parametric catastrophe insurance placed for the 2026 to 2027 coverage year. The renewal runs from 5 June 2026 to 5 May 2027 and transfers risk from earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, hurricanes and floods of medium to high severity, and has two components: a 400 million peso Loss Management Fund and the 10 billion peso parametric cover, structured to guarantee a timely financial response to high-severity catastrophes. Agroasemex, S.A., a Mexican government insurance institution, is the conduit for the global market capacity supporting the arrangement, with the parametric cover placed on a reinsurance basis to protect the insurer, and it has served the same role for the country's catastrophe bonds over two decades in partnership with reinsurers, development banks and capital markets investors. Mexico operates a federal strategy for Financial Management of Disaster Risks with insurance arrangements running from mid-year, has been a beneficiary of World Bank facilitated catastrophe bond protection since the groundbreaking CAT-Mex Ltd. transaction of 2006, and was most recently in the cat bond market in May 2024 securing $420 million of parametric protection against earthquakes and Atlantic hurricanes.
insights: The sovereign's stated reason for choosing parametric cover is the benefit rather than the price: predictable, responsive and fast-paying protection. Mexico has been buying this for twenty years and has converged on speed as the thing worth paying for.

Agroasemex is the structural detail worth keeping. A state insurance institution acting as conduit means the sovereign reaches reinsurance and capital markets through a regulated insurer rather than directly, which is the pattern a government without its own insurer cannot copy and the reason Mexico can renew annually at scale.
Pairing a 400 million peso Loss Management Fund with the parametric layer is a retention-and-transfer split: the fund absorbs the frequent losses and the parametric cover the severe ones.
Doubling coverage in a single renewal is a demand signal rather than a supply one, and it dates precisely: June 2026, following the 2024 catastrophe bond renewal at $420 million.

records.title: Arcadis and Jupiter Intelligence Introduce PRICE Framework to Help Organizations Close the Climate Adaptation Investment Gap
records.summary: Arcadis and Jupiter Intelligence launched the PRICE Adaptation Framework on 10 June 2026, a methodology for comparing climate adaptation options, quantifying return on investment and prioritising resilience spending. The five steps are: Pinpoint loss drivers, Rank adaptation options, build the Investment case by quantifying avoided losses and ROI, set a Capital strategy connecting resilience decisions to funding, and Execute and evidence by translating planning into measurable delivery. It is supported by Arcadis Climate Risk Nexus and Enterprise Decision Analytics and by Jupiter's Adaptation Hub. Two test cases are reported: in the flood-prone Meyerland neighborhood of Houston, an analysis of 100 single-family homes found positive ROI for dry floodproofing at 52 per cent of locations assessed; in Slovenia, a modeled flood wall for an industrial facility that had suffered up to US$60 million of losses in a single event showed a projected ROI of 245 per cent. Arcadis reports applying the approach with the State University of New York, Northeast US regional transit clients and major real estate owners. The release cites UNEP's 2025 Adaptation Gap Report on adaptation finance needs of $310 to $365 billion a year by 2035, 12 to 14 times current flows, and a $14 damage avoided per $1 of coastal protection.
insights: The Houston result is the useful number: dry floodproofing cleared a positive ROI at only 52 per cent of 100 homes assessed, so a blanket retrofit programme in a flood-prone neighborhood would be half uneconomic on this method, which is an argument for screening rather than for coverage.

The two test cases sit at opposite ends of the distribution, 52 per cent of homes marginal against a 245 per cent ROI on a single industrial flood wall, which shows the method mainly separates concentrated high-value exposure from dispersed residential exposure.

The C step, capital strategy, is what distinguishes this from a risk analytics product: the framework's claim is that it connects an avoided-loss calculation to a funding route, which is the step most climate risk tools stop short of.
Both vendors are commercial and the framework is their joint product, so the ROI figures are self-reported and carry no independent verification.

records.title: Florida TaxWatch Looks at the Broward Countywide Resilience Plan 2025
institutions: Broward County Board of County Commissioners
Bureau of Economic and Business Research
records.summary: Florida TaxWatch evaluates Broward County's Countywide Resilience Plan 2025 on behalf of county taxpayers, asking whether it rests on sound data, sets measurable benchmarks, is financially feasible, assigns clear roles and has legal force. The plan pairs engineered and nature-based adaptations in two tiers (2050 and 2070) totalling $28.0 billion in 2024 dollars, of which about $9 billion is public and $19 billion falls on private property. TaxWatch finds the modeling strong and the plan economically feasible, but judges the funding sources non-dedicated and the private share unexplained. It concludes that the near-term implementation strategy approved on June 9, 2026, a $20 million annual grant program leveraged 5-to-1, largely answers its earlier financial feasibility concerns.
insights: Tier 1 (2050) capital cost is estimated at $20.1 billion and Tier 2 adds $7.9 billion, for $28.0 billion in 2024 dollars, with annual costs of $201 million and $280 million.

Of the $28 billion, the public share is about $9 billion and private property improvements (seawalls, storage, swales) about $19 billion, and TaxWatch finds it unclear how owners will fund their share.

Recurring annual economic benefits are estimated at $1.1 billion (Tier 1) and $5.2 billion (Tier 2), with non-recurring benefits of $20 billion and $51 billion, modeled with the V-ARIO input-output model over 2025 to 2125.
The adaptations include 190+ miles of enhanced seawalls, 159 flood control structures, 33 new pump stations, 41 upgraded crossings and 1,247 acre-feet of storage, selected from 47 modeled scenarios.
On June 9, 2026 the Board approved a near-term strategy: a $20 million annual grant program, leveraged 5-to-1 to $100 million a year and $1.5 billion over 15 years, for 263 Tier 1 projects.

Candidate funding sources include FEMA grants, WIFIA, Resilient Florida grants, the Clean Water SRF, a county sales surtax, stormwater fees, revenue and general obligation bonds and a resilience bond, none of them dedicated.

records.title: Total Catastrophe Bond Issuance Hits $16.1bn Year to Date in 2026, 144A Cat Bonds Over $15.8bn
records.summary: An Artemis market report on catastrophe bond issuance in 2026, recording total settled issuance across Rule 144A deals and analysed private transactions of $16.1 billion year to date, with settled 144A issuance alone above $15.8 billion. The breakdown is almost $15.44 billion of 144A property catastrophe bonds, almost $385 million of 144A cat bonds on other lines such as specialty, and just over $286 million of private cat bonds or cat bond lites. Seventy-one issuances had settled with a further seven in the pipeline, projecting at least 78 by 30 June against the previous first-half record of 72 set in H1 2025, so 2026 will break the record for the most deals to market and settle in a first half. The seventy-first to settle was the California Earthquake Authority's $425 million Sutter Re 2026-1. The article's initial projection for H1 2026 total issuance was about $16.96 billion, second only to the $17.56 billion of H1 2025, and it carries two dated updates: on 10 June, after new Kilimanjaro III Re offerings for Everest, the projection rose to just over $17.49 billion, and on 12 June the author judged the market on course for new second-quarter and first-half records. Issuance was already more than $3.5 billion ahead of H1 2024.
insights: The article is a snapshot of a moving number and says so in its own text, revising its projection twice within three days from $16.96 billion to over $17.49 billion. Any figure taken from it has to be cited with its update date.

The composition is the more durable finding: property catastrophe risk is about 96 per cent of 144A issuance, and private cat bonds are under 2 per cent of the total. A resilience-linked security entering this market enters an overwhelmingly property-catastrophe channel.

Deal count breaking a record while dollar volume does not is a market-structure signal: average deal size is falling, which usually means new and smaller sponsors are reaching the market. That is the direction a public-sector resilience sponsor would need.
The California Earthquake Authority's $425 million Sutter Re 2026-1 is named as the settling deal, which puts a public-sector sponsor in a market otherwise dominated by re/insurers.

records.title: Home Insurance and the Unraveling of Florida Communities
records.summary: An article in The Conversation of 9 June 2026, by a researcher who has spent over a decade studying how property markets adapt to the changing financial realities of climate change in Florida, the Netherlands and beyond. It opens on Shore Acres, a low-lying bayfront neighbourhood of St Petersburg, in November 2024, two months after Hurricane Helene pushed several feet of water into homes there even though the storm's centre stayed far offshore, and days after Milton made landfall nearby as a major hurricane, the two arriving within 13 days of each other. What the author found was starkly unequal recovery on a single street: dozens of older homes from the postwar building boom gutted, interiors piled in the street, for-sale signs on many of them, alongside pristine newer homes raised on posts far above their neighbours in line with newer building codes and showing no sign a storm had passed. The argument is that these costs are driven by more than major disasters: soaring property insurance rates are repricing life in Florida and will worsen as hurricanes intensify, and the current way of managing those risks and costs is not the only option.
insights: The elevated houses are the finding. On one street, homes built to the newer code were untouched while their postwar neighbours were gutted, which is an unusually clean natural experiment in what a building standard is worth, observed rather than modelled.

Helene put several feet of water into Shore Acres with its centre far offshore, which is the same lesson the MetroCat trigger design encodes: surge is not proportional to proximity or to landfall intensity, and an instrument keyed to wind at landfall can miss the loss entirely.
For-sale signs on the damaged homes and none on the elevated ones is the distributional consequence stated plainly: the households that cannot afford to rebuild to code are the ones who leave.

records.title: CDP Launches AI-Powered Adaptation & Action Explorer to Help Subnational Governments Turn Climate Risk Into Action
records.summary: CDP announced the launch of the Adaptation & Action Explorer, an AI-powered platform built with Google.org Fellowship support that combines climate hazard data from Google Earth Engine with disclosures from more than 1,000 subnational governments in over 80 countries. The tool lets cities, states and regions assess climate risk by location, review adaptation plans and project pipelines, find peer solutions and query the data through an AI assistant. It is intended to help governments prioritise interventions and present investable adaptation projects to funders.
insights: The platform draws on CDP data from more than 1,000 disclosing governments across 80 countries, covering 16% of the global population.
Over 94% of disclosing governments reported being impacted by climate hazards in 2025.
In 2025, reporting cities, states and regions identified 2,871 projects requiring a total of $114.3 billion in investment.
Map-based hazard data from Google Earth Engine covers eight major climate hazards.
The open-source platform was built over a six-month pro bono Google.org Fellowship.

records.title: The Weekly: The Blended Capital Stack That Could Move Resilience Finance at Scale
institutions: Metropolitan Water District of Southern California
records.summary: An argument that funding climate resilience is a coordination problem rather than a capital problem, built on a historical parallel. In 2025, climate-driven disasters in the United States caused an estimated $115 billion in damages across 23 separate billion-dollar events, and the article's contention is that the capital to address the underlying risk already exists while the coordination to move it does not. Drawing on a piece by Lily Bui of SoCal Grantmakers, it recalls that early twentieth century Los Angeles outgrew its local water supply and that reaching the Colorado and Owens Rivers required new institutions, new financing mechanisms and unprecedented coordination across jurisdictions: California created the Metropolitan Water District, and voters approved bonds during the Great Depression to finance the Los Angeles and Colorado River Aqueducts, turning a fragmented system of local wells into a regional network able to sustain growth at scale. The article proposes the same shift for resilience finance, from isolated wells to a coordinated watershed in which resources are intentionally pooled, directed and circulated across geographies, sectors and time horizons.
insights: The framing claim is falsifiable and useful: capital is not the constraint, coordination is, and the evidence offered is that $115 billion of 2025 losses coexists with available capital that does not move.

The Metropolitan Water District precedent is the strongest part of the argument, because it shows a fragmented local system being consolidated by creating an institution and a financing mechanism together, and doing so during the Great Depression.

The watershed metaphor is operationalised as pooling across geographies, sectors and time horizons, the last of which is the hard one: resilience benefits accrue over decades while most funding cycles are annual.
This is a weekly newsletter format, so the substance is the argument and the cited figures rather than original analysis, and the Bui article it draws on is the primary source.

records.title: AI Is Closing the Data Gaps That Have Limited Disaster Prediction for Decades
records.summary: The article argues that as historical baselines lose predictive value (the 'end of stationarity'), AI is filling data gaps in disaster prediction. It describes AI vegetation risk tools used by utilities to prevent wildfire ignitions, the Pacific Disaster Center's AI-enriched DisasterAWARE platform, Google's Groundsource dataset of flood events mined from news, and AI tools extending severe weather and hail forecasts. It notes that free, high-quality hazard data could change who has access to risk information currently sold by catastrophe modelers.
insights: Utilities spend about $8 billion a year on vegetation management; PG&E operates over 100,000 miles of power lines.
Overstory says six of the ten largest North American utilities are clients, and Inland Power and Light reported reducing hazard trees by 88%.
DisasterAWARE is used by more than 20,000 disaster management and humanitarian practitioners worldwide; a $1 million federal grant for an AI warning system on O'ahu was frozen in April.
Google's Groundsource, announced in March 2026, built a dataset of 2.6 million historical flood events across more than 150 countries and supports urban flash flood forecasts up to 24 hours ahead.
An NSF tool can flag severe weather outbreaks a week ahead, and FLASH Weather AI forecasts hail size and arrival up to 55 minutes ahead.

records.title: Updated Climate Bonds Resilience Taxonomy Methodology (CBRT v1.1)
records.summary: Annexes I to VI of the Climate Bonds Resilience Taxonomy methodology document, version 1.1, June 2026. The taxonomy defines the target climate impact that each adapting measure addresses, and Annex I sets out how an adapting measure is assessed against a global threshold in four steps. First, define the investment context for the assessment, setting boundaries that correspond to the specific implementation of the measure, which may be more granular than the activity or even the asset it sits in: installing water-efficient fixtures and fittings is assessed in the specific context in which they are installed. Three further considerations may apply, setting out the investment's context of vulnerability to climate change, an explicit statement of intent to reduce the vulnerabilities identified, and a clear direct link between the investment and that vulnerability. Second, establish an appropriate timescale, normally the expected time horizon for implementing the measure, covering the expected lifespan of both the measure and the activity it is implemented in. Third, use the investment-appropriate global threshold defined in the taxonomy, subject to further development and refinement including by Technical Working Groups. Fourth, define a counterfactual against which progress toward the threshold can be measured.
insights: The counterfactual requirement is what separates a resilience taxonomy from a green one: an adapting measure has no emissions to count, so the only way to say it worked is against a stated alternative, and requiring that alternative be defined up front is the discipline the field has been missing.

Assessment at the level of the specific implementation rather than the activity or the asset is the move that makes ordinary capital expenditure eligible: a fixture in a building can qualify without the building qualifying.

The three-part intent test, vulnerability context, stated intent, direct link, is designed to stop adaptation-washing, where spending that would have happened anyway is relabelled once a taxonomy exists.
Global thresholds remain subject to development by Technical Working Groups, so the taxonomy is a framework with the numbers still to come, and an issuer cannot yet self-certify against it.
Tying the timescale to the lifespan of both the measure and the activity it sits in prevents the common trick of claiming a long-lived benefit from a short-lived intervention.

records.title: Making Resilience & Public Finance Function
records.summary: This essay argues that state and local governments are becoming the most consequential actors in closing the gap between climate risk and investment, and that resilience will be won through their finance functions rather than through Chief Resilience Officers, who rarely control budgets, debt or reserves. It urges philanthropy and nonprofits to engage finance officers, budget directors, treasurers and housing finance agencies, and to reframe risk as a direct fiscal burden. It identifies housing finance agencies as a key entry point, since they can embed resilience criteria in mortgage products, bond issuance and development incentives, and it calls for adapting existing tools rather than building new systems.
insights: Chief Resilience Officers are described as advisory: they do not control budgets, issue debt or set reserve policies.
Housing Finance Agencies are singled out as leverage points because they can standardize products, aggregate demand and embed resilience criteria in mortgages and bond issuances.
Existing tools named for adaptation to risk reduction include tax-exempt bonds, revolving loan funds and housing finance programs.
The placement of the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund in EPA rather than Treasury is cited as an example of environmental programs separated from financial infrastructure.
Embedding resilience in reserve policies, capital improvement plans and debt structures is presented as a way to shift capital toward risk reduction without new systems.

records.title: The Impacts of Climate Change Are Already Here: How Resilient Are We?
records.summary: This report summarizes a Resilience First roundtable held on 2 June 2026 at London SXSW, convening senior representatives from insurance, finance, transport, health, and telecommunications to assess organisational climate resilience. It finds preparedness improving but uneven, with persistent gaps in asset resilience, infrastructure planning, and long-term scenario analysis. Key themes include cascading cross-sector interdependencies, the underfunding of adaptation relative to mitigation, data gaps for physical risk quantification, and the need for CFO-level financial framing to unlock resilience investment.
insights: Capital continues to flow predominantly toward mitigation rather than adaptation, driven by short-term incentive structures and decision-making frameworks that fail to capture long-term resilience value, a persistent structural barrier identified by cross-sector practitioners.

Investment decisions in organisational resilience are ultimately driven by CFOs, making translation of climate risk into financial risk language (cost of inaction, quantified externalities) a prerequisite for unlocking capital.

Human health impacts, including the northward spread of tropical diseases and heatwave effects on workforce productivity and safety, were identified as the most compelling near-term catalyst for corporate resilience action, framed as a duty-of-care obligation.

Cascading cross-sector risks (where failure in one system triggers disruption across others) represent a leading dimension of climate vulnerability, yet no unified or widely accessible framework exists to map these interdependencies.

Data gaps for physical climate risk quantification are a binding constraint: scientific data exists but is not communicated in ways accessible to business decision-makers, and confidentiality concerns further inhibit cross-sector data sharing.

Preparedness is uneven across organisations and sectors: while climate resilience is increasingly integrated into core business strategy with growing risk intelligence capabilities, significant gaps persist in asset resilience, infrastructure planning, and scenario analysis.

Participants called for embedding resilience into policy cycles, asset planning, and system design coherently across sectors and geographies, with cross-sector coordination currently fragmented, lacking centralised oversight and weak local-to-national integration.

records.title: Low Cost, High Yield: The Adaptation and Resilience Investment Opportunity for Infrastructure
records.authors: Karina Whalley, Alma Djelic, Anthony Schrapffer, Matthieu Renard
records.summary: This IFC/AXA Climate report (June 2026) makes a quantitative financial and policy case for adaptation and resilience (A&R) investment in infrastructure, focused on emerging markets and developing economies (EMDEs). Using three Brazilian infrastructure assets (a 1,000 km, 500 kV transmission line in Mato Grosso, a water reservoir in Southeastern Brazil, and a São Paulo motorway concession), the report models NAV impacts and IRRs of targeted A&R measures under intermediate- and high-emissions scenarios. Headline findings: $8.6 protected per dollar invested in T&D, $6.3 in water, and $2.2 in roads; IRRs up to 886%. The report catalogues seven financing mechanism categories, maps structural barriers to A&R investment, and profiles live instruments including a USD 340 million blended finance fund, a USD 1.3 billion water facility, and the world's first CBI-certified resilience bond.
insights: Across three Brazilian infrastructure business cases, targeted A&R measures costing less than 10% of NAV protect $2.2–$8.6 in asset value per dollar invested over the asset's lifetime, with IRRs ranging from 56% (road bundle, short loan) to 886% (T&D firebreaks, 15-year loan); these high IRRs reflect the low cost of selected measures relative to avoided climate losses, not full project economics.

Without A&R, cumulative climate hazards erode approximately 22% of NAV under intermediate-emissions scenarios and up to 30% under high-emissions scenarios across the assets studied, confirming physical climate risk as a material valuation concern for infrastructure investors and lenders.

Loan maturity is the single most important financing lever: extending loan tenor from 6 to 15 years can double IRRs for road A&R measures, while interest rate variations produce comparatively minor effects, a critical insight for DFIs and development banks structuring concessional finance.

Firebreaks for the Mato Grosso transmission line reduce annual service outages from 10.8 to 1.6 days (85% reduction) and cut NAV losses from 30.3% to 7.6% under the high-emissions scenario, at a cost of only ~3% of NAV, the clearest documented unit-economics proof point in the report.

Climate impacts already cost low- and middle-income countries an estimated USD 390 billion annually (1–2% of GDP); without action, losses could increase 12–22% in middle-income and up to 33% in low-income countries by 2100, with the global cost of inaction estimated at USD 1.27 trillion between 2022 and 2100.

records.title: Climate Resilience as Strategy: Scaling Corporate Action on Physical Risks from Climate Change
records.authors: Verena Radulovic, Tessa Ide, Tucker Van Aken, Dee Yang
institutions: Center for Climate and Energy Solutions (C2ES)
Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures
records.summary: This June 2026 report by C2ES and Systemiq, based on interviews with over 40 organizations including two dozen companies, assesses where corporations stand on physical climate risk management and what is needed to scale action. Key findings: 65% of public companies cite physical climate risk in filings, but only 25% of those acting have taken strategic measures. Without adaptation, major companies globally face projected annual losses of $1.2 trillion by the 2050s. The report proposes four practical infrastructure elements (a guidance catalog, a maturity model, a standardized corporate climate resilience framework, and sector-specific playbooks), and documents significant valuation, governance, and financing gaps holding companies back.
insights: Major companies globally face projected annual losses of $1.2 trillion annually by the 2050s from physical climate risk if no adaptation action is taken, with large- and mid-cap companies already experiencing average annual losses of $88 billion in asset damage and $1.1 trillion in business interruption.

65% of public companies cite physical climate risk in SEC filings, more than double the 2001 share, but only 25% of those that have begun acting have taken genuinely strategic measures such as adapting products, services, or delivery models.

Among companies that have invested in operational resilience, 82% report positive financial or reputational results, 68% cite increased investor interest, 67% report improved insurance terms, and 56% say they have secured better lending conditions, per MSCI Institute.

A Bloomberg study of 2,900 companies found those with 10% higher physical climate risk exposure faced a weighted average cost of capital 22 basis points higher than peers; Dow Jones companies with insignificant physical risk exposure generated returns approximately 1.7x higher than peers with moderate exposure over the past decade.

FM Global's resilience credit program, premium offsets that clients reinvest in engineering improvements, had grown to $825 million (a 10% premium offset for eligible policies) by 2026 and driven a potential reduction in economic impact of nearly $80 billion, illustrating a scalable insurer-corporate co-investment model.

Adaptation finance reached an all-time high of $63 billion annually in 2021/22, but tracked private sector adaptation finance averaged only $4.7 billion per year for 2019–2022, a severe gap relative to need and indicative of the capital allocation problem the report targets.
records.publisher: Center for Climate and Energy Solutions

records.title: The Weekly: Hail and Tornadoes Are Now the Most Expensive Insured Peril in America
institutions: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety (IBHS)
records.summary: This issue of The Weekly argues that severe convective storms (hail, tornadoes and derechos) now generate more cumulative insured losses than tropical cyclones and have become the most expensive insured peril of the century in the US. It warns that investors calibrated to historical storm maps may be underestimating exposure as damage spreads into the Southeast, Mid-Atlantic and Northeast. It lists the main failure points for commercial property, chiefly roofs, and the retrofits that reduce them, and notes state mandates tying insurance discounts to IBHS FORTIFIED Commercial standards.
insights: In 2025, 21 of the 23 billion-dollar US disasters were severe convective storms.
Munich Re puts US severe thunderstorm losses at $56 billion for 2025, and the average per-event cost is 31% higher than a decade ago.
Hail claims account for 50% to 80% of all severe storm losses, and roofs in hail-prone areas last half as long as elsewhere.
