Alabama, Louisiana and Mississippi mandate that insurers offer premium discounts for properties meeting IBHS FORTIFIED Commercial standards.
A linked Realtor.com analysis finds insurance premiums on new-construction homes up to 38% lower than on older homes.
A cited study found each dollar invested in forest fuel treatments yielded $3.73 in expected benefits.

records.title: Three Examples of How Incremental Change Led to Resilience
institutions: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety
University of Alabama Center for Risk and Insurance Research
records.summary: Abby Ross, CEO of The Resiliency Company, traces three cases in which localized resilience measures grew into national models: Firewise USA, the IBHS FORTIFIED standard in Alabama, and soft-story seismic retrofit ordinances in California. Each case shows a slow path from pilot to policy, accelerated when technical standards were tied to insurance pricing, grants or mandates. She argues that early proof points rarely look like proof at the start and that funding local programs and tying standards to dollars is how new markets are created.
insights: Marin County grew from nine Firewise sites in 2017 to roughly 90 by 2025, backed by $86 million in cumulative community investment; Firewise communities fix 3.5x more defensible space vulnerabilities per parcel.

Alabama required insurer discounts for qualifying coastal properties in 2009, created Strengthen Alabama Homes grants in 2011 and extended discounts statewide in 2015; grants now reach up to $10,000 and wind premium discounts up to 55%.
A 2025 University of Alabama study of more than 40,000 properties after Hurricane Sally found FORTIFIED Roof homes had 73% fewer claims and 72% lower total losses.
More than 90,000 FORTIFIED homes span 34 states, and IBHS issued more than 20,000 designations in 2025.
San Francisco's 2013 soft-story ordinance covers about 5,000 buildings housing 180,000 residents, and Los Angeles's 2015 ordinance up to 13,500 buildings.

records.title: DEQ Announces $1.6M Nature-Based Flood Resilience Project in Bladenboro
institutions: North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality
records.summary: North Carolina's Flood Resiliency Blueprint awarded $1.6 million to the Bladenboro South Main Street Flood Resiliency Project, a nature-based scheme to create floodplain storage and restore natural streamflow so as to reduce recurring flooding in downtown Bladenboro. The town has been hit three times in eight years, by Tropical Storm Debby in 2024, Hurricane Florence in 2018 and Hurricane Matthew in 2016, with extensive damage to businesses and homes, and has already relocated businesses out of the floodplain. The project works by clearing and widening a blocked culvert to increase outlet capacity and restore natural streamflow, and pairs that with planting trees and native plants in the floodplain to stabilise stream banks, which together create over 3.9 million gallons of floodplain storage, enough to cover 12 acres at one foot depth, while controlling erosion and improving water quality and wetland habitat. The vendor is Resource Environmental Solutions, and the announcement names the state senator and representative who helped secure it.
insights: The intervention is mostly a culvert: clearing and widening a blocked outlet is the core engineering, with planting added for bank stability and water quality, which makes the nature-based label partly a co-benefit on a drainage fix.
3.9 million gallons of storage for $1.6 million gives a directly comparable unit cost against the Swannanoa and Rosman awards under the same programme.

Three major floods in eight years is the pattern that justifies capital spending rather than repeated recovery, and the town had already relocated businesses out of the floodplain before seeking this award.
Delivery is through a private ecological restoration vendor rather than a nonprofit or the municipality, which is a different delivery model from the same programme's other awards in the same month.
records.publisher: North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality

records.title: SEC Proposes Rescission of Climate-Related Disclosure Rules
records.summary: The SEC formally proposed rescinding its 2024 Climate-Related Disclosure Rules in their entirety, arguing the rules exceed the agency's statutory authority. Follows the March 2025 vote to cease defending the rules and the Eighth Circuit's September 2025 order requiring the Commission to determine the rule's fate. Materially changes the federal disclosure landscape for physical and transition climate risk.
insights: The proposal is to rescind the climate disclosure rules in their entirety on the ground that they exceed the agency's statutory authority, with policy reasons offered as independent and additional rather than primary.

The procedural history is the substance: rules adopted March 2024, stayed April 2024 pending Eighth Circuit litigation, defence abandoned March 2025, and the petitions held in abeyance from September 2025 until the Commission either reconsiders by notice-and-comment or renews its defence. This rescission is that reconsideration.

Materiality is named as the organising principle, with the Commission stating that disclosure obligations should avoid the practical effect of dictating corporate behaviour and be imposed only where expected benefits justify the costs.

The rules being rescinded covered greenhouse gas emissions, management of climate-related risks and the financial statement effects of severe weather events, so the physical-risk disclosure that resilience analysis depends on is inside the scope of the rescission.
A 60-day comment period from Federal Register publication is the remaining procedural step.

records.title: Funding Climate Resilience Is a Coordination Problem, Not a Capital Problem
records.summary: This opinion piece by Lily Bui of SoCal Grantmakers argues that the primary barrier to climate resilience finance is coordination failure, not capital scarcity, with 2025 U.S. climate disasters causing an estimated $115 billion in damages from 23 events. Using the Los Angeles aqueduct as a historical analogy, it outlines a blended capital stack model where philanthropy funds pre-development, CDFIs and impact investors translate projects for institutional capital, and public funding scales de-risked projects. Three case studies illustrate the model: Florida affordable housing with IBHS FORTIFIED standards, the EPA's Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund, and post-LA-fire recovery through the Resilient LA Delta Fund.
insights: In 2025, U.S. climate-driven disasters caused an estimated $115 billion in damages across 23 separate billion-dollar events, yet the article's central argument is that sufficient capital exists, the gap is structural coordination, not volume.

Adaptation and resilience projects (forest management, urban cooling, early warning systems, home hardening) rarely align with a single funding source and remain heavily dependent on philanthropic and public funding, unlike climate mitigation (solar, wind, EVs) which has legible repayment structures for private capital.

The article proposes a tiered blended capital stack: philanthropy absorbs early-stage and pre-development risk; CDFIs and impact investors bridge and translate; public capital scales and de-risks; private institutional capital enters only after uncertainty is reduced, each layer performing a distinct, non-substitutable function.

The Resilient LA Delta Fund uses a Robert Wood Johnson Foundation guarantee alongside philanthropic capital to de-risk CDFI lending for post-Los Angeles wildfire recovery and resilience projects, with the explicit goal of eventually attracting larger private and institutional capital as repayment performance stabilizes.

Climate resilience districts using tax increment financing are highlighted as a promising place-based mechanism to capture value and reinvest it in long-term resilience infrastructure, potentially reducing dependence on episodic grant funding.

The EPA's Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund is cited as a federal catalytic capital model that coordinates grants, concessional debt, private investment, and technical assistance through community lenders and green banks, though it is noted as currently stalled amid political and legal challenges.

records.title: Galapagos Capital R$126M Brazil ILS: LATAM Capital Markets Come of Age
records.summary: The article reports Galapagos Capital's R$126 million Letra de Risco de Seguro (LRS) issuance in May 2026, the largest under Brazil's domestic insurance-linked securities regime and the first placed with a syndicate of five institutional investors. It explains the SSPE structure licensed by SUSEP, the supply chain of law firms, collateral managers and trustees the market is building, and why the early deals transfer credit insurance rather than catastrophe risk. It argues that the framework is structurally ready for parametric catastrophe ILS for flood and drought.
insights: The May 2026 deal is Galapagos's third transaction after R$100 million in December 2025 and R$13.5 million in April 2026, and cumulative LRS issuance across Brazilian SSPEs is about R$273 million.
The underlying risk is credit insurance on a major Latin American retailer's consumer credit book, not a natural catastrophe trigger.

SUSEP Joint Resolution 9/2024 (February 2024) set up the trustee agent framework with collateral segregation, payment priority and trigger documentation that makes multi-investor syndication feasible.
Four SSPEs are authorized: Andrina (IRB Re, first mover with a R$33.7 million surety deal in May 2025), Galapagos Capital, Ariel and a Lockton-linked platform.
The 2024 Rio Grande do Sul floods produced insured losses above R$3 billion, which the article names as the natural demand base for catastrophe LRS.
Global ILS outstanding was USD 56 billion at end-2025 with USD 24.7 billion issued that year, per Swiss Re.

records.title: US Exposed to $375 Billion-$1 Trillion in Aggregated Uninsured Flood Losses From a Range of Extreme Events
records.summary: Moody's uses its RMS US Inland Flood HD model to compare the insurable value of US residential property with homes carrying NFIP coverage, county by county, and so quantify the flood insurance protection gap. Under a 1-in-100-year scenario aggregated uninsured residential loss exposure is $375 billion with a 65% protection gap; a 1-in-500-year scenario triples it to over $1 trillion, and an RCP 4.5 scenario raises it about 25% to around $472 billion by 2050. The report argues that this gap is a credit risk for state and local governments, because uninsured losses shift recovery costs onto households, local budgets and federal aid. It stresses that credit impact depends on the size of uninsured losses relative to a county's capacity to absorb them, and offers uninsured loss exposure ratios as a second lens.
insights: In a 1-in-100-year flood, less than 2% of counties, across 11 states, carry 65% of uninsured loss exposure (around $245 billion), each with potential losses above $1 billion.

Counties with potential uninsured losses above $5 billion are concentrated in Florida, Louisiana, South Carolina and Texas, with county protection gaps of 45%-75%; in a 1-in-500-year flood they extend to 11 states, some inland, with gaps of 50%-100%.

Flood insurance take-up is low even in the highest-risk Gulf and Atlantic coastal areas, at 10%-30%, partly because mortgage flood requirements follow FEMA SFHA maps that omit much pluvial, surge and sea-level-rise risk.

Private flood policies have roughly doubled since 2020 but are still only about 10% of policies in force, while NFIP policies fell by a similar number, so the national gap has not materially narrowed; NFIP caps coverage at $250,000.

Counties in six states (Florida, Kentucky, Louisiana, South Dakota, South Carolina, Texas) have uninsured loss exposure ratios above 10% in a 1-in-100-year flood, rising to 16 states in a 1-in-500-year flood.

Hurricane Helene rainfall (24.2 inches over three days near Asheville) exceeded the 1-in-1,000-year return period; Buncombe County's modeled protection gap is around 88%, and Moody's moved its Aaa outlook to negative in March 2025 and back to stable on 15 April 2026.

records.title: Climate Adaptation Finance as the Next Frontier of Public Financial Management
institutions: ICAEW (Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales)
records.summary: ICAEW argues that adaptation finance is emerging as the central priority for public financial management, warning that without robust outcome-based metrics public climate finance will remain fragmented and input-driven. Cites the $212B/year adaptation funding gap and Standard Chartered's $1:$12 benefit estimate to argue for stronger PFM systems to measure and optimize adaptation investments.
insights: The framing question is not whether to fund adaptation but whether public financial systems can measure it: without robust metrics, adaptation finance stays fragmented and input-driven rather than outcome-oriented.

Adaptation has no single universal metric equivalent to carbon emissions in mitigation finance, which is why governments fall back on proxy indicators for exposure, sensitivity and adaptive capacity, and why spending is not comparable across countries or sectors.

Public adaptation finance is described as running through four interlinked channels, domestic budget allocations, concessional and multilateral finance, risk transfer mechanisms, and blended structures, with African Risk Capacity's parametric cover named as the rapid post-disaster liquidity example.

The Netherlands Delta Programme and Bangladesh's cyclone early warning are offered as cases where indicators are integrated into governance, against many developing countries where the same indicators sit fragmented across institutions and outside fiscal decision-making.
The UK's Climate Change Act 2008 is cited as a model for institutionalising climate risk in public financial management through a legally binding assessment and adaptation planning cycle.

records.title: Resilience-Adjusted Credit Risk: Operationalising Climate Adaptation in Financial Decision-Making
records.authors: Cambridge Institute for Sustainability Leadership (CISL), Banking Environment Initiative
institutions: UK Centre for Greening Finance and Investment (CGFI)
records.summary: Cambridge Institute for Sustainability Leadership's Banking Environment Initiative introduces the Resilience-Adjusted Credit Risk (RACR) framework, a forward-looking approach that integrates physical climate risk exposure, insurance adequacy, and resilience measures into core credit metrics such as probability of default and loss given default. The framework provides banks a method to operationalise climate adaptation in lending decisions.
insights: The framework's central move is to make adaptation investment a credit variable: it adjusts probability of default and loss given default to reflect both hazard exposure and the borrower's capacity to reduce it, recognising avoided loss as a PD and LGD reducer.

Current credit frameworks are described as assuming insurance is a static condition of lending, and the Insurance Adequacy component replaces that assumption with coverage verification, premium trajectory and an uninsurability horizon.

Six barriers are named as self-reinforcing rather than independent: prudential regime gaps, a revenue paradox in which adaptation benefits are not captured, low observed climate bad debts, attribution failures that hide climate losses inside standard risk categories, a horizon mismatch between credit tenor and physical risk, and a widening insurance blind spot. Invisible losses suppress urgency, which suppresses investment, which perpetuates the absence of evidence.

The framework is deliberately modular, letting banks begin with qualitative overlays and triage screens and add quantitative integration as data infrastructure develops, which is an adoption path rather than a standard.

Scaling is argued to require four things no single institution can build: a common adaptation taxonomy, shared data and modelling infrastructure, resilience-linked insurance pricing that rewards verified vulnerability reduction, and recognition of resilient assets in capital requirements. The EU Infrastructure Supporting Factor, the Monetary Authority of Singapore capital relief pilot and PRA SS5/25 are cited as early signals.

records.title: The Weekly: Local Communities Are Taking Wildfire Mitigation Into Their Own Hands
records.summary: This weekly newsletter's feature reports that wildfire-prone communities in the US West are funding their own detection technology as federal mitigation support stalls and technology gets cheaper. In Eagle County, Colorado, the Cordillera Metro District, a special tax district, is installing 1,000 solar-powered smoke sensors funded from a budget surplus. It links the shift to the legal limbo of FEMA's BRIC program and delayed state reimbursements. The news roundup covers research pricing wildfire risk into municipal borrowing costs, projected Florida premium increases and a study of how physical adaptation affects equity prices.
insights: Cordillera's sensor system costs between $300,000 and $400,000, affordable enough to fund through a budget surplus, and staff say it buys about 45 minutes in a fire.
In ground-based sensor trials, responders received wildfire alerts 37 minutes before a 911 call.
FEMA's BRIC program was canceled in April 2025 and reinstated after a federal court order in March 2026, and $11 billion in planned state reimbursements was delayed.
Cited research finds wildfire exposure raises municipal bond interest rates by about 0.36% for high-risk communities, and mitigation can reduce or eliminate the premium.
A cited University of Zurich study of 13,500+ US firms finds pre-hurricane physical protection offsets 26-37% of negative stock reactions.

records.title: Scalable Investment Platforms, Not Capital, Are Holding Back Climate Adaptation Finance in Asia
records.summary: An Eco-Business report from Temasek's Ecosperity summit in Singapore, on a panel discussing the bankability of climate adaptation and resilience. Jeb Victorino, investment director at the Netherlands-based investment firm Climate Fund Managers, argues that scalable investment platforms rather than scarce capital are the main bottleneck for climate adaptation finance in Asia: there is ample private money looking at climate-aligned opportunities in the region but no multiplier effect from structures that can absorb capital at scale and channel it into resilience projects. The opportunity he identifies is in innovating and creating replicable platforms and repeatable capital structures so that investors can fund at scale even with limited resources, enabling private capital to match the public sector's magnitude in financing adaptation. He cites a debt-for-nature transaction structured three years earlier in which Ecuador exchanged about US$1.628 billion of its existing international bonds for a new US$656 million marine bond used to protect 150,000 hectares of mangroves in the Galapagos area, and says similar transactions were replicated for Vietnam and the Philippines through a US$1 billion blended finance facility targeting water, sanitation and oceans infrastructure in emerging markets.
insights: The panel's diagnosis is that the bottleneck is replicable structures rather than capital, so the constraint it identifies is transaction design and repeatability rather than the supply of money.

The Ecuador numbers are the concrete ones: $1.628 billion of old bonds exchanged for a $656 million marine bond, so the conservation funding comes out of the discount on distressed sovereign debt rather than from new money.

Replication is the claim to test. The same structure reaching Vietnam and the Philippines through a $1 billion facility is the multiplier the panel describes, and it is a resilience structure being deliberately templated rather than built bespoke.
Naming 150,000 hectares of mangroves ties the financial structure to a physical protective asset, which is what distinguishes a debt-for-nature swap from a general-purpose refinancing.

records.title: Understanding PPPs for climate adaptation and resilience: A guide for city and regional authorities
records.authors: Federico Aili, Valerie Brown, Leon Kapetas, Fani Gelagoti
records.summary: A guide for city and regional authorities on using public-private partnerships for climate adaptation, written by Resilient Cities Network with Grid Engineers. It explains PPP concepts, contract models such as DBFOM and its variants, payment mechanisms and revenue schemes, the finance structure of a PPP and the preparation cycle from identification to long-term contract management. Its distinctive content is climate risk allocation: distinguishing frequent, extreme and rare events and internal from external risks, on the argument that transparent risk sharing is what keeps a project financially viable while protecting the public interest. It is deliberately cautionary, naming unequal negotiating power, limited transparency, unclear incentives and lock-in to costly inflexible contracts as real risks, and stops short of design and implementation guidance.
insights: The guide's central technical contribution is a climate risk allocation framework that separates frequent, extreme and rare events and internal from external risks, rather than treating climate risk as one category to be assigned to one party.

It defines a PPP by performance-based payment, a long-term agreement in which the private partner designs, finances, builds, operates or maintains a public asset and is paid on performance, which is what connects it to outcomes-based finance rather than to procurement.
Bankability is named as the thing a well designed PPP improves for adaptation projects, which is the specific market failure that makes adaptation hard to finance at municipal scale.

Three illustrative applications carry the argument: a stormwater PPP in an emerging market country, a revenue-generating urban dune system for coastal protection, and a flood-resilient bus rapid transit PPP. The dune example is the clearest case of a resilience asset carrying its own revenue line.

The guide is explicit that PPPs are not a quick fix and that many local authorities lack the legal, institutional and capacity base to negotiate them, so it positions itself before the design stage rather than as an implementation manual.

records.title: IBHS's FORTIFIED Program Surpasses 100,000 Designations
institutions: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety (IBHS)
Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety
records.summary: The Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety (IBHS) announced in May 2026 that its FORTIFIED® program (a voluntary, beyond-code construction and re-roofing standard designed to reduce storm losses from high winds, hurricanes, and wind-driven rain), has surpassed 100,000 designations nationwide. More than half of those designations were earned in the past three years, driven by state grant programs in Alabama, North Carolina, and Louisiana, insurer incentives, and industry partnerships. Independent research following Hurricane Sally (2020) confirmed that FORTIFIED homes suffered significantly less damage than conventionally built homes, validating the program's loss-reduction claims and its role in stabilizing insurance markets.
insights: FORTIFIED has surpassed 100,000 designations nationwide as of May 2026, with more than 50% earned in the last three years, indicating accelerating adoption rates driven by public-private investment.

Post-Hurricane Sally (2020) independent research by the University of Alabama confirmed FORTIFIED-standard homes experienced significantly less damage than conventionally constructed neighbors, providing real-world loss-reduction proof points for insurers and capital allocators.

State grant programs are the primary demand catalyst: Alabama's Strengthen Alabama Homes (SAH) grant, North Carolina Insurance Underwriting Association grants covering 18 coastal counties, and Louisiana's Fortify Homes Program have each driven large-scale regional adoption.

Alabama Insurance Commissioner explicitly linked FORTIFIED adoption to reduced claims and a stronger state insurance market, framing resilient construction as a market-stabilization tool, a direct signal to insurers and reinsurers pricing wind risk.

The program has expanded from single-family residential to commercial buildings and multifamily communities, broadening the addressable market and opening pathways to institutional and portfolio-scale resilience investment.

A first-of-its-kind alliance with GAF to certify FORTIFIED roofing contractors addresses workforce and supply-side constraints that could otherwise cap adoption, representing an industry infrastructure investment in resilience delivery capacity.

Additional states (Kentucky, Maine, Minnesota, Mississippi, Oklahoma), are developing or considering mitigation grant legislation, indicating a policy pipeline that could substantially grow the designation count and associated loss-reduction impact.
records.publisher: Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety

records.title: DEQ Announces $1.2M for Flood Resilience Projects in Swannanoa and Rosman
institutions: North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality
records.summary: North Carolina's Flood Resiliency Blueprint awarded more than $1.2 million for two flood resilience projects in Swannanoa and Rosman, both in the French Broad River Basin and both in communities that had not previously received Blueprint funding. Together the projects will create nearly 9 million gallons, or 27 acre-feet, of flood water storage, restore 3,000 feet of tributary streams and three acres of wetlands, stabilise streambanks and install natural stormwater infrastructure. In Swannanoa, $822,780 goes to the regional nonprofit RiverLink to lead a project on a river severely damaged by Hurricane Helene, creating 1.6 million gallons of storage and capturing and filtering pollutants, with the site identified during field inspections for a damage assessment. In Rosman, the award goes to Conserving Carolina to work on 30 acres of former agricultural fields, slowing flood waters and creating floodplain storage to protect downstream infrastructure and property. The release places these in programme context: the Blueprint had previously funded more than $8.8 million across 16 projects in the French Broad River Basin, and has now funded 84 projects across six river basins totalling more than $43 million.
insights: The programme reports its output in hydrological units rather than dollars alone, 9 million gallons of storage from $1.2 million, which is the kind of unit cost a state can use to compare nature-based against grey alternatives.

Both awards go to regional nonprofits, RiverLink and Conserving Carolina, rather than to municipalities, so the delivery model routes state resilience money through land-focused civil society organisations.
Deliberately funding basins and communities that had not yet received Blueprint money is a distributional rule inside the programme rather than a competitive outcome.
At 84 projects across six river basins for more than $43 million, the average award is around $500,000, which sets the scale of project this instrument is designed for.
Restoring 30 acres of former agricultural fields to floodplain is land use change financed as flood infrastructure.
records.publisher: North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality

records.title: Parametric Insurance for Natural Disasters: Frequently Asked Questions
records.summary: This Congressional Research Service Insight (updated May 2026) provides a primer on parametric (index-based) disaster insurance for Members of Congress, prompted by the FEMA Review Council's May 2026 recommendation to develop a parametric funding model for Public Assistance grants. It explains the mechanics of parametric versus indemnity insurance, outlines advantages (speed, flexibility, coverage breadth) and disadvantages (basis risk, regulatory gaps), and surveys U.S. and international examples including CCRIF payouts, state and municipal parametric wind and flood policies, Puerto Rico earthquake/hurricane coverage, and wildfire catastrophe bonds issued by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power.
insights: CCRIF paid nearly $19.3 million to Dominica within 14 days of Hurricane María in 2017, and $85 million to five Caribbean countries within two weeks of Hurricane Beryl in 2024, demonstrating parametric insurance's speed advantage over traditional indemnity claims that can take months or years.

The FEMA Review Council (May 2026) recommended developing a parametric funding model for Public Assistance grants as a lump-sum formula grant, signaling a potential federal policy shift that could reshape disaster recovery finance for state and local governments.

Basis risk is the central underwriting challenge: the New Orleans School District's 2024 parametric wind policy (100 mph trigger) did not pay out after Hurricane Francine despite school facility damage, illustrating how trigger design can leave real losses uncompensated.

The Los Angeles Department of Water and Power has issued three parametric wildfire catastrophe bonds since 2020, each with a different trigger, transferring wildfire risk directly to capital market investors, a replicable structure for utility wildfire exposure.

New York City used parametric flood coverage in 2023 as a financing mechanism for an emergency assistance program specifically targeting low- and moderate-income households, linking parametric instruments to distributional equity outcomes.

Puerto Rico purchased parametric coverage for both hurricanes and earthquakes in 2023 to satisfy FEMA's requirement to maintain insurance after receiving Public Assistance, showing how federal conditionality can drive parametric market adoption.

Most parametric policies in the U.S. are purchased by public-sector entities; the retail market (Jumpstart, StormPeace, FloodFlash, Recoop) is growing but remains nascent, indicating significant unmet demand and market-building opportunity.

records.title: Advancing Adaptation in Southeast Asia
records.authors: Ashwin Balasubramanian, Mekala Krishnan, Annabel Farr
records.summary: This McKinsey Global Institute article (May 2026) quantifies the adaptation gap in Southeast Asia across 11 countries and 20 intervention measures. The region currently spends ~$12 billion per year on adaptation against a $37 billion annual need today and ~$84 billion by 2050 under a 2°C scenario. More than 80% of required spending targets measures with benefit-to-cost ratios above 3:1, rising to ~7:1 at 2°C. The article identifies barriers to finance, outlines roles for businesses, insurers, banks, institutional investors, and governments, and highlights blended finance, parametric insurance, resilience bonds, and land-value capture as key instruments.
insights: Southeast Asia faces an annual adaptation gap of ~$25 billion today ($37B needed vs. $12B spent), widening to ~$72 billion by 2050 at 2°C warming ($84B needed); this gap persists even as the region already spends ~$18 per capita per year on adaptation.

More than 80% of required adaptation spending in Southeast Asia targets measures with benefit-to-cost ratios above 3:1; at 2°C the average BCR across measures rises to ~7:1, making adaptation economically compelling relative to inaction.

Active cooling (air conditioning) alone accounts for 48% of the $84B annual adaptation cost at 2°C, with heat-related measures (heat stress + heat waves) comprising 71% of total spending, signaling large addressable markets for cooling technology and efficiency finance.

By 2050, ~91% of Southeast Asia's population could live in climate-hazard-exposed areas (vs. ~50% today), with heat wave exposure rising from 16% to >80% of the population, materially increasing physical risk for asset owners and lenders in the region.

Even if adaptation spending grew in proportion with GDP growth, only ~$39B (46%) of the $84B 2050 annual need would be met, demonstrating that economic growth alone cannot close the gap and that dedicated financing mechanisms are required.

Adaptation cost in some countries (e.g., Indonesia, Philippines) would require close to 40% of average monthly income per person, highlighting severe distributional constraints and the need for subsidies, social protection, and concessional capital to reach lower-income populations.

Less than 15% of flood-exposed coastlines in Southeast Asia are adequately protected (vs. ~25% globally), and outside Singapore fewer than 20% of people have air conditioning access, quantifying the current protection deficit for infrastructure investors and insurers.

records.title: Jamaica Targets Upsized $200m of Parametric Insurance from New IBRD CAR Jamaica 2026 Catastrophe Bond
records.summary: The Government of Jamaica raised the target size for its third catastrophe bond, IBRD CAR Jamaica 2026, to $200M of parametric named-storm and hurricane protection, facilitated by the World Bank. The upsizing reflects strong ILS investor appetite and continued use of cat bonds by sovereign issuers to transfer hurricane risk away from public balance sheets.
insights: This is a sponsor returning to the market immediately after a full payout: Jamaica's second cat bond was exhausted paying $150 million in full after Hurricane Melissa in October 2025, with funds reaching the government within weeks, and the third issuance upsized from $150 million to $200 million.

The upsizing came with tightening rather than widening pricing: risk margin guidance narrowed from an initial 6.5 to 7.25 percent range to 6.75 to 7 percent, against an initial expected loss of 2.48 percent, so investor appetite absorbed a larger deal after a total loss.

The structure is a per-occurrence parametric named storm and hurricane cover issued by the IBRD under its global debt issuance facility and Capital-At-Risk notes programme, so the sovereign accesses capital markets protection through a multilateral rather than directly.
The term covers four hurricane seasons to maturity in May 2030, which sets the sovereign's protection horizon and its re-entry date.

Jamaica's sponsorship history, $185 million in 2021, $150 million in 2024 and $200 million in 2026, is a rare case of a sovereign parametric programme with a demonstrated payout and continuous renewal.

records.title: The Weekly: Why This Wildfire Season is Already Breaking Records
records.summary: This edition of The Epicenter's weekly newsletter updates its wildfire hazard briefing for the 2026 season, arguing that wildfire has become a structural cost driver rather than a periodic catastrophe. It attributes rising losses to three drivers: climate change and fire suppression policy, population growth in the wildland urban interface, and assets not built to withstand fire, compounded by underinsurance. It lists private-sector levers including modern building materials and land use policy, new detection and management technology, parametric wildfire insurance and private capital for forest management. A news roundup covers a proposed federal reinsurance backstop, parametric climate insurance and FEMA reform.
insights: The 2025 Los Angeles fires produced $40 billion in insured losses, the largest wildfire insurance loss ever recorded.
By May 1st 2026, 1.8 million acres had burned across the US, the highest year-to-date total since 2017.
From 1990 to 2020 the number of homes in the wildland urban interface grew by 47%, and it now encompasses nearly a third of US homes.
The Forest Service spent nearly four times as much fighting fires in 2020 as in 1989 (inflation adjusted), and costs could rise as much as 84% by 2050.
One in seven US homes is uninsured, and California's FAIR Plan has more than doubled in size since 2020.

records.title: Wildfires: The Drivers Putting People and Assets At Risk
records.summary: Part I of The Epicenter's wildfire briefing identifies why US wildfires are becoming more frequent and costly. It names three drivers: climate change and historical fire suppression policy making fires more frequent and intense, migration into the Wildland Urban Interface increasing exposure, and vulnerable assets including outdated codes and retreating insurance coverage. It documents rising federal firefighting and recovery spending and the disproportionate burden on lower-income households.
insights: In 2025 more than 8,200 California wildfires burned about 507,000 acres, including the Los Angeles fires that took 30 lives and caused more than $53 billion in damages.
Homes in the Wildland Urban Interface grew 47% from 1990 to 2020, and the WUI now holds nearly a third of US homes.
The annual area burned by high-severity wildfires in the American West has increased about 8x since 1985.
FEMA allocated about $4.5 billion in post-wildfire funding in 2016 to 2020, 8x the $500 million of 2001 to 2005.
Interior's Wildland Fire Management budget was $1.9 billion in 2025 with $6.5 billion requested for 2026.
California's FAIR Plan has more than doubled its policy count since 2020, and 17,000 policyholders were told in August 2024 they would lose fire coverage.

records.title: Wildfires: Opportunities For the Private Sector
institutions: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety
records.summary: Part II of The Epicenter's wildfire briefing sets out four levers through which private capital can reduce wildfire frequency, severity and cost: modern building materials, codes and land use; technology for risk identification and fire management; new insurance models; and private financing for forest management. It gives company and program examples for each, including home-hardening platforms, fire-tech startups, AI-driven and parametric wildfire insurance, and Colorado's public-private home mitigation program. It explains how Forest Resilience Bonds and Environmental Impact Bonds fund forest treatments that beneficiaries repay from avoided costs.
insights: A 2021 California Building Industry Association analysis found only 1% of homes built after 2010 were damaged in nine of the most destructive fires since 2017, attributed to post-2007 hardening codes.
Colorado's Wind and Wildfire Home Protection Mitigation Program offers grants and forgivable loans up to $30,000, financed through the CDFI Impact Development Fund.
From 2018 to 2022 a $4 million Forest Resilience Bond issued by Blue Forest Conservation funded restoration treatments on 14,545 acres of the Tahoe National Forest.
The Nature Conservancy's nature bond models have allocated $350 million across 134 projects.

Kettle builds parametric wildfire and commercial products with machine learning; Descartes Underwriting writes parametric fire policies for California businesses; Tahoe Donner's parametric policy rewards proactive forest management.
In an Environmental Impact Bond, investors fund treatments designed by federal land agencies and beneficiaries repay them with interest from avoided wildfire costs.

records.title: Louisiana Orders Every Property Insurer to Discount Fortified Homes by January 2027
institutions: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety (IBHS)
records.summary: Louisiana Regulation 136 (Fortified Homes Premium Discounts), promulgated via LDI Bulletin 2026-04 signed April 29, 2026, mandates that every property and casualty insurer authorized in the state provide premium discounts on FORTIFIED-designated residential properties by January 1, 2027. Discounts are set by a Louisiana-specific benchmark table built by the NAIC using Verisk and Moody's hurricane catastrophe models across three IBHS designation levels (Roof, Silver, Gold) and three geographic regions. The regulation eliminates insurer discretion on discount levels, making premium reduction a compliance requirement rather than a voluntary offering.
insights: Louisiana mandates FORTIFIED home premium discounts effective January 1, 2027, removing insurer discretion, discounts are set by a state-prescribed benchmark table, making this one of the most prescriptive home-hardening insurance incentive regimes in the U.S.

The benchmark discount table was built by the NAIC's Catastrophe Risk Management Center of Excellence using two industry-standard hurricane catastrophe models (Verisk/AIR and Moody's/RMS), providing a replicable, model-driven methodology that other states could adopt.

Three IBHS FORTIFIED tiers (Roof, Silver, Gold) are modeled at varying mitigation levels, and discounts are regionalized across North, Central, and South Louisiana, enabling geographic granularity that maps to actual hurricane risk gradients.

Modeled hurricane expected loss reductions are converted directly into premium discounts after adjustment for insurer expense loads derived from publicly available Louisiana homeowner rate filings, creating a transparent actuarial bridge between physical risk reduction and policyholder savings.

The regulation creates a direct financial incentive linkage between home-hardening investment (IBHS FORTIFIED designation) and insurance cost, which could accelerate adoption of beyond-code construction standards and reduce insurer loss exposure in hurricane-prone areas.

Carriers face operational compliance requirements across rating systems, underwriting workflows, and policyholder documents, insurers or producers unable to demonstrate discount application by January 1, 2027 face regulatory exposure.

Because the methodology document is publicly available and the discount benchmarks are posted publicly by the Louisiana Department of Insurance, the actuarial assumptions underpinning the discounts are contestable by carriers through the modeling layer, creating a defined channel for industry pushback.

records.title: The Weekly: Why Small Moves Beat Big Mandates in Resilient Real Estate
records.summary: The feature revisits The Resiliency Company's commercial real estate risk mitigation playbook and argues that broad adoption of incremental changes, rather than system-wide mandates, is the practical route to resilient real estate. Because developers, lenders and contractors who shape a building's risk rarely bear it, small steps that each actor can take independently can shift behaviour without waiting for the whole value chain. It gives examples for investors, developers and contractors and stresses that pre-development is where leverage is highest.
insights: Commercial buildings in Florida, California and Texas have seen 31% year-over-year and 108% five-year increases in insurance premiums, per a Deloitte report.
Investors are urged to model insurance costs on a realistic escalation curve so the committee sees the asset by year seven.
Developers can require above-code resilience in a single RFP, such as wind-rated glazing in Miami or higher stormwater design in Houston.
Contractors can replace 'act of God' clauses with named perils tied to time and cost consequences; construction projects worldwide are delayed by weather 45% of the time.
The author revises the playbook's earlier claim that 'the time for incremental change has passed'.

records.title: How Incremental CRE Actions Add Up to Resilience
records.summary: The article argues that commercial real estate resilience will come from many small, stakeholder-specific changes rather than wholesale system change, revising the call in The Resiliency Company's Risk Mitigation Playbook. It lists two incremental actions each for lenders, investors, developers and owners, design teams, contractors and insurers, such as re-underwriting storm-affected loans, modeling insurance escalation in pro formas, and naming perils in subcontracts. It identifies pre-development as the point of greatest leverage.
insights: Lenders are urged to re-underwrite any asset hit by a storm or fire during the loan term and track the top 5% most-exposed loans quarterly using FEMA risk index reports.
A Deloitte report cited in the Playbook found 31% year-over-year and 108% five-year insurance premium increases for commercial buildings in Florida, California and Texas.
Investors are urged to replace flat insurance cost lines in pro formas with a modeled escalation curve.

Contractors are urged to replace 'act of God' clauses with named-perils lists and price weather delays on projected rather than historical data; projects worldwide are delayed by weather 45% of the time.
Insurers are urged to show on one renewal what specific measures such as a FORTIFIED roof would have done to the premium.
The risk in CRE lands mostly on owners, insurers and communities, not on the developers, lenders and contractors who shape it.

records.title: The Weekly: The Link Between Housing Resiliency and Affordability
records.summary: This weekly newsletter's feature summarises a Brookings Institution analysis linking homeowners' insurance cost increases to household adaptive capacity. Using Treasury homeowners' insurance data for 2018 to 2022, FEMA's National Risk Index and Census data, Brookings sorted US ZIP codes into four groups by exposure and resources. It argues that the largest dollar increases fall on wealthy households best able to respond, while lower-resourced households facing smaller increases are more likely to go uninsured, widening the wealth gap. It points to policies including stronger BRIC funding, parcel-level risk disclosure, land use reform and pricing that links mitigation to premiums.
insights: Between 2018 and 2022, average annual premiums in high-wealth, high-risk ZIP codes rose by over 10%, or $204, nearly four times the increase in the most economically vulnerable communities.
Brookings classifies 8% of ZIP codes as low-risk and well-resourced, 18% adaptable, 18% vulnerable and 54% at risk of quietly going uninsured.
In California, communities at greatest financial risk from insurer retreat often overlap with those that historically faced barriers to homeownership.
Recommended responses include parcel-level climate risk disclosure and pricing mechanisms that link risk mitigation to insurance premiums.
Between 2014 and 2024, 100% of the 100 worst power outages in the central US were caused by extreme weather (Union of Concerned Scientists).

records.title: Flood Risk, Insurance, and Housing in the United States
records.summary: This NBER working paper (Qin & Voorheis, May 2026) uses confidential linked administrative and survey microdata from the US Census Bureau's Environmental Impacts Frame to provide the first comprehensive household-level analysis of flood risk distribution in the United States from 1999–2023. Key findings overturn aggregate-data conclusions: high-income households (especially the top 1%) are disproportionately exposed to flood risk; the share of households in floodplains has remained stable despite population growth; and a vulnerable subpopulation of low-income, uninsured homeowners in single-family homes, only ~1.74% of floodplain households, faces compounded risk across income, structure, and property-damage dimensions. Insurance cost burdens are sharply regressive, with premiums consuming 10–15% of income for the lowest-income vigintile versus under 1% for the top.
insights: Aggregate-data analyses produce aggregation bias: they show a monotonically decreasing income gradient in flood risk exposure, but household-level microdata reveal a non-monotonic relationship where the top 1% of income earners have ~19% floodplain exposure, higher than any other income group, including the lowest quartile (~16%).

The share of US households in floodplains has remained essentially stable from 1999–2023 (e.g., parcel-level FEMA exposure held between 14.2–14.4%), despite absolute counts rising from ~11 million to ~15 million, reflecting overall population growth rather than increasing relative flood risk exposure.

Only ~1.74% of floodplain households are simultaneously low-income, uninsured, and in single-family homes, the group vulnerable across all three dimensions of income, structure type, and property damage risk.

Insurance cost burdens are sharply regressive: premiums average 10–15% of household income for the lowest income vigintile of homeowners, versus below 1% for the top income vigintile, even as absolute premium levels are higher for high-income owners.

Renters face higher floodplain exposure rates than homeowners (18% vs. ~12% by end of sample period), but are not liable for structural property damages, their primary risks are personal property loss and dislocation.

When second homes are included, top-income households' floodplain exposure rises from ~18% to ~27%, and the top 1% income group holds 7% of total floodplain home value versus ~3.5% of non-floodplain home value, indicating severe concentration of at-risk asset value.

Black and Hispanic homeowners are more likely to be uninsured in both floodplain and non-floodplain areas; in floodplains, uninsured homeowners without a mortgage were ~4 percentage points more likely to be in a floodplain than insured homeowners (~15% vs. ~11%) in 2023.

records.title: Africa’s Climate Bet: Can a New $750m Fund Make Infrastructure Withstand a Hotter Future?
records.summary: The Development Bank of Southern Africa joined the Africa Finance Corporation's $750 million Infrastructure Climate Resilient Fund, signed at the Africa We Build Summit in Nairobi on 23 April. The fund, managed by AFC Capital Partners, blends concessional and commercial capital and puts climate risk assessment into every stage of a project. The Green Climate Fund provides first-loss capital through a $253 million equity pledge, and the fund expects to mobilise up to $3.7 billion in total financing across 10 to 12 projects.
insights: The Infrastructure Climate Resilient Fund targets $750 million and expects to mobilise up to $3.7 billion in total financing across 10 to 12 projects.
The Green Climate Fund pledged $253 million, described as its largest equity investment in Africa, and provides first-loss capital to attract other investors.
Other backers include the European Investment Bank, the Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority and several African pension funds; DBSA joined on 23 April.
AFC puts Africa's losses to climate shocks at 2 to 5 percent of GDP a year and adaptation needs at up to $50 billion a year.
Target sectors are renewable energy, transport and logistics, digital infrastructure and industry, with each investment screened for weather exposure, emissions pathway and governance.

records.title: Cayman Considers Catastrophe Bond, More Parametric Insurance to Expand Hurricane Protection
records.summary: An Artemis report, drawing on the Cayman Compass, that the government of the Cayman Islands is considering expanding its hurricane protection ahead of the 2026 Atlantic season by potentially issuing its own catastrophe bond while simultaneously expanding its parametric insurance coverage. The islands are highly hurricane-prone and very low-lying, which makes them extremely vulnerable to storm surge. Minister for Finance and Economic Development Rolston Anglin said the ministry had decided to increase natural catastrophe coverage, explaining that the current coverage level had been in place for a considerable period while exposure had increased, the country had grown, and there were more assets at risk. Two options are described: the government issuing its own catastrophe bond, or increasing its coverage in CCRIF SPC, formerly the Caribbean Catastrophe Risk Insurance Facility, a regional catastrophe fund providing specialised parametric insurance to Caribbean and Central American governments. Anglin said all options would be looked at, including catastrophe bonds, increasing traditional coverage and parametric solutions, and assessed holistically, and on the cat bond specifically that it comes down to cost and whether the cost justifies going down that route.
insights: The minister states the decision rule out loud: it comes down to cost, and to whether the cost justifies the route. That is a finance ministry saying what would actually make it issue, rather than an argument that it should.
The stated reason for needing more cover is growth, not climate: the country has grown and there are more assets at risk, so the buyer attributes rising exposure to development rather than to hazard.

The choice between issuing a bond and buying more CCRIF cover is the choice between bespoke and pooled, and it is the decision a small sovereign faces that a large one does not. CCRIF exists because Cayman alone is too small to interest the market efficiently.
The instrument is being considered rather than placed, so the durable content is the reasoning; whether Cayman issued is a separate fact to check later.

records.title: Mayor Wu Releases 2030 Climate Action Plan to Reduce Carbon Emissions and Strengthen Climate Resilience
records.summary: Mayor Michelle Wu announced Boston's 2030 Climate Action Plan, an implementation plan for reducing community-wide greenhouse gas emissions 50 percent by 2030 and reaching carbon neutrality by 2050 while increasing resilience to sea level rise and extreme weather. The plan covers buildings, transportation, energy, workforce development, coastal resilience and protection from extreme weather, and is framed as a shift from city government goals to citywide coordinated action. Progress is to be tracked through 22 metrics on a public implementation dashboard.
insights: Boston reports being on track for a 48 percent emissions reduction by 2030 through existing programmes alone, so the plan's additional actions are closing a two-point gap rather than carrying the whole target.

The resilience half is specific about instruments of control rather than spending: screening City capital projects for future climate risk, the Coastal Flood Resilience Overlay District, Net Zero Carbon Zoning, and the Building Emissions Reduction and Disclosure Ordinance.

The regional argument for coastal protection is asset based: New England's prosperity is said to depend on Boston's hospitals, universities, highway and rail network and food systems, which is the case for protecting infrastructure that is not the city's own.
The strategies are projected to support approximately 67,000 full-time jobs annually, which is the economic rather than avoided-loss side of the case.

Accountability is designed in as 22 tracked metrics on a public dashboard over five years, covering buildings meeting the zoning and disclosure standards, heat pumps and weatherisation, tree plantings for cooling, transit ridership and climate job training graduates.

records.title: First Street Expands Climate Risk Coverage from Real Estate to Companies and Infrastructure
records.summary: First Street launched two new analytical modules, a Company Module that connects physical climate risk to corporate earnings, credit, and valuation across operating footprints and supply chains, and a Complex Assets Module covering transportation, data centers, energy, and industrial campuses. Extends the firm's property-level methodology to corporate and infrastructure asset analysis.
insights: The expansion is a move from asset-level hazard modelling to financial translation: the Company Module connects site and supplier disruption through to earnings, credit and valuation, so an analyst can judge when physical risk becomes material to the P and L.

The Complex Assets Module extends analysis from individual properties to infrastructure systems, transport networks, data centres, energy systems and industrial campuses, and identifies the specific segments driving vulnerability rather than scoring a whole asset.

The stated gap being closed is consistency: investors lacked a single framework in which property-level exposure, supply chain interdependency and financial outcome could be evaluated together, which is what pricing across due diligence, underwriting and capital allocation requires.
The organisation's own path, founded as a research nonprofit and now selling an enterprise suite, is a case of peer-reviewed public-interest modelling becoming commercial risk infrastructure.
Coverage is claimed across billions of buildings worldwide with models quantifying likelihood and severity of flood, wildfire and extreme temperature into damage, downtime and financial loss.

records.title: The Weekly: Building Codes Can't Keep Up. Here's How States Can Take Back Control.
records.summary: This edition of The Weekly condenses an article by Alexis M. Pelosi arguing that US homes can be fully code-compliant yet uninsurable, because building codes update slowly while catastrophe models used by insurers move fast. It proposes that states adopt a 'Resiliency Code' overlay in high-hazard areas, citing Colorado's Wildfire Resiliency Code Board and New Jersey's Climate-Adjusted Flood Elevation standard. The proposed framework has four parts: a code board, certificates insurers recognize, fast-track permitting and a retrofit fund.
insights: Average premiums are up 24% since 2021 and roughly 1.9 million policies have been dropped nationwide.
Insurer mitigation requirements now act as de facto building codes built on proprietary models with no public accountability.
The proposed framework comprises a Resiliency Code Board, Resiliency Certificates, a Resiliency Fast-Track and a Resiliency Prepared Fund of grants and loans.
Colorado counties and fire districts in high-risk areas must implement the Wildfire Resiliency Code by July 1, 2026.
Disaster losses cost the housing market the equivalent of one month of new home construction each year.

records.title: Climate Health Implementation Manual
records.summary: The Climate Health Implementation Manual (CHIM) serves as a comprehensive guide for integrating climate considerations into health systems, emphasizing the critical need for climate-resilient systems to achieve universal health coverage. It provides practical tools and strategies across governance, data management, workforce training, sustainable procurement, and waste management, encouraging multisectoral collaboration to enhance health outcomes amidst climate challenges.
insights: The CHIM is a roadmap for integrating climate health considerations into existing health systems.
Building climate-resilient health systems is essential for achieving universal health coverage.
Nearly 50% of the World Bank's health commitments support climate action as part of health system strengthening.
Climate-smart investments can lower operating costs and enhance health service reliability during extreme weather events.
Environmental sustainability in health procurement can achieve cost savings and ensure supply security.
Pooling and regional procurement can enhance environmental criteria without sacrificing cost-effectiveness.
New procurement contracts can leverage innovative structures like Product-as-Service to ensure accountability.
Blended finance mechanisms can effectively support the development of climate-smart health products.

records.title: New Method to Raise Investment Funds for Projects That Restore Coastal Wetlands for Climate Adaptation
institutions: Center for Coastal Climate Resilience at UC Santa Cruz
records.summary: A new methodology has been developed to create investment opportunities for coastal wetland restoration and protection projects, by quantifying their storm protection benefits. This innovative approach enables the generation of Coastal Resilience Assets, which can be sold to investors, ultimately aiming to address the funding gap for nature-based climate adaptation solutions.
insights: The new methodology quantifies the dollar value of storm protection provided by coastal wetlands.
Coastal Resilience Assets can be sold to private and public investors, creating a new funding avenue for wetland restoration projects.
A web-based calculator has been released to help project developers assess the financial value of mangrove conservation.
The approach shifts funding from traditional debt-based models to proactive investments in nature-based solutions.
The methodology has been evaluated and published by Verra, ensuring a standardized approach to resilience credits.
Wetlands like mangroves have shown significant storm damage reduction, with estimates of $4.1 billion saved during Hurricane Ian.
The framework provides a clear investment opportunity for parties interested in reducing climate risks.
California is positioned as a global leader in developing mitigation markets to support coastal community resilience.
This methodology helps demonstrate the economic value of nature-based solutions, encouraging investment in flood risk reduction.
The project emphasizes the need to improve accountability and transparency in climate adaptation financing.

records.title: Building Codes Can't Keep Up With Climate Risk. Here's How States Can Take Back Control.
records.summary: The article argues that building codes lag climate risk, so insurers, through underwriting conditions on mitigation, have become de facto setters of building standards outside public processes. It notes states are legislating physical resilience through hardening incentives and mandated insurance discounts, backed by NCOIL model legislation. It proposes that states adopt 'Resiliency Codes' overlaying existing codes in high-hazard areas, citing Colorado's Wildfire Resiliency Code Board and New Jersey's Climate-Adjusted Flood Elevation. It sets out a four-part framework of a code board, certificates recognized by insurers, a permitting fast-track and a retrofit fund.
insights: Average homeowners premiums have risen 24% since 2021 and roughly 1.9 million policies have been dropped nationwide.
NCOIL released model legislation in 2024 tying grants and insurance rate reductions to 'beyond code' resilience standards.
New Jersey's REAL initiative adopted a Climate-Adjusted Flood Elevation based on projected sea-level rise through 2100.

The proposed framework has four parts: a Resiliency Code Board, Resiliency Certificates recognized by insurers, a Resiliency Fast-Track of permitting incentives, and a Resiliency Prepared Fund of grants and loans for retrofits.
The article warns that letting proprietary insurer models set standards creates informal rules with no public accountability, citing a 2025 California legislative report.

records.title: Coastal Resilience Benefits From Restoration and Protection of Mangroves and Tidal Marshes
records.authors: Siddharth Narayan; Michael W. Beck; Borja G. Reguero; Scott Settelmyer; Pelayo Menendez; Stefanie Simpson
institutions: Center for Coastal Climate Resilience at UC Santa Cruz
records.summary: Verra's SDVM003 v1.0 is a Sustainable Development Verified Impact Standard (SD VISta) methodology that quantifies the coastal flood risk reduction delivered by restoring or protecting mangroves and tidal marshes as a 'coastal resilience asset', measured in USD of avoided annual property damage. It applies globally and sets out project and impact-area boundaries, baseline scenarios, crediting periods and monitoring. Benefits are computed with an avoided-damages (expected damage function) approach, either by a scenario method using flood models with Manning's n roughness, or by a deemed estimate method drawn from published global datasets. An optional claim covers the reduction in people at risk of coastal flooding. The assets may not be used for offsetting.
insights: The asset unit is USD: the reduction in damage to property at risk of coastal flooding each year, computed as expected annual damage in the baseline minus the project scenario.
Crediting periods run between 10 and 50 years; baselines must be reassessed at least every five years for protection projects and every ten years for restoration projects.
Storm conditions must be assessed for at least four return periods, one of them 1 in 100 years, and total water level is mean sea level plus astronomical tide plus storm surge plus wave runup.
The project impact area extends twice the project's shore-parallel length or 10 km on each side, whichever is greater, landward to the 1-in-100-year floodplain.

In the deemed estimate worked example, two data points from Menendez et al. (2020) average to expected annual property benefits of USD 3000 per hectare; a protection example uses USD 21 710 per hectare.
Development of v1.0 was funded by AXA XL, Builder's Vision and the UCSC Center for Coastal Climate Resilience, and assets generated under it must not be used for offsetting.

records.title: Climate Risk Threatens REIT Revenue: First Street Analysis of 45,000 Properties Across 65 REITs
records.summary: Analysis of 45,000 properties across 65 publicly traded REITs found that climate disruption already costs ~1.1% of revenue ($3.1B). Under a 1-in-100-year severe-weather scenario, average losses reach ~15% of revenue and total losses near $43B, with nearly one-third of firms potentially losing 20%+ of annual revenue. Highlights material physical-risk exposure in listed real estate.
insights: The exposure is already in earnings rather than pending: climate disruption is said to cost the typical REIT about 1.1 percent of annual revenue, roughly $3.1 billion across the index, before any tail event.

The tail is severe and concentrated: 98 percent of REITs would lose revenue in a 1-in-100-year event, more than half would lose at least 10 percent and nearly a third more than 20 percent, with an index-wide 1-in-100 loss of about $43 billion and a 1-in-500 loss near 30 percent of annual revenue.

Self-insurance is emerging as the response to cover becoming expensive or unobtainable, with some REITs reserving against loss rather than paying premiums, which moves the risk onto the balance sheet where it is less visible.

The report's own framing is that real estate is a geographic commitment, so unlike other asset classes the exposure cannot be relocated, and US assets are more than 80 percent of global REIT locations with heavy concentration in California, Texas and Florida.

REITs already using forward-looking climate data showed nearly 7 percentage points less revenue at risk in severe scenarios, a relationship the report explicitly cautions is not necessarily causal, and wildfire is currently the most severe hazard while wind is expected to become the primary driver of future losses.

records.title: Scaling Up Investment for a Resilient Power Sector: The Role of Robust Disaster-Risk Financing
records.summary: The document discusses the urgent need for increased financial investment in the power sector to manage escalating climate and disaster risks, with developing countries requiring up to $365 billion annually by 2035. It highlights a significant gap in funding and emphasizes the importance of effective deployment of disaster risk financing (DRF) strategies. A layered risk management approach, incorporating insurance and contingent financing, is essential for maintaining liquidity and enabling rapid recovery in the power sector, ultimately linking financial resilience with broader economic growth and infrastructure improvements.
insights: Developing countries need $310 to $365 billion annually for climate adaptation by 2035.
International public finance for adaptation dwindled to $26 billion in 2023.
The investment need for climate adaptation is 12 to 14 times greater than current funding.
Disaster risk financing (DRF) can sustain liquidity and speed up recovery processes.
Risk layering in DRF includes mechanisms for risk retention, contingent financing, and risk transfer.
Mexico's catastrophe bond program showcases effective use of DRF in disaster management.
Regional risk pools, like the CCRIF, provide cost-effective insurance solutions for small island states.
Systemic financial planning is crucial to avoid ad hoc borrowing and fiscal crises after disasters.
Integrating DRF considerations in public-private partnerships can enhance investment resilience.
Physical resilience measures must complement financial protection mechanisms for effective climate adaptation.

records.title: 2026 Behavioral Health Report
records.authors: Katie Patton, Clara Petrucelli, Maggie Jackson, Austin Miller, Allison Oakes
records.summary: The 2026 Behavioral Health Report highlights a significant worsening of the behavioral health crisis in the U.S. since the COVID-19 pandemic, with nearly one in four adults experiencing mental illness and drastic increases in substance use mortality. It underscores disparities in treatment access, particularly among young adults and multiracial individuals, while emphasizing the rising demand for telehealth services amidst a backdrop of provider shortages and burnout. The projected economic impact of untreated mental health issues is substantial, calling for a coordinated response to enhance accessibility and effectiveness in behavioral health services.
insights: The prevalence of mental illness has increased by 5.7 percentage points, affecting nearly 23.4% of adults in 2024.
Telehealth for behavioral health treatment accounted for 65.6% of all telehealth visits in 2024, representing a significant shift in care delivery.
Untreated mental illness is projected to impose a substantial economic burden on the U.S., estimated to exceed $477.5 billion annually.
Over 65% of adults cite financial barriers as a primary obstacle to accessing behavioral health services.
The shortage of psychiatrists is acute, with less than 10% of behavioral health providers being MDs or DOs, primarily led by master-level clinicians.
Emergency department visits for alcohol and substance use disorders grew from 33.8% to 39.1% between 2018 and 2024.

records.title: The Weekly: How Maryland Is Spending Its Conservation Dollars in Pennsylvania
records.summary: The lead feature describes how Maryland, through the Conowingo Pay for Success Program, pays for nitrogen reductions in Pennsylvania and other parts of the Susquehanna watershed and credits them toward its own Chesapeake Bay nutrient-reduction obligations. The program uses $25 million in Maryland funding, administered by the Susquehanna River Basin Commission, and buys a unit of outcome (pounds of nitrogen kept out of the Bay) rather than reimbursing practices, with applicants competing on cost per pound. The legal basis was Maryland's 2022 Conservation Finance Act, which lets the state spend conservation funds outside its borders if the receiving state credits Maryland. The article names three preconditions for replicating the model and notes interest from Washington, California, Missouri and Arizona; a digest follows on wildfire insurance, insured losses and corporate adaptation.
insights: The Conowingo Pay for Success Program uses $25 million in Maryland funding, administered through the Susquehanna River Basin Commission, to buy pounds of nitrogen kept out of the Chesapeake Bay.
Applicants compete on cost per pound of nitrogen reduced, so projects are selected and paid on results rather than on specific practices.
Maryland's 2022 Conservation Finance Act authorised spending conservation funds outside the state, provided the receiving state credits Maryland for the outcomes.
The Chesapeake Bay watershed covers 64,000 square miles from upstate New York to Maryland and Virginia, and each state has nutrient-reduction targets under the Chesapeake Bay Watershed Agreement.
The template has three preconditions: an agreed quantifiable outcome, authority to spend across borders, and a coordinating body to run procurement.
The digest cites a Swiss Re finding that wildfires, storms and floods were a record 92% of global insured losses.

records.title: Where Rising Climate Risks and Insurance Costs Will Hit Hardest
records.summary: The report discusses how rising climate risks and homeowners insurance costs are exacerbating affordability issues, particularly in disadvantaged communities. It highlights the increasing premiums that homeowners face in climate-exposed areas and the variable impact on different demographics, emphasizing the role of adaptive capacity in determining how households respond to these challenges. Without proactive policy changes, the instability in the homeowners insurance market may further entrench existing wealth disparities and barriers to homeownership.
insights: Rising premiums in the homeowners insurance market threaten affordability and access to homeownership for many Americans.
Low-income homeowners are particularly vulnerable, often dropping or reducing coverage in response to increased insurance costs.
Disadvantaged communities, especially low-income Black and Latino families, bear a larger financial burden from climate risks and insurance instability.
Adaptive capacity, or the ability to respond to climate risks, varies significantly across different demographic groups and regions.
The insurance market instability is influenced by a lack of political will to address systemic climate risks.
ZIP codes categorized as 'adaptable' face the highest premium increases but typically have higher wealth, allowing residents to absorb those costs more easily.
Vulnerable and at-risk ZIP codes, even with smaller absolute premium increases, may experience greater financial strain relative to their lower wealth.
The relationship between race and insurance premium changes indicates that Black-majority ZIP codes are more likely to experience significant impacts from insurance market instability.
California serves as a significant case study for understanding the relationship between climate risks, insurance, and housing affordability.
Future policies should integrate housing considerations with climate resilience strategies to combat growing disparities.

records.title: Urban Planning for Climate Resilience: Evaluating Multi-Level Network of Resilience Plans in Miami-Dade County
records.authors: Sarbeswar Praharaj; Shouraseni Sen Roy; Sofia Bond; Mirna Obeid; Tyreke Walker
records.summary: An article in Sustainable Cities and Society by five University of Miami authors, evaluating the network of resilience plans in Miami-Dade County through an in-depth content analysis of 37 plans. The question is not whether individual plans are good but whether multi-level, cross-sectoral strategies across a network of plans are coordinated toward a unified long-term outcome. The authors build methods for assessing a network of plans on equity, integration with other proposals, dynamic relationships across governance levels, and measurable frameworks for assessing the co-benefits of implementation. They find that flood resilience and environmental management dominate while health and equity remain underrepresented; that the plans converge on expanding green space, improving canal systems and installing flood barriers while their approach to greenhouse gas mitigation stays loosely defined; and that neighbourhood-level plans consistently outperform city and county plans on most indicators. Their conclusion is that weak integration and limited feedback across the planning network, together with the absence of co-benefit evaluation mechanisms, undermine coordinated climate-resilience governance. The introduction cites the IPCC's Sixth Assessment estimate that without adaptation, flooding alone will cause $14 to $20 trillion in infrastructure and property damage by 2100, with over 1 billion people at risk of coastal hazards each year.
insights: Neighbourhood plans outperforming city and county plans is the finding with the most consequence for financing, and it runs against how resilience capital is actually organised: money is raised and allocated at the county and city level, where the plans are weakest, while the strongest plans sit at the scale with no balance sheet.

The absence of co-benefit evaluation mechanisms is named as a governance failure, and it is the same gap the Rebuild by Design CRA guidebook runs into from the financing side: a park that is also a stormwater asset cannot be underwritten on a benefit nobody measures.

Thirty-seven plans for one county is itself the finding about integration. A network that large with weak feedback produces convergence on visible interventions, green space, canals and barriers, and divergence on the things that need coordination.
Health and equity being underrepresented across the network matters for instrument design, because those are the benefits that justify public and concessional capital rather than commercial capital.

records.title: California Can’t Afford to Wait: The Fiscal Case for Sustained Resilience Investment
records.summary: The resource argues that California urgently needs to increase its investments in resilience to mitigate the financial impact of climate risks, as the state faces a growing gap between the necessary funding and available revenue. Climate disasters exacerbate costs for citizens and governments, highlighting the need for innovative funding strategies to ensure long-term resilience investment amidst a volatile budget environment.
insights: California's economic losses from climate disasters could reach up to $131 billion due to wildfires alone in 2025.
The state is projected to face structural deficits of approximately $35 billion annually starting in 2027-28.
Under-investment in resilience leads to multiplied costs, including significant financial impacts on households and local governments.
Insurance companies are withdrawing from high-risk areas, increasing liability for the California FAIR Plan.
California's reliance on personal income tax and capital gains complicates the sustainability of resilience funding.
Many existing resilience programs depend on non-durable funding sources, limiting their longevity and effectiveness.
Other states have successfully implemented dedicated revenue strategies for climate adaptation, demonstrating viable funding alternatives.
Proactive investment in resilience can reduce emergency response costs and stabilize insurance markets.
Dedicated revenue for resilience can complement existing funding mechanisms while addressing California's unique fiscal context.

records.title: The Weekly: "Wood Utility" Facilities Could Improve Wildfire Resilience
records.summary: This edition of The Weekly makes the case for 'wood utility' facilities that process forest biomass into building materials, using Regenerative Forest Solutions' Timbershed initiative in Sonoma County, California as its example. It argues that missing sawmill capacity leaves woody biomass in forests, adding to wildfire risk and insurance costs, and that such facilities need concessionary finance and state grants to start. The rest of the edition summarizes outside news on parametric flood insurance, California's insurance commissioner race and wildfire technology.
insights: In Sonoma County 10 million board feet of timber went unharvested last year, enough lumber for 500 single-family homes.
Sonoma County home insurance rates rose 40% between 2014 and 2024, the biggest jump in the Bay Area.
California must grow its sawmill infrastructure by 95 percent to meet its wildfire reduction goals.
Converting woody biomass into durable wood products can offset forest treatment costs by 39% to 50%, per Temra Costa.
Costa says concessionary finance is needed to start, most likely through state grant programs.
Climate-related disasters wipe out the equivalent of one month of construction investment each year.

records.title: Should Wood Be a Public Utility?
