Six homeowners insurance groups are now expanding in California under the Sustainable Insurance Strategy, compared to zero in 2025, a measurable early market-stabilization signal that capital allocators can track as a recovery indicator.

The Department saved consumers $6.6 billion through rate filing scrutiny across property, commercial, and auto lines from 2019–2025, and separately refunded $3.3 billion in auto premiums during the pandemic, quantifying the financial stakes of regulatory intervention in insurance pricing.

The strategy mandates that insurers write policies covering at least 85% of properties in distressed areas (662 distressed ZIP codes as of the snapshot), creating a first-ever legal obligation for insurers to serve high-risk communities, a structural shift that changes the investability calculus for insurers operating in California.

The FAIR Plan, California's insurer of last resort, held 668,609 homeowner and commercial policies as of December; reducing reliance on the FAIR Plan is a central goal, with short-term increases treated as a market-stress indicator and long-term decreases as a recovery signal.

Introduction of catastrophe modeling in rate-making is a landmark regulatory change: for the first time, California insurers can use forward-looking risk models in rate filings, aligning premium pricing more closely with physical climate risk, a move with direct implications for how insurers and reinsurers price wildfire exposure.

records.title: Homeowners Insurance: Premiums Generally Tracked Inflation but Rose More in Disaster-Prone Areas
records.summary: The GAO report on homeowners insurance reveals that while premiums have tracked inflation nationally, disaster-prone areas experience significantly higher increases, particularly in states like Florida, Louisiana, and Oklahoma. Availability and affordability of insurance in these regions are declining due to rising losses from natural disasters, prompting the implementation of mitigation strategies and regulatory reforms aimed at improving the insurance landscape. Homeowners are encouraged to adopt risk-reducing measures like FORTIFIED construction, and emerging alternatives such as parametric insurance are gaining attention.
insights: Homeowners insurance premiums rose nationwide but more significantly in disaster-prone areas.
In disaster-prone regions, premiums increased by 25% or more from 2019 to 2024.
33 states are exploring grant programs to encourage homeowners to improve resilience against natural disasters.
FORTIFIED roofs are shown to reduce insurance losses compared to traditional roofs.
Regulatory approval times for premium increases vary significantly by state, impacting insurance availability.
Stakeholders support federal policies that incentivize risk mitigation through tax credits or deductions.
Insurance availability can improve with effective risk management and mitigation strategies.
The National Flood Insurance Program highlights the federal role in providing insurance in high-risk situations.
Insurers must demonstrate that their premium calculations are justified based on risk assessment.

records.title: The Weekly: Takeaways From 2025's Climate Disasters
records.summary: The issue reviews 2025 US climate disasters: 23 billion-dollar events causing $115 billion in damage with no hurricane landfall. It draws three lessons: the Los Angeles wildfires stressed insurance, rebuilding and real estate at once; repeated severe storms eroded affordability, strained local budgets and shifted insurance risk inland; and the Texas floods exposed a gap between mapped risk and actual vulnerability. It notes regulatory responses in California, the need for state resilience offices as federal assistance is denied, and low insurance penetration in Texas flood zones.
insights: 2025 had 23 billion-dollar disasters causing $115 billion in damage, with no hurricane making landfall.

The Los Angeles wildfires caused $40 billion in insured losses, the largest wildfire insurance loss on record; total home value loss is estimated at $8.3 billion and lot values remain 15-20% below pre-fire norms.
Twenty-one separate severe storms each caused over $1 billion in damage, totalling $42 billion in insured losses, with hail driving premium increases across the middle of the country.

The Texas floods caused an estimated $18-22 billion in damage; First Street found FEMA's flood maps vastly underestimated the risk and Neptune Research Group found low insurance penetration even in high-risk zones.

CSAA and Mercury will raise California home insurance rates 6.9%, the first increases approved under the Sustainable Insurance Strategy, in exchange for expanded wildfire-area coverage and home-hardening discounts.
50-80% of homeowner claims after severe convective storms are due to hail damage.

records.title: What 2025's Costliest Disasters Mean for U.S. Real Estate, Insurance, and Public Infrastructure
institutions: Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety
University of Alabama Center for Risk and Insurance Research
records.summary: The article reviews the 23 billion-dollar weather and climate disasters that struck the US in 2025, estimated at $115 billion in damage and 276 deaths, and draws out consequences for real estate, public infrastructure and insurance. It examines the Los Angeles wildfires, the cumulative cost of severe convective storms, and the Texas floods in turn. It finds the federal government is no longer a reliable backstop for disaster aid, that hail and severe storm losses are shifting insurance pressure inland, and that low flood insurance take-up left Texas losses on homeowners. It closes by noting states adopting building codes, resilient infrastructure and financing mechanisms.
insights: In 2025 the average gap between billion-dollar disasters fell to 10 days, against 100-plus days typical in the 1980s and 1990s.

The Los Angeles wildfires are put at $250-275 billion in total economic cost and $40 billion in insured losses; Realtor.com estimates $8.3 billion of home value erased in Pacific Palisades and Altadena, with values still 15-20% below pre-fire norms.
California received $5.7 billion in FEMA aid for the fires, but the additional $33.9 billion requested had not been issued.
Twenty-one severe storms each caused $1 billion or more in 2025 damage, totalling $51 billion, and US severe convective storm insured losses reached $42 billion in the first nine months of 2025.
Only 7% of Texas homes carry flood insurance, rising to 28% in FEMA high-risk zones, so most of the $18-22 billion flood losses fell on homeowners.
Six states offer incentives to build or upgrade to FORTIFIED homes, and a growing number require insurers to offer FORTIFIED discounts.

records.title: Let’s Stop Pretending Capital Will Flow to Nature-Based Solutions on Its Own
records.summary: The article discusses the significant gap in funding for nature-based solutions, emphasizing that despite billions of dollars allocated for such projects, very little capital is flowing due to underdeveloped ideas and a lack of experienced project developers. The focus is on the necessity of bridging the gap between project developers and investors to facilitate funding and achieve substantial climate impact.
insights: Billions earmarked for nature-based solutions remain unused due to underdeveloped projects.
Most nature-based projects are not investment-ready, stalling capital flow.
Investors are reluctant to share deal preferences, leading to blind pitches from project teams.
Successful projects often come from experienced project teams that can navigate complex funding structures.
There is a significant shortage of project developers qualified to advance climate initiatives.
Developing a project into an investable asset requires extensive time and resources.
Blending grants with commercial financing can enhance project viability and attract investment.
Project developers are crucial for connecting capital to viable nature-based solutions.
A systematic approach is needed to empower developers and effectively scale nature-based projects.

records.title: Climate Change Risk Index and Municipal Bond Disclosures of United States Drinking Water Utilities
records.authors: Zia J. Lyle, Jeanne M. VanBriesen, Constantine Samaras
records.summary: The study analyzes the climate risk exposure of 1,455 municipal drinking water utilities in the U.S., revealing that 67 million customers are served by high-risk utilities, especially in the West and Northeast. It highlights significant gaps in climate risk awareness and disclosures in municipal bonds, emphasizing the financial implications of climate change on utilities and the need for targeted assistance and better governmental support for climate adaptation planning.
insights: 67 million customers are serviced by drinking water utilities classified as high climate risk.
36% of municipal bonds analyzed were issued by high-risk utilities without any mention of climate change.
65% of the 146 highest risk utilities did not mention climate change in their bond statements.
A total bond debt of approximately $39.3 billion is represented by analyzed utilities, with $9.2 billion from those at high climate risk.
The developed climate risk index can help identify utilities needing targeted assistance for climate resilience.
Governmental support is essential to assist high-priority utilities in preparing for climate change.

records.title: The Weekly: The Risky Rise of State-Backed Reinsurance
institutions: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety (IBHS)
records.summary: This newsletter issue condenses Matt Posner's argument that states leaning on public and quasi-public reinsurance backstops shift catastrophic risk onto taxpayers through state-backed funds, residual markets and post-event assessments. Florida's Citizens Property Insurance Corporation and Florida Hurricane Catastrophe Fund are the example, with statewide assessments when losses exceed reserves. It lists five harms: transferring losses created by poor policy, distorting price signals, undermining building policies, setting a bailout precedent and misallocating public dollars. The digest notes the California FAIR Plan's $750 million wildfire catastrophe bond and an OECD report on climate risk in real estate.
insights: Florida's state-backed entities function as taxpayer-supported risk backstops and can levy mandatory statewide assessments on policyholders when losses exceed reserves.
Public reinsurance mutes the warning that rising reinsurance prices give about loss frequency and severity.
The expectation of rescue leads insurers to rely on public support, developers to keep building in risky places and homeowners to delay mitigation.
California's FAIR Plan issued a $750 million catastrophe bond tied solely to wildfire risk, the largest of its kind, though critics argue it may shift risk without helping policyholders.
Of 13,000 homes destroyed in the Los Angeles fires, only seven had been completely rebuilt.

records.title: C-PACE CRE Lending Is Suddenly Seeing Record Deals
records.summary: This CNBC article reports on record growth in Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy (C-PACE) financing, driven by institutional investor appetite for long-duration, fixed-rate, senior-lien instruments secured by tax assessments on commercial real estate. Nuveen closed a $465 million C-PACE deal for The Geneva office-to-residential conversion in Washington, D.C., the largest in history, and originated $2.1 billion across 53 deals in 2025. Peachtree closed a $176.5 million deal for the Rio Hotel & Casino in Las Vegas. Cumulative C-PACE investment reached nearly $10 billion through 2024, with 40 states now holding enabling policies.
insights: Nuveen originated $2.1 billion in C-PACE loans across 53 deals in 2025 alone, implying an average deal size of ~$40 million, and has originated over $5 billion in total, establishing it as the dominant institutional C-PACE lender.

The single largest C-PACE deal in history closed in January 2026: a $465 million loan from Nuveen for The Geneva office-to-residential conversion in Washington, D.C., demonstrating the instrument's scalability for major urban adaptive reuse.

Cumulative U.S. C-PACE investment reached nearly $10 billion through end-2024, with double-digit annual growth over the past five years; active state programs expanded from 6 in 2015 to 32 across 40 states by 2026.

97% of Nuveen's C-PACE project pipeline combines energy efficiency and climate resiliency upgrades rather than pure renewable energy, signaling that cost reduction and physical risk mitigation, not decarbonization optics, are the primary commercial drivers.

C-PACE's senior tax-lien security structure makes it attractive to long-term institutional investors (insurance companies, pension funds) in a higher-for-longer rate environment where traditional CRE bank lending has contracted sharply; banks represent ~50% of CRE lending but have pulled back on new construction.

Peachtree's retroactive C-PACE structure for the Rio Hotel & Casino ($176.5M) illustrates the instrument's use as rescue capital, allowing owners to recapitalize recently completed projects and pay down senior bank debt, extending the product's utility beyond construction financing.

Peachtree aggregates and securitizes C-PACE loans sold to insurance companies, creating a capital markets pipeline that links building-level resilience upgrades to institutional fixed-income portfolios.

records.title: States Should Not Become Reinsurers of Last Resort
records.summary: The op-ed argues that states expanding public and quasi-public reinsurance backstops are making a long-term fiscal mistake, because such mechanisms transfer catastrophe risk to taxpayers without reducing it. Using Florida's Citizens Property Insurance Corporation and Florida Hurricane Catastrophe Fund as the example, it explains how post-event assessments make policyholders statewide subsidise high-risk rebuilding. It sets out five objections: public reinsurance transfers losses created by poor policy, mutes price signals, undermines building practices, sets a bailout precedent and misallocates public dollars. It proposes instead state resilience authorities, resilient revolving loan funds, required local risk analysis, financing from private co-beneficiaries, and alignment of existing housing finance tools.
insights: Florida's state-backed entities can levy mandatory assessments, effectively taxes, on policyholders statewide when losses exceed reserves, whether or not they were affected.
Public reinsurance redistributes risk rather than reducing it, and rising reinsurance prices are a signal that state backstops suppress.
The piece cites data that every $1 of resilience investment saves $11 to $33 in future losses as the case for funding state resilience authorities.
Taxing property insurers to fund resilience has precedent in Strengthen Alabama Homes, but the author favours reallocating premium tax dollars already collected.
Resilient revolving funds, such as the Resilient Virginia Revolving Loan Fund, can use state credit to finance roofs, floodproofing, elevation and hardening and recycle capital as loans are repaid.
States can condition grants, infrastructure funding or credit support on local risk disclosure and analysis.

records.title: Supporting Investor Action on Physical Climate Risk: Adaptation and Resilience Priorities for 2026
institutions: Institutional Investors Group on Climate Change
records.summary: An IIGCC insight by Lucia Graham-Wood setting out how institutional investors are beginning to bring physical climate risk into corporate engagement, and what IIGCC will provide its members in 2026. It cites S&P Global's estimate that without adaptation climate change could cost companies up to USD 1.2 trillion annually by the 2050s. Investors are opening engagements in sectors with large fixed asset bases, utilities, mining, oil and gas and infrastructure, and the suggested first questions are a company's process for appraising physical risk, direct operational disruption against indirect supply chain effects, insurance implications including premium affordability and coverage availability, and what adaptation options are under way. Corporate disclosure is thin but emerging, with utilities and real estate furthest ahead, and some companies classify physical risk as immaterial without explanation. Asset-level vendor data is incomplete and inconsistent, and the insight points to a GARP report benchmarking 13 vendors. The work builds on IIGCC's Climate Resilience Investment Framework and the updated Physical Climate Risk Appraisal Methodology, PCRAM 2.0, whose fourth case study covers a last-mile logistics warehouse in Spain and was developed with AXA IM Alts, Mott MacDonald and Swiss Re.
insights: Insurance appears here as a diligence question rather than as a product: premium affordability and coverage availability are things an investor asks a company about, which makes the insurance market a transmission channel into equity analysis rather than a separate sector.

The measurement problem is stated precisely and is the reason this is hard: unlike decarbonisation, which has a single metric in emissions, physical and nature-related risk cannot be reduced to one number, so there is nothing to benchmark a portfolio against.
Companies declaring physical risk immaterial without explanation is the specific disclosure failure investors are told to push on, and it is more tractable than asking for better modelling.
PCRAM 2.0 is the methodology described, and this document is a clean route to it: the publisher's own page for the methodology carries injected spam.
records.publisher: Institutional Investors Group on Climate Change

records.title: State of Finance for Nature 2026: Nature in the Red, Powering the Trillion Dollar Nature Transition Economy
records.authors: UNEP, with ELD Initiative and Global Canopy
records.summary: UNEP's 2026 State of Finance for Nature finds that for every dollar invested in nature, $30 flow to nature-negative activities ($7.3T in 2023). Only $220B supported nature-based solutions, with private finance contributing just $23B. Introduces a Nature Transition X-Curve framework to phase out harmful subsidies and scale high-integrity NbS, calling for $571B/year by 2030.
insights: The headline is a ratio rather than a gap: $7.3 trillion a year flows into nature-negative activities against $220 billion supporting nature-based solutions, roughly 30 to 1.

The public and private shares are inverted between the two sides: most of the $7.3 trillion nature-negative flow is private, at $4.9 trillion from utilities, industrials, energy and basic materials plus $2.4 trillion in harmful subsidies, while 90 percent of protective investment is public and only 10 percent private, with private NbS spending at $23 billion.

The stated requirement is a 2.5 times increase in NbS investment to $571 billion a year by 2030 to meet CBD, UNFCCC and UNCCD goals, paired with turning around the nature-negative flows, which the report treats as one transformation rather than two.
Reforming and repurposing existing capital flows, public and private, is named as the most powerful available tool, which puts subsidy reform ahead of new money in the sequence.
International public finance for NbS was 22 percent above 2022 and 55 percent above 2015, so the public side is growing while the private side remains the binding constraint.

records.title: When Actuaries See the Future: Climate Risk, Insurance, and Your Wallet
records.summary: The excerpt discusses how actuaries view climate change not merely as an environmental issue but as a critical matter of risk management that influences insurance markets and financial products. It highlights the growing recognition of climate risk in insurance pricing, the impact on households, and the interconnected nature of these risks as they compound. The urgency of understanding and addressing climate risk is emphasized, promoting a shift from panic or denial to a more informed conversation about probabilities and management.
insights: Actuaries are trained to assess long-term risks, translating future climate hazards into present-day financial implications.
Climate risks are actively being incorporated into insurance premiums and financial products, reflecting real economic ramifications.
The definition of risk differs from uncertainty; risk has measurable probabilities while uncertainty embodies unknown factors.
Natural disasters and climate events are increasingly interconnected, leading to cascading risks that complicate insurance modeling and pricing.
Insurance premiums are rising, making it financially unrealistic for many households to maintain coverage, leaving significant assets exposed.
Geographic and climatic changes, especially in states like Florida and California, reveal early signals of risk that are often overlooked by the general public.
The concept of climate as a threat multiplier highlights how it exacerbates existing vulnerabilities across various sectors.
Market responses to rising hazards often occur before individual recognition of risk, pointing to broader systemic issues in risk pricing.
Government-backed insurers are bearing a significantly higher risk as private insurers withdraw from high-risk markets.
A shift in perspective is needed to address climate change as an issue of financial risk management rather than solely an environmental crisis.

records.title: From Wildfire Risk to Resilience: The Investment Case for Action
records.summary: World Economic Forum report builds the investment case for proactive wildfire resilience, covering avoided-loss valuation, insurance dynamics, nature-based fuel management, and blended-finance instruments. Targets investors, insurers, and public agencies with a portfolio of intervention archetypes ready for capital deployment.
insights: The spending asymmetry is the core finding: UNEP is cited that more than half of wildfire expenditure goes to response while planning receives around 0.2 percent of total wildfire budgets, so the money sits almost entirely downstream of the risk.

Three independent return estimates are assembled: roughly $210 in avoided future economic losses per $1 invested in wildfire-resistant construction in Los Angeles rebuilding, NIBS benefit-cost ratios of about 2:1 to 8:1 for measures such as WUI code compliance, and a US Chamber of Commerce estimate of more than $22 in lost future activity per $1 not invested in preparedness.

The paper's proposal is explicitly an instrument question: scaling financial instruments that let investors earn returns from avoided losses, which is the Benefit to Instrument link rather than another case for prevention.

The protection gap is quantified at around 56 percent of global wildfire losses uninsured between 2000 and 2023, attributed to insurers withdrawing from high-hazard regions over rising losses, modelling uncertainty and pricing constraints.

Four pillars are proposed to make prevention financeable, finance and insurance, tech and data and governance, nature-based solutions, and community coordination, with the stated requirement that prevention be measured, priced and financed over multiple years rather than annually.

records.title: The Weekly: The Data Story Behind America's Billion-Dollar Climate Disasters
records.summary: This edition of The Weekly reports how Climate Central took over the US billion-dollar weather and climate disasters database after NOAA discontinued it in May 2025, hiring the scientist who had led NOAA's program. It argues that disaster cost data underpin risk pricing and capital allocation, and warns that NCAR faces similar threats. The rest summarizes outside news on wildfire recovery, climate insurance litigation and disclosure.
insights: Climate Central reports that 23 separate US events in 2025 cost $115 billion in damages.
NOAA's billion-dollar disasters database, maintained since 1980, was discontinued in May 2025.
Climate Central hired Adam Smith, who led NOAA's program for 15 years, and relaunched the database by October 2025 with data through June 2025.
The National Center for Atmospheric Research has been targeted for 'breaking up' by the Trump administration.
On average the US had just 10 days between billion-dollar disasters in 2025, compared with over 80 days in the 1980s.

records.title: Global Risk Pooling Mitigates Financial Risk From Drought in Hydropower-Dependent Countries
records.authors: Rosa Isabella Cuppari; Tamlin M. Pavelsky; Gregory W. Characklis
institutions: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
records.summary: An article in Nature Communications by Rosa Isabella Cuppari, Tamlin M. Pavelsky and Gregory W. Characklis on pooling drought risk across hydropower-dependent countries. More than 50 countries rely on hydropower for over a quarter of their electricity generation, 56 by the paper's own count, and for some, hydropower sales are also an important source of government revenue, which makes them vulnerable to drought and the revenue losses that follow: the first half of 2023 alone saw an 8.5 per cent decline in global hydropower generation from drought, with China down 20 per cent. Governments can absorb the losses of publicly owned generators, but doing so creates fiscal pressure and can lead to lower bond ratings. Index-based financial instruments are an alternative, though data collection and index design are hard. Using remotely sensed hydrometeorological data the authors construct index insurance contracts to manage drought-related financial risk, and find that low correlations in drought across these countries allow cost reductions when the risks are pooled: pooling the contracts yields average savings of 54 per cent against managing the same risk individually through reserves.
insights: A 54 per cent saving against self-insurance through reserves is the number to carry. It is a direct measure of what diversification is worth in adaptation finance, and it is large enough to change a finance ministry's choice between holding a reserve and buying cover.

Using remotely sensed data solves the constraint that kills index insurance in data-poor places: no ground station network is required, which is why the approach travels to the countries that need it most.

The causal chain the paper states is specific and priced: drought cuts hydropower revenue, the government absorbs the loss, and the fiscal pressure lowers the bond rating, with the pooled insurance interrupting it at the first step.
Low cross-country drought correlation is the whole basis of the result and also its fragility: a synchronised multi-basin drought would break the pool.

records.title: Uncertainty Surrounding Federal Disaster Funding Looms over State Budgets
records.summary: This Pew Charitable Trusts article (January 2026) examines how growing uncertainty around federal disaster assistance, particularly potential restructuring of FEMA, is straining state budgets already under fiscal pressure. It documents specific funding disruptions in 2025 (cancellation of the Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities program, halted Hazard Mitigation Grant Program allocations, delayed Emergency Management Performance Grants), state-level responses such as New Mexico's $30M contingency appropriation and new disaster reserve funds in Minnesota and Massachusetts, and two competing federal reform proposals: raising the public assistance threshold fourfold and shifting to an advance-funding model. An Urban Institute analysis found six states would have received zero federal post-disaster aid from 2008–2024 under the higher threshold scenario.
insights: An Urban Institute study found that six states (Arizona, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Ohio, and Pennsylvania), would have received no federal post-disaster public assistance between 2008 and 2024 if the Trump administration's proposed fourfold increase in the damage threshold were applied retroactively; Virginia would have lost $534M (88% of total funding received) and Iowa $497M ($155 per capita).

Nearly 73% of counties that experienced a presidentially declared disaster in the prior 10 years still had outstanding FEMA reimbursement claims more than two years old, totaling between $237M and $665M, forcing local governments to use bonds or short-term financing to bridge cash flow gaps.

New Mexico passed emergency legislation in 2025 allocating an additional $30M to its Appropriation Contingency Fund for rapid disaster response, citing slower and smaller FEMA reimbursements, illustrating how federal funding uncertainty is directly triggering state budget action.

The Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities (BRIC) program was canceled in April 2025, placing stormwater infrastructure projects in Louisiana and New Jersey on hold pending legal resolution, demonstrating how federal mitigation grant disruptions cascade into specific capital project delays.

States have not received Hazard Mitigation Grant Program allocations since spring 2025 and FEMA halted Emergency Management Performance Grants in October 2025, compressing state and local capacity to fund both preparedness and risk-reduction projects simultaneously.

A proposed shift from reimbursement-based to advance-funding grants could accelerate disaster recovery cash flow for counties, but carries the risk of underestimating long-term recovery costs since initial damage assessments frequently miss full scope, creating a structural mismatch between speed and fiscal adequacy.

records.title: Tackling the Insurance Protection Gap: Leveraging Climate Mitigation and Nature to Increase Resilience
records.summary: The resource analyzes the widening insurance protection gap exacerbated by climate change and nature loss, emphasizing the need for integrated approaches that combine traditional insurance mechanisms with nature-based solutions to enhance resilience. It highlights critical barriers faced by the insurance industry, such as affordability, lack of awareness, and inadequate risk management, while advocating for collaborative efforts among stakeholders, including governments and the private sector, to address climate-related challenges effectively and improve coverage across communities.
insights: The insurance protection gap is widening, particularly in developing economies, due to rising climate risks and inadequate insurance models.
Integrating nature-based solutions into insurance frameworks is essential for improving resilience and reducing vulnerability to climate impacts.
Public investment in ecosystem protection offers a cost-effective strategy for enhancing insurance coverage and economic stability.
Affordability issues and unpredictable climate risks hinder insurance uptake, especially in high-risk areas.
Governments are increasingly stepping in as insurers of last resort due to market inadequacies, requiring careful design to avoid maladaptive behaviors.
Health risks related to climate change are rising, with potential impacts on health insurance costs and socio-economic inequality.
Collaborative public-private partnerships are crucial for effectively managing the insurance protection gap and fostering a holistic approach to climate risk management.

records.title: Connecticut Atlas of Disaster
institutions: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection
Connecticut Institute for Resilience and Climate Adaptation
records.summary: A state profile of federally declared climate disasters in Connecticut from 2011 to 2024 and the federal money that followed them. It counts 11 climate disaster declarations and $564.3 million in FEMA and HUD post-disaster funding, or $158 per capita, mapped by planning region against social vulnerability and power reliability. It sets out four recommendations for funding resilience before disasters, including new dedicated funding sources such as an insurance surcharge, and catalogues state actions such as SB 9, which created Resiliency Improvement Districts.
insights: Connecticut had 11 federally declared climate disasters in 2011 to 2024, with $351 million in FEMA obligations and $214 million in HUD CDBG-DR funds, $564 million in total.

The atlas estimates that $3.7 billion of climate infrastructure could be supported through a small insurance surcharge, and recommends surcharges on property and casualty coverage as a dedicated funding source.

Connecticut's SB 9, signed in June 2025, gives towns Resiliency Improvement Districts to fund adaptation capital projects and requires sellers, landlords, lenders and insurers to disclose a property's flood history.
The Corbin District redevelopment in Darien was Connecticut's first C-PACE project to finance climate resiliency, with $63 million in CounterpointeSRE financing.
The report recommends mandating that insurers price in mitigation measures, on the model of the NFIP Community Rating System.
Greater Bridgeport received the most post-disaster assistance in the state, $84 million, and has the highest social vulnerability score, 0.81.

records.title: Climate Resilience Districts: A Powerful Tool Waiting for California
records.summary: California Forward, working with Resilient Cities Catalyst, examines why the Climate Resilience District created by SB 852 in 2022 remains almost entirely unused, as groundwork for a Resilience District Incubator and a statewide call for pilot communities. A CRD is a special district that one or more local governments may form to address climate mitigation, adaptation or resilience within a defined project area, which can be a single neighbourhood or an entire region, and it can draw on a wide range of revenue-raising tools including tax increment financing, under which the district locks in today's property values and borrows against future growth. The article's argument is that California local governments face climate costs they cannot meet from a tax base constrained by Proposition 13's limits on property tax revenue, and that CRDs are the vehicle the legislature built for exactly that gap. To date only one CRD exists, the Sonoma County Regional Climate Protection Authority, and even that uses its district as a regional governance structure without having used any of the financing tools available to it.
insights: The instrument exists in statute and is unused, which is a different problem from a missing instrument: one district in four years, and that one has not used any of its financing powers, so the binding constraint is adoption capacity rather than legal authority.

Proposition 13 is named as the reason the ordinary tax base cannot fund resilience in California, which makes tax increment financing through a special district the workaround rather than a preference.

Tax increment financing locks in present property values and borrows against future growth, so the district is betting that resilience investment raises the value it captures, which ties repayment to the benefit.
The project's own next step is a statewide call for pilot communities, so the document is a diagnosis written to be acted on rather than a retrospective.

records.title: Governor Ron DeSantis Announces Major Insurance Rate Relief as Florida’s Reforms Deliver Results
records.summary: A press release of 12 January 2026 from the Florida Chief Financial Officer's office reporting that Governor Ron DeSantis announced statewide insurance rate relief for Florida homeowners, with Citizens Property Insurance policyholders seeing premium reductions from Spring 2026 at renewal. The approved rates give the vast majority of Citizens policyholders statewide a decrease, with a statewide average reduction of 8.7 per cent: over 330,000 policyholders across all 67 counties see decreases and more than 150,000 receive reductions of 10 per cent or greater. South Florida, which had some of the highest litigation-driven insurance costs in the state, sees the largest reductions: approximately 27,000 homes in Broward County at an average 14.1 per cent, approximately 42,000 in Miami-Dade at 14.0 per cent, approximately 26,000 in Palm Beach at 11.9 per cent, and more than 1,000 homeowners in Monroe County at 11.3 per cent with over 8,000 wind-only policies reduced or held flat. The release attributes the reductions to comprehensive insurance and tort reforms, with statements to that effect from the Governor, Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia and Insurance Commissioner Mike Yaworsky.
insights: Premiums are reported FALLING by 14 per cent in Miami-Dade, which runs against the direction of travel most Florida insurance reporting describes and is the figure the release is built around.

The attribution is the state's, not a measurement. The release credits tort and litigation reform and says nothing about hazard, exposure or physical risk reduction, so the causal claim is asserted by the parties announcing it and is untested in the document.

The county pattern is the analytically interesting part: the largest reductions land where litigation costs were highest, not where hazard is lowest. If that holds, a material share of what Florida homeowners were paying was legal-system cost rather than risk cost, which is a different problem from the one adaptation finance is built to solve.

Citizens is the state insurer of last resort, so its rate filing is a public-sector price rather than a market one. Its movements are policy decisions as much as actuarial ones, which is the caveat to attach to any use of these figures.

The wind-only policies in Monroe County are called out separately as reduced or held flat, which is worth noting: the most hazard-exposed coverage in the most exposed county is the one that did not fall.

records.title: The Weekly: Why Construction Sites Need Resilience Planning
records.summary: This weekly newsletter's feature argues that the active construction site is the most vulnerable and least planned-for stage of commercial real estate development with respect to climate risk. Drawing on an interview with Ryan Companies' Chief Sustainability Officer, it describes how Hurricane Ian in September 2022 damaged two in-process senior living projects, causing 70-day delays, expired pricing guarantees and storage costs. It points to the Risk Mitigation Playbook for construction-phase strategies, arguing that modest upfront costs save more on the back end. The roundup covers adaptation explainers, NOAA cuts, sinking dams and adaptation venture capital.
insights: Hurricane Ian damaged two Ryan Companies senior living projects in progress, with schedule delays of 70 days.
One project incurred $3.5 million in insurance claims with $1 million paid out of pocket; the second $1.6 million in claims and $620,000 out of pocket.
Weather-related delays affect an estimated 45% of construction projects globally.
Work that had already passed inspection had to be redone after wind-driven rain soaked drywall and mechanical systems.
At 2°C of warming, benefits of resilience spending against heat and extreme weather outweigh costs by seven to one (statistic of the week).

records.title: Despite Federal Backsliding, US States and Municipalities Are Still Planning for Climate Resilience
records.summary: Manann Donoghoe of Brookings Metro maps the US federal climate resilience system and the sub-national planning that has grown despite it. Since 1980 there have been over 400 billion-dollar disasters costing $2.9 trillion, and in 2024 a major disaster was declared every four days. Unlike 87 per cent of countries globally, the US has no federal legal or policy structure coordinating nationwide resilience planning; instead at least 39 programmes across at least 10 agencies have accreted through the 1988 Stafford Act, the 1974 Housing and Community Development Act, WIFIA, the 1976 Energy Conservation and Production Act and others, with FEMA, EPA and NOAA managing most. From 2019 to 2023 FEMA spent an average $39.5 billion a year on disaster response and recovery, and GAO projects $26 to $134 billion a year by 2050; between FY2010 and FY2018, 88 per cent of FEMA grants targeting resilience were available only after a federal disaster declaration. The Disaster Recovery Reform Act, the IRA and the IIJA increased pre-disaster funding, but post-disaster funding still dwarfs it: BRIC requests rose every year to $5.7 billion in 2023 against roughly $1 billion of available funds. BRIC has also benefited wealthier communities, with 78 per cent of 2023 funding going to East and West Coast states, because the National Risk Index underweights vulnerability and overweights exposure, so communities with higher property values and thus higher expected losses are prioritised over communities where poverty and rental precarity drive vulnerability. Heatwave deaths, which are not eligible for federal disaster declarations, now exceed deaths from all other disasters combined. At the sub-national level, 272 entities have undertaken resilience or adaptation planning since 2005, publishing 347 plans, with 55 including major cities planning two or more times; thirteen states have appointed a chief resilience officer.
insights: The distributional finding is the most consequential: the National Risk Index underweights vulnerability and overweights exposure, so a federal allocation tool routes mitigation money toward high property values, and 78 per cent of 2023 BRIC funding went to coastal states as a result. The scoring rule, not the appropriation, is what makes the programme regressive.

BRIC demand at $5.7 billion against roughly $1 billion available is a five-to-one oversubscription, which means the binding constraint is appropriation rather than pipeline, the opposite of the diagnosis in the urban resilience finance literature.

88 per cent of FEMA resilience grants between FY2010 and FY2018 required a disaster declaration first, which is the structural reason the US system pays for recovery: the money is legally attached to the event it was meant to prevent.

Heatwave deaths now exceed all other disaster deaths combined and heat is not eligible for a federal disaster declaration, so the largest and fastest-growing mortality risk sits entirely outside the funding architecture.

State-level mandates work: California and Massachusetts require municipal planning and produce over 24 per cent of all US plans between them, which is the clearest evidence in the report that a legal requirement rather than a grant is what generates plans.

Resilience planning is not partisan at the sub-national level, with Louisiana, Mississippi, Florida and South Carolina all carrying plans or a chief resiliency officer, and the pattern breaks only in interior red states facing drought and heat rather than hurricanes.

records.title: Challenges and Opportunities in Scaling Climate-Resilient Housing Solutions in the United States
records.authors: Nadia A. Seeteram, Linda Shi, Katharine J. Mach, Alizé Carrère, Trinish Chatterjee, Anna Garner, Radley M. Horton
records.summary: The resource underscores the pressing need for scaling climate-resilient housing solutions in the United States, particularly in coastal communities, by analyzing insights from expert interviews. It highlights significant barriers such as policy inadequacies, financing limitations, and affordability issues, while stressing the necessity for government intervention and multi-sectoral collaboration to foster long-term resilience against climate risks.
insights: Current risk reduction strategies are largely insufficient, focusing on small-scale actions.
Affordability and climate resilience are interconnected concerns in U.S. housing markets.
Government intervention and multi-stakeholder collaborations are crucial for fostering resilient housing.
Regulatory barriers and insurance behaviors hinder effective housing solutions.
Data accessibility related to climate risk is essential for informed decision-making.
Managed retreat programs present opportunities but raise social justice concerns.

records.title: A New Financing Model for Frontline Solutions
records.summary: The article describes an innovative blended-finance model that pools philanthropic grants, concessionary capital, and outcome-based payments to support under-resourced communities facing extreme weather risks. By structuring investments around pay-for-success contracts and rigorous impact measurement, the approach creates a revolving fund that recycles repaid capital into new resilience projects. This model aligns incentives among donors, service providers, and local stakeholders to scale community-led infrastructure and social initiatives while sharing risk and demonstrating tangible cost savings.
insights: The argument is that this is an allocation problem rather than a capital shortage: US strategic philanthropy reached $557 billion in 2023 while climate resilience and decarbonisation solutions took under 2 percent of overall giving, and donor advised funds hold more than $326 billion of which only a fraction is deployed catalytically.

Philanthropy is positioned as first-loss capital and guarantee capital whose function is to de-risk an unproven investment thesis so that debt and equity investors can participate, which makes grant money an underwriting input rather than a substitute for investment.
Restricted grants are named as the mechanism that keeps organisations in survival mode, tying them to programme outputs on short cycles rather than to long-term outcomes.
Technical assistance grants are given the same de-risking role as first-loss capital, creating a pathway for investors into early-stage models.

A $50 trillion intergenerational wealth transfer over the next decade is offered as the reason to mainstream these tools now, with next-generation holders described as wanting philanthropy and investment integrated in one portfolio.

records.title: Active Construction Sites Are Climate Risk Blind Spots: Lessons from Hurricane Ian
records.summary: Through an interview with Joe Rozza of Ryan Companies, the article shows how Hurricane Ian in September 2022 damaged two mid-construction senior living projects in Florida and set off cascading schedule, cost and insurance effects. It argues active construction sites are a distinct and overlooked phase of climate vulnerability. It lists Risk Mitigation Playbook recommendations, including site-specific risk assessments, parametric insurance, longer material pricing guarantees and site hardening.
insights: Forty-five percent of construction projects globally face weather-related delays.
Schedule delays after Ian reached 70 days and material costs jumped 5 to 20 percent as pricing guarantees expired.
One project recorded $3.5 million in insurance claims with about $1 million paid out of pocket; the second $1.6 million with $620,000 out of pocket.
Rozza says Ryan Companies was carrying the force majeure risk and would have bought parametric insurance had it had the playbook guidance.
The playbook recommends extending material pricing guarantees two or three months beyond anticipated completion dates.

records.title: Cat Bonds on the Nile: A Risk-Sharing Approach to the Nile Waters Dispute
records.summary: The excerpt discusses the introduction of the Grand Ethiopia Renaissance Dam (GERD) and the resulting disputes among Ethiopia, Sudan, and Egypt over water rights and environmental risks. It introduces the concept of catastrophe bonds (cat bonds) as a potential financial solution to address the concerns of downstream countries regarding environmental disasters while allowing Ethiopia to develop its resources. The proposal involves creating structured financial instruments that manage risk, although complexities arise in defining trigger events and addressing the impacts on the countries involved.
insights: The GERD, completed by Ethiopia, is Africa's largest hydropower project but has led to conflicts with Sudan and Egypt over water resource management.
Ethiopia aims to increase electricity access with the dam, while Egypt and Sudan argue that it threatens their water resources and flood security.
International law principles regarding equitable resource sharing are invoked by all parties, highlighting the complexity of the dispute.
Catastrophe bonds could provide a financial mechanism to address risks associated with the dam, serving as a compromise between Ethiopia's development and downstream countries' protection.
The World Bank could facilitate this cat bond arrangement, helping to mitigate risks without adding debt to Ethiopia's balance sheet.
Defining trigger events for cat bond payouts presents challenges, as not all impacts can be easily quantified or attributed directly to the dam.
The proposal raises questions about the fairness of risk-sharing among countries with different capacities for negotiation and water management.
Complex humanitarian conditions in Sudan complicate its participation in negotiations regarding any financial arrangements.
There is potential for this cat bond approach to serve as a model for resolving other transboundary water disputes globally.

records.title: Resilience Isn’t About Bouncing Back. It's About Building Differently. [Episode 29]
records.summary: Abby Ross of The Resiliency Company describes an organisation whose stated goal is to mobilise as much capital as possible into resilient infrastructure, on the premise that infrastructure will be rebuilt anyway and is currently being rebuilt to the standard that already failed. She calls it a do tank rather than a think tank, working on the conditions for success: new financial vehicles, new networks and new commercial businesses. The concrete mechanism she describes is resilient home lending. After a disaster a homeowner must know the engineering solutions exist, sort through competing standards, assemble contractors who understand resilience, and then find the money, and the resilient rebuild costs roughly $25,000 more than rebuilding to code. A lower-rate loan, an eight percent conventional rate against seven and a half for a resilient home, is reported to be enough incentive to change the decision. She notes most banks have never done resilient home lending and many have never done construction lending. On the commercial side, partners representing about $2.5 trillion in market capitalisation co-authored a playbook, From Vulnerability to Value, aimed at the misalignment that the people holding the risk in what is built are not the people deciding what gets built. She notes that state and local governments are the largest asset owners and that municipal bonds have funded 80 percent of US infrastructure.
insights: The lending mechanism is precisely specified and small: a roughly $25,000 gap between a code rebuild and a resilient rebuild, closed by a half-point rate reduction, is reported to be sufficient to change the homeowner's decision.

Post-disaster is named as both the moment of maximum openness to change and the cheapest moment to build resilience in, which makes the speed of assembling lenders and contractors the determining variable.

The commercial real estate misalignment is stated directly: the parties holding the risk in a finished building are not the parties deciding what gets built, so the intervention has to reach investors, pre-development, contractors, owners and tenants along the chain.

Municipal bonds having funded 80 percent of US infrastructure, with state and local governments as the largest asset owners, locates the largest available lever for resilience standards in public debt markets rather than in private capital.
Most banks have never made a resilient home loan and many have never made a construction loan, so the constraint on the product is lender capability rather than borrower demand.

records.title: Physical Climate Risk Creates Challenges and Opportunities in US Municipal Finance
records.authors: Aayushi Mishra, Adavit Arun, Evan Kodra, Erika Smull, Owen Woolcock, Tom Doe, Justin Marlowe, Auroop R. Ganguly
institutions: Harvard University Graduate School of Design
University of Chicago Harris School of Public Policy
records.summary: This Nature Cities review article examines how physical climate risks (flooding, wildfires, sea level rise, and extreme heat), interact with the US $4.2 trillion municipal bond market to create a "climate-debt doom loop." The authors identify three reinforcing challenges: climate risk is systematically underpriced in bond markets (a 10% increase in SLR exposure yields only a 5.3 basis point rise in credit spreads); abrupt repricing could severely disadvantage fiscally fragile, high-risk municipalities; and municipal adaptation planning is structurally misaligned with municipal finance. The paper proposes innovations including standardized climate disclosures, a federal infrastructure finance authority, parcel taxes, resilience bonds, and state credit enhancement programs to disrupt the loop.
insights: A 10% increase in sea level rise exposure corresponds to only a 5.3 basis point rise in municipal bond credit spreads, concentrated in longer-dated bonds, short-term bonds show no meaningful climate risk adjustment, indicating systemic underpricing across the $4.2 trillion municipal bond market.

Predominantly Black communities pay an estimated 0.44% more in annualized borrowing costs, a 'Black tax' totaling $110 million in 2019 alone, while a separate study found a racial penalty of 19 basis points totaling $900 million annually across the municipal bond market, linking structural racism to compounded climate-financial vulnerability.

The US infrastructure funding gap stands at $2.6 trillion, and adaptation projects require governments to cover roughly one-third of costs just to break even; a debt-only approach to adaptation can worsen short-term fiscal health and accelerate the climate-debt doom loop.

Insurer withdrawal from high-risk states (Florida, Louisiana, California) is shifting disaster cost burden to municipalities and state-backed last-resort plans, increasing reliance on debt markets that do not yet price climate risk adequately, a structural feedback that reinforces the doom loop.

Bond defaults due to natural disasters have been rare (only 12 in the past 15 years), but the Paradise Redevelopment Agency default post-2018 Camp Fire and Clyde, TX's 2023 default illustrate emerging precedents that could trigger abrupt investor repricing.

Virginia Beach's $567 million voter-backed flood bond and Miami's $400 million Forever Bond represent contrasting outcomes: the former used participatory design to ensure benefits outweigh debt service; the latter produced mixed equity results, illustrating how instrument design determines distributional impact.

records.title: How Two LA Nonprofits Are Making Wildfire-Resilient Rebuilding Accessible
institutions: San Gabriel Valley Habitat for Humanity
Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety
records.summary: The post describes how the Resilient LA Delta Fund, set up by The Resiliency Company through Resilient Los Angeles, pays for the extra cost of rebuilding homes burned in the Eaton and Palisades fires to a higher wildfire standard. The fund covers the resiliency delta, the gap between rebuilding to code and meeting the IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home Plus standard, through targeted grants and loans. It has chosen two nonprofits for pilots: Greenline Housing Foundation in Altadena and San Gabriel Valley Habitat for Humanity. It argues that philanthropic capital routed through trusted community organizations can close the resilience gap and serve as a model for post-disaster recovery elsewhere.
insights: The added upfront cost of wildfire resilience is typically 2 to 3% on top of total construction costs.
Grants cover only the incremental cost of upgrading to IBHS WPH+, and homeowners must already have funding to rebuild to code and commit to full certification.
Habitat's volunteer labor and donated materials make the per-home resiliency delta far smaller than 2 to 3%, so modest grants stretch across more families.
Habitat's standard model builds code-compliant homes, and a Delta Fund grant bridges it to fire-resilient construction.
A Wildfire Grants Guidebook came out of a collaboration among The Resiliency Company, Insurance for Good, the Environmental Defense Fund and the Resources Legacy Fund.

records.title: Hurricane Loss Mitigation Program 2025 Annual Report
records.summary: The Hurricane Loss Mitigation Program 2025 Annual Report, prepared by the Florida Division of Emergency Management and dated 1 January 2026, under Governor Ron DeSantis and Executive Director Kevin Guthrie. It is the programme's statutory annual accounting of a recurring $10 million appropriation and its sub-allocations, which in this reporting year include $6.5 million, $7 million, $3 million and $2.8 million lines. Mitigation is the report's dominant vocabulary, appearing 86 times against 66 for hurricane and 8 for resilience.
insights: A recurring annual appropriation is a different instrument from a one-off programme. A standing $10 million line means Florida funds hurricane loss mitigation as an operating commitment rather than as a response, which is what lets a delivery capability persist between storms.
The report is where the money behind Florida's mitigation grant programmes is enumerated, so it shows the budget constraint those programmes operate under rather than the mechanism they use.

The vocabulary throughout is mitigation rather than resilience, because Florida's statutory language predates the resilience framing; a search on resilience alone would miss the state's largest standing mitigation commitment.
An annual report is evidence of delivery rather than of design: it reports what was spent rather than what an instrument was intended to do.

records.title: Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) Case Studies
records.authors: Alexander Tellides; Allison Shao; Claire McLean; Daniel Gunton; Pei Li Chua
records.summary: The case studies volume accompanying Rebuild by Design's Community Reinvestment Act work, published January 2026 and running to 221,940 characters. Its inner title is Mobilizing Private Investments in Equitable Climate Infrastructure Under the New Community Reinvestment Act Guidelines, a final report prepared for Rebuild by Design by a capstone team of Alexander Tellides, Allison Shao, Claire McLean, Daniel Gunton and Pei Li Chua and dated March 2025. Where the bank guidebook argues the case to lenders, this volume carries the evidence: background, methodology and sectioned case material on mobilising private investment into equitable climate infrastructure under the CRA.
insights: This and the bank guidebook are a deliberate pair from one publisher and should be read as one body of work, with the guidebook as the argument and this as the evidence. They were checked for duplication rather than assumed distinct: 0 of 40 sampled passages of the guidebook appear here.

The two documents carry different dates internally. The capstone report is dated March 2025 and the published volume January 2026, so the research predates the publication by most of a year and predates the guidebook's account of the 2024 rescission.
A capstone team rather than a staff research unit produced the underlying report, so the analysis was commissioned rather than institutional.

records.title: Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) Bank Guidebook
records.summary: A guidebook from Rebuild by Design, dated January 2026, on using the Community Reinvestment Act to finance community-wide resilience infrastructure in low and moderate income communities before extreme weather strikes rather than after it. It opens with the exposure: citing Climate Central, the US has experienced 426 extreme weather events with damages over $1 billion since 1980, costing over $3.1 trillion, and those events fall disproportionately on low and moderate income communities, particularly ones shaped by the legacy of redlining. The CRA was created to counter the economic effects of redlining and has long funded affordable housing, small business and community development, and in 2023 it was updated to call explicitly for investments in disaster preparedness and climate resilience. Those updates were rescinded in 2024, and the guidebook's position is that banks can still fund resilient infrastructure under the 1995 rules. Its central observation is that the CRA has not yet been used to fund large-scale community-wide infrastructure at all, which is why guidance on what is possible is the gap it sets out to fill. Community-wide infrastructure means neighbourhood to large-scale projects that reduce extreme weather and sea level rise risk while supporting everyday wellbeing, the worked example being a park that captures rainwater in a flood and serves as community space the rest of the time.
insights: The argument is an alignment argument rather than an obligation one: lowering community risk lowers the bank's own risk, because the assets on the bank's books are the property, loans and mortgages inside the community being protected. CRA credit is then a second benefit rather than the motive.

The regulatory history matters more than the guidance. A 2023 amendment naming disaster preparedness and climate resilience was rescinded in 2024, so the route this guidebook describes runs through the 1995 rules and depends on an interpretation rather than on an explicit authorisation.

That the CRA has never funded large-scale community-wide infrastructure is the finding rather than the premise: a statute with decades of deployment in exactly the most exposed communities has no track record on the asset class.

The multi-benefit framing is what makes a project CRA-eligible and resilient at once, and it is also the hardest thing to underwrite: a park that is a stormwater asset in a flood has a benefit stream that only partly shows up in any single year's cash flow.

records.title: In the Hot Seat: Financing Asia's Heat Resilience
records.summary: A study of how to finance heat resilience in Asia, structured around the roadblocks to private financing, the business case for heat-resilience investment, and five routes for leveraging private capital: risk transfer products, project de-risking instruments, results-based incentives, capital markets, and market creation. It then sets out four enablers for scaling: policy and regulatory strengthening, development finance institutions and multilateral development banks as mobilisers of private capital, insurers as critical enablers, and data, technology and measurement. The framing is that global priorities are shifting from mitigation to adaptation while roughly 90 per cent of private climate fund investment has historically gone to mitigation.
insights: Heat is treated as a HORIZONTAL threat rather than a sector hazard, cutting across health, labour productivity, infrastructure and agriculture, which is why the report argues it resists the project-by-project financing model used for flood defence.

The five capital routes are ordered by maturity rather than by size: risk transfer products first, then project de-risking, results-based incentives, capital markets and finally market creation, which is the honest sequence for an asset class that does not yet exist at scale.

Insurers are named as critical ENABLERS rather than as capital providers, which is the distinction that matters: their contribution is pricing and data that let other capital in, not their own balance sheets.

The report sets heat resilience against a long policy record rather than treating it as new: France's multi-ministry heat strategy after the 2003 heat wave and India's first heat action plan in 2013 are given as the precedents that private finance has not yet matched.

COP30 is used as the timing argument, with Beat the Heat, a health sector adaptation plan for Brazil and an Extreme Heat Risk Governance Framework all launched within four days, plus adaptation indicators expected in the Global Goal on Adaptation framework.

The commercial signal offered is small and concrete, from HVAC systems to cooling vests for drivers at the Singapore Grand Prix, which sets the current state of heat-resilience commercialisation against the financing ambition.

records.title: Building Corporate Climate Resilience: Key Insights from the 2025 Corporate Climate Resilience Foresight Series
institutions: Center for Climate and Energy Solutions (C2ES)
records.summary: A synthesis of the 2025 Corporate Climate Resilience Foresight Series, six dialogues convened by C2ES and Resilience First with forty senior leaders from 24 organisations across manufacturing, energy, technology and financial services. It presents a strategic framework for corporate climate resilience and finds that awareness of climate risk has grown substantially while translating it into sustained action has not, because companies face competing priorities, data limitations and governance structures not designed for long-term systemic threats. Leading organisations are framing resilience as a source of competitive advantage rather than a cost centre.
insights: Resilience is framed as a systems problem rather than an organisational one: individual preparedness fails when supply chains, infrastructure and communities remain vulnerable, which is why a company cannot buy its way to resilience alone.

Governance is identified as the determinant rather than budget: organisations that embed climate into core decision processes, engineering standards and strategic planning achieve more comprehensive resilience than those that fund resilience projects separately.

Heat and water are reported as universal threats across all sectors and geographies represented, cascading into operations, workforce, finances and communities, which is a narrower and more actionable finding than a general hazard list.

The reported driver of internal resource allocation is external: customer requirements, investor expectations and regulatory frameworks, which means the lever on corporate resilience spending sits with counterparties and supervisors rather than with the company.
Early integration is claimed to cost significantly less than retrofitting or responding to disruption, which puts the corporate case on timing rather than on the size of the eventual loss.

The two host organisations are an insurer and a broker, Zurich Insurance for the community stakeholder dialogue and Marsh McLennan for the corporate governance dialogue, so the risk transfer industry convened the governance conversation.

records.title: United Nations Plan of Action on DRR for Resilience
institutions: United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction
Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
records.summary: The 2025 progress report on the UN Plan of Action on Disaster Risk Reduction for Resilience, subtitled Pooling capacities and resources for prevention, published by UNDRR in Geneva. The Plan is supported by more than fifty UN funds, programmes, specialised agencies and related organisations, and 34 of them reported progress in 2025. The report carries a special focus on pooling capacities and resources for prevention, and functions as the UN system's own accountability record against the Sendai Framework rather than as an analysis of any financing instrument.
insights: The Plan's coverage is the striking fact: more than fifty UN entities support it, from the IMF and World Bank to UPU and WIPO, which makes disaster risk reduction a system-wide obligation rather than a UNDRR programme.

Reporting is partial and the report says which entities reported: 34 organisations submitted progress in 2025 against the larger list of supporters, so the coverage boundary is visible rather than implied.
The special focus is on pooling capacities and resources for PREVENTION rather than response, which is an allocation claim about where disaster money should sit in the cycle.
It is published under CC BY-NC IGO with an explicit note that the work may be freely quoted with acknowledgement, which makes it a citable source without a licence question.
UNDRR names its core donors, Sweden, Norway, Japan, Switzerland and Finland among others, and states that the views are the authors' rather than the donors'.

records.title: Harnessing nature for resilience
records.summary: A Marsh article on nature-based solutions as part of climate risk management, arguing they address a dual challenge: increasing resilience to physical climate risk while reversing the decline of the natural ecosystems that have historically been the first line of defence. It sets out layered green and gray protection, combining wetlands, marshes, dunes and urban green infrastructure with levees and flood walls, and then turns to financing: quantifying the protective value of nature in financial terms is named as the crucial step toward mainstreaming, and the nature finance landscape is surveyed across sustainability-linked bonds, direct investment in natural asset companies, environmental and biodiversity credits, and sustainable forestry and agriculture.
insights: The measured result the article rests on is an insurance one: research along Florida's coastline found that the frequency of insurance claims approximately halved in areas of high coastal habitat protection, even after accounting for other flood risk factors.

That is the specific form the article says mainstreaming requires, quantifying the protective value of nature in FINANCIAL terms, because a claims-frequency effect is something an underwriter can price where an ecological benefit is not.

The UK's Biodiversity Net Gain legislation is given as the live example of a regulatory instrument creating a funding stream for natural flood risk management, and the article notes other regions are exploring similar frameworks.

The nature finance landscape is split by maturity rather than by type: sustainable forestry and agriculture are named as offering more immediate investable opportunities with attractive returns, while biodiversity credits and nature technology are said to require further development and policy support.

The WEF Global Risks Report 2026 is cited as ranking extreme weather events and biodiversity loss and ecosystem collapse as the top global risks over ten years, which is the framing that makes the two problems one.

Hybrid green and gray systems are described functionally: natural buffers reduce flood surges, dissipate wave energy and manage stormwater, complementing engineered defences, with co-benefits in biodiversity, urban heat relief and carbon sequestration.

records.title: Climate Resilience Grant Program in New York
records.summary: The Nature Conservancy's Climate Resilience Grant Program funds New York based community organisations for projects that conserve lands and waters delivering multiple climate benefits, including flood mitigation, migration corridors, carbon storage, water quality and recreation, and also funds climate-focused planning, strategy development and capacity building. The programme is grounded in the Resilient and Connected Network, a mapping of landscapes covering 33 per cent of the continental United States built by more than 100 Nature Conservancy scientists over a decade, and directs grants toward New York's role as the connector between the central and northern Appalachians. Alongside grants the programme protects natural floodplains and shorelines, including projected future floodplains, through land acquisitions and conservation easements.
insights: In its first three years the programme funded 39 projects with 23 organisations, deploying roughly $1.2 million at an average grant of about $31,000 against a $50,000 cap, so grants are sized to early-stage capacity gaps rather than to capital projects.

The Resilient and Connected Network, mapped by more than 100 Nature Conservancy scientists over a decade, covers 33 per cent of the continental United States and is the prioritisation layer the grants are allocated against, which makes this a data-directed conservation capital programme rather than an open call.

The Orange County Land Trust used a grant to add 423 acres, creating about 3,000 acres of contiguous protected forest running from New Jersey to the Catskills, which is how a small grant leverages a land transfer of much larger scale.

The Genesee Valley Conservancy acquired 200 acres of wetland for eventual transfer to New York State, a structure in which private conservation capital temporarily bridges to public ownership and de-risks state land acquisition.

The programme funds conservation easements and acquisitions in PROJECTED FUTURE floodplains and shorelines rather than only current ones, which anticipates moving flood boundaries instead of locking in static regulatory maps.

It explicitly targets organisations with limited capacity, infrastructure and resources, positioning philanthropic grant capital as a first mover into gaps that larger public or private finance does not reach.

Flood mitigation, water quality, carbon storage, habitat and recreational access are co-delivered by the same parcels, which is the multi-benefit stack any future payment-for-ecosystem-services or green bond structure over this land would have to value.

records.title: ʻĀina Restoration Through Community Governance to Advance Climate Resilience in the Hawaiian Islands
records.summary: A NOAA Climate Resilience Regional Challenge project summary for ʻĀina Restoration through Community Governance to Advance Climate Resilience in the Hawaiian Islands, led by the University of Hawaiʻi Sea Grant College Program with an award of $68,497,799. The goal is a reinvigorated moku system, a Native Hawaiian framework for traditional land tenure and contemporary biocultural stewardship, delivered by a collaborative of fourteen state and county agencies, academia, national and local nonprofits and collectives of Indigenous and local stewards, with activities centred on five moku, one each on Kauaʻi, Oʻahu, Molokaʻi, Maui and Hawaiʻi. Six actions: conserving and restoring forests and watersheds by removing invasive species and planting native vegetation as green breaks and food forests to reduce wildfire risk and sediment loading onto coral reefs; enhancing regional community-based coastal stewardship through shoreline management and adaptation strategies, wetland restoration in two wildlife sanctuaries, transfer of 423 acres on Maui to the public domain for shoreline restoration and sea level rise adaptation pathways, managing tourism pressure on the Pololū Trail, and an inventory of historic and cultural coastal sites; restoring marine abundance through loko iʻa fishponds, limu and coral reefs, including expanding a high school aquaculture programme to restock native mullet statewide; sharing knowledge across island-scale and statewide networks; reducing risk and improving disaster resilience through community-led wildfire management, a homeowner's hazard handbook and support for community resilience hubs; and advancing community governance models that address historical power imbalances and expand community-based monitoring.
insights: The award is structured around a governance system rather than a hazard: restoring the moku framework is the intervention, and the flood, fire and reef work are what it delivers, which inverts the usual grant logic.

Land transfer of 423 acres into the public domain is a property-rights instrument inside a federal grant, and it is what makes the shoreline restoration and the sea level rise adaptation pathway on that land possible at all.

The wildfire chain is causally explicit, invasive removal and native planting reduce both fire risk and sediment loading onto reefs, so one action buys a terrestrial and a marine benefit, which is the multi-benefit case adaptation appraisal usually cannot count.
Advancing community governance to address historical power imbalances is named as a funded action rather than as a principle, which makes it a deliverable that can be assessed.

$68.5 million to a Sea Grant programme rather than to a state agency puts a university in the fiscal agent role for a fourteen-partner collaborative, which is a capacity choice as much as a funding one.

records.title: Regional Adaptation for Climate Resilience of Monterey Bay Coastal Communities
records.summary: A NOAA Climate Resilience Regional Challenge project summary for Regional Adaptation for Climate Resilience of Monterey Bay Coastal Communities, led by the California Marine Sanctuary Foundation with an award of $71,100,000. The project addresses the region's highest priority climate risks, flooding and wildfire, through four integrated strategies, each using nature-based approaches. Regional collaboration and capacity building centres on the new Monterey Bay Climate Adaptation Action Network as the hub for collective planning and coordination, with a focus on representation by tribes and disadvantaged communities and inclusive membership across universities, community-based organisations, nonprofits, research institutions and all levels of government. Flood risk reduction implements nature-based solutions that strengthen shorelines and restore and expand floodplains and salt marshes to accommodate flood waters that would otherwise damage homes and infrastructure. Wildfire risk reduction targets the large, high-intensity fires becoming more common, aiming to reduce risk to the more than 120,000 residents living in coastal watersheds classified as high or very high wildfire risk, with Indigenous knowledge central to the strategy. Workforce development trains young adults, college students and professionals through local and state colleges, universities and community-based nonprofits specialising in wetland restoration, with recruitment emphasised from disadvantaged communities. The programme behind it is the Climate Resilience Regional Challenge, funded by approximately $575 million that Congress appropriated through the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022 for competitive award to coastal resilience projects.
insights: A $71.1 million single award out of a $575 million national programme means roughly one dollar in eight went to this one region, so the Challenge concentrated rather than spread its money.
Bundling flood and wildfire into one award is unusual and matters: these hazards are normally funded by different programmes, and combining them is what lets one regional network manage both.
Workforce development inside a capital award is the recognition that the constraint on deploying nature-based solutions at this scale is people who can design and build them, not money.
The award funds creating the Monterey Bay Climate Adaptation Action Network rather than assuming one exists, which is the same origination-capacity gap Glasgow and Marin County each paid to close.
The 120,000 residents in high or very high wildfire risk watersheds is the beneficiary count this award would be evaluated against, and it is stated up front.

records.title: NOAA Climate Resilience Regional Challenge
records.summary: The NOAA Climate Resilience Regional Challenge programme page, describing a $573 million competitive grant investment administered by NOAA's Office for Coastal Management for collaborative projects that increase coastal communities' resilience to extreme weather. The programme names four components it treats as important: risk reduction, community engagement, regional coordination and enduring capacity.
