The page carries the programme's own reported outcomes to date, including over 300 community adaptation plans, more than 3,100 acres of habitat restored, 6,570 acres of land acquired for conservation, over 2,000 acres of nature-based infrastructure, more than $174.8 million invested in infrastructure with $79.4 million dedicated to resilience planning, over 56,000 individuals engaged, $2.85 million invested in education, $1.125 billion in economic activity against a reported 213 per cent return on investment, $24.66 million invested in workforce development, 6,006 jobs created, $1.61 million in research and monitoring and $72.6 million in habitat restoration. It links to the funded project map, a fellowship programme and grantee resources.
insights: The programme reports a 213 per cent return on investment and $1.125 billion in economic activity against a $573 million appropriation, which is a self-reported figure from NOAA's own economic impact estimate and should be traced to that source before being cited.
Enduring capacity is named as one of four core components alongside risk reduction, which means the programme funds institutional durability rather than only projects.

The split between infrastructure investment at over $174.8 million and resilience planning at $79.4 million puts roughly a third of the programme into planning, which is unusually high for a federal infrastructure programme.
Land acquisition at 6,570 acres exceeds habitat restoration at 3,100 acres, so the programme is buying exposure out of harm's way as much as rebuilding ecosystems.

records.title: West Virginia Atlas of Disaster
institutions: Department of Housing and Urban Development
records.summary: The West Virginia Atlas of Disaster (January 2026), produced by Rebuild by Design, is a county-level risk and federal spending diagnostic for West Virginia's 1.8 million residents. It documents 23 federally declared disasters (2011–2024), $951M in FEMA and HUD post-disaster funding ($531 per capita, 9th highest nationally), and an ASCE infrastructure grade of D. All 55 counties face high flood risk; 28 have had five or more disasters. The report quantifies costs of inaction, maps social vulnerability hotspots, and recommends shifting to pre-disaster mitigation finance, including a small insurance surcharge projected to unlock $1.3B in resilient infrastructure investment.
insights: West Virginia received $951M in FEMA and HUD post-disaster funding from 2011–2024 ($531 per capita), ranking 9th highest nationally in per capita disaster spending, signaling chronic underinvestment in pre-disaster mitigation relative to post-disaster outlays.

AECOM estimates the cost of inaction at $55B in the next decade for coastal storm and flood-event-related damages nationwide; the U.S. Chamber of Commerce documents a 13:1 benefit-cost ratio for hazard mitigation investment, and every $1 not invested can cost up to $33 in lost future economic activity.

A small insurance surcharge mechanism is estimated to support $1.3B in resilient infrastructure investment in West Virginia alone, illustrating how modest insurance-sector policy changes can unlock significant pre-disaster capital.

All 55 West Virginia counties face high flood risk; 46% of state roads, 57% of fire stations, 38% of schools, and 37% of commercial properties are projected at flood risk by 2050, creating a broad infrastructure liability with direct implications for municipal credit quality and insurance pricing.

McDowell County holds the highest Social Vulnerability Index score (0.87) in the state, and historically redlined neighborhoods nationally face 25% higher flood risk and temperatures 4.7°F hotter during heat waves, equity dimensions that affect where mitigation capital is most needed and least available.

Lincoln County leads West Virginia with 12 disaster declarations in 13 years, demonstrating that repetitive-loss geographies are identifiable and targetable for pre-disaster investment and risk transfer instruments.

The June 2016 West Virginia flash flood cost $1B, damaged 1,500+ roads and bridges, and killed 23 people, quantifying the single-event infrastructure liability that resilience investments are designed to avoid.

records.title: Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) Community Guidebook
records.authors: Joie Zhang, Pei Li Chua, Daniel Gunton, Claire McLean, Allison Shao, Alex Tellides
records.summary: The CRA Community Guidebook, published by Rebuild by Design in January 2026, is a practical toolkit for community-based organizations (CBOs) in low- to moderate-income (LMI) neighborhoods seeking to leverage the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) to fund climate resilience infrastructure. It explains the CRA's regulatory framework, identifies qualifying multi-benefit projects (green infrastructure, resilience hubs, stormwater systems, coastal barriers), and provides step-by-step guidance for engaging banks, CDFIs, and regulators. The guide makes the financial case for banks, citing a 27% average ROI on adaptation investments and $13 in avoided damages per $1 spent on preparedness, and documents examples including a $100B U.S. Bancorp community benefits plan and $7M post-Harvey CDFI lending in Houston.
insights: Every $1 spent on disaster preparedness saves $13 in damages, cleanup, and lost economic activity, a ratio the guide uses to make the business case for CRA-eligible climate infrastructure investments to banks.
The average ROI for climate adaptation investments is cited as 27%, framing resilience as one of the most cost-effective forms of risk management for bank loan portfolios.

From 1998–2018, 57% of disaster-impacted U.S. counties contain census tracts where banks may receive CRA credit, indicating substantial geographic overlap between climate exposure and CRA eligibility.

Between 2011 and 2024, extreme weather cost $117.9 billion in federal disaster relief, affected 80% of states, and struck 99.5% of congressional districts, establishing the scale of unaddressed climate risk in CRA-eligible communities.

Community advocacy via CRA public commenting has generated large commitments: U.S. Bancorp ($100B, 5-year plan), JPMorgan Chase ($30B racial equity commitment), Flagstar/NYCB ($28B community benefit agreement), and BBVA Compass ($10B plan including $2.1B in LMI mortgages).

CRA-eligible climate projects span three scales: small ($2K–$25K/unit, e.g., weatherization, solar for LMI homes), medium ($250K–$5M, e.g., resilience hubs, green schoolyards), and large ($10M–$1B+, e.g., stormwater systems, coastal barriers), each with distinct bank/CDFI funding pathways.

Regulators (OCC, Federal Reserve, FDIC) have explicitly affirmed that both pre-event resilience plans and post-event disaster recovery activities in LMI areas qualify for CRA credit, creating a regulatory pathway for proactive climate investment.

CDFIs serve as critical intermediaries between banks and communities: one example shows ECLF and DC Green Bank co-funding solar installation on affordable housing generating 2,500+ MWh of renewable energy annually.

records.title: Premium Discounts for Structures Built or Retrofitted According to Building Standards Established by the Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety (IBHS)
institutions: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety (IBHS)
records.summary: This is the 2026 legislative report from the Louisiana Department of Insurance (LDI) implementing Act 533 of 2024, which mandates that all admitted insurers file actuarially justified premium discounts for homeowners who build or retrofit to the IBHS FORTIFIED® Roof standard. As of July 1, 2026, over 40 insurer groups have filed approved discounts ranging from 1% to 54%, applied primarily to the wind and hail portion of premiums. The report serves as the official public registry of approved FORTIFIED® Roof discounts under Louisiana law, directly linking mitigation investment to insurance cost reduction.
insights: Over 40 distinct insurer groups have filed IBHS FORTIFIED® Roof discounts in Louisiana as of July 1, 2026, with approved discounts ranging from 1% (Farmers Property & Casualty condo/landlord) to 54% (FCCI/Monroe Guaranty/HDI Global/Universal Fire & Casualty in highest-risk zones), demonstrating a wide but real market for risk-differentiated pricing based on mitigation.

Most insurers apply discounts specifically to the wind and hail portion of the premium rather than total premium, meaning the effective percentage reduction on total premium may be lower than the stated discount, a critical nuance for cost-benefit analyses of FORTIFIED® Roof retrofits.

Zone-tiered discount structures (e.g., Louisiana Citizens Property Insurance Corporation: 7.2% Zone 3 to 24.3% Zone 1; State Farm: 19%–39% for homeowners) reveal that insurers price mitigation benefit proportionally to underlying hazard exposure, providing implicit actuarial validation that FORTIFIED® Roofs reduce wind/hurricane losses most in high-risk coastal areas.

The Liberty Mutual/Safeco group offers a 40% discount under an 'IBHS Home' designation, and Chubb's Executive Risk Indemnity offers 45.62%, among the highest in the registry, suggesting that for high-value or commercially underwritten policies, FORTIFIED® Roof certification can materially reduce insurance cost of ownership.

State Farm's discount range of 19%–39% for homeowners and 7%–20% for manufactured homes, combined with USAA's 19%–37% range, indicates that the two largest personal lines writers in the U.S. have filed actuarially justified discounts, lending market legitimacy to FORTIFIED® Roof as a standardized risk-reduction metric.

records.title: Texas Windstorm (TWIA) Sponsoring $450m Alamo Re 2026-1 Catastrophe Bond
records.summary: The Texas Windstorm Insurance Association (TWIA), Texas's residual market property insurer, is sponsoring Alamo Re Ltd. Series 2026-1, a new catastrophe bond targeting at least $450 million in capital markets reinsurance against Texas named storms and severe thunderstorms. The issuance comprises three tranches (Class A $200M, Class B $200M, Class C $50M) on an indemnity trigger and annual aggregate basis, with Hannover Re fronting via retrocession. If completed alongside existing in-force cat bonds, TWIA's total cat bond risk transfer could approach or exceed its 1-in-50-year probable maximum loss funding requirement of ~$2.28 billion, potentially displacing traditional reinsurance sources entirely in 2026.
insights: TWIA is targeting $450M in new cat bond capacity via Alamo Re 2026-1 across three tranches, with spread guidance ranging from 6–7% (Class A, lowest risk) to 11–12% (Class C, highest risk), illustrating the cost curve for layered catastrophe risk transfer in a residual market context.

Prior to this issuance, TWIA held $2.45B in outstanding cat bond risk transfer (Alamo Re and Bluebonnet Re combined); with ~$900M maturing in June 2026, the effective in-force position would drop to $1.55B, making the $450M deal necessary to approach its legislative 1-in-50-year PML funding requirement of ~$2.28B.

TWIA's 1-in-50-year PML mandate requires only ~$2.28B total risk transfer in 2026, meaning the $450M issuance slightly overshoots the net-new requirement of ~$330M, giving the board optionality to redeem older tranches or reduce traditional reinsurance purchases.

The deal structure uses a Bermuda-based special purpose insurer (Alamo Re Ltd.) with Hannover Re as the ceding reinsurer in a retrocession fronting arrangement, a repeating structure TWIA has used across multiple prior cat bond issuances, demonstrating the replicability of this SPI/fronting model for residual market insurers.

Class B and C tranches carry initial expected losses of 3.63% and 5.01% respectively, with attachment probabilities of 4.49% and 5.65%, these metrics quantify the pricing of mid- to lower-layer Texas windstorm risk for capital market investors.

TWIA has been a continuous cat bond sponsor since 2014, and if 2026 in-force coverage is maintained, the capital markets could fund the near-entirety of its reinsurance tower, a notable structural shift away from traditional reinsurance for a state-backed residual insurer.

records.title: Catastrophe Bond and ILS Market Report, Q2 2026
records.summary: The Artemis Q2 2026 Catastrophe Bond & ILS Market Report documents a record $11.3 billion of cat bond issuance across 48 transactions in Q2 2026, surpassing the previous quarterly record by $842 million (8%). H1 2026 issuance reached nearly $18 billion, making 2026 the second-largest issuance year ever behind 2025's $25.6 billion record. The outstanding cat bond market reached a record $65.6 billion at end-June 2026. The report also features Verisk analysis showing U.S. severe thunderstorm insured losses rising from ~$4 billion annually (1998–2005) to over $40 billion (2021–2025), and a Twelve Securis essay on combining public and private ILS for portfolio efficiency.
insights: Q2 2026 cat bond issuance hit a record $11.3 billion, 73% above the 10-year quarterly average, marking the fourth consecutive Q2 issuance record and the first quarter ever to exceed $11 billion.

H1 2026 issuance of ~$18 billion already exceeds full-year issuance for every year in the market's history except 2025 ($25.6 billion), signaling sustained structural growth in cat bond capital supply.

The outstanding cat bond market reached a record $65.6 billion at end-June 2026, up 7% from year-end 2025's then-record $61.3 billion, demonstrating compounding market growth driven by issuance outpacing maturities.

Average cat bond spreads tightened to 6.63% in Q2 2026 (from 7.23% in Q2 2025), and the average multiple fell to 2.29 (from 3.14), the lowest Q2 multiple since 2021, a direct indicator of reinsurance market softening and strong investor demand compressing risk pricing.

Nine new sponsors entered the cat bond market in Q2 2026, a quarterly record, including sovereigns (Tajikistan, Kyrgyz Republic via Asian Development Bank) and insurers from Germany (Gothaer) and Florida, broadening the geographic and counterparty diversity of the asset class.

U.S. severe thunderstorm average annual insured losses increased ~10x from ~$4 billion (1998–2005) to over $40 billion (2021–2025), driven by both exposure concentration growth (claims rising from 1.3M to 3.5M annually) and claim severity (residential reconstruction costs up 63.7% between 2014–2024), with direct implications for multi-peril cat bond structures re-introducing aggregate features.

Texas accounted for 95% of all Q1 2025 national CAT claims, with five ST events each exceeding $1 billion in Texas in 2024 alone, a concentration risk relevant to sponsors and investors in US multi-peril and Texas-specific cat bond tranches.

records.title: Statewide Resilience Plan, Fiscal Year 2026-27
records.summary: Florida's Statewide Resilience Plan (SRP) for Fiscal Year 2026-27 allocates $160 million in grants across 23 new projects and three supplemental awards to municipalities and water utilities throughout the state. Projects target stormwater infrastructure, wastewater treatment plant hardening, lift station rehabilitation and relocation, and pump station upgrades in coastal and flood-prone communities including Miami-Dade County, the Florida Keys, Fort Myers, Vero Beach, and Broward County. The program addresses compounding flood and sea level rise risks to water and wastewater systems.
insights: The plan is an award schedule rather than a strategy document: it lists named grantees, project names and dollar awards, so it is a record of where state resilience money actually went.

Water and wastewater utility resilience dominates the funded list, with treatment plant flood mitigation, electrical system upgrades, lift stations and pump stations recurring across Fort Myers, Miami-Dade, Clearwater, Key Largo, Cooper City, Palm Beach County and Marathon.

Several of the largest line items are additional funding for awards made in a previous cycle, including $21.4 million and $5.8 million to the South Florida Water Management District and $7.2 million to Fort Myers, so the plan is partly topping up projects that were previously underfunded.
Every award carries the caveat that it remains subject to further review for activity and expense eligibility, so the published figures are commitments rather than disbursements.

records.title: New Laws Sponsored by Commissioner Lara to Strengthen Consumer Protections and Wildfire Resilience Take Effect January 1
institutions: California Infrastructure and Economic Development Bank
records.summary: The California Department of Insurance announces nine laws sponsored by Commissioner Ricardo Lara taking effect January 1, 2026. They create a grant program for fire-safe roofs and Zone Zero mitigation (AB 888), authorise grants for the nation's first publicly available wildfire catastrophe model (SB 429), require regular review of the Safer from Wildfires discount regulations (AB 1), and speed wildfire claim payouts (SB 495). They also extend the non-renewal moratorium to commercial policies (SB 547) and let the FAIR Plan access catastrophe bonds through IBank and take lines of credit or loans (AB 226). Two health insurance laws are included.
insights: SB 495 requires insurers to pay 60 percent of contents limits, capped at $350,000, to total-loss wildfire survivors without an itemised inventory, and gives at least 100 days for proof of loss.
AB 226 lets the FAIR Plan, if authorised by the Commissioner, access catastrophic bonds through the California Infrastructure and Economic Development Bank and enter lines of credit or loans.
SB 429 authorises grants to establish the nation's first publicly available wildfire loss catastrophe model.
AB 888, the California Safe Homes Act, creates a grant program for fire-safe roofs and mitigation within five feet of homes (Zone Zero).
SB 547 extends the one-year non-renewal moratorium to commercial policies, including HOAs, condominiums, affordable housing and non-profits.

records.title: Come Dream, Come Build Affordable Homes [Episode 28]
records.summary: Nick Mitchell-Bennett runs a community development organisation in Brownsville, Texas, in a persistent-poverty region where more than 20 percent of the population has lived below the federal poverty line for at least 30 years. He describes three linked innovations: a small-dollar loan product built as an alternative to payday lending, which has made over 160,000 loans totalling about $158 million at roughly $900 each and saved borrowers an estimated $160 million in fees and interest against a Texas payday loan; a modular housing programme begun after winning the Wells Fargo Affordable Housing Breakthrough Challenge in December 2020, now roughly doubling output each year toward 36 units, with buyers choosing among 29 design options online while the factory builds standard boxes; and homebuyer readiness counselling that takes six to twelve months. His most pointed argument is about insurance. As carriers leave or price out, buyers and rental owners are pushed toward non-admitted carriers with less regulation, while Texas insurer capitalisation rules have not been updated in 25 years. He is confident a company can pay a single apartment fire and doubtful it could pay after a category five hurricane destroyed a whole portfolio, which means the certificate of insurance held by tax credit investors and lenders may be worth less than it appears.
insights: The insurance warning is a capital adequacy argument with a direct effect on affordable housing finance: tax credit investors and lenders accept a certificate of insurance as sufficient, while the carrier behind it may be non-admitted and capitalised under rules 25 years old, so the protection standing behind the investment may not survive a correlated loss.

Market exit pushes borrowers into what he calls the payday lending market of insurance, the lightly regulated non-admitted segment, which mirrors the credit market dynamic his own loan product was built to counter.

The small-dollar loan result is measurable at scale: over 160,000 loans averaging about $900, roughly $158 million lent, and about $160 million saved against the payday alternative, so avoided cost roughly equals principal advanced.

Modular construction is used to remove cost without removing choice, with 29 buyer-selected options presented against a standardised factory product, on the argument that limited choice is not what drives cost down.

Philanthropic capital is distributed very unevenly by place, cited as roughly $950 per head in New York City against about $21 to $25 in the Rio Grande Valley and about two dollars on Indian reservations, which constrains which communities can pursue catalytic capital at all.

records.title: The Spatially Variable Effects of Mangroves on Flood Depths and Losses from Storm Surges in Florida
records.authors: Siddharth Narayan, Christopher J. Thomas, Kechi Nzerem, Joss Matthewman, Christine Shepard, Laura Geselbracht, Michael W. Beck
institutions: Center for Coastal Climate Resilience at UC Santa Cruz
records.summary: This peer-reviewed study (Cell Reports Sustainability, 2025) uses a catastrophe-industry-standard, kilometer-scale flood and loss model to quantify the spatially variable economic benefits of mangrove forests in reducing storm surge property damages in Florida. Mangroves reduce average annual storm surge losses by $67 million in Collier County (~$270,000/km²/year), with 73% of benefits accruing for storms with return periods under 50 years. During Hurricane Irma (2017) mangroves avoided ~$725 million in damages (14%); during Hurricane Ian (2022), ~$4.1 billion (30%). The study provides critical evidence for treating mangroves as quantifiable natural infrastructure in insurance pricing and coastal risk management.
insights: Mangroves reduce average annual storm surge losses in Collier County, Florida by $67 million, equivalent to ~$270,000 per km² per year, an order of magnitude higher than a prior county-level estimate of $38,000/km²/year from Sun and Carson.

73% of annual mangrove flood-loss reduction benefits accrue for storms with return periods under 50 years, and over 55% for return periods under 30 years, within a typical US home mortgage lifetime, making these benefits financially tangible to lenders and homeowners.

During Hurricane Irma (2017), mangroves avoided ~$725 million in storm surge property damages (14% reduction); during Hurricane Ian (2022), ~$4.1 billion (30% reduction), across a smaller spatial footprint of roughly 250 km² of mangrove forest in Collier County.

Mangroves always reduce flood losses for properties landward of the mangrove edge (100% of landward hexagons show net benefit in all three event cases), but can increase damages for properties inside or seaward of mangrove forests due to surge impoundment, a critical spatial nuance for underwriters and planners.

The study uses an insurance-industry catastrophe risk model (Moody's RMS), making findings directly legible to (re)insurers, risk pricing analysts, and bond issuers: the methodology supports integration of mangrove value into premium structures, cat bond design, and resilience investment incentives.

Over $4 billion in avoided storm surge damages during the 2017 and 2023 hurricane seasons in south Florida was attributable to mangroves, yet less than 3% of post-Sandy federal recovery funding went to green infrastructure, indicating a major allocation gap.

records.title: The Living Laboratory of Norfolk [Episode 27]
institutions: United States Army Corps of Engineers
United States Department of Housing and Urban Development
records.summary: Kyle Spencer, who leads resilience for the City of Norfolk, describes a programme that has grown from one or two people into a team of about ten funded from the general fund, and a coastal flood protection project being delivered with the Army Corps of Engineers. The city is roughly 95 percent built out, so the design uses flood walls, a hybrid flood wall and levee, pump stations and storm surge gates of the kind built in New Orleans after Katrina. His argument for acting before a storm is a return figure: recent studies put roughly $13 back for every dollar spent on resilience investment, and he contrasts this with the Army Corps pattern of completing a feasibility study, shelving it, and implementing only once a storm releases the money. Norfolk's living laboratory with RISE, originating in the HUD response to Hurricane Sandy and topped up by the state, lets the city buy proven products, and the competitive challenge process has been used to justify sole-source procurement. On insurance, the city has about 80 percent flood insurance uptake among those in the floodplain against a typical 30 to 50 percent, and wants to keep it after the flood defences are built, since a Harvey-scale rainfall would overwhelm any stormwater system; the city is exploring a community-based approach to covering deductibles so that higher deductibles can keep policies affordable without leaving households exposed.
insights: The insurance design problem is stated precisely: once large flood control systems are built, households have an incentive to drop flood cover, but residual risk remains, so the city wants to preserve its unusually high 80 percent uptake rather than let protection substitute for insurance.

A community-based mechanism to pay deductibles is floated as the way to keep premiums affordable through higher deductibles without leaving households exposed, which places a collective instrument between the household and the insurer.

Acting before the storm is argued from a roughly $13 return per dollar of resilience investment, set against the Army Corps pattern of shelving a feasibility study until a disaster releases the funding.
The non-federal match can come from state or any non-federal source, which is what determines the pace of a large Corps project and makes state appropriation the binding constraint.

The Defense Community Infrastructure Program is used as a funding source outside the fence line, tying military mission readiness to municipal resilience spending on roads and stormwater backflow prevention.

records.title: Where to Restore and Conserve? A Regional Benefit Cost Analysis of Coral Reef Protection and Restoration for Coastal Flood Resilience
records.authors: Borja G. Reguero, Camila Gaido, Curt D. Storlazzi, Valerie Pietsch McNulty, Denise I. Perez, Michael W. Beck
records.summary: This peer-reviewed study provides one of the first regional-scale, spatially explicit benefit-cost analyses (BCA) of coral reef conservation and restoration for coastal flood risk reduction in the U.S. Virgin Islands (Saint Croix, Saint John, Saint Thomas), designed to meet FEMA Hazard Mitigation Grant Program requirements. Using hydrodynamic modeling (XBeach, SWAN) and FEMA HAZUS damage functions, the study finds that current reefs prevent $43.6 million USD in annual flood damages and protect 481 people. Ecological restoration (ER) and hybrid restoration (HR) are both cost-effective, with up to 10.9 km of coastline meeting a BCR threshold of 1.5, opening pathways to federal hazard mitigation funding for nature-based solutions.
insights: Current coral reefs in the U.S. Virgin Islands prevent $43.6 million USD in annual flood damages and protect 481 people per year, representing 87% of the region's $51.4 million USD annual flood risk.

Reef degradation (1 m elevation loss) would nearly double annual flood damages across reef-fronted areas, increasing expected annual damages from $45.4M to $88.7M, a 95% increase, demonstrating the asset value of existing natural infrastructure.

Ecological restoration (ER) achieves BCR thresholds exceeding 1.5 along 10.9 km of coastline and BCR >3 along 6.9 km, despite providing less absolute flood mitigation than hybrid restoration (HR), because ER costs ($1,500/linear meter) are roughly half those of HR ($3,057/linear meter).

Hybrid (gray-green) restoration delivers greater absolute flood risk reduction but lower cost-effectiveness than ecological restoration, illustrating the tradeoff between maximizing total protection and maximizing return on investment, HR is best suited for highest-risk shoreline segments.

Conservation and restoration priority areas are strongly correlated (Pearson r = 0.86), meaning areas with the greatest existing reef protection value also tend to be the best candidates for restoration investment, simplifying spatial prioritization for allocators.

The study was funded under FEMA's Hazard Mitigation Grant Program and is explicitly designed to meet federal BCA requirements, marking a replicable template for unlocking pre- and post-disaster mitigation grants for nature-based solutions globally.

In June 2023, FEMA awarded $38.6 million to the first-ever coral reef restoration hazard mitigation project in Puerto Rico, establishing policy precedent that complements this analytical framework and signals growing federal investability of reef-based solutions.

records.title: The Weekly: Climate Migration and the Resilience Belt
records.summary: This newsletter edition reports that rising insurance premiums and utility costs in disaster-exposed markets are reversing the 70-year migration from the Rust Belt to the Sun Belt. Through an interview with Hunter Maats of Resilience Investments, it frames the shift as an investment opportunity created by mispriced risk, with insurance pricing becoming a forward indicator of housing value. It sets out options for receiving cities, such as workforce development and urban wealth funds or community asset trusts built on land bank assets, and for Sun Belt jurisdictions, including insurance reform modelled on the UK's Flood Re and municipal revenue from distributed energy.
insights: The top 20 markets in the Summer 2025 WSJ/Realtor.com Housing Market Ranking were all in the Midwest and Northeast.
80% of Florida's $4 trillion in real estate value sits in coastal counties, exposing a property-tax-dependent municipal base.
Flood Re is described as charging a £10.80 levy on every policy over 25 years to cover the most at-risk homes while letting the private market return.
Urban wealth funds or community asset trusts managing land bank parcels in Detroit and Cleveland are proposed as revenue sources not tied to taxes.
A projected shortage of 2.1 million skilled trades workers by 2030 is cited as an opening for workforce development in receiving cities.
Detroit's lowest annual minimum temperature is about 8.7°F warmer than in 1970.

records.title: How Three Climate-Vulnerable Areas Rebuilt with Resilience, Kept Insurance, and Increased Home Values
institutions: Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety (IBHS)
records.summary: Written for homeowners rebuilding after the Eaton and Palisades fires, this article presents three US cases where rebuilding to IBHS resilience standards kept homes insurable and raised their value. It covers Florida's FORTIFIED premium discounts, the Strengthen Alabama Homes grant program and its effect on home prices and losses, and KB Home's Dixon Trail community in Escondido built to the Wildfire Prepared Home Plus standard. It argues that insurers reward clear, science-based construction standards adopted at scale, a model California can learn from.
insights: Insurers in Florida offer discounts of 20% to 60% for homes built to the IBHS FORTIFIED standard, which has reduced premiums by up to 60% according to SageSure.
Strengthen Alabama Homes offers grants of up to $10,000 with no income limit, has fortified more than 50,000 roofs, and homeowners can save as much as 55% on premiums, particularly wind coverage.

FORTIFIED homes sold for 6.8% more than conventionally built homes in a University of Alabama study, and a 2022 study found returns on FORTIFIED roofs of 8.1% inland to 72% on the coast at the Gold designation.
When Hurricane Sally hit in 2020, FORTIFIED construction produced 55% to 74% fewer overall losses than conventional construction.

Dixon Trail in Escondido, California, built by KB Home to the Wildfire Prepared Home Plus standard, is described as the first purpose-built wildfire-resilient neighbourhood in the US, and such homes can save up to 21% on premiums.

The article cites a figure that every $1 spent rebuilding with resilience can save $210 in avoided future losses, and a Mercury Insurance executive says certified homes are much more likely to be renewed.

records.title: Why Remediation Is the First Step to Real Resilience
institutions: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety
records.summary: This article argues that resilient rebuilding is incomplete without remediation of the contaminants that fires and floods leave behind. It reviews evidence of toxic releases after the Los Angeles fires, Florida hurricanes and Hurricane Harvey, and identifies fragmented regulation and high cleanup costs as barriers. It recommends treating contamination prevention and cleanup as one process, through non-toxic resilient materials, runoff control, land-use planning, post-disaster mitigation bonds and one-stop funding that combines rebuilding with remediation.
insights: The first half of 2025 was the costliest six months of US weather events on record, at an estimated $101.4 billion in damage.
During the 2024 hurricane season, flooding in Florida released nearly 92 million gallons of pollutants; Hurricane Harvey damaged at least 14 Superfund sites and more than 40 industrial facilities.
About 25% of surveyed Eaton and Palisades survivors could not get their properties tested for contaminants.
Debris clearing after the 2018 California fires cost an estimated $3 billion, and cleanup of a single toxic site after Harvey an estimated $115 million.
After Harvey the Houston area raised more than $2.5 billion in bonds for catch basins and buyouts, and NY Rising integrated cleanup, reconstruction and over 35,000 contamination tests after Sandy.

records.title: Handbook for Livable and Resilient Cities: Chapter 4 Instruments, Enforcement, Monitoring, and Evaluation
institutions: Global Facility for Disaster Reduction and Recovery
records.summary: Chapter 4 of the GFDRR Handbook for Livable and Resilient Cities, on the instruments cities use to implement risk-informed urban planning and on enforcing, monitoring and evaluating them. It covers regulatory and incentive instruments, zoning and land-use controls, building codes, financial and land management tools, and capacity building and public engagement, and treats the central challenge as coordinating disaster risk management and climate risk management components with the instruments that execute them. Worked examples include graduated planning controls in Australia's Hawkesbury-Nepean Valley and land value capture funding flood resilience in Barranquilla, Colombia.
insights: Land value capture is presented as an accessible starting instrument for cities with limited capacity, with betterment levies and capital gains tax named as the most popular forms, and Barranquilla in Colombia given as a case where a betterment levy funded resilience and road infrastructure.

Zoning is framed as the instrument that prevents the CREATION of new risk rather than reducing existing risk, by defining where urbanisation and critical infrastructure should be avoided, which separates it cleanly from retrofit instruments.

Building codes are described as translating hazard and risk information into technical requirements for materials, design loads and construction practice, and the chapter argues most current codes still address gravity, earthquake and wind while needing to evolve for floods, wildfires and extreme temperatures.

A city without hazard and risk assessments is told to treat that as a short-term priority, because every downstream instrument in the chapter depends on the assessment to define compatible land uses and development standards.

Plans are required to be flexible enough to absorb new hazard information by updating zoning, land use, performance standards and building regulations, which makes the instrument set a cycle rather than a one-time adoption.

Australia's Hawkesbury-Nepean Valley is used to show graduated planning controls in a hazard-prone area, with land use, construction type, density and setbacks all varying by vulnerability level rather than by a single flood line.
records.publisher: Global Facility for Disaster Reduction and Recovery

records.title: Public Development Banks’ Climate Commitments 2025: Trends and Progress of PDB Climate Ambition
records.authors: Neil Chin, Shreya Bansal, Arjun Rawal
records.summary: The report 'Public Development Banks’ Climate Commitments 2025' assesses the role of Public Development Banks (PDBs) in climate finance, identifying both progress and significant gaps in climate ambition across different institutions. It highlights the importance of capacity building and regional collaboration to enhance PDBs' effectiveness in meeting climate goals by 2025, emphasizing the need for a structured, long-term approach to support less ambitious banks in improving their climate commitments.
insights: Public Development Banks (PDBs) are essential to achieving climate and development goals.
The share of PDBs aligning with the Paris Agreement has increased from 28% in 2020 to 45% by 2025.
High ambition PDBs control a considerable amount of assets totaling USD 9.3 trillion, significantly influencing climate finance distribution.
Capacity building initiatives are often short-term and fragmented, lacking the necessary support for institutional transformation.
There is a critical need for enhanced support for PDBs with limited climate commitments to mobilize broader climate finance participation.
Collaborative efforts in countries like Brazil are vital for creating enabling conditions that elevate PDB climate ambition.
Machine learning and AI tools are being utilized for analyzing and categorizing climate commitments to improve data accuracy.
Peer-to-peer learning and knowledge sharing are essential for sustaining institutional capacity after initial support.

records.title: The End of Climate Finance as Usual: QV Looks Ahead to 2026
records.summary: Quantified Ventures' Tee Thomas argues that as federal climate funding faltered in 2025, practical finance innovation moved to local actors, and illustrates it with three QV engagements. The Freshwater Trust used analytics on 36,000 irrigated fields in the Snake River watershed to price a phosphorus target at $210 million and fund it through a centralized vehicle with a $5 million line of credit. The Great Outdoors Foundation's Conservation Acceleration Fund front-loads capital against slow grant cycles in Iowa. Montgomery County Green Bank is designing a municipal resilience finance program that bundles efficiency, water, energy and infrastructure upgrades.
insights: The Freshwater Trust assessed 36,000 irrigated fields covering nearly 300,000 acres and identified 2,000 projects that would meet regional phosphorus targets, priced at $210 million for the watershed, with 20 percent of the area producing 80 percent of the benefit.

A centralized vehicle, Irrigation Incentives LLC, aggregates federal, state, private and utility money, and a $5 million line of credit advances payments so producers do not carry costs; 23 upgrades were completed in a year with more than 115 queued.

The Great Outdoors Foundation raises about $15 million a year that catalyses another $150 million; QV designed interim financing that front-loads capital while grant and donor money arrives over two to five years.
Montgomery County Green Bank, building on its Resilience Dedicated Fund, is designing a municipal resilience finance program as a local market maker for resilience products.
The common thread is financing designed around measured outcomes rather than program rules.

records.title: Rhode Island Offers a Blueprint for Financing Coastal Climate Resilience
institutions: Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management
records.summary: The article presents Rhode Island as a model for financing coastal and inland climate resilience as federal adaptation funding recedes. It describes how the legislature, the Department of Environmental Management and the Rhode Island Infrastructure Bank coordinate statewide prioritisation of about 10,000 assets with a bond-backed revolving loan fund and grants. The Municipal Resilience Program made workshop participation a condition of grant access, bringing all 39 cities and towns to the table. Woonsocket's Truman Drive greenway shows a small planning grant unlocking larger federal and state funds, and the Resilient Rhody Infrastructure Fund and the Act on Coasts extend this to multi-million-dollar projects.
insights: The Rhode Island Infrastructure Bank has awarded $24-25 million in resilience grants since 2019, but demand exceeds funds by 4-5x; one round had 41 proposals totalling $52 million for $12 million.
The Resilient Rhody Infrastructure Fund is a revolving loan fund with $10 million authorised and another $20 million expected in 2026; RIIB says each $1 supports $3 of projects.
A $25,000 planning grant for Woonsocket's Truman Drive unlocked $500,000 from EPA's SNEP program and $2 million from the RIIB, with RIDOT covering the 25% local match.
The Act on Coasts requires DEM to produce a plan by end of 2025 prioritising assets by vulnerability and value to the state.
RIIB has already loaned out $2 billion for clean water projects.

records.title: The Growth Story Behind Insurance-Linked Securities
records.summary: This CFA Institute blog post by Mariagiovanna Guatteri surveys the growth and maturation of the insurance-linked securities (ILS) market as of mid-2025. The global catastrophe bond market has surpassed $56 billion in outstanding size, with 2025 on pace to be the largest issuance year on record at $17.2 billion through mid-year. The piece covers performance (Swiss Re Global Cat Bond Index returned 9.89% in the first ten months of 2025), risk events including the Los Angeles wildfires ($40 billion in insured losses) and a $150 million World Bank catastrophe bond payout for Jamaica after Hurricane Melissa, and the expanding role of parametric and index-based structures in institutional portfolios.
insights: The catastrophe bond market surpassed $56 billion in outstanding notional size in 2025, exceeding prior records, with $17.2 billion in new issuance in the first half of the year alone, more than 75% of which included wildfire bond coverage.

The Swiss Re Global Cat Bond Index returned 9.89% in the first ten months of 2025, and since 2002 cat bonds have produced positive monthly returns nearly 90% of the time, demonstrating low correlation to traditional financial markets.

The Los Angeles wildfires in early 2025 caused approximately $40 billion in insured losses, the largest wildfire-related insured loss on record, stress-testing ILS structures without triggering widespread market disruption.

Hurricane Melissa triggered a 100% payout of a $150 million World Bank Catastrophe Bond for Jamaica, illustrating both the sovereign risk-transfer utility and the full-loss tail risk embedded in parametric structures.

Institutional allocators typically target 1%–3% of portfolio exposure to ILS; modeling suggests allocations up to 10% could improve portfolio metrics, but investors remain cautious given the asymmetric, event-driven return profile.

Diversification within the ILS market has broadened beyond US hurricane: recent issuances include $182 million for UK flood, $105 million for Canada earthquake and severe convective storms, and $100 million for French terrorism coverage.

Inflation has an indirect positive effect on ILS: higher insured asset values increase demand for risk transfer (widening spreads) while floating-rate coupons tied to Treasury money market funds directly benefit investors in high-rate environments.

Innovation in deal structure, particularly index-based solutions and parametric products, is expanding the addressable market by enabling faster payouts and more efficient risk transfer, supporting continued institutionalization.

records.title: The Weekly: Climate Risk Literacy in Commercial Real Estate
records.summary: This weekly newsletter's feature draws three takeaways on climate risk literacy from the Risk Mitigation Playbook, developed by The Resiliency Company with professionals from over 55 companies for commercial real estate. It argues that a shared risk language across lenders, developers, designers and owners lets teams set risk tolerance and make site-selection and design decisions that reflect future conditions. It stresses that risk data should be refreshed continuously, citing Prologis and a JLL pre-sale flood assessment. It closes that insurance repricing and disclosure requirements make early risk literacy the foundation for every other resilience strategy.
insights: The Risk Mitigation Playbook was developed with professionals from over 55 companies.
Prologis runs physical risk analysis on its entire global portfolio and refreshes that data daily to feed its investment process.
A JLL assessment found significant hidden flood exposure in a retail property before sale, allowing the owner to retrofit flood barriers and preserve the investment return.
A developer cited by NAIOP revised site selection and building design after portfolio hazard mapping, adding reinforced storm shutters and reducing glass facades.
A JLL survey found 45% of commercial real estate leaders plan to select only climate-resilient buildings by 2030.

records.title: The Commercial Real Estate Climate Imperative: A New Playbook for Navigating Risk
records.summary: This Epicenter article introduces the Risk Mitigation Playbook, a guide for commercial real estate development produced by a coalition of The Resiliency Company, JLL, Ryan Companies and the Urban Land Institute. It argues that CRE's reliance on historical weather, standard codes and predictable insurance has become a liability as losses and premiums rise. It presents case studies in which resilience built into design and underwriting preserved asset value, cut insurance costs or attracted tenants, and concludes that front-loading resilience delivers the largest returns.
insights: Global insured losses from weather-related catastrophes reached $137 billion in 2024, and commercial building insurance costs in Florida, California and Texas rose 108% over five years.

JLL research cited finds 53% of US commercial real estate investment over the past decade occurred in markets facing acute climate risk, and 30% of banks hold material climate risk in real estate portfolios representing $627 billion in loans.
Only 21% of natural hazard-prone jurisdictions have adopted current hazard-resistant building codes.
Trammell Crow's Park 8Ninety near Houston raised its site with soil from a 25-foot-deep lake dug in 2015, and stayed dry through Hurricane Harvey's 50 inches of rain.

The Eddy Apartments in Boston elevated critical systems, cutting potential flood loss from $10 million to $1 million and insurance premiums by 90%; in Cape Coral a climate risk assessment revealed potential losses over $6 million on a $36 million retail asset.
Studies cited show $4 to $7 in returns for every dollar spent on adaptation and resilience in buildings.

records.title: Rating Action: Moody's Ratings Downgrades City of Corpus Christi, TX's Issuer and Related Ratings to A1; Outlook Negative
records.summary: Moody's Ratings downgraded Corpus Christi, TX's issuer, general obligation limited tax, sales tax revenue, and combined utility revenue ratings two notches to A1 (from Aa2/Aa3) in December 2025, with a negative outlook, citing acute water supply depletion risk. The city anticipates demand will exceed supply by April 2027, with a Level 1 Emergency threshold potentially triggered by November 2026. The city carries ~$2 billion in total debt and is pursuing groundwater, effluent reuse, and well-drilling projects to avert crisis. ESG factors were explicitly material to the action.
insights: Corpus Christi's water supply is projected to be insufficient to meet demand by April 2027, a Level 1 Emergency threshold could be triggered as early as November 2026, giving the city fewer than 12 months of implementation margin at the time of rating action.

The two-notch downgrade (Aa2→A1 issuer; Aa3→A1 utility) on ~$2 billion in outstanding debt directly demonstrates how acute physical water stress can translate into measurable credit deterioration for a U.S. municipal issuer.

Persistent drought along the Texas Gulf Coast and heavy industrial water use are the primary supply drivers; the Lake Corpus Christi and Choke Canyon reservoirs (Western Supply) have not received sufficient rainfall for replenishment, accelerating the emergency timeline.

The city is pursuing three near-term supply diversification interventions: groundwater access from the Evangeline Aquifer, effluent reuse for industrial users, and well drilling (Nueces Groundwater Program Western Well Field targeted for completion May 2026), all running parallel to the emergency trigger date, leaving near-zero margin for delay.

Financial reserves are projected to decline to 31% of FY2026 revenue due to capital spending; if the fund balance ratio falls below 25%, Moody's has signaled a further downgrade, quantifying a specific fiscal threshold linked to physical risk.

The utility restructured its rate design to shift revenue toward fixed charges and reduce volumetric rates, improving coverage stability even amid residential conservation, a replicable structural response to demand-side uncertainty under water stress.

Resident median income is ~82% of national median, constraining the city's political capacity to levy the significant rate increases and debt issuance required to fund water supply solutions, creating a distributional equity tension between fiscal necessity and affordability.

records.title: Advancing Adaptation: How Evolving Hazards Could Shape the Agenda
records.authors: Mekala Krishnan, Olivia White, Sylvain Johansson, Sven Smit, Annabel Farr, Kanmani Chockalingam
records.summary: The McKinsey Global Institute report “Advancing adaptation: how evolving hazards could shape the agenda” examines how rising physical climate risks, from sea-level rise and extreme heat to shifting precipitation patterns, will reshape investment and policy priorities over the coming decades. It quantifies growing exposures, highlights the substantial adaptation financing gap, and outlines a three-horizon framework for scaling resilience, from near-term protective measures to systemic integration and long-term transformational change. The report calls for stronger data and standards, greater public-private collaboration, and targeted nature-based and engineered solutions to mobilize the estimated trillions needed for effective adaptation.
insights: The framing claim is that change is uneven in three dimensions at once: not everywhere, not in the same way, and not all at once. Freezing is expected to decline, and drought or flood risk may fall in small areas even while rising elsewhere, so an adaptation cost model cannot assume monotonic increase.

About 40 percent of the Earth's landmass already experiences severe heat, destructive wildfire, prolonged drought or severe flooding, and some 35 percent experiences freezing days, so the baseline is current weather extremes rather than a future scenario.

Heat stress, defined as more than four weeks a year of high temperature and humidity affecting labour productivity, expands by roughly 25 percent of global landmass at 1.5 degrees and more than 50 percent at 2 degrees, with already-exposed regions going from about 12 weeks to more than 16.

Hazards are defined using protection standards typical of developed economies, which is a consequential methodological choice for a global cost estimate because it sets the level of protection being priced.

The authors state they are not climate scientists and that the results are directional assessments rather than high-resolution predictions, offered as the basis for an order-of-magnitude assessment of adaptation costs and benefits. The companion report prices 20 proven, cost-effective adaptation measures.

records.title: Advancing Adaptation: Mapping Costs from Cooling to Coastal Defenses
records.authors: Mekala Krishnan, Olivia White, Sylvain Johansson, Sven Smit, Annabel Farr, Kanmani Chockalingam
records.summary: The document provides a comprehensive analysis of adaptation costs associated with various climate hazards, focusing on eight types of hazards including heat stress, wildfires, droughts, and flooding. It assesses current protection measures, future adaptation costs, and the efficacy of different adaptation strategies across demographic groups. The research utilizes external climate models to estimate exposure to these hazards and emphasizes the importance of establishing clear thresholds for protection standards.
insights: The study examines eight climate hazards grouped into four categories: heat, wildfire, drought, and flooding.
Adaptation measures can be sector-specific or cross-cutting, addressing vulnerabilities and exposures in diverse contexts.
Costs of adaptation are estimated based on both capital expenditures and operational expenses through 2050.
A variety of thresholds are used to define hazards, which influence exposure estimates and the required adaptation measures.
Maladaptation poses risks wherein adaptation efforts can inadvertently create new vulnerabilities or negative consequences.
The analysis aligns with IPCC data regarding climate hazard confidence and their projected impacts across different global regions.
The findings suggest that as global temperatures rise, higher levels of adaptation will be necessary to mitigate increasing climate risks.
Uncertainties inherent to climate modeling necessitate ongoing research and flexibility in adaptation planning.
Demand for adaptation measures could increase significantly as populations face growing exposure to various climatic hazards.
The research highlights the need for continuous assessments to evaluate the effectiveness and economic viability of adaptation strategies.

records.title: Massachusetts Atlas of Disaster (2011-2024)
institutions: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
records.summary: This Rebuild by Design atlas documents the 11 federally declared climate disasters Massachusetts experienced between 2011 and 2024 and the more than $541 million in FEMA and HUD post-disaster funding they drew. It maps disaster occurrences, federal assistance, social vulnerability and hazard exposure county by county, and describes rising property insurance costs and very low flood insurance take-up. It reviews state programs such as the 2018 Environmental Bond Act, the Municipal Vulnerability Preparedness program and the ResilientMass Plan, and argues for a dedicated state funding source for adaptation, notably a small surcharge on property insurance.
insights: Massachusetts had 11 federally declared major climate disasters from 2011 to 2024, costing more than $541 million in FEMA and HUD post-disaster funding, about $77 per capita.
Bristol and Suffolk counties each had eight disasters, the highest in the state; Hampden County had the highest federal spending and the highest social vulnerability score.
Homeowners faced a nearly 16% property insurance premium increase in 2025, and fewer than 2% of Massachusetts homes carry NFIP flood insurance.

Bill S.572/H.938 would levy a 2% surcharge on real estate property insurance, expected to raise $80-95 million a year for adaptation; the atlas states $6.7 billion of climate infrastructure could be supported this way.
In 2025 the MVP program received $110 million in funding requests and awarded almost $29 million in grants.
Recommends shifting post-disaster federal dollars to pre-disaster funding and requiring insurers to price mitigation, modelled on the NFIP Community Rating System.

records.title: Lessons on Recovery and Resilience in a Survey of L.A. Fire Survivors
records.summary: This article summarises a Department of Angels survey of fire survivors released in October, nine months after the Eaton and Palisades fires. It identifies three problems: exhausted displacement coverage, worse claim outcomes for owners of damaged but standing homes, and poor access to contamination testing. It recommends enforcing displacement coverage, expanding testing and case managers, and describes insurance models that finance resilience, including resilience endorsements, resilience credits, premium discounts and community-based policies.
insights: 12% of Altadena and 20% of Pacific Palisades residents have exhausted displacement coverage, rising to 23% and 29% within the next year.
Survivors with damaged but standing homes are four times more likely to experience claim denials and six times more likely to have all claims rejected than those who lost everything.
55% of homes tested had contaminant levels above thresholds; insurance covered testing for 29% of standing-home residents while 27% paid out of pocket.
Over half of survivors want a case manager but only 6% have one, and more than 80% support investment in fire-safety upgrades.
California's FAIR Plan now offers up to 25% premium reductions for properties meeting wildfire safety standards.

records.title: Finding Inspiration in an Atlas of Solutions [Episode 24]
institutions: United States Department of Housing and Urban Development
records.summary: Amy Chester of Rebuild by Design describes two bodies of work. The first is the original competition, which carved a portion out of roughly $65 billion of disaster recovery funds and offered it to interdisciplinary teams on three conditions: work with communities and local governments on the ground, develop something that would not otherwise have been done, and address multiple challenges with multiple benefits. Ten teams worked across the region, projects were taken to the public for support, and seven were awarded. The Hoboken resiliency park is the worked example, a concrete structure beneath a park that pumps and holds water from twenty surrounding blocks while functioning as ordinary public space above; Hoboken has paired it with a waterfront park, an interior flood wall and streets redesigned for both pedestrian safety and water retention. The second body of work is the atlas series, which lets anyone look up their own county's federally declared disasters from 2011 to 2024, see how much FEMA and HUD money arrived and what that is per capita, and connect to their congressional representative. She notes an internal analysis, initially unpublished, finding that disaster funding to red and blue states was broadly similar, and a separate finding that 77 percent of New York City parks will intersect a future flood zone.
insights: The competition's conditions functioned as the instrument: money was offered only for work co-developed with communities, that would not otherwise have happened, and that delivered multiple benefits, which is outcome-shaping through eligibility rather than through evaluation.

Governments are described as reluctant to publish a big idea because they fear being held accountable for implementing it, which is a political constraint on ambition that later funding availability exposed.

The atlas turns federal disaster spending into a constituent-level fact, county by county and per capita, with a route to a representative, which makes an accountability instrument out of data that was already public.
Treating parks as major infrastructure is supported by the finding that 77 percent of New York City parks will intersect a future flood zone, which makes the parks budget a flood budget.
The unpublished red-state and blue-state comparison of disaster funding found broadly similar totals, which is evidence against a partisan-allocation reading of federal disaster money.

records.title: The Weekly: The Real Infrastructure Behind the Cloud
records.summary: The lead feature argues that the AI-driven boom in data center construction is placing critical digital infrastructure in climate-exposed US regions. Drawing on an XDI analysis of nearly 9,000 data centers, it makes three points: facilities are only as resilient as the roads, water and communications they depend on; insurance for data centers in high-risk places such as New Jersey may become prohibitively expensive or be withdrawn; and targeted retrofits can sharply reduce the number of high-risk facilities. It gives Equinix's Miami data center as an example of resilient design.
insights: The US data center industry is expected to reach $309 billion by 2030.
XDI analysed nearly 9,000 operational and planned data centers worldwide; the WEF estimates climate-driven inefficiencies and damages to data centers could cost $3.3 trillion cumulatively by 2055.
Retrofits such as flood barriers, better drainage and stronger roofs could reduce high-risk facilities by 72% by 2050, lowering insurance costs (XDI).
Insurance for data centers in high-risk locations such as New Jersey is on track to become prohibitively expensive or be withdrawn.
Equinix's Miami data center sits 14 feet above sea level with critical infrastructure a further 18 feet up, giving 32 feet of surge clearance, and is built for Category 5 winds.
25 states have introduced legislation to improve climate adaptation.

records.title: New Analysis of Home Sales Makes Economic Case for Resilient Coastal Forests
institutions: Center for Coastal Climate Resilience at UC Santa Cruz
records.summary: A new study highlights the economic benefits of mangrove forests for coastal homeowners in Florida, revealing that proximity to these natural features can preserve home values by $20,000 to $60,000 during storm events. The research provides the first market-based evidence showing homebuyers value the storm-protective qualities of mangroves, encouraging financial support for their protection and restoration.
insights: Homes near mangroves in coastal Florida experience smaller price declines after storms compared to those further away.
The average financial protection per $1 million home from mangroves ranges from $20,000 to $40,000, with some instances up to $60,000.
This study is the first to use housing market data to quantify the storm-protection value of mangrove ecosystems.
Strong financial incentives exist for insurers, developers, and investors to support mangrove conservation due to their economic benefits.
The research indicates that homebuyers actively perceive and are willing to pay for the protective benefits of mangroves.
Mangrove protection aligns with broader climate adaptation strategies, offering economic and ecological advantages.
The study supports the concept of valuing ecosystems and biodiversity within financial markets.
Protection and restoration of mangroves can mitigate climate change impacts and increasing hurricane frequency.
Additional benefits of mangroves include protection of non-housing assets like agricultural land, infrastructure, and tourism.
Future work is needed to develop financial tools to facilitate investment in mangrove conservation.

records.title: Fintech Innovation in Green Finance: A Disruptive Force or a Complementary Tool?
records.authors: Fengsheng Chien, Yunqian Zhang, Muhammad Sadiq
institutions: Fuzhou University of International Studies and Trade
records.summary: The resource analyzes the significant role of FinTech innovation in advancing green finance, highlighting its benefits in transparency and efficiency, especially within developed economies, while also addressing the challenges faced by emerging markets due to regulatory gaps. It discusses various innovative solutions, including central bank digital currencies and regulatory sandboxes, aimed at fostering climate tech investments, particularly in countries like Nigeria and Indonesia, and emphasizes the necessity for tailored global policies to promote equitable integration of FinTech in the green finance sector.
insights: FinTech significantly improves the transparency and efficiency of green finance markets, especially in developed economies.
Emerging markets face structural challenges in green finance, but FinTech tools can help improve access to funds and risk management.
The uncontrolled growth of FinTech in emerging markets can lead to increased financial risks, including cybersecurity threats.
Countries with strong regulatory frameworks experience higher yields from the integration of FinTech in green finance.
CBDC implementation in Nigeria demonstrated a reduction of interest rates by 4.5% for SMEs in the renewable sector.
Regulatory sandboxes can create exempt environments to foster climate-tech investments while maintaining regulatory stability.
Fintech innovations are potential enablers for achieving climate goals through improved lending practices.

records.title: Risk Ownership in a Time of Rising Climate Costs: Rethinking Who Pays, Who Benefits, and How We Move Forward
records.authors: Nuin-Tara Key, Carolyn Kousky, Joshua Mendoza
records.summary: The second installment in a blog series discusses the escalating economic risks due to climate change and the need to rethink risk ownership. As the costs of climate-related shocks increase, current financing systems for resilience are found lacking. This blog emphasizes aligning responsibility, incentives, and investments across sectors to effectively manage risk and integrate resilience as a mainstream investment rather than an afterthought.
insights: The rising costs of climate change are straining households, businesses, and communities, necessitating a reevaluation of risk ownership.
Current systems for financing resilience are fragmented and ill-equipped to address today's climate threats.
Measuring and valuing avoided losses is crucial to encourage investments in risk mitigation.
Bridging the communication gap between engineers, financial decision-makers, and budget managers is essential for scaling resilience solutions.
Insurance alone cannot solve the funding gap for resilience; collaborative, multi-sector approaches are needed.
New models for risk ownership must emerge, recognizing the shared nature of climate-related risks.
Innovative financing tools can unlock demand for resilience investments, making them more appealing for stakeholders.
Public-private funding pools and resilience districts can provide alternative paths for funding resilience projects.
Stakeholder incentives must be aligned to ensure that all parties benefit from mitigation efforts without unfairly bearing costs.

records.title: Funding and Financing Options for Resilience Investments
records.authors: Nuin-Tara Key, Carolyn Kousky, Tai Michaels
records.summary: The first part of a blog series by CA FWD and Insurance for Good discusses the urgent need for funding and financing strategies to enhance climate resilience amid rising climate change costs. Highlighting key challenges and options for resilience investments, it emphasizes the critical role of both funding and financing in mitigating the economic impacts of climate change and adapting communities effectively.
insights: Climate change is projected to reduce global income by at least 20% over the next 25 years.
Extreme weather events cost the world $16 million per hour, accumulating to $2 trillion over the last decade.
Many communities struggle to implement adaptation projects due to insufficient funding.
Funding refers to actual dollars for investments, while financing includes methods to manage large sums over time.
There are five primary strategies for securing funds for resilience investments: use current budgets, save over time, pay later via debt, use insurance-like financing, and seek grants.
Budget constraints and competing priorities hinder local and state governments from adequately addressing climate adaptation.
Projected future losses are often not tracked on balance sheets, complicating cash flow management for investments.
Many markets fail to fully price climate risks, limiting the effectiveness of insurance and lending.
Community benefits from resilience investments are often diffuse, complicating funding and recognition of their value.

records.title: Reflection Group on Mobilising Climate Resilience Financing: Final Report
records.authors: Reflection Group on Mobilising Climate Resilience Financing
records.summary: The final report of the Reflection Group on Mobilising Climate Resilience Financing, published through the European Commission's climate site on 2 December 2025. Its disclaimer is explicit: the considerations are compiled under the aegis of the Group's members, it is not an official Commission document, it does not reflect an official Commission position, and nothing in it commits the Commission or precludes any policy outcome. Its recommended actions are organised by actor rather than by theme, in four sets: the public sector; joint action by public and market operators; the competent authorities, meaning sector ministries, standards offices and regional and local governments; and insurance. The body covers the state of play and expectations for climate resilience, the business and economic case for resilience split into economic risks and opportunities, business risks and opportunities and the alignment of the two, climate resilience communication including improved understanding of risks and public-private dialogue, and filling information gaps and improving data structure and accessibility.
insights: The recommendations are organised by actor rather than by theme, so the report says who does each thing rather than what should happen, and it gives insurance a section of its own rather than folding it into the private sector.

Separating the business case from the economic case, and then devoting a section to aligning them, concedes the thing most resilience advocacy elides: what is worth it to a society is not automatically worth it to a firm, and the gap between them is where an instrument has to sit.

The disclaimer matters for how it is cited: this is expert-group advice carrying no Commission commitment, so it is evidence of what was recommended in Europe in late 2025 rather than of what the EU intends.

A dedicated chapter on information gaps and data accessibility puts it alongside the IIGCC record on incomplete asset-level vendor data and the WMO record on underfunded climate services. Three independent sources now name information as a binding constraint rather than a preliminary.

records.title: The Long-Term Benefits of Nature-Based Solutions [Episode 22]
institutions: United States Army Corps of Engineers
records.summary: Leonard Nelson, CEO and co-founder of Natrx, makes the asset-versus-liability case for nature-based coastal infrastructure. Hard, impervious structures speed water up, which is what makes storm surge dangerous, while reefs, oyster beds and woody debris slow it down; and where a sea wall or road is a depreciating liability from the moment it is built, a nature-based installation is an asset that gains value over time. His economic argument is that traditional construction is now expensive enough, in materials and in the multi-year study, permitting and mitigation cycle it requires, that nature-based approaches frequently come out cheaper. He notes that the long lead times of conventional waterfront construction push designers to overbuild because they get only one attempt, which inflates both budgets and timelines, whereas nature-based techniques can be adapted incrementally. On permitting he reports broad regulatory consensus, citing the Army Corps of Engineers' Engineering With Nature programme, and describes offering agencies simple habitat-to-impact ratios, where a sea wall scores negative. He also names the obstacle plainly: inertia in a roughly $10 trillion global heavy infrastructure market where people are used to doing things the way they are used to doing them.
insights: The framing that carries the financial weight is asset versus liability: a sea wall or road begins depreciating on completion, while a nature-based installation accrues value, which changes how the investment should be carried and financed rather than only how it is justified.

Overbuilding is presented as a consequence of process, not of engineering caution: a five-year permitting and mitigation cycle means one attempt, so designers oversize, which is a procurement-driven cost that incremental nature-based approaches avoid.
Habitat-to-impact ratios are used as the simple metric offered to resource agencies, and a sea wall scores negative on it, which is how permitting consensus is built without case-by-case argument.

The stated impediment is mindset inside a roughly $10 trillion global heavy construction market rather than cost or regulation, and clients who seriously evaluate the option with an economic benefit almost always choose it.
The company's path ran through RISE's federally originated innovation lab, which is a concrete instance of public catalytic funding producing a scaling private supplier.

records.title: Resilience Taxonomy for U.S. Infrastructure
records.summary: Kestrel 360's "Resilience Taxonomy for U.S. Infrastructure" (December 2025) is a practitioner-facing methodology document that codifies how the firm identifies and scores resilience features across nine municipal infrastructure sectors, roads/bridges, multimodal transportation, K-12 schools, higher education, airports, drinking water, wastewater, electric utilities, and healthcare. Drawing on benchmarking of over 15,000 municipal bond series covering more than $3T par, Kestrel maps sector-specific resilience indicators to its Sustainability Scores, citing a $4–$10 return per $1 invested in infrastructure resilience, and positions these scores as inputs for investors pricing physical and transition risk in the U.S. municipal bond market.
insights: Kestrel has benchmarked over 15,000 series of municipal bonds covering more than $3T par value, giving the taxonomy an empirical foundation rare in ESG/resilience rating methodologies.

The document cites a $4–$10 return for every $1 spent on infrastructure resilience, sourced from WRI (2025) and the Global Commission on Adaptation (2019), providing a high-level BCR range relevant to capital allocators evaluating resilience investments.

Resilience features are embedded directly into Kestrel's Sustainability Scores (Environmental and Social sub-scores) rather than treated as a separate overlay, meaning resilience quality already influences bond-level scoring visible on Bloomberg and Investortools, key distribution channels for institutional fixed-income investors.

The taxonomy organizes indicators at two levels, community (equitable access, pre-disaster planning, emergency preparedness) and organization (vulnerability assessments, resilience plans, contingency plans), enabling both equity-focused and credit-focused users to locate relevant disclosures.

Sector-specific indicators reveal high granularity: e.g., airport runways extended for heat adaptation, bidirectional EV bus chargers with vehicle-to-grid capability at K-12 schools, and High Temperature Low Sag (HTLS) conductors for electric utilities, each representing capital expenditure line items that practitioners and engineers can verify in bond documents.

The framework explicitly links resilience to financial materiality: 'Sustainability and resilience are likely to become material drivers of asset valuations as the growing frequency of extreme weather events affects insurance markets and federal emergency support,' signaling a pricing-shift argument for allocators.

records.title: The Resilience Dividend: How Adaptability Builds Long Term Value
records.summary: The article discusses the increasing importance of resilience in the face of climate change and socio-economic disruptions. It emphasizes that traditional corporate efficiency is becoming a liability, while adaptability and resilience are emerging as essential components for long-term value creation. The narrative highlights the need for financial systems and businesses to innovate and invest in resilience-oriented practices, as they grapple with rising risks associated with climate-related shocks.
insights: Political uncertainty is affecting financial and corporate stability, prompting a shift toward resilience as a performance benchmark.
Traditional notions of efficiency are exposed as vulnerabilities in an unpredictable world, highlighting the need for flexibility.
Resilience is defined as the capacity to live and thrive amid change, rather than merely returning to the status quo.
Climate-driven disasters are straining insurance models, leading to higher premiums and reduced coverage in affected areas.
Resilience investments can yield significant economic returns, with a report suggesting that every dollar invested may generate four dollars in benefits.
Barriers to resilience investment include policy failures, mispricing of climate risk, and short-term market focuses.
Creating equitable resilience is essential, as social inequalities affect outcomes and benefits.
Resilience needs to shift from a project-oriented approach to a structural principle integrated into decision-making across sectors.
The concept of resilience is gaining traction as a foundation for long-term growth and competitiveness in turbulent times.
Addressing climate risk will require innovative financial mechanisms and systemic integration of resilience in fiscal frameworks.

records.title: CCRIF SPC Annual Report 2024 - 2025
records.summary: CCRIF SPC, the Catastrophe Risk Insurance Facility of the Caribbean and Central America, reports on 2024-2025. Established in 2007 after Hurricane Ivan, it is the world's largest parametric insurance programme and the first multi-country, multi-peril risk pool, created to close the liquidity gap and give governments rapid access to funds after a disaster without adding to their debt. It now has 35 members, has made 82 payouts totalling over US$483 million over two decades, offers seven products and carries US$1.4 billion of coverage purchased. Cover spans tropical cyclones, earthquakes, excess rainfall, and the fisheries and electric and water utilities sectors, with payouts made within 14 days of an event so governments, public utilities and public entities can meet urgent needs, stabilise budgets and accelerate recovery. Risk pooling secures better reinsurance prices and so makes cover more affordable to members. In 2024 Hurricane Beryl produced US$84.5 million in payouts to seven members including governments, electric and water utilities and a tourist attraction. The report notes the protection gap is widening: in developing countries only 5 per cent of natural-hazard losses are insured, against about 50 per cent in developed nations. Alongside insurance, CCRIF funds scholarships and internships for Caribbean youth, small community resilience grants and capacity building for regional organisations.
insights: The 14-day payout is the product, not a service level: CCRIF was built to close a liquidity gap rather than an indemnity gap, so speed rather than completeness of cover is what it sells.

US$483 million of payouts over eighteen years against US$1.4 billion of coverage currently purchased shows a facility whose value is in the tail: most years pay nothing and the structure has to survive them.
