records.summary: A Resilient Cities Network report, lead-authored by Sadiq Currimbhoy of Resilient Horizons with four R-Cities contributors, arguing for a portfolio approach to financing city resilience rather than the project-by-project route cities are pushed toward. It follows a March 2024 convening on investing in resilience and was published in September 2025. The report treats a city's resilience needs as a portfolio to be financed as a whole, which changes what an investor is being asked to underwrite and what a city has to be able to show, and connects that to observable market signals including insurance non-renewal rates in the counties most exposed to climate risk.
insights: The portfolio framing is the argument, not a presentational device: financing a bundle rather than a project changes the diligence burden, the tenor and who can plausibly hold the risk, and it is the structural answer to the fact that individual municipal resilience projects are too small and too slow to attract institutional capital.
R-Cities is registered in New York, Amsterdam and Singapore, and the report is written for cities in all three regions, so its claims should not be read as US-specific even where the evidence is.

The report reaches for insurance market data, non-renewal rates by county exposure as of December 2024, as evidence about CITY FINANCE rather than about insurance, using the insurer's withdrawal as a signal of fiscal exposure.

records.title: How Do We Protect Our Homes from the Growing Threat of Wildfires? [Episode 4]
records.summary: Mark Brown, executive officer of the Marin Wildfire Prevention Authority and formerly a deputy fire chief with 30 years at Marin County Fire, makes the case for shifting effort from suppression to pre-fire work, on the grounds that firefighters start every fire behind. His subject is Zone Zero, the combustible-free zone within five feet of a home, and the problem he is solving is adoption at community scale: the risk one household carries depends on what its neighbours do, and homeowners facing a long inspection list do nothing. The structural approach he describes aims to create a market for Zone Zero services where none exists. On finance, his stated first objective is insurance availability rather than price, and he reports that parts of Marin have seen a 200 to 300 percent increase in homes covered by the California FAIR Plan, with one community at roughly 27 percent of homes on FAIR Plan policies, which cover wildfire only and so require a wraparound policy for everything else.
insights: Availability is named as the problem to solve before price: the objective is to restore insurability first and discuss premium reduction second, which reverses the usual framing of mitigation as a route to cheaper cover.

The residual market is carrying the shift in measurable terms: a 200 to 300 percent rise in FAIR Plan coverage in parts of Marin, and roughly 27 percent of homes in one community on FAIR Plan policies, which cover wildfire alone and require a second wraparound policy.

Avoided-loss evidence is offered from the 2017 Thomas Fire at Montecito, where prior fuel breaks and home hardening accompanied 1,300 homes impacted and 12 structures destroyed, and where one crew could do the work that would otherwise need four.

Wildfire risk is treated as a collective good rather than a private one, since a hardened home reduces its neighbours' risk, which is the argument for a community-scale intervention rather than a per-household subsidy.

A single-mission public authority funded solely for wildfire mitigation is put forward as the institutional innovation, on the argument that a general fire department can only give mitigation a fraction of its attention.

records.title: From Disaster to Blueprint: How Greenline's Model Could Transform Post-Fire Recovery
records.summary: The profile describes how the Greenline Housing Foundation responded to the January 2025 Eaton Fire in Altadena with the Eaton Fire Relief Fund, a blended capital stack of philanthropy and debt. The fund provides interim housing and rental assistance, rebuilding grants to close the gap between insurance or FEMA payouts and rebuilding costs, and an anti-speculation landbanking program financed with impact and CDFI debt. It presents the model as a template for community-based post-disaster rebuilding and closes with four recommendations for organizations seeking to replicate it.
insights: Nearly half (48%) of Black-owned homes in Altadena were destroyed or seriously damaged by the Eaton Fire, most owned by people over 65.
Greenline deployed over $500,000 in interim housing assistance to 28 families through corporate leases and subsidized subleases.
A $1.35 million commitment from the California Endowment and Walgreens anchors rebuilding grants of up to $250,000 per family for 50 families, aimed at insurance shortfalls of $150,000 to $300,000.

Debt from impact investors, the California Wellness Foundation and CDFIs, including a Program-Related Investment from Clearinghouse CDFI, funds landbanking of 10 lots by October 2025 and 40 more by July 2026, with capital returned on each lot sale.
The recommendations are to build relationships before disaster, favour partnership over competition, match capital types to need and time horizon, and align stakeholder interests.

records.title: Global Landscape of Climate Finance 2025
records.authors: Baysa Naran, Varun Shankar, Pedro de Aragão Fernandes, James Dixon, Joe Burnett, Sasha Abraham, Sean Stout, Jake Connolly, Costanza Strinati
records.summary: The Global Landscape of Climate Finance 2025 report reveals significant growth in global climate finance, which reached USD 1.9 trillion in 2023, driven largely by private sector contributions and addressing emerging economies' financing disparities. With a growing emphasis on innovative financing solutions for adaptation and resilience, the report underscores the necessity for enhanced collaboration and transparency in funding mechanisms to meet net-zero goals and emphasizes the need for substantial investments across various sectors, particularly clean energy and agriculture, to effectively tackle climate challenges.
insights: Private climate finance contributions surpassed USD 1 trillion for the first time in 2023.
Mitigation finance dominated global climate flows with USD 1,780 billion allocated in 2023.
Emerging economies require more catalytic capital to enhance climate finance access.
Investment in clean energy is increasingly driving GDP growth in countries like China.
Despite growth, a substantial gap remains, necessitating USD 6 trillion annually to meet climate goals by 2030.
Adaptation finance tracking faces challenges that may lead to underestimation of actual flows.
Public finance fell by 14%, highlighting the need for increased national development finance contributions.
Collaborative efforts between public and private sectors are critical to mobilize sufficient capital for climate action.
A notable disparity in adaptation finance needs exists, particularly in vulnerable regions like Sub-Saharan Africa.

records.title: How Do We Make Permanent Affordable Housing a Community Asset? [Episode 3]
records.summary: Ashon Nesbitt, CEO of the Florida Housing Coalition, explains the community land trust as a structural answer to the expiry of affordability: the trust retains the land under a ground lease, removing it permanently from the speculative market, so that public subsidy is not lost when a subsidy term ends. The financing problem he describes is that CLT mortgages are still written as one-off transactions, and his organisation has built standards and a certification so that lenders can underwrite them against known criteria and the resulting mortgages can reach the wider financial system. He then joins that to resilience: because a CLT property is intended to stand in perpetuity, it is worth building to a standard above Florida's already strong code, and he argues the mortgage will follow the insurance, so that if financing becomes unavailable in high-hazard areas property values fall in exactly the communities already devalued. He names the perverse incentive directly, that insurance priced on replacement cost can raise the premium on a more resilient and more expensive building, and asks how the risk reduction can be credited back.
insights: The load-bearing argument is a pricing one: insurance priced on replacement cost penalises a more resilient, more expensive building, so the risk reduction the owner paid for is not credited. He asks for lower cost of capital or insurance savings to close the gap, and states that those mechanisms do not exist in Florida today.

A lending certification for community land trusts is being used as the bridge from one-off CLT mortgage transactions to standardised products the broader financial system can absorb, which is the same standard-as-market-access move the insurance argument asks for and has not yet won.

The mortgage follows the insurance: if coverage becomes unobtainable, financing follows, and depressed property values land on communities that were already devalued, which makes insurance availability a credit and wealth question rather than only a coverage one.
Permanent affordability and resilience are argued to reinforce each other, because a property held in perpetuity justifies a higher build standard than a property whose affordability term expires.
Florida's building code is described as already exceeding most states, so the live question is incentivising building above code rather than raising the floor.

records.title: Preparing Regulation for Climate-Resilient Restoration: Learning From Emerging Technologies
records.authors: Mary C. Fisher; Marissa L. Baskett; Andrew C. Baker; Ashley Kidd; Michael R. Springborn; Tyler A. Scott
records.summary: A perspective in Conservation Letters, volume 18 issue 4, first published 22 August 2025, arguing that the gap between the literature on climate-resilient ecosystem restoration and its practice is partly created by regulation. Current paradigms in resource and environmental management, and the regulatory structures attached to them, can unintentionally contribute to the implementation gap. The authors' proposal is to borrow regulatory approaches developed for emerging or disruptive technologies, specifically regulatory greenhouses or sandboxes and risk-weighted regulation, and apply them to restoration interventions that account for climate change. The work was funded by NSF DISES award 2108002, with additional support to one author from the University of California Agricultural Experiment Station.
insights: Risk-weighted regulation is the transferable idea: it scales the regulatory burden to the expected harm of an intervention rather than treating every novel action as high risk, which is the same logic a lender applies to a borrower.

A regulatory sandbox is a financing question disguised as a permitting one. An intervention that cannot be trialled cannot build the evidence a funder needs, so the regulatory bottleneck and the capital bottleneck are the same bottleneck at different points.

The author list spans population biology, economics and public policy with a University of Miami coral scientist among them, which is why the restoration examples reach beyond terrestrial conservation.
The record was staged with a July date and the journal states 22 August 2025 as first publication.

records.title: ResilientMass Finance Strategy
records.authors: Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs, ResilientMass
records.summary: The ResilientMass Finance Strategy presents a comprehensive framework for Massachusetts to tackle climate change impacts through a whole-of-government approach, requiring an investment range of $90 billion to $130 billion until 2050. It emphasizes proactive investments in critical infrastructure, community engagement, and adaptable financing mechanisms to enhance resilience, streamline project delivery, and ensure equitable access to resources across all communities.
insights: Massachusetts faces increasing climate-related challenges, requiring an estimated investment of $90 billion to $130 billion for resilience measures by 2050.
Early interventions can significantly reduce costs, with potential savings of $6 to $13 for every dollar invested in resilience.
The strategy promotes community engagement and equitable access to financial resources, especially for disadvantaged populations, during project implementation.
Innovative financing models, including pay-for-performance contracts, are essential for sustainable and effective investment in resilience projects.
A centralized tracking framework is crucial for monitoring project progress and ensuring accountability in resilience investments.

records.title: More Resilient by Design: North Carolina’s Flood Resiliency Blueprint
records.authors: North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality
institutions: North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality
records.summary: More Resilient by Design: North Carolina's Flood Resiliency Blueprint, the Spring 2025 update from the Department of Environmental Quality's Division of Mitigation Services. The Blueprint exists by statute: in 2021 the General Assembly passed Section 5.9(c) of Session Law 2021-180 directing DEQ's Division of Mitigation Services to develop it, and in 2022 Section 22 of Session Law 2022-75 added guidance on how the Blueprint should use data to support decision making and to reduce the cost and complexity for local governments of developing projects that reduce flood risk. Separately, Session Law 2021-180 Section 40.7(a) as amended by Session Law 2022-43 Section 2(a) appropriated $96,000,000 to DEQ for flood mitigation projects in prioritised river basins, to be used after the initial draft Blueprint was completed.
insights: The appropriation is conditioned on the planning artifact existing first: $96 million for flood mitigation in prioritised river basins, available only once the draft Blueprint was complete. North Carolina's version of that sequence builds one statewide data product rather than funding workshops municipality by municipality.

The legislature's stated aim is to reduce the cost and complexity for local governments to develop projects, which writes the project-preparation gap into statute as the thing the money is meant to fix.
Prioritising by river basin rather than by jurisdiction lets the allocation see upstream and downstream together, which a municipality-by-municipality grant programme cannot do.

The document is labelled a Spring 2025 update while the record carries August 2025. The label is the document's own and the discrepancy is recorded rather than resolved, since no precise publication date appears.
records.publisher: North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality

records.title: What If a Once-In-A Generation Hurricane Were to Hit South Florida This Year?
records.authors: Chris Lafakis, Adam Kamins, Theresa Lederer, Jacob van Nieuwkerk
records.summary: A Moody's special report, published 21 August 2025, modelling the macroeconomic consequences of a rare Category 5 hurricane making landfall at Homestead, Florida in 2025, using Moody's RMS catastrophe models and the Moody's Economic Exposure Database. Economic losses along the storm path total $232 billion, with 90 per cent, or $212 billion, concentrated in Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach counties, which together account for 33 per cent of Florida's GDP and between 33 and 46 per cent of state GDP in transportation and warehousing, information, retail and wholesale trade, finance and insurance, professional and business services and real estate. Wind damage to buildings drives the majority of losses, with the remainder from storm surge and precipitation-induced flooding. Both scenarios modelled exceed $200 billion, which would make it the costliest hurricane in US history, surpassing Hurricane Katrina's inflation-adjusted $195 billion. The moderate scenario assumes $144 billion of federal assistance modelled on the Katrina response, under which homeowners insurance premiums rise 60 per cent from Q4 2025 within five years and nearly triple by end-2036. The severe scenario assumes no supplemental federal relief: insurers become insolvent or non-renew widely, premiums rise 200 per cent within five years and quadruple by end-2036, insurance becomes unaffordable and drives outmigration. Miami-Dade gross metro product falls 30 per cent in Q4 2025, far worse than a typical recession, and remains 5 per cent below baseline in the severe scenario. Population falls 7 per cent temporarily under the moderate scenario and nearly 20 per cent under the severe one by 2030. Insurance costs are currently about 6.5 per cent of the cost of owning and operating a home in Miami and rise to 20 per cent by 2030 under the severe scenario, lowering house prices 12 per cent.
insights: The insurance channel, not the physical damage, does the lasting harm: insurance costs rising from 6.5 to 20 per cent of the cost of owning a home is what lowers house prices 12 per cent and drives the outmigration, so the permanent loss runs through the premium rather than through the wind.

The two scenarios differ only in whether federal aid arrives, and that single variable moves the five-year premium increase from 60 per cent to 200 per cent and the population loss from 7 per cent to nearly 20 per cent. Federal disaster relief is therefore an insurance-market stabiliser as much as a rebuilding fund.

$232 billion of loss with 90 per cent in three counties is the concentration figure any Florida resilience instrument is sized against, and those same three counties carry a third of state GDP, so the fiscal and the physical exposure coincide exactly.

A 30 per cent quarterly decline in Miami-Dade gross metro product is far outside recession experience, which is the report's argument that a Category 5 in Miami is not a large disaster but a different category of event.

Permanently higher insurance costs reduce the labour force and therefore GDP growth indefinitely, so the modelled recovery is incomplete under both scenarios: the economy does not return to its pre-event path.

records.title: Managing Climate Risk: Implications for Local Governments
records.summary: The resource highlights the growing challenges local governments face in managing climate risks due to extreme weather events, emphasizing their critical role in adaptation against fiscal constraints. It calls for comprehensive frameworks prioritizing data transparency, consistent funding for adaptation projects, and equitable investment to protect low-income communities. The need for innovative insurance models and effective governance structures is underscored to ensure communities are prepared for climate impacts while balancing socio-economic equity.
insights: Local governments are primarily responsible for climate adaptation, affecting their fiscal capacity and tax revenues.
Public trust in local governments is higher than in other levels of government, providing a unique opportunity for local leaders.
High climate risks can result in declining property values, which have negative implications for local tax revenue.
Data transparency and collaboration with insurers are essential for informed risk management and decision-making.
Innovative insurance models, such as parametric insurance, are necessary to address climate risks effectively.
Effective adaptation governance requires clear authority and frameworks to prioritize investment in resilience.
Consistent funding is crucial for long-term adaptation efforts and can be sourced from diverse channels.
Disinvestment strategies may be necessary in chronic threat areas to optimize resource allocation.
Research is urgently needed to better understand climate risk impacts on municipal finance and lower-income communities.

records.title: Managing Basis Risks in Weather Parametric Insurance: A Quantitative Study of Diversification and Key Influencing Factors
records.authors: Hang Gao; Shuohua Yang; Xinli Liu
records.summary: An article in The Geneva Papers on Risk and Insurance, volume 51 pages 84 to 111 for 2026, received 16 August 2024, accepted 31 July 2025 and published online 19 August 2025, by Hang Gao of China Agricultural Reinsurance Corporation with Shuohua Yang and Xinli Liu. Weather parametric insurance pays on a weather index rather than a loss assessment, which improves claims efficiency, reduces moral hazard and improves fairness, but its market share stays limited because of basis risk, the mismatch between actual loss and payout, appearing either as actual loss without payout or payout without actual loss. The paper isolates basis risk as a structural feature of the parametric trigger, decoupled from its financial consequences for insurer or policyholder, and studies it through Monte Carlo simulations of diversified contract portfolios. Three findings: portfolio basis risk and its volatility both decrease as the number of contracts rises; basis risk follows deterministic patterns set by the ratio of the exposure-to-weather-station distance to the hazard footprint radius, which gives a geometry-driven reference; and hazard event severity does not significantly affect basis risk, so catastrophic severity should not hinder the development of parametric insurance. The conclusion is that basis risk is inherent but manageable through portfolio strategy and geospatial optimisation, and that this is most actionable for insurers, who can diversify at a scale individual policyholders cannot.
insights: The distance-to-footprint-radius ratio turns basis risk into a stated geometry rather than a judgement, so whether a given set of measurement stations is well or badly sited becomes a calculation rather than an opinion.

Finding three removes a standing objection: severity does not drive basis risk, so the argument that parametric cover is unsuited to catastrophic perils does not survive. That matters for every sovereign and ecosystem parametric record here.

The insurer-versus-policyholder asymmetry is the practical conclusion. Basis risk is manageable by diversification, and only a party holding many contracts can diversify, so a single municipality or trust buying one parametric policy cannot reduce its own. That is an argument for pooled structures rather than bespoke ones.
Isolating basis risk from its financial consequences is the methodological move that makes the result general: the geometry holds whoever bears the mismatch.
records.publisher: The Geneva Papers on Risk and Insurance - Issues and Practice

records.title: How Should Climate Policy Integrate Community Knowledge? [Episode 2]
records.summary: Manann Donoghoe, a climate resilience researcher in Brookings Metro's Center for Community Uplift, describes a project building a comparative resilience index across US communities, scored zero to one from publicly available datasets, and then using it as an identification tool rather than a ranking: find the communities scoring high, visit them, and learn from civic leaders what the data cannot show. He argues the drivers worth testing are civic infrastructure, public infrastructure, community organisation strength and wealth. On policy he identifies two openings that survive a changed federal climate posture, disaster policy reform and home casualty insurance, both of which address climate impacts without using the vocabulary of climate change. His closing argument is that the next wave of innovation should be in funding mechanisms that transfer resources to communities and households for resilience building, on the model of international adaptation funds, and he frames resilience investment as something that should be targeted as routinely as inflation or unemployment.
insights: The proposed next frontier is explicitly a funding-mechanism question rather than a policy-language one: a domestic pot of capital, modelled on international adaptation funds, that under-resourced communities can draw on for disaster risk reduction and infrastructure.

Disaster policy and home casualty insurance are named as the two live openings for resilience work under a federal posture hostile to climate framing, because both are addressed in their own vocabulary rather than as climate policy.

The resilience index is designed as an identification tool for positive cases, not a scoring of failure: the stated purpose is to direct policy attention to communities where something is working and to scale what is found there.
An estimated 137 million people, 41 percent of the US population, live in areas regularly affected by major disasters, and FEMA declared a major weather-related disaster every four days in 2024.

The data half of the index is presented as insufficient on its own, with the qualitative site visits treated as a required second pass rather than as colour, which is a methodological commitment rather than a presentational one.

records.title: Investing in Cities: Strengthening Urban Resilience Finance
records.authors: Jessie Press-Williams, Allison Ahern, Wadeisor Rukato
records.summary: The Cities Climate Finance Leadership Alliance, Howden and the Resilient Cities Network convened a high-level roundtable during 2025 London Climate Action Week on public-private models for unlocking urban climate resilience investment, and this reflection summarises the anonymised takeaways. CCFLA research puts city climate mitigation needs at approximately $4.3 trillion a year through 2030. Seven themes emerged: coordination is the constraint rather than capital, since deployment is hampered by fragmented planning and incoherent instruments; blended finance lacks a clear definition and needs creative application of grants, concessional loans and philanthropic capital to de-risk long-term infrastructure; insurance can unlock capital by making projects bankable and by supplying risk expertise, but must be embedded from project design rather than added afterwards; replicable models and aggregation across cities diversify risk and cut transaction costs; restrictive regulation, particularly in developing economies, blocks investment and sandboxing could help; partnerships need clear roles and better matchmaking in a fragmented ecosystem; better data on avoided losses and co-benefits lowers the cost of capital; and investment models should be inclusive rather than purely commercial. The Glasgow case from the Global Risk and Resilience Fellowship, a joint Howden and R-Cities programme, embedded an insurance professional in city leadership to bridge the gap between Glasgow's £30 billion Greenprint for Investment and what banks require. Glasgow learned to reframe climate risk from liability to investment opportunity, but it still took nearly three years to mobilise £4 million.
insights: The Glasgow numbers are the most useful thing in the document: a £30 billion investment prospectus and three years to mobilise £4 million, which puts the real constraint at origination capacity rather than at capital availability.

The stated remedy for that gap was a person, an insurance professional embedded in city leadership, which says the missing input was underwriting fluency inside the public body rather than a new instrument.

The roundtable's insurance point is a sequencing claim: insurance has to be embedded at project design to make a project bankable, because retrofitting coverage onto a finished design cannot change the risk that was built in.
Participants assert there is no shortage of capital, which shifts the entire diagnosis from mobilisation to pipeline, and is the opposite of how the adaptation finance gap is usually framed.
The takeaways are anonymised and summarised, so nothing here is attributable or verifiable against a named institution's position.

records.title: The Economic Commitment of Climate Change
records.authors: Maximilian Kotz, Anders Levermann, Leonie Wenz
institutions: Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research
Mercator Research Institute on Global Commons and Climate Change
records.summary: The resource titled 'The Economic Commitment of Climate Change' synthesizes research on the economic impacts of climate change, revealing a projected median reduction in global income of 17% by mid-century, driven by updated methodologies incorporating subnational data and historical trends. It presents an empirical analysis of the relationship between climate conditions and economic growth, highlighting disparities in impacts on different socio-economic regions, particularly poorer nations. The findings underscore the importance of climate mitigation efforts, adaptation strategies, and the ongoing discourse on climate justice.
insights: The revised estimates show a 17% reduction in global income by mid-century due to climate change.
Methodological updates were made to improve robustness against data inaccuracies, particularly related to Uzbekistan.
The likelihood of damages exceeding mitigation costs has increased to 91% under the new analysis.
Committed damages are especially pronounced in regions with historically low emissions and socioeconomic resilience.
Different climate variables show varied individual impacts on economic output, evidencing the complexity of climate-economy interactions.
The analysis highlights that poorer regions have experienced lower growth rates than their richer counterparts, potentially influenced by climate change.
Future economic damages can be projected by applying estimated empirical model parameters to climate scenarios.
Mitigation costs are assessed as the difference in per capita GDP under various scenarios to evaluate trade-offs.

records.title: When Affordability Is a Challenge, How Do We Address Extreme Weather? [Episode 1]
records.summary: Krista Egger, vice president of Building Resilient Futures at Enterprise Community Partners, argues that affordable housing and climate resilience are one problem rather than two, because the households least able to absorb a shock are the ones living in the least resilient stock. She describes Enterprise's Green Communities certification, now running about 10,000 new certifications a year against a cumulative total near 200,000 homes, and the several state and city housing departments that already condition their affordable-housing allocations on it. The unbuilt piece is financial: she wants a mechanism by which insurers would recognise the certification as evidence that a property will withstand a given hazard, and price it. The conversation also covers self-insurance and risk pools formed among affordable-housing owners as a response to withdrawing coverage, industrialized construction and the shortage of lenders experienced in financing it, and Enterprise's regional Resilience Academies, which combine peer learning, hazard identification across a portfolio and pass-through grant funding.
insights: A green building certification is being proposed as an insurance-pricing signal, not only a design standard: the ask is that insurers treat Green Communities certification as evidence a property will withstand a hazard and reduce premiums accordingly. That link does not exist yet, which is the gap the episode names.

Several state and city housing departments already use the certification to allocate affordable-housing funding, so the standard has become a public-capital allocation rule ahead of becoming a private-capital pricing rule.

Affordable-housing owners are responding to coverage withdrawal by self-insuring and by forming risk pools among like-minded owners, a sector-level risk-transfer response rather than a per-property one.
Financing, not engineering, is the named barrier to industrialized construction: there are few lenders experienced with the instrument types it needs.

Extreme heat is described as causing more fatalities than any other climate disaster while attracting less attention, because the building survives and the occupants do not, which keeps it out of loss statistics built on structures.

records.title: Federal Judge Temporarily Halts BRIC Grant Program Termination
records.summary: This NACo news article reports on the federal court-ordered temporary halt to the Trump administration's termination of FEMA's Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities (BRIC) grant program. On April 4, 2025, FEMA announced it would not allocate $750 million for BRIC that year and would cease funding previously approved projects. Twenty states sued, and in August 2025 a federal judge ruled the administration lacked authority to repurpose Congressionally allocated funds. Since its 2020 launch, BRIC had awarded more than $5 billion in grants for hazard mitigation projects including flood control, wildfire prevention, stormwater management, and building code strengthening, covering up to 75% of project costs.
insights: FEMA's BRIC program awarded more than $5 billion in hazard mitigation grants since its 2020 launch, covering up to 75% of project costs for flood control, wildfire prevention, stormwater management, and building code upgrades.

The Trump administration's April 2025 cancellation withheld $750 million in BRIC allocations for FY2025 and halted funding for previously approved, in-progress projects, creating immediate pipeline disruption for county-level mitigation investments.

A federal court temporarily blocked reallocation of the BRIC funds in August 2025, ruling the administration lacked authority to repurpose Congressionally appropriated funds, a significant separation-of-powers constraint on executive rescission of pre-disaster mitigation grants.

The ruling does not release funds to states but prevents their use for non-BRIC purposes, leaving counties in a legal limbo: projects cannot proceed, but funds cannot be permanently redirected either.

Counties in disaster-prone areas face a forced shift from proactive mitigation spending to reactive post-disaster recovery dollars, a dynamic that historically increases total federal disaster expenditure and reduces community resilience.

The cancellation signals a federal policy shift toward state and local responsibility for disaster preparedness, reducing the federal match that made large-scale infrastructure mitigation projects financially viable for local governments.

NACo and the Intergovernmental Disaster Reform Task Force are actively lobbying Congress for federal disaster reform, indicating the BRIC dispute is part of a broader intergovernmental conflict over disaster finance architecture.

records.title: Insurance for a FAIR Future
records.summary: The document discusses the challenges faced by FAIR Plans in providing insurance coverage in the context of increasing climate-related risks. As private insurers withdraw from high-risk areas, property owners are increasingly reliant on state-backed FAIR Plans, leading to a cycle where these plans absorb more high-risk policies and face rising costs, threatening their financial viability. The document proposes rethinking the structure and operation of FAIR Plans to ensure continued availability of property insurance and promote resilience measures.
insights: FAIR Plans are under significant stress due to climate-fueled extreme weather events, leading to increasing enrollment and rising costs.
Private insurers are retreating from high-risk areas, resulting in more reliance on state-backed FAIR Plans as the insurer of last resort.
The current structure of FAIR Plans leads to unsustainable financial models that require bailouts from private insurers.
Effective changes to FAIR Plans are needed to maintain their role in the property insurance market and prevent a 'cycle of doom' where costs continue to rise.
Incorporating hazard mitigation and climate adaptation measures could improve the sustainability of FAIR Plans and reduce risk exposure.
Access to affordable insurance is disproportionately affected for low-income communities, necessitating targeted subsidies and support.
Proposed reforms include not allowing insurers to recoup assessment costs from policyholders and encouraging community-level hazard mitigation.
The financial health of FAIR Plans could be strengthened by retaining policyholder surpluses and investing in higher-yield options.
Authorize FAIR Plans to sell catastrophe bonds as a means to enhance their financial stability and manage catastrophic risks.
Implementing community-based insurance products linked to hazard mitigation could foster cooperation between insurers, governments, and homeowners.

records.title: The Carbon Cost of Coastal Adaptation: A Performance Evaluation Methodology for Nature-Based Solutions
institutions: Harvard University Graduate School of Design
Salata Institute for Climate and Sustainability at Harvard University
records.summary: The article discusses the potential of low-carbon, nature-based solutions for coastal adaptation, highlighting the importance of redesigning coastal infrastructure to reduce carbon emissions. It emphasizes the need for collaboration among designers, builders, and policymakers to adopt more sustainable materials and practices, thereby improving coastal resilience while minimizing environmental impact.
insights: Nature-based solutions (NbS) offer substantial benefits over traditional concrete and steel approaches, including reduced carbon emissions and cost savings.
Using lower-carbon alternatives and sourcing materials locally can significantly decrease the carbon footprint of coastal resilience projects.
Replacing high-emission materials, such as traditional fill, with sustainable options can lead to lower emissions and improved carbon impact.
Increasing vegetation at coastal sites not only enhances carbon sequestration but also contributes to biodiversity and public health.
Simple design modifications can significantly decrease the amount of material used, directly reducing emissions associated with coastal adaptation infrastructure.
Implementing nature-based solutions at scale can lead to net positive environmental outcomes, reversing the trend of contributing to climate change.
Collaboration among stakeholders from project inception is crucial to effectively integrating low-carbon materials and practices.
Establishing carbon limits and updating codes for infrastructure can help institutionalize nature-based solutions as the standard practice.
Potential global emissions reductions from implementing these strategies in coastal projects could equal 40 years worth of New York City's emissions.
Designers and engineers play a critical role in shifting the approach to coastal resilience towards sustainability.
records.publisher: Salata Institute for Climate and Sustainability

records.title: Scaling Finance and Investment for Climate Adaptation: Input Paper for the G20 Sustainable Finance Working Group
records.summary: The document serves as an input paper for the G20 Sustainable Finance Working Group, advocating for scaled finance and investment in climate adaptation due to the stark disparity in funding compared to mitigation efforts. It outlines essential strategies and challenges in mobilizing resources, particularly in developing countries, emphasizes innovative financing mechanisms like blended finance and resilience bonds, and underscores the importance of public-private partnerships and effective coordination among stakeholders to enhance climate resilience efforts across multiple sectors.
insights: Current adaptation finance is severely inadequate, with only $76 billion mobilized in 2022 compared to $1.3 trillion for mitigation.
Blended finance and innovative instruments are crucial for attracting private sector investment in climate adaptation.
Developing countries face significant barriers such as lack of data and insufficient institutional frameworks impeding adaptation investments.
Public-private partnerships are essential for enhancing private investment in climate-resilient infrastructure.
Innovative financial mechanisms like resilience bonds and debt-for-adaptation swaps can provide alternative funding solutions for adaptation.

records.title: Climate Change and Insurance: Embracing Resilience for Private Market Survival
records.authors: John A. Roper, David G. Casagrande, Paolo Bocchini
records.summary: The resource examines the impact of climate change on the insurance industry, highlighting the increasing risks from natural disasters and the urgent need for private insurance in risk management. It advocates for collaborative efforts between public and private sectors to fund resilience through innovative financing mechanisms, such as resilience bonds, and emphasizes the importance of investing in resilient infrastructure, especially in vulnerable communities, to mitigate damages and enhance the financial sustainability of insurers.
insights: Private insurance is crucial for managing natural disaster risks, but climate change is challenging its sustainability.
There is a concerning gap between actuarial risk and premium pricing, which disproportionately impacts vulnerable communities.
Investments in resilience can lead to significant long-term savings and improved recovery times from disasters.
Public-private partnerships are essential for addressing funding challenges in resilience but face organizational hurdles.
Innovative financing like resilience bonds can create mutual benefits for both public and private sectors, enhancing community resilience.

records.title: Bracing for Impact: A Systems Strategy for Climate Resilience in the US
records.authors: Dee Yang, Tucker Van Aken, Laurie Schoeman
records.summary: Systemiq's July 2025 strategic blueprint for closing the US resilience gap. It opens with the exposure: 27 billion-dollar weather disasters in 2024 causing $183 billion in direct damages, a projected $1.2 trillion a year in physical climate risk costs to global companies by mid-century, $1.5 trillion of potential climate-driven devaluation of US homes, and at least $6.6 trillion of cost to the US economy over twelve years. Against that, every $1 of pre-disaster mitigation saves an estimated $13, and the resilience dividend, the economic, social and environmental benefits beyond avoided losses, is often twice the value of avoided losses. Capital needed is put at $100 to $200 billion a year. The report names seven systemic barriers: adaptation is not mainstreamed and its benefits are not visible; incentives reward recovery over prevention because insurance, mortgage and lending systems rarely price risk reduction, with flat mortgage rates and uniform premiums subsidising inaction; the financing ecosystem lacks taxonomies, scalable instruments, catalytic capital mechanisms and project preparation; private sector engagement ignores shared system dependencies; capacity is constrained across sectors; the solution set is poorly defined with no shared framework for comparing and sequencing interventions; and coordination mechanisms are lacking. The strategy works across three fronts. Framing: quantify the case for resilience with context-specific models, clarify the resilience toolbox as a shared typology, and embed resilience in investment frameworks and capital allocation. Coordination: cross-sector resilience networks, regional innovation hubs as living labs, and open-source resources. Execution: expand the pipeline of investable projects through project development facilities, develop innovative financing mechanisms such as resilience bonds structured around triple dividends.
insights: The second barrier is stated bluntly: insurance, mortgage and lending systems rarely price risk reduction, and flat mortgage rates and uniform premiums actively subsidise inaction, so the financial system pays for recovery and charges nothing less for prevention.

The proposed instrument, a resilience bond structured around triple dividend metrics, is the direct answer to that barrier, because it would make the avoided loss, the growth and the co-benefits all cashflow-relevant rather than only the first.

Project development facilities are named as the missing layer between a resilience plan and an investable project, and the report observes that BRIC did this nationally before its cancellation, so the gap is a policy decision rather than an unsolved design problem.

The report is explicit that the resilience dividend is often twice the avoided loss, which means an appraisal that counts only avoided damages understates the return by roughly a factor of three and is the main reason the $13:1 ratio understates the case.
Every recommendation is paired as bottom-up and top-down, which follows from the diagnosis that the failure is coordination rather than either local initiative or national funding alone.

records.title: Standards, Not Pricing: How Insurers Can Bend the Market Toward Safety as Climate Hazards Intensify
institutions: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety
records.summary: The essay argues that insurers can send risk signals through safety standards rather than price, and should reframe the insurance crisis as an insurability crisis. It draws on two precedents: William Henry Merrill, whose 1893 electrical risk assessment for insurers led to Underwriters Laboratory, and William Haddon Jr., whose work led to federal motor vehicle safety standards and the insurer-backed Insurance Institute for Highway Safety. It proposes IBHS standards such as FORTIFIED and Wildfire Prepared as the equivalent for homes, while noting they are not yet commonplace or demanded by consumers. It calls on insurers to partner across the housing ecosystem and invest in tools that scale demand.
insights: Underwriters Laboratory, now UL Solutions, grew from Merrill's insurer-commissioned assessment at the 1893 Chicago World's Fair and is the largest safety standard organization in the world, with $3 billion in annual revenue.
The Insurance Institute for Highway Safety evolved from an insurer research body on auto claims and is now the de facto global standard setter for automobile safety.
IBHS FORTIFIED and Wildfire Prepared standards are not yet commonplace outside certain parts of the country, and consumers do not yet demand them as they do UL or IIHS standards.
Insurability is framed as a shared responsibility built from many independent decisions across design, land use, building codes and construction, with insurers as final arbiters.
The author notes standards-based alignment already works for almost 4 billion electrical appliances and 300 million cars in the US, and argues it can work for 82 million US homes.

records.title: U.S. Municipalities Are Battling Growing Flood Risk with Innovative Insurance Solutions
records.summary: This article from InsTech describes the growing flood insurance gap facing U.S. municipalities and profiles Fremont, California as the first U.S. city to purchase a citywide parametric flood insurance policy, enabled by Floodbase's satellite- and AI-driven flood monitoring technology and distributed by specialty insurer Amwins. The piece argues that FEMA payouts are slow, partial, and may disappear under the current administration, making parametric insurance (which pays out within days of a trigger event, without damage assessments), a compelling alternative. Fremont's 2017 flood retroactively illustrates a modeled payout of over $710,000 under the new policy structure.
insights: Flood costs the U.S. an estimated 1–2% of GDP annually, yet municipal flood risk remains largely underinsured; California municipalities alone saw $5–7 billion in economic losses in 2023, of which 80% was uninsured.

Hurricanes Milton and Helene (2024) caused a combined insured loss of $44 billion against total economic losses of $112 billion, implying an insurance gap of roughly $68 billion for a single hurricane season.

Fremont, CA became the first U.S. municipality to purchase a citywide parametric flood insurance policy; Floodbase's retroactive modeling estimates a payout of over $710,000 had the policy been active during the 2017 atmospheric river event.

Parametric flood insurance pays out within days of a trigger event because no damage assessment is required, directly addressing municipalities' reported frustration with FEMA's slow and often incomplete reimbursements.
Unlike FEMA payouts, parametric insurance proceeds can be used for loss of tax revenue, a major but previously uninsurable economic loss category for flood-affected municipalities.

Floodbase uses satellite imagery, near-real-time national stream gauge data, and AI to provide continuous global flood monitoring, enabling trigger-based parametric policies at city scale, a capability previously unavailable for flood peril.

The potential elimination of FEMA under the Trump administration heightens urgency for municipalities to adopt alternative risk transfer instruments; parametric insurance is positioned as a scalable substitute.

Parametric flood insurance is well-established for earthquake, drought, and wildfire but has been technically constrained for flood due to real-time modeling challenges at scale, Floodbase's technology represents a market-opening breakthrough for this peril.

records.title: Climate Risk Capital Modelling: Market Trends
records.summary: Lloyd's report on how its syndicates measure, manage and model climate change risk in their capital models, drawn from responses to the Climate Change Questionnaire that Actuarial Oversight issued in 2024. It defines climate risk across three types, physical, litigation and transition, and reports market practice against each, isolating the syndicates that Lloyd's own high-level assessment suggests are materially exposed. The exercise is explicitly exploratory and is intended to shape Lloyd's capital and validation guidance and climate risk oversight from 2026 onward. It is a state-of-the-market report and not a gap analysis against the CP10/25 consultation, which it largely predates.
insights: LITIGATION RISK IS TREATED AS A THIRD CATEGORY ALONGSIDE PHYSICAL AND TRANSITION, defined as disputes arising from a party's contribution to climate change, from the physical consequences, or from the laws and duties related to it. Most climate risk frameworks carry only two.

Lloyd's set explicit materiality criteria rather than asking every syndicate the same question: more than 37.5 per cent of one-in-200 gross losses from LCM5 weather perils as a share of syndicate ECA for physical risk, more than 10 per cent of gross written premium in D&O and general liability for litigation risk, and more than 3 per cent investment exposure to transition-exposed sub-sectors.

Those criteria put 38 syndicates in the physical bucket, 41 in the litigation bucket and only 3 in the transition bucket, which is a striking asymmetry: litigation exposure is broader across this market than transition exposure.

The identified gap is not that syndicates model climate badly but that some do not quantify it at all: a small proportion cannot quantify physical climate risk exposure and a larger proportion cannot quantify climate litigation risk, including some Lloyd's assesses as materially exposed.

Lloyd's is careful that not adjusting a vendor catastrophe model is not automatically wrong, because its oversight of Principle 2a already tests whether present-day climate change is suitably captured, so the absence of an adjustment is a question rather than a finding.

The transition-risk sector list is taken from the Bank of England's CBES scenarios, the sectors with gross value added losses above 30 per cent, which ties a Lloyd's capital exercise directly to a central bank stress-testing framework.

records.title: IDB Launches Disaster Risk Instruments and Expands Coverage
records.summary: The Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) and IDB Invest announced a multi-instrument expansion of disaster risk financial protection for sovereign and private clients in Latin America and the Caribbean. Key elements include: a $1 billion increase in the Contingent Credit Facility for Natural Disasters (reaching $5 billion total by 2026), a $1 billion expansion of Climate Resilience Debt Clauses (reaching $4.2 billion total by 2026), a new Regional Disaster-Risk Transfer Program connecting countries to reinsurance and capital markets (initially targeting Belize, Honduras, and Panama), and a first-of-its-kind MDB private-sector Business-Resilience Program from IDB Invest offering debt principal deferrals and tenor extensions of up to two years.
insights: The IDB is expanding disaster-risk coverage by a combined $2 billion across two instruments, $1 billion added to its Contingent Credit Facility for Natural Disasters (now $5 billion total) and $1 billion added to Climate Resilience Debt Clauses (now $4.2 billion total), all targeted at Latin America and the Caribbean by 2026.

Climate Resilience Debt Clauses allow eligible sovereign borrowers to temporarily pause debt-service payments after qualifying natural disasters, freeing fiscal space for emergency response without triggering default; the IDB's total coverage reaches $4.2 billion by 2026.

The new Regional Disaster-Risk Transfer Program is designed specifically for small and vulnerable economies with limited market access, channeling extreme-event risk from hurricanes, floods, droughts, earthquakes, and wildfires to reinsurance and capital markets, with Spain and France as potential bilateral supporters.

IDB Invest's Business-Resilience Program is the first multilateral development bank mechanism to extend debt-clause protections to private-sector borrowers across agribusiness, infrastructure, energy, and tourism, allowing principal deferrals and tenor extensions of up to two years, setting a benchmark for MDB innovation in development finance.

The package builds on the IDB's 'Ready and Resilient Americas' regional program launched in March, signaling a systematic institutional shift toward pre-arranged, contingent financial instruments rather than post-disaster emergency lending.

The expansion of eligible countries under the Contingent Credit Facility and the inclusion of regional risk-pooling mechanisms suggest a scalable model for sovereign catastrophe liquidity that could be replicated by other MDBs or regional development banks.

records.title: Mass Ready Act
records.authors: Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs, Gvr. Maura Healey, Lt. Gvr. Kim Driscoll
records.summary: The Mass Ready Act is a comprehensive $2.9 billion initiative designed to enhance Massachusetts' infrastructure, protect natural resources, and strengthen local economies. It focuses on improving flood resilience, upgrading essential utilities, safeguarding water quality, and promoting food security while streamlining environmental processes. The Act aims to create robust communities for future generations, ensuring environmental preservation and public health.
insights: The Act allocates significant funds for infrastructure improvements, including $764 million for state property upgrades and $401.6 million for dam and flood control projects.
Investments in local economies and agriculture are emphasized, with $125 million dedicated to food security programs.
The establishment of a Resilience Revolving Fund will provide low-interest loans for community resilience projects.
The Act addresses environmental protection with $505 million invested in clean water infrastructure and PFAS contamination remediation.
Provisions for enhancing biodiversity and protecting wildlife habitats are included, ensuring sustainability for future generations.
Streamlining environmental permitting processes is intended to reduce costs and expedite housing development.
The focus on modernizing policies around agriculture and animal health aims to foster economic viability in the sector.
Investments in recreational and green spaces are designed to improve community quality of life and environmental health.
The bill aims to create a comprehensive approach to managing climate challenges while focusing on public health and safety.

records.title: Global Assessment Report (GAR) on Disaster Risk Reduction: Resilience Pays: Investing and Financing for Our Future
institutions: United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction
records.summary: The Global Assessment Report (GAR) 2025 emphasizes the urgent need for investment in disaster risk reduction (DRR) as a response to the increasing economic and humanitarian impacts of climate change. Highlighting the escalating costs of disasters, the report calls for proactive risk management strategies, effective financial instruments, and international cooperation to enhance resilience and sustainable development, particularly for vulnerable populations, while advocating for improved methodologies in disaster cost assessments to better capture the full range of impacts.
insights: Disaster costs have increased significantly over the decades, with the economic burden reaching unprecedented levels due to climate-related events.
Investment in disaster risk reduction (DRR) is not only necessary but economically beneficial, with strategies like risk transfer and innovative financing offering favorable returns.
Vulnerable populations, including refugees, face heightened risks from climate change, necessitating proactive investment in mitigation and resilience-building efforts.
Innovative financial solutions, like blended finance, resilience bonds, and catastrophe bonds, play a crucial role in funding disaster risk management initiatives.
Data gaps often lead to underestimations of disaster impacts, underscoring the need for improved methodologies in disaster cost assessments.
Disasters disrupt education and economic stability, with multi-hazard events leading to cascading economic effects that require comprehensive risk management strategies.
Access to early warning systems and disaster insurance remains uneven, reinforcing the necessity for improved coverage, especially in developing regions.
records.publisher: UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction

records.title: How Catastrophes Limit Prosperity – Weather Disasters Are a Growing Burden, Also for Many Industrialized Countries
records.summary: Weather disasters are increasingly costly for major economies, with losses relative to gross national income rising significantly since the 1980s. An analysis finds that countries like the USA, Germany, and India are experiencing heightened financial burdens from these events, emphasizing the need for preventative investments to mitigate future costs.
insights: Significant increase in weather disaster losses has been observed in eight of the ten largest industrialized countries since the 1980s.
The USA, Germany, and India reported the highest average losses in relation to their gross national income over the past five years.
In the US, weather-related losses increased to approximately five times the levels seen from 1980 to 1989.
Flooding and severe thunderstorms are major contributors to weather-related losses in North America and Europe.
Investment in prevention strategies can yield substantial returns, potentially saving $10 for every $1 spent.
China has effectively reduced average weather disaster losses relative to its economic output through significant investments in flood protection.
The percentage of uninsured losses remains high in many countries, complicating the financial recovery from disasters.
Japan's high level of prevention measures significantly mitigates its risk from natural disasters.
In Brazil, a combination of floods and droughts poses severe threats to economic stability, exacerbated by climate change.
The insurance gap underscores the need for improved coverage and risk management strategies across all regions.

records.title: Connecticut Public Act 25-33 (Substitute Senate Bill No. 9)
records.summary: Connecticut Public Act 25-33, Substitute Senate Bill No. 9, an act concerning the environment, climate and sustainable municipal and state planning and the use of neonicotinoids and second-generation anticoagulant rodenticides. Its first two sections, both effective 1 July 2026, are flood insurance disclosure mandates. Section 1 requires every insurer that delivers, issues for delivery or renews a homeowners or renters policy for a residential dwelling in the state to give the insured a notice prescribed or approved by the Insurance Commissioner explaining clearly, conspicuously and in plain language that the policy does not cover loss caused by flood, and that insurance is available under separate flood policies, with information on flood insurance eligibility and access. Section 2 requires each creditor in a mortgage loan transaction, not later than ten days before closing, to notify the applicant in writing that standard homeowners policies do not cover flood damage and related losses, that flood damage may occur regardless of whether the property is in a designated flood zone, and that the applicant may wish to consult a licensed insurance producer or surplus lines broker.
insights: The operative provision is a flood disclosure delivered ten days before mortgage closing, which fixes the moment of disclosure to a point where the buyer can still act on it rather than at contract signature.

The clause that flood damage may occur regardless of whether the property is in a designated flood zone is a direct legislative answer to the map-inadequacy half of the same recommendation. The state cannot fix a federal map, so it requires the disclosure the map fails to make.

Placing the duty on the creditor as well as the insurer is the load-bearing choice. The lender has the borrower's attention ten days before closing and carries the collateral risk, so the disclosure lands at the moment a buyer can still act on it.
Disclosure is the cheapest resilience instrument available to a legislature: no capital, no risk transfer, no subsidy. Whether it changes behaviour is the open question the act does not answer.

The act bundles flood disclosure with municipal planning and with rodenticide regulation, which is how a disclosure mandate passes. Recorded because a reader searching for flood insurance law would not expect to find it here.

records.title: Local Governments Can Be Champions For Flood Management: A Case Study From Algonquin, Illinois
records.summary: The article profiles how the Village of Algonquin, Illinois, a Chicago suburb, moved from reactive flood response to a programmatic green infrastructure approach built on a 2005 natural area inventory and two 319 Watershed Plans drafted in 2013. It sets out how the work was paid for: village-owned land, Illinois 319 grants, local matching funds, county stormwater ordinances that collect in-lieu fees from developers, and a Conservation Design ordinance requiring new development to leave space for nature. It reports that flooding has improved despite rising rainfall and that naturalized areas cost far less to maintain than conventional landscaping. It closes with steps other local governments can take.
insights: Algonquin's public works lead brought in over $1.6M in grant funding over 20 years, each grant matched by village budget.
The traditional landscape contract costs $431,000 a year for about 220 acres, while the natural areas contract costs $150,000 a year for about 470 acres.
McHenry and Kane Counties' Stormwater Management Ordinances let the village collect in-lieu fees from new development to restore wetlands, detention basins and streams.
Illinois average annual precipitation rose 11% (36 to 40 inches) over the past century and storms over 2 inches nearly doubled, per Illinois State Water Survey Bulletin 75.
Over half the projects in the Jelkes Creek-Fox River watershed plan and over one-third in the Woods Creek plan have been completed.
Residents initially resisted native vegetation but, within 3 to 5 years of projects, began requesting more of them.

records.title: The Compelling Investment Case for Climate Adaptation
records.authors: Carter Brandon, Bradley Kratzer, Aarushi Aggarwal, Harald Heubaum, Celine Novenario
records.summary: The report highlights the significant returns on investment for climate adaptation measures, emphasizing that $1 invested can yield over $10.50 in benefits due to avoided losses and various economic, social, and environmental advantages. It calls for a shift in perception to view adaptation not as a cost but as a lucrative investment opportunity crucial for achieving resilient development despite a current funding gap of $359 billion annually.
insights: Extreme weather events are increasing in frequency and intensity, leading to significant economic damages.
The annual adaptation finance gap is estimated at $359 billion, indicating a critical need for enhanced funding.
Investing in adaptation can yield high returns, with $1 generating over $10.50 in benefits over a decade.
Adaptation investments create a 'triple dividend' of avoided losses, induced economic growth, and social/environmental benefits.
Health-focused adaptation projects can achieve returns exceeding 78%, improving public health and productivity.
Disaster risk management investments yield high returns, averaging nearly 36%, by safeguarding lives and infrastructure.
Water-related adaptation efforts average around 19% returns, highlighting the importance of water management.
Adaptation efforts can also help reduce greenhouse gas emissions, creating synergies between adaptation and mitigation.
Improved data collection and analysis is needed to accurately assess the benefits of adaptation investments.
Failing to invest in adaptation not only exposes communities to risks but also misses out on substantial socio-economic benefits.

records.title: Investing in Resilience: Three Case Studies in Climate Adaptation
records.summary: A Ceres brief drawn from a roundtable of its Investor Network, presenting three investor case studies in climate adaptation: IFM Investors on how infrastructure equity owners create long-term value through adaptation, Breckinridge Capital Advisors on incorporating forward-looking climate data into municipal bond credit assessment, and Impax Asset Management on engaging companies to improve risk disclosure and management. It argues adaptation is both a risk management necessity and a multi-trillion-dollar market opportunity, and identifies risk assessment, disclosure quality and adaptation financing as the obstacles that keep it underfunded.
insights: More than 90 per cent of global climate finance still goes to mitigation, and adaptation investment is projected to cover only one sixth of expected physical climate risk costs by 2030, which is the allocation gap the brief is written against.
The stated potential return on adaptation investment is up to $43 for each $1 spent, against annual losses of up to $1.2 trillion by 2050 for the world's largest companies without adaptation.

All three investors report that markets misprice tomorrow's climate realities today, which they treat as a barrier to adaptation funding and simultaneously as the source of the opportunity for long-horizon capital.

IFM applies adaptation at acquisition rather than after it: climate risk screening in due diligence, an explicit willingness to buy the inland asset over the coastal one at equal characteristics, and a required climate transition plan covering adaptation for every acquired asset.

Breckinridge applies forward-looking climate projections rather than historical trends inside municipal bond credit assessment, which is one of the few concrete routes by which physical risk reaches a price in this brief.

The brief names investors' most common error as looking only at direct operations while ignoring supply chains, infrastructure networks and communities that transmit climate shocks across a whole portfolio.

records.title: Strengthening the Investment Case for Climate Adaptation: A Triple Dividend Approach
records.authors: Carter Brandon; Bradley Kratzer; Aarushi Aggarwal; Harald Heubaum
records.summary: This WRI working paper (June 2025) introduces the AdapTDR database, a first-of-its-kind compilation of 320 climate adaptation investments totaling $133 billion, approved by multilateral development banks and international climate finance institutions across 12 countries from 2014 to 2024. Using the triple dividend of resilience (TDR) framework alongside standard cost-benefit analysis, the study finds that $1 invested in adaptation yields over $10.50 in benefits, with an average EIRR of 26.7%. Second and third dividends (induced economic and social/environmental benefits) are double the value of avoided losses, and nearly half of investments generate mitigation co-benefits, opening pathways to carbon finance and private capital mobilization.
insights: US$1 invested in adaptation yields over $10.50 in benefits over a 10-year period; 320 evaluated investments cost $133 billion total and may generate $1.4 trillion in benefits, with an average EIRR of 26.7% and median EIRR of 20.3%, well above the informal 10% MDB threshold.

Second and third dividends (induced economic development and social/environmental benefits) are, on average, double the value of first-dividend avoided losses, meaning over half of all monetized adaptation benefits accrue regardless of whether a climate disaster occurs, fundamentally de-risking the investment case.

Nearly half (44.7%) of all 320 evaluated adaptation investments are expected to generate GHG emissions reductions, with energy (85.7%) and forestry (75%) subsectors showing the highest rates; this creates direct eligibility for carbon finance layered onto adaptation structures.

Health and disaster risk management subsectors show the highest average EIRRs (78.5% and 35.9% respectively), driven primarily by avoided mortality valuations; sustainable agriculture and forestry show high returns (27.2% and 39.5%) via poverty-reduction and mitigation co-benefits.

Water subsectors (supply/sanitation: 19.4% avg. EIRR; flood management: 18.2%) are systematically undervalued, less than 20% of water investments monetize avoided losses, suggesting realized returns are substantially higher than reported.

Only 8.4% of the 320 investments valued all three dividends in monetary terms, and 74% of projects citing avoided-loss benefits did not monetize them, confirming that current EIRRs and BCRs are underestimates across the portfolio.

records.title: New Jersey's Flood Risk = Financial Risk
records.summary: Rebuild by Design's parcel-level analysis of New Jersey flood exposure, covering all 3.4 million residential, commercial and industrial parcels in the state and classifying each into one of four displacement risk groups. The headline figures are that nearly 1.3 million New Jerseyans live in high flood risk areas, half of them lower income residents who may lack the resources to relocate, and that by 2050 nearly one in six land parcels statewide will face high flood risk, threatening $435.9 billion in present property value and $5.9 billion in annual property tax revenue. The report also examines insurance rates and non-renewal risk, noting that some of the highest-flood-risk counties are also seeing higher non-renewal rates, and sets the exposure against a housing market with a 0.5 per cent homeowner vacancy rate and 3.6 per cent for renters. Its three recommendations are to create reliable state funding for resilient infrastructure, raised through a bond act or a minimal surcharge on certain insurance types to buy down risk; to expand the Blue Acres voluntary buyout programme with case management and social services; and to plan for short and long term migration.
insights: The framing turns flood risk into fiscal risk: $5.9 billion in annual property tax revenue at severe risk by 2050 is a state and municipal revenue exposure, not a property owner's loss, which is what makes it a public finance problem.

The funding recommendation names two specific instruments, a state bond act or a minimal surcharge on certain insurance types to buy down risk, the second of which uses the insurance system to capitalise mitigation.
Non-renewal risk is found to concentrate in the same counties as the highest flood risk, so insurance withdrawal compounds rather than offsets the exposure.

A 0.5 per cent homeowner vacancy rate is the binding constraint on the relocation recommendations: the analysis classifies parcels by displacement risk into a market with almost nowhere for displaced households to go.

The parcel-level method across all 3.4 million properties is what allows displacement risk groups at all, and it is paired with the state's Atlas of Disaster finding of 14 federal disaster declarations from 2011 to 2024 costing over $7.9 billion.

records.title: Climate Risk and Local Government Debt Decisions
records.authors: Bin Li, Chensheng Wang, Wendai Lv
institutions: Research in International Business and Finance
records.summary: This peer-reviewed empirical study examines how climate risk shapes local government debt decisions across 277 Chinese prefecture-level cities from 2010–2020, using urban investment bonds (municipal investment bonds) as a proxy for government debt. Using fixed-effects, spatial Durbin, and instrumental variable models, the study finds that rising physical climate risk (measured by frequency of extreme weather events) significantly increases local government debt balances. Two primary mechanisms are identified: expanding infrastructure investment demand and contracting land-based fiscal revenues. Spatial spillover effects and policy heterogeneity, particularly interactions between low-carbon pilot mandates and debt-control policies, further shape debt outcomes. The findings carry direct implications for green bond instrument design, fiscal resilience, and intergovernmental transfer policy in climate-stressed jurisdictions.
insights: Climate risk (measured by extreme weather event frequency) increases local government bond balances by a coefficient of 0.139–0.144 (significant at 5%) across 277 Chinese prefecture-level cities over 2010–2020, confirming that physical risk systematically drives expansionary debt behavior.

Two transmission mechanisms are empirically validated: (1) investment demand expansion, greater local government infrastructure investment demand amplifies climate risk's effect on debt (interaction term LGI×Risk: 2.120, p<5%); and (2) revenue pathway contraction, higher housing prices attenuate climate risk's debt impact (HP×Risk: −0.007, p<1%), meaning declining real estate markets force heavier borrowing.

Spatial Durbin Model results reveal significant spatial spillover: climate risk in one city raises debt in neighboring cities (indirect effect: 0.393, p<1%), while the direct effect is negative (−0.262, p<5%), yielding a positive total effect (0.131, p<10%). This means debt policy responses propagate regionally and cannot be managed in isolation.

Policy heterogeneity is decisive: low-carbon pilot city designation amplifies climate risk's debt effect (coefficient 0.280, p<1%), while key debt-mitigation province designation renders the effect statistically insignificant (coefficient −0.037), demonstrating that strict debt oversight can override climate-driven borrowing impulses.

When both low-carbon and debt-control policies apply simultaneously, climate risk's effect on debt is also insignificant (coefficient 0.121), suggesting the two policy frameworks partially cancel each other out, a governance conflict with direct implications for financing climate adaptation.
records.publisher: Research in International Business and Finance

records.title: How Climate Change May Be Reshaping the Landscape for Municipal Debt Issuances
records.summary: This article examines the impact of climate change on the municipal bond market, highlighting how rising natural disaster costs are reshaping the financial landscape for municipalities in the U.S. It notes that despite the growing evidence of climate risks, municipal bonds are often issued without adequate pricing for these risks, leading to questions about long-term financial stability for municipalities reliant on bonds for infrastructure and disaster recovery.
insights: Municipalities face escalating costs due to climate change impacts, leading to increased borrowing from the municipal bond market.
Climate risks are not currently factored into the pricing of municipal bonds despite clear evidence of their impact.
Research indicates a minimal effect on bond yields, even for issuers with significantly higher climate risk exposure.
Rating agencies prioritize short-term financial metrics over long-term climate risk assessments in their evaluations.
Disaster recovery has historically relied on federal assistance, creating a false sense of security for investors.
Legislative restrictions in certain states hinder the consideration of climate risks in investment decisions.
The demand for municipal debt often overshadows underlying climate-related risks due to limited supply.
Future municipal debt issuance may rise as federal funding becomes more available for climate-resilient infrastructure.
Municipal bond investors need to reassess their evaluations by incorporating climate risk alongside traditional metrics.
The evolving reality of climate change will eventually necessitate a shift in how municipal bonds are priced and perceived.

records.title: Partnerships Mark Early Phases of Los Angeles Recovery
institutions: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety
records.summary: Francis Bouchard reports from the May 2025 Milken Global Meeting on how Los Angeles is approaching recovery from the January 2025 Altadena and Palisades fires. He describes partnership, system-level engagement and local leadership as the defining features of a recovery that will be locally led because federal funding is unclear. The piece introduces the Resilient LA Delta Fund, which offers grants, subsidized loans and market-rate instruments to cover the gap between code-level insurance payouts and the cost of rebuilding to the IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home standard. It argues that insurers should reframe their role from pricing peril to reducing risk.
insights: $650M of philanthropic funds were raised in the first weeks after the fires, still almost $40B short of what rebuilding needs.
Local leaders aim to rebuild 12,000 homes as a community, and the Delta Fund could harden as many as 12,000 homes.
The 'resilience delta' is defined as the gap between what standard insurance payouts cover (code-level rebuilding) and the cost of building to the highest wildfire resilience standard.

The Delta Fund is a partnership of The Resiliency Company, Marsh McLennan, Momentus Securities, IBHS and the Dept of Angels, with a June design event supported by Morgan Stanley, Insurance for Good and SidePorch.
The author raises catastrophe bonds, insurance-linked securities and blended capital stacks as possible sources of capacity for struggling insurers.

records.title: Building Momentum: Flood and Coast: Innovative Financing for Climate Adaptation
records.authors: Callum Ellis, Morgan Jones, Ed Kilcommons, and Swenja Surminski
records.summary: The excerpt discusses the urgent need for innovative financing strategies to support climate adaptation efforts in response to rising risks from extreme weather events, particularly coastal erosion and flooding. It highlights the significance of collaboration among government entities, local authorities, and private investors to develop scalable funding mechanisms.
