Federal and local collaboration is vital, as illustrated by the improvements being made with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers.
Sustainable urban planning and water management are essential ongoing efforts to combat climate-related challenges.

records.title: Climate Adaptation Finance: The Challenge for Institutional Investors and Commercial Banks
records.summary: A November 2024 World Economic Forum article by Baker McKenzie partners examines why institutional investors and commercial banks have contributed less than 3% of climate adaptation finance, while developing countries face an annual gap of $187–$359 billion this decade and need a fourfold increase in adaptation flows. The piece identifies five structural barriers (definitional gaps, data scarcity, disclosure constraints, long timelines, and risk-pricing difficulty), and spotlights two instruments as scalable solutions: debt-for-impact swaps (illustrated by Ecuador's 2023 $656M marine conservation-linked bond) and blended finance deployed through public-private partnerships.
insights: Private sector actors, institutional investors and commercial banks, contribute less than 3% of total climate adaptation finance, despite adaptation representing a critical component of Paris Agreement goals.

The UN Environment Programme estimates a financing gap for developing countries of $187–$359 billion per year this decade, and the Global Center on Adaptation and Climate Policy Initiative state that adaptation finance flows must increase fourfold.
Although adaptation finance has grown in real terms, it has fallen as a share of overall climate finance, signaling that mitigation continues to crowd out adaptation in capital allocation.

Ecuador's 2023 debt-for-nature swap, exchanging $1.6B face-value sovereign bonds for a $656M marine conservation-linked loan, is the largest such transaction to date and illustrates how political risk insurance and development bank guarantees can enable sovereign debt restructuring to redirect savings to conservation and adaptation.

Ecuador directed more than $300M of debt-restructuring savings to marine conservation around the Galápagos Islands, demonstrating the potential scale of fiscal space created by debt-for-impact mechanisms.

Five structural barriers constrain private adaptation finance: (1) absence of standardized definitions/classification equivalent to green loan principles; (2) insufficient project-level climate risk data; (3) disclosure and data-sharing constraints; (4) return timeline mismatches; and (5) difficulty pricing risk when value is primarily in avoided damages rather than monetary revenue.

The EU Taxonomy Regulation provides a classification pathway that can qualify adaptation activities as 'green,' enabling use of EU Green Bonds, a key enabler for European capital markets to label and fund adaptation projects.

records.title: States Are Exploring Paths to Finance Climate Resilient Infrastructure
records.summary: Pew reviewed legislation and policy announcements across all 50 states for 2023 and 2024 to map how states are funding and financing climate-resilient infrastructure. The framing figure is a state backlog of nearly $1 trillion for deferred maintenance and needed upgrades to public infrastructure, against which aging and undermaintained systems are increasingly exposed to more frequent disasters, extreme heat, heavy rainfall and drought, all of which raise maintenance costs. The article catalogues the strategies states are using, distinguishing those spending the historic Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act allocations from those experimenting with their own funding and financing mechanisms, and presents them as a snapshot of approaches with named adopters rather than as a ranking. The emphasis throughout is that resilience spending competes with other essential priorities such as health care and education, so the question states are answering is how to manage rising costs while meeting those obligations too.
insights: The scale is set by deferred maintenance rather than by new adaptation: a backlog of nearly $1 trillion across states means most resilience spending is catching up on existing assets, not building new protection.

A 50-state scan of 2023 and 2024 legislation is the method, which produces a menu of mechanisms with named adopters and makes the article useful as a source of state precedents rather than as an argument.
IIJA implementation and home-grown state mechanisms are treated as two different things, so a state's approach depends on whether it is deploying federal money or raising its own.
The competition with health care and education is stated explicitly, which is the political constraint any state-level resilience instrument has to survive.

records.title: Is Physical Climate Risk Priced? Evidence from Regional Variation in Exposure to Heat Stress
records.authors: Viral V. Acharya; Timothy Johnson; Suresh Sundaresan; Tuomas Tomunen
records.summary: Acharya, Johnson, Sundaresan and Tomunen test whether physical climate risk is priced by exploiting regional variation in exposure to heat stress, and they test it across three asset classes at once: municipal bonds, corporate bonds and equities. They find consistent evidence across all three that local exposure to heat stress is associated with higher yield spreads for bonds and higher conditional expected returns for stocks. Using heat stress rather than a coastal hazard is the design choice that makes the result general: heat exposure varies regionally across the whole country rather than concentrating on a coastline, so the test is not confined to the flood-exposed jurisdictions where most climate pricing work is done. The paper was awarded the Q-Group's 2022 Jack Treynor Prize and was revised in November 2024 from a September 2022 original.
insights: Finding a consistent premium across municipal bonds, corporate bonds and equities is the strength of the paper: a result in one asset class can be a local artefact, and the same sign in three is much harder to explain away.

Heat stress is the methodological choice that matters, because it varies across the entire country rather than along a coast, so the finding is not limited to the flood-exposed jurisdictions that dominate this literature.
A higher yield spread on municipal bonds in heat-exposed regions means the cost of public capital already reflects a hazard most municipal adaptation planning treats as secondary to flooding.

Higher conditional expected returns on equities in exposed regions is the equity-market counterpart: investors require compensation, which is the same thing as a higher cost of capital for firms in those places.

records.title: WMO: Climate Services Support Climate Action
records.summary: A World Meteorological Organization press release of 7 November 2024 announcing its multi-agency State of Climate Services report. The finance figure is the reason to hold it: of the US$63 billion being spent on climate adaptation, nearly a third goes toward climate-informed investments, and an estimated US$4 to 5 billion of that explicitly supports climate services and early warning activities. In 2024 one third of National Meteorological and Hydrological Services provide climate services at an essential level and nearly one third at an advanced or full level, with Asia and Africa making the clearest gains on the back of targeted adaptation funding, while Latin America and the Caribbean face growing need for early warning against forest fires and drought. On losses, over 2020 to mid-2024 floods were the most frequently reported disaster, heat-related hazards became the leading cause of death at 57 per cent of reported weather, water and climate deaths globally, and storms produced 59 per cent of economic losses, per EM-DAT data cited in the report. The Secretary-General's stated position is that the cost of no action is several times higher than the cost of action.
insights: The $4 to 5 billion for climate services inside $63 billion of adaptation spending is roughly 7 per cent, and climate services are the input every other adaptation investment depends on for its own targeting. A thin allocation to the information layer is a structural finding rather than a budget detail.

Deaths and losses decouple across hazards: heat kills most, at 57 per cent of reported deaths, while storms cost most, at 59 per cent of economic losses. A financing instrument tuned to economic loss will systematically underweight the hazard that kills, which is why heat is hard to insure.

The release notes that continued investment is not translating into capacity at National Meteorological and Hydrological Services, which is an intermediation finding of the same shape as the Ford Foundation record: money increases while the institutions it is meant to build do not.

Reported deaths are falling while economic losses rise, which the release attributes to better early warning and disaster risk management. That is an avoided-loss benefit statement with an attribution attached.

records.title: The Economic Cost of Extreme Weather Events: Could Cost Economy $2 Trillion over the Last Decade
records.summary: The Oxera report, commissioned by the International Chamber of Commerce, reveals that extreme weather events have caused an estimated $2 trillion in economic losses globally over the past decade, impacting 1.6 billion people, particularly in vulnerable developing economies that face escalating risks and disproportionate economic impacts. The findings underline the urgent need for enhanced climate action and financial investment to mitigate future disruptions and address the inequalities exacerbated by climate change.
insights: Extreme weather events have resulted in $2 trillion in economic losses globally over the last decade.
Approximately 4,000 extreme weather events affected 1.6 billion people between 2014 and 2023.
Economic damages from extreme weather have accelerated, with $451 billion in losses reported in the last two years alone.
Developing economies are disproportionately impacted, with some single events costing more than the entire annual GDP of certain countries.
Climate change is an immediate problem, with ongoing adverse economic impacts felt in real-time.
Extreme weather events exacerbate existing social and economic inequalities.
Investment decisions are increasingly influenced by risks associated with extreme weather, potentially limiting growth in certain regions.
Migration and displacement due to climate-related events are likely to become pressing global issues.

records.title: The Weekly: Voting, the Candidates, and Climate Disasters
records.summary: This short pre-election issue links climate disasters to the 2024 US election through four summarised news items. It reports that North Carolina's voting system proved resilient after Hurricane Helene because of earlier policies such as no-excuse absentee and early voting. It notes that disasters shift political views only slowly, that climate migration is largely missing from immigration debate, and that presidents hold direct power over post-disaster capital allocation through FEMA.
insights: Of 80 early voting sites expected to open in disaster-impacted areas of Western North Carolina, only 4, in Buncombe County, could not open.
$5 million in state and federal emergency funding was used to support election communications and voting after Helene.
No single climate disaster shifts attitudes on its own, but cumulative experience can narrow the partisan gap on climate policy.
Trump indicated curtailing FEMA funds and suggested disaster funding to states could depend on political support, such as withholding wildfire support from California over water allocation.
Harris gave no explicit disaster or resilience plan but bolstered FEMA funds after Helene and Milton.

records.title: Conceptual Note on Adaptation
institutions: Network for Greening the Financial System
records.summary: The NGFS Conceptual Note on Adaptation (November 2024) is the network's first comprehensive exploration of climate adaptation and its implications for financial stability. It makes the case that central banks and supervisors should integrate adaptation into their mandates of price and financial stability, covering: the economic costs of insufficient adaptation (up to USD 1,266 trillion total inaction costs through 2100; ~1% GDP/year losses for low-income countries 2000–2019); the triple dividend of adaptation investment (up to USD 12 in economic benefit per USD 1 invested); an adaptation finance gap of USD 194–366 billion/year in developing countries; and the 60% global insurance protection gap (USD 280B total economic losses vs. USD 108B insured in 2023). The note identifies four priority areas for central banks and supervisors: metrics/disclosure, regulatory frameworks, enabling adaptation finance, and international collaboration.
insights: Extreme weather events linked to climate change reduced GDP by approximately 1% per year on average for low-income countries between 2000 and 2019; in some EMDEs, unmitigated climate change could reduce GDP by more than 12% by 2050.
The total cost of inaction from 2025 to 2100 is estimated at up to USD 1,266 trillion, and 32 million individuals are at risk of falling into poverty by 2030 due to insufficient adaptation.

Adaptation investment returns are high: the World Bank estimated a 1:4 dividend; more recent research (Standard Chartered/KPMG/UNDRR, 2024) finds USD 12 in overall economic benefit for every USD 1 invested. Every USD 1 billion invested against coastal flooding yields USD 14 billion in avoided economic damages.

The annual adaptation finance gap in developing countries ranges from USD 194 billion to USD 366 billion, 10 to 18 times current financing flows, and is projected to widen to USD 315–565 billion by 2050. Only ~4% of global climate finance goes to adaptation, with 98% from public sources.

In 2023, 60% of global exposures were uninsured (total economic losses USD 280B vs. insured losses USD 108B). Annual insured losses have grown 5–7% per decade for 30 years. Closing insurance protection gaps is a direct financial stability concern for central banks and supervisors.

Risk-based insurance pricing and impact underwriting can create feedback loops that incentivize physical adaptation: higher premiums for climate-exposed assets signal risk and encourage investment in flood barriers, elevated structures, or managed retreat, ultimately reducing vulnerability and premiums.
records.publisher: Network for Greening the Financial System

records.title: Adaptation Gap Report 2024: Come Hell and High Water - As Fires and Floods Hit the Poor Hardest, It Is Time for the World to Step Up Adaptation Actions
records.summary: The Adaptation Gap Report 2024 underscores the urgent need for enhanced climate adaptation actions globally, particularly for vulnerable populations disproportionately affected by climate-related disasters. It highlights significant financial gaps in adaptation efforts and advocates for innovative financing, capacity-building, and effective planning to create equitable and resilient responses to climate change. The report calls for better alignment between Nationally Determined Contributions and National Adaptation Plans, emphasizing the necessity for transformational approaches to close the adaptation finance gap and support sustainable development.
insights: The world is on track for a temperature rise of 2.6-3.1°C, necessitating urgent adaptation measures.
Estimated adaptation finance needs for developing countries range from $387 billion to $975 billion annually.
While international public adaptation finance flows increased to $28 billion in 2022, this remains inadequate to meet the urgent needs of vulnerable nations.
The adaptation finance gap is particularly severe in highly vulnerable countries, hindering their ability to effectively respond to climate impacts.
Over 87% of countries have national adaptation planning instruments, but implementation quality and alignment with Nationally Determined Contributions vary significantly.

records.title: The Weekly: Gaps in Flood Insurance, Local Microgrids, and North Carolina's Deficit
institutions: Disability Resource Center of the Panhandle
records.summary: This short edition of The Weekly summarizes flood insurance gaps, the vulnerability of mobile and manufactured homes in Hurricanes Helene and Milton, microgrids deployed after Helene, and ReBuild NC's funding deficit and displaced applicants. It closes with evidence that climate risk and insurance costs are beginning to depress some home values.
insights: Only 4% of Americans have flood insurance, and 95% of flood policies are written by the NFIP.
14% of homes in Western North Carolina and 11% in Tampa Bay are mobile or manufactured homes.
ReBuild NC has a deficit of over $150 million, with 2,700 applicants helped and 1,600 still awaiting assistance.
North Carolina appropriated $273M for Hurricane Helene, which cannot be used for earlier disasters.
Florida property values in 2020 were 5% below their pre-2008 high in one analysis.

records.title: Rising to the Challenge: Success Stories and Strategies for Achieving Climate Adaptation and Resilience
records.authors: Jia Li; Esther Naikal; Thomas Kerr; Stéphane Hallegatte
records.summary: This is the executive summary of the World Bank's 2024 report Rising to the Challenge, which frames adaptation and resilience as inseparable from development. It finds that about one-fifth of the world's population, 1.2 billion people in 103 countries, is both exposed to climate hazards and highly vulnerable, and that income growth halved the share at high risk between 2010 and 2021. Readiness assessments in 44 countries show major gaps in sector implementation, macrofiscal risk and monitoring. Case studies show public and private actors scaling adaptation, while barriers such as difficulty monetising resilience benefits and credit vulnerabilities limit private investment.
insights: 1.2 billion people across 103 countries (86 percent of global population) are both exposed to at least one climate-related hazard and highly vulnerable.
The share of global population at high risk from climate hazards fell from 36 to 18 percent between 2010 and 2021.

A 10 percent increase in GDP per capita is associated with a 1.5 percentage-point decline in the share of population at high risk and a 5 percent reduction in people pushed into extreme poverty by 2030.
More resilient power, water, sanitation and transport assets cost about 3 percent more but could yield $4.2 trillion in net benefits, $4 per $1 invested.
Only 5 percent of total climate finance ($63 billion per year in 2021-22) is counted as adaptation finance.
Barriers to private resilience investment include difficulty monetising benefits, unclear metrics and credit vulnerabilities that raise capital costs.

records.title: Sovereigns: Climate Performance and the Cost of Capital
records.authors: Kamesh Korangi, Josephine Richardson, Hazel Ilango
records.summary: The resource discusses the interplay between sovereign climate performance and the cost of capital, emphasizing the significant role that government policy decisions play in the climate transition. It employs an advanced regression model to explore how climate factors influence government bond yields, identifying key drivers and the evolution of their impact over time, particularly highlighting the unique dynamics within ASEAN and Western European nations.
insights: Government policy decisions are crucial in mitigating climate risks and shaping the financial stability of sovereigns.
The correlation between climate performance and government bond yields has been increasing, particularly since 2018.
ASEAN countries exhibit unique challenges regarding climate vulnerability and bond yield interactions compared to other regions.
Research indicates that higher emissions correlate with increased bond yields in certain contexts, especially in relatively developed regions like Europe.
Effective climate policies can help mitigate credit risks associated with sovereign debt, potentially lowering the cost of capital for climate-related investments.
The significance of climate-related factors in bond yields can vary significantly over time and by region, indicating a nuanced relationship.
The use of advanced regression models, including SHAP analysis, provides deeper insights into the factors influencing bond yields beyond traditional economic measures.
Innovative financial mechanisms linked to climate performance could enhance investor confidence and improve the credit ratings of vulnerable countries.
Higher climate readiness generally correlates with lower bond yields, although this relationship can vary based on specific socio-economic factors.
Transition risks associated with climate change may not be fully priced into the sovereign debt markets yet, leading to potential mispricings.

records.title: Understanding Global Concessional Climate Finance 2024
records.authors: Baysa Naran, Tinglu Zhang, Ishrita Gupta
records.summary: The 'Understanding Global Concessional Climate Finance 2024' report underscores the urgent need to significantly increase concessional capital finance to meet Paris Agreement goals, especially for vulnerable regions. It highlights trends from 2019 to 2022, revealing a 50% increase in international concessional climate finance to USD 81 billion, though still far below fossil fuel subsidies. The report emphasizes the necessity of blended finance, public-private collaboration, and innovative funding mechanisms to address substantial funding gaps in adaptation and resilience projects, while recommending improvements in coordination and impact metrics.
insights: Concessional capital finance needs to increase fivefold by 2030 to achieve climate goals.
In 2022, international concessional climate finance reached USD 81 billion, a 50% increase from 2019, but still low compared to fossil fuel subsidies of USD 1.3 trillion.
About 33% of total international concessional finance went to least-developed countries (LDCs), highlighting their critical financing needs.
Blended finance can effectively lower project risks and attract diverse investor types through innovative capital structures.
Technical assistance is crucial for enhancing the commercial viability and impact of climate finance projects.
The presence of risk buffers, like first loss and subordinate equity, increases the attractiveness of investments for institutional players.
Concessional finance has been shown to quadruple private investments for every dollar of donor capital utilized.

records.title: Aligning Community, Conservation, and Defense Priorities in the Fort Huachuca Sentinel Landscape
records.authors: Chris Wolff; Reed Benoit; Shaun O’Rourke
records.summary: The Fort Huachuca Sentinel Landscape faces severe groundwater depletion affecting ecosystems, military operations, and the local economy. Collaborating with various stakeholders, QV has developed financial strategies and secured over $4 million for groundwater recharge projects. This initiative also aims to establish an $80 million endowment for long-term conservation and operational needs, serving as a model for similar landscapes nationwide.
insights: Groundwater depletion threatens ecosystems and military readiness in Fort Huachuca.
Collaboration among diverse stakeholders is crucial for effective resource management.
Innovative financing can bridge gaps in existing funding mechanisms for conservation.
Secured funding of over $4 million supports immediate and sustainable groundwater recharge projects.
An $80 million endowment is being structured for long-term stewardship and operational needs.
The partnership model could be replicated across other US Sentinel Landscapes.
Aligning priorities among local communities, conservation agencies, and military partners enhances project success.
A phased investment plan helps manage funding effectively across different stakeholders.
Blended finance approaches accelerate project implementation and ensure ongoing funding.
Demonstrating measurable outcomes strengthens support for conservation initiatives.

records.title: Why Private Capital Is Indispensable to Close the Great Development and Climate Financing Divide
records.summary: This World Economic Forum article (October 2024), co-authored by the UN Special Envoy for Financing Sustainable Development and WEF's Lead for Sustainable Finance, argues that the SDG financing gap in emerging and developing economies has grown from $2.5 trillion annually (2017 estimate) to $4.2 trillion, constituting a "great financial divide." Private capital mobilization reached an all-time high of $21.9 billion in 2022 but represents less than 20% of total funds mobilized. The piece calls for blended finance structures, MDB/DFI de-risking mechanisms, and enabling policy environments, citing Egypt's $14.7 billion green project pipeline as a replicable model, to attract commercial capital to climate, energy, water, and nature investments in developing markets.
insights: The SDG financing gap in emerging and developing economies has grown from $2.5 trillion/year (2017) to $4.2 trillion/year (2024), driven by COVID-19 impacts, geopolitical fragmentation, and rising debt burdens.

Private capital mobilization for sustainable development reached an all-time high of $21.9 billion in 2022 but still represents less than 20% of total development funds mobilized, illustrating the scale of the structural gap between available and needed private finance.

Renewable energy projects in emerging markets cost up to three times more than in developed countries, with the cost premium driven primarily by macroeconomic risk factors rather than project-specific risks, making de-risking instruments the critical lever.

External public debt service in developing economies rose from 5% of public revenues in 2010 to 8.8% today, with a growing number of countries spending more on interest payments than on development efforts, crowding out public climate and resilience investment.

Egypt's Nexus of Water, Food and Energy programme created a green project pipeline worth $14.7 billion using government and concessional financing as a catalytic layer to unlock private-sector engagement, offered as a replicable model for other developing economies.

WEF's Mobilizing Investment for Clean Energy in Emerging Economies Network published a 'Playbook of Solutions' referencing over 100 policy measures, finance mechanisms, and de-risking solutions that have successfully catalyzed private capital for clean energy in emerging markets.

Global leaders at WEF's Sustainable Development Impact Meetings identified three priority action areas: (1) collaboration across the investment value chain to make projects bankable, (2) strategic deployment of scarce public funds to catalyze commercial capital, and (3) enabling policy environments through strategic reforms.

records.title: The Weekly: 5 Early Insights From Hurricane Helene
records.summary: This issue of The Weekly offers five early takeaways from Hurricane Helene in 2024. It reports that climate change worsened the storm's rainfall, that hurricanes now threaten inland places such as Asheville once seen as climate havens, and that adaptation is growing harder as hazards become less predictable. It notes utilities face rebuilding costs and pressure to harden grids, and cites Hunters Point in Cortez, Florida, as a disaster-resistant development that kept power and stayed insurable. It closes with webinars and a recovery fund for supporting affected communities.
insights: A rapid attribution study by the Berkeley lab found climate change caused over 50% more rainfall during Helene in Georgia and North Carolina.
As of October 1, 1.6 million customers, out of 6 million who lost power, were still without electricity.
Asheville published a 2016 article saying it was ready for the next flood, then became one of the hardest-hit communities in 2024.

Hunters Point in Cortez, Florida, is 31 hurricane-resistant homes with steel roofs, seam-mounted solar and batteries for 10 days of limited power; insurers have covered them while others exit Florida, with prices from $1.25M.
First Street estimates 57 banks with $627 billion in real estate loans could face material financial risk from climate change.

records.title: Assessing the Impact of Climate Resilience
records.summary: An asset manager's account of why measuring the impact of climate resilience investments is harder than measuring climate mitigation, and what to do about it. The argument is that mitigation impact has a universal quantitative yardstick, greenhouse gases emitted or avoided, and resilience has none: the data is mainly qualitative and situation-specific, it depends on assumptions about local and regional climate effects over long timescales, and the underlying benefit is harm avoided against a counterfactual that did not occur and a baseline that itself moves. Wellington sets out approaches it thinks help investors work through those difficulties while still holding resilience as an impact investment class.
insights: The measurement problem is stated precisely: the impact of a resilience investment is loss avoided relative to a counterfactual that did not happen, which requires assumptions rather than observation.

A second and subtler difficulty is the moving baseline: the level of protection a flood defence provides must be measured against a future flood regime that is itself changing, so the denominator shifts while the intervention is in place.

Mitigation is used deliberately as the reference case rather than as a rival: the absence of an equivalent to tonnes of CO2 avoided is what makes resilience impact resist the standard impact-investing toolkit.
The recommended answer is a mix rather than a metric, combining qualitative and quantitative data for a holistic assessment, which is an admission that no single number will do the work.
The research base is a named scientific partnership with Woodwell Climate Research Center rather than a vendor risk score, which is unusual among asset managers writing on physical risk.

records.title: Global Landscape of Climate Finance 2024: Insights for COP29
records.authors: Baysa Naran, Barbara Buchner, Matthew Price, Sean Stout, Maddy Taylor, Dennis Zabeida
records.summary: The 'Global Landscape of Climate Finance 2024' report examines the resilience and growth of climate finance, which reached USD 1.46 trillion in 2022, yet underscores the urgent need for increased funding to meet the estimated annual requirement of USD 7.4 trillion by 2030. It highlights disparities between advanced economies and emerging markets and developing economies (EMDEs), the importance of innovative financing solutions, and the critical need for collaboration, data standardization, and capacity building to enhance the effectiveness of climate finance across sectors.
insights: Climate finance has more than doubled from USD 674 billion in 2018 to USD 1.46 trillion in 2022.
Public sources accounted for 85% of clean transport finance outside China, while private investments are increasingly dominant in the buildings and infrastructure sectors.
Adaptation finance in EMDEs grew faster than mitigation finance, indicating a shift toward urgent climate resilience investments.
There is a significant climate finance gap, especially for least developed countries (LDCs) and small island developing states (SIDS), necessitating increased international public finance support.
Standardization of data and disclosure practices is crucial for improving trust and accountability in climate finance efforts.
Domestic climate finance is becoming increasingly vital, with significant growth in regions like Latin America and South Asia.
Enhanced interoperability among finance providers is needed to maximize resource efficiency and address the fragmented climate finance landscape.
Concessional finance and innovative instruments like debt-for-climate swaps are necessary to promote climate resilience in debt-distressed regions.

records.title: Insurance and Climate Risks: Policy Lessons from Three Bounding Scenarios
records.authors: Carolyn Kousky, Galen Treuer, Katherine J. Mach
institutions: Miami-Dade County Office of Innovation and Economic Development
records.summary: The resource examines the evolving landscape of insurance markets in Florida amid increasing climate risks, particularly related to hurricane and flood threats. It analyzes three different scenarios, exploring how near-term policy decisions will affect long-term outcomes for insurance markets, housing, and local economies. The scenarios emphasize the need for proactive investments in risk reduction, equitable policy-making, and the potential consequences of inaction as climate hazards intensify.
insights: Insurance markets in high-risk regions like Florida are experiencing significant stress due to escalating climate hazards.
Public-sector insurance programs are increasingly absorbing risks as private insurers withdraw from high-risk areas.
Sustainable adaptation strategies must directly address rising risks rather than merely shifting them to different sectors.
Inequitable access to insurance can exacerbate income inequality, particularly after disasters strike low-income communities.
Near-term regulatory decisions regarding insurance can have profound effects on future disaster recovery and socioeconomic well-being.
records.publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

records.title: The Weekly: U.S. Bridges, Climate Superfund Bill, and Lahaina Homes Still Standing
institutions: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety
records.summary: This edition of The Weekly curates five items: Jay Koh of The Lightsmith Group on the investment case for adaptation, climate-driven deterioration of US bridges, New York's Climate Superfund Bill, climate disaster impacts on people with disabilities, and an IBHS study of homes that survived the Lahaina fire. It frames each as evidence that adaptation needs capital and that building to available standards reduces losses.
insights: New York's Climate Superfund Bill, passed in June 2024, is expected to raise $3B per year for 25 years from the largest emitters, with a third invested in vulnerable communities.
One study found one in four steel bridges will collapse by 2050; the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law allocates $110B to repair US infrastructure including bridges.
Colorado officials estimate needing 5x the annual amount currently provided ($143B) to update affected infrastructure.
70% of deaf evacuees lived in unsanitary conditions for a month after a disaster versus 7% of hearing evacuees, per the U.S. Census Bureau.
The August 2023 Lahaina fire destroyed over 2,000 homes and buildings; IBHS found homes with certain materials and reduced vegetation were more likely to survive.

records.title: California Insurers Begin Giving Discounts for Fire-Proofed Homes
records.summary: California has implemented a new program requiring property insurers to offer discounts for homeowners who mitigate wildfire risks, making it the first state in the nation to do so. However, the discounts are often minimal and may not significantly encourage homeowners to invest in fire-proofing measures. Experts suggest that while the long-term benefits may improve as data on effectiveness becomes available, immediate savings are limited and may not justify the costs of the required mitigation measures.
insights: California is the first state to mandate discounts for wildfire mitigation in property insurance.
Discounts for fire-proofing measures, such as fire-resistant windows, are often minuscule, with some homeowners seeing as little as a $14 saving on a $13,800 premium.
There is a lack of reliable data on the effectiveness of individual wildfire mitigation steps, which has led insurers to offer minimal discounts.
Experts warn that small savings could limit the success of the discount program, making it difficult for homeowners to invest in necessary mitigation upfront.
The California discount program could serve as a model for other states, though many are currently hesitant to implement similar requirements without further data.
A range of property-clearing and design improvements are listed under the state-mandated discounts, but the depth and effectiveness of these strategies remain uncertain.
The approach to discounts varies among insurers, creating inconsistencies that may confuse policyholders.
It's projected that discounts may grow over time as the insurance industry gains more understanding of mitigation effectiveness.
Insurers have cautioned that discounts alone cannot cover the costs of retrofitting homes, and state incentives may be necessary to encourage adoption of wildfire safety measures.
Historical examples from other states, such as Alabama's wind-mitigation discounts, suggest that acceptance and participation may increase as the success of such programs becomes evident.

records.title: Beware How Financial Markets Are Pricing in Climate Risk: An Inconsistent Approach and General Lack of Understanding Is Heightening Risk
records.summary: The financial markets are currently employing an inconsistent approach to pricing climate risk, resulting in a heightened level of uncertainty and risk across the board. This lack of understanding and uniformity in addressing climate-related risks in financial evaluations is exacerbating vulnerabilities in investment and economic stability.
insights: Financial markets lack a consistent methodology for pricing climate risk.
Inconsistencies in climate risk evaluation increase overall market vulnerability.
A general misunderstanding of climate risk among investors is prevalent.
The current approach may lead to mispricing of assets affected by climate change.
There is a critical need for standardized frameworks to assess climate risk.
Market participants often underestimate the long-term impacts of climate change.
Failing to accurately price climate risk could lead to significant financial losses.
Greater transparency and communication are needed regarding climate-related financial risks.

records.title: Integrating Climate Adaptation into Physical Risk Models
records.authors: Wong De Rui; Rick Lord; Kim Kee Bum; Kuntal Singh; Nina Khalili; Rohini Samtani; Tory Grieves
records.summary: GIC and S&P Global Sustainable1 argue that physical climate risk models understate or misrank investment risk because they ignore adaptation, and prototype a method that adds adaptation measures to physical risk assessment. Applied to real estate held by S&P Global REIT Index constituents, it projects cumulative excess costs from climate hazard exposure of US$536bn to US$559bn by 2050, 26% to 28% of the index's real estate asset value. It estimates return ratios for four building-scale adaptations and sizes the market for them. It also shows building-scale adaptation captures only a small share of projected costs, so public investment in large-scale protection is also needed.
insights: Under SSP3-7.0 with no adaptation, index properties could incur US$110bn by 2030, US$310bn by 2040 and US$559bn by 2050 in cumulative excess costs, 28% of real estate asset value as of July 2024.
Wet and dry floodproofing could offset physical hazard costs by US$3.55 for every US$1 invested, and green and cool roofs could save US$7.45 per US$1.
Annual demand for these adaptation solutions is estimated at about US$29bn globally through 2050, or US$726bn cumulatively.
Cumulative net benefits of the four measures studied total US$45bn by 2050 under the medium-high scenario, just 8% of projected cumulative hazard costs.
89% of index constituent assets will be materially exposed to extreme heat by the 2050s, against 1%, 9% and 13% for coastal, pluvial and fluvial flood.

records.title: Federal Land Leasing, Energy, and Local Public Finances
records.summary: The resource highlights a significant legislative disparity in revenue distribution from fossil fuel versus renewable energy projects on federal land, where fossil fuel revenue is shared with states and local communities while renewable energy revenues primarily benefit the federal government. It underscores the public's strong support for reforming policies to establish a revenue-sharing mechanism for renewable energy similar to that of fossil fuels, emphasizing the need for local community involvement in revenue allocation decisions to enhance economic benefits and social acceptance of energy developments.
insights: Revenue from fossil fuel projects is shared with states and local communities, while renewable energy revenues largely stay with the federal government.
The Public Land Renewable Energy Development Act (PLREDA) seeks to establish a revenue-sharing mechanism for renewable energy projects on federal land.
Bipartisan support exists for reforming current policy to allow states and local communities to benefit from renewable energy revenues.
Public opinion shows overwhelming support for equitable revenue distribution from energy projects, with 89% of respondents favoring revenue sharing for renewables.
73% of respondents believe that local communities affected by energy development should influence revenue allocation decisions.
records.publisher: Salata Institute for Climate and Sustainability

records.title: How Local Governments Avoid Floodplain Development Through Consistent Implementation of Routine Municipal Ordinances, Plans, and Programs
records.authors: A R Siders, Jennifer Niemann-Morris, Miyuki Hino, Elizabeth Shields, Lidia Cano Pecharroman, Tess Doeffinger, Logan Gerber-Chavez, Ju-Ching Huang, Alexandra Lafferty, Salvesila Tamima, Caroline Williams, Armen Agopian, Christopher Samoray, Katharine J Mach
institutions: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
records.summary: This study examines how local governments in New Jersey effectively limit floodplain development through the consistent application of routine municipal ordinances, plans, and programs. The analysis reveals that a significant majority of towns have successfully avoided new housing development in floodplains from 2001 to 2019 by utilizing common land use management tools rather than relying on innovative legal measures. The findings challenge prevailing narratives about floodplain development and highlight the importance of having a few high-quality management tools, consistent implementation, and local official commitment.
insights: 85% of towns in New Jersey limited new floodplain housing development from 2001 to 2019.
126 towns in New Jersey managed to put none of their new housing in floodplains during the study period.
Robust floodplain avoidance is achievable through routine administrative practices without the need for legal innovations.
The quality and consistent implementation of floodplain management tools are more critical than their quantity.
Local government capacity is a weak predictor of floodplain development outcomes, counter to expectations from previous studies.
Coastal and populous towns can also effectively limit floodplain development despite common assumptions about their vulnerability.
The study indicates a need to focus on municipalities that are successfully avoiding floodplain development to understand best practices.
Developments in floodplains often lead to increased flood risks, emphasizing the importance of managing local land effectively.
Local commitment and coordination among officials greatly influence the successful implementation of floodplain avoidance strategies.

records.title: G20/OECD Report on Approaches for Financing and Investing in Climate‑resilient Infrastructure
records.summary: The G20/OECD report emphasizes the urgent need for financing climate-resilient infrastructure, particularly in developing countries facing climate risks. It advocates for integrating climate resilience throughout the infrastructure lifecycle, fostering adaptive planning and collaboration among governments, communities, and the private sector. By leveraging innovative financial instruments, project preparation facilities, and nature-based solutions, the report aims to mobilize resources for sustainable infrastructure that meets both economic and climate resilience goals.
insights: Developing countries face significant infrastructure investment gaps while being highly vulnerable to climate impacts.
Integrating climate resilience across the infrastructure lifecycle can enhance economic returns and public safety.
Adaptive planning and collaboration are essential for effective climate-resilient infrastructure development.
Innovative financing mechanisms, including blended finance and public-private partnerships, can attract investment for resilience-focused projects.
Nature-based solutions offer co-benefits that enhance climate resilience and community well-being.
Transforming infrastructure plans into bankable projects is crucial for mobilizing investment, particularly in developing regions.
Community engagement plays a vital role in the successful implementation of climate-resilient infrastructure projects.
Investment in flood-resilient infrastructure has the potential to create substantial job opportunities.

records.title: Climate Resilience and Risk Reduction in the U.S. Virgin Islands
institutions: U.S. Virgin Islands Department of Planning and Natural Resources
Southeast and Caribbean Disaster Resilience Partnership
records.summary: NOAA's project summary describes a $69,000,000 Climate Resilience Regional Challenge award to the U.S. Virgin Islands Department of Planning and Natural Resources. The project buys four at-risk land parcels, one on each main island, for a new Territorial Park System, forms a Water Working Group for Climate Resilience and Nature-based Solutions, and creates a U.S. Virgin Islands Climate Corps to train young adults in restoration work. It frames the benefits as water security, flood and drought protection, habitat and workforce capacity. The Challenge was funded with about $575 million that Congress appropriated through the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022.
insights: The award is $69,000,000, led by the U.S. Virgin Islands Department of Planning and Natural Resources with the Trust for Virgin Islands Lands and the Trust for Public Lands facilitating purchases.
Four naturally and culturally significant parcels will enter a new Territorial Park System for perpetual conservation.
The Climate Corps will train 12 to 20 young people (ages 18 to 30) on each island, spending about 50,000 to 75,000 labor hours on adaptation projects.
The program runs on St. Croix in 2025 and 2027, and on St. Thomas and St. John in 2026 and 2028.
In 2022 Congress appropriated approximately $575 million through the Inflation Reduction Act for the competitive Climate Resilience Regional Challenge.

records.title: Leveraging Cooperative Extension to Build an Enduring Capacity Resilience in Rural Agricultural Communities Across Coastal Virginia, Maryland, and Delaware
institutions: Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University
records.summary: This NOAA Climate Resilience Regional Challenge project summary describes a $1,973,267 award to Virginia Tech's Biological Systems Engineering department to build climate resilience capacity in rural agricultural communities of the Delmarva region. Partners will run a needs assessment and community listening sessions, focusing on low-income, minority and agricultural communities, then design educational programming. The aim is enduring capacity among extension professionals and rural localities to start adaptation and resilience projects.
insights: The award to Virginia Tech Biological Systems Engineering is $1,973,267.
The project covers coastal Virginia, Maryland and Delaware (the Delmarva region), where agriculture anchors the local economy.
It begins with a needs assessment and community listening sessions targeted at low-income, minority and agricultural communities.
It uses Cooperative Extension to build lasting local capacity to initiate climate adaptation projects.

records.title: Bristol Bay Guardians
records.summary: NOAA's profile of a Climate Resilience Regional Challenge award of $1,999,470 to The Nature Conservancy and Igiugig Village in Southwest Alaska. The project expands community-based environmental monitoring in Igiugig and aims to build a regional guardians network modelled on Canada's Indigenous Guardians programs. It invests in local training and uses Indigenous knowledge to guide natural resource management in a region dependent on sockeye salmon.
insights: The award is $1,999,470 to The Nature Conservancy with Igiugig Village.
The project will build a regional guardians network based on Canada's Indigenous Guardians programs.
It expands community-based monitoring in Igiugig and shares the approach with nearby tribal communities.
The Bristol Bay region supports more wild salmon populations than anywhere else on Earth, and climate impacts are already apparent there.

records.title: Bristol Bay Climate Adaptation Planning Program
records.summary: NOAA's profile of a Climate Resilience Regional Challenge award of $2,000,000 to the Bristol Bay Native Association in Alaska. The project, led by a consortium of 31 federally recognized tribes, will center Indigenous knowledge in regional climate adaptation planning. Its three phases establish a Bristol Bay Regional Resilience Collaborative to coordinate planning, education and implementation.
insights: The award is $2,000,000 to the Bristol Bay Native Association.
The project is led by a consortium of 31 federally recognized tribes in a remote region of Alaska.
It will establish the Bristol Bay Regional Resilience Collaborative in a three-phase project.
The funding comes through NOAA's Climate Resilience Regional Challenge.

records.title: Southwest Louisiana and Central Acadiana Resilient Future
records.summary: This NOAA Climate Resilience Regional Challenge project story describes a $1,998,800 award to Tulane University's ByWater Institute for regional resilience planning in Southwest Louisiana and Central Acadiana. The project analyses existing plans, characterises climate risk, prioritises projects and develops engineering reports to move them toward implementation. It also sets up a regional collaborative for continued coordination across governments, including tribal governments.
insights: The ByWater Institute at Tulane University received $1,998,800 under the Climate Resilience Regional Challenge.
Activities include analysing existing plans, characterising climate risk, defining best practices, prioritising projects, evaluating policies and developing engineering reports.
A regional collaborative is to provide continued coordination, implementation, evaluation and resource sharing beyond the award.

The funding targets foundational gaps: technical and data information, community use of data and tools, coordination between governments at all scales including tribal, and assessing the robustness of existing resilience projects.

records.title: Strengthening Opportunities for Adaptive Response
institutions: United States Conference of Catholic Bishops
records.summary: This NOAA Climate Resilience Regional Challenge project story describes a $2,000,000 award to Catholic Relief Services for the Strengthening Opportunities for Adaptive Response (SOAR) project in the Federated States of Micronesia. The project aims to elevate the priorities of vulnerable coastal and remote island communities and provide technical and financial resources to jumpstart priority resilience projects. It targets 30,000 individuals across 39 coastal communities in Chuuk and Yap.
insights: Catholic Relief Services, with the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops, received $2,000,000 under the Climate Resilience Regional Challenge.
SOAR aims to reach 30,000 individuals across 39 coastal communities, 14 in Chuuk and 25 in Yap.
The project provides technical and financial resources to jumpstart priority resilience projects and build collaboration beyond the award.
It builds a learning network that leverages existing research, encourages natural resource stewardship and generates evidence to expand coastal resilience work.

records.title: Building Resilience to Extreme Weather in Northeast Ohio
records.summary: NOAA's Climate Resilience Regional Challenge awarded $1,310,142 to the Northeast Ohio Black Health Coalition to set up a resilience hub of 30 community-based organizations in a region with high poverty rates and climate vulnerability. The coalition will address barriers to climate resilience, invest in climate literacy and public engagement, and secure funding for executable resilience projects. The project builds on efforts to address the disproportionate impact of extreme weather and flooding in the region while building capacity among newer community-based organizations.
insights: The award to the Northeast Ohio Black Health Coalition is $1,310,142.
The resilience hub joins 30 community-based organizations.
One stated aim is securing funding to implement executable resilience projects, so the award is capacity-building ahead of project finance.

records.title: Growing Regional Resilience Coordination on Aquidneck Island
records.summary: NOAA's Office for Coastal Management profiles a $1,999,777 Climate Resilience Regional Challenge award to the Aquidneck Land Trust (formerly City of Newport) for island-wide resilience on Aquidneck Island, Rhode Island. The project partners the land trust with Newport, Middletown, Portsmouth and Naval Station Newport. It will provide technical assistance, capacity building and strategies, and implement nature-based projects against flooding, sea level rise and water pollution. The land trust has already conserved over 2,800 acres.
insights: The award is $1,999,777, with the Aquidneck Land Trust as recipient (formerly City of Newport).
The land trust warns that at current development rates all remaining unprotected open space on the island will be developed by 2050.
The land trust has conserved over 2,800 acres in prior projects.
Planned projects use nature-based solutions to address flooding, sea level rise and water pollution.
The partnership spans three municipalities and Naval Station Newport.

records.title: Regional Collaboration for Better Resilience Outcomes in the Puget Sound Basin
records.summary: This NOAA Climate Resilience Regional Challenge project summary describes a $1,999,963 award to King County, Washington, to fund staffing and programming for the Puget Sound Climate Preparedness Collaborative. The collaborative links local and county governments, tribes and regional agencies building resilience to climate change. The funding will strengthen regional capacity, partner with Coast Salish tribes on climate impacts, and build a knowledge base of climate preparedness resources.
insights: King County, Washington received $1,999,963.
The Puget Sound basin holds more than five million people and 19 federally recognized Coast Salish tribes.
Funds support staffing and programming for the Puget Sound Climate Preparedness Collaborative.
The project will partner with Coast Salish tribes and build a regional knowledge base of preparedness resources.

records.title: Enhancing the United Houma Nation’s Short-, Mid-, and Long-Term Coastal Resilience
records.summary: This NOAA Climate Resilience Regional Challenge project summary describes a $56,573,066 award to the United Houma Nation for coastal resilience in southern Louisiana. The Tribe's five-phase plan combines traditional knowledge with current planning and technology, and the award funds four of those phases. It covers hardening the central and satellite community resilience hubs, expanding communications, and developing a community-led migration strategy with land stewardship capacity.
insights: The United Houma Nation's project was awarded $56,573,066 under the Climate Resilience Regional Challenge.

The Tribe's administrative building serves as a shelter and distribution site during disasters for residents of all six parishes the Nation covers, and will be strengthened for flood, wind and energy resilience with nature-based infrastructure.
Satellite hubs across the six parishes will be upgraded to current wind and flood building science and serve as convening spots before and after disasters.
Community-led migration is framed as returning relocation decisions to tribal citizens, given a history of forced movement, and funds strategy development and land stewardship mechanisms.
The Climate Resilience Regional Challenge draws on approximately $575 million appropriated by Congress in 2022 through the Inflation Reduction Act.

records.title: The Washington State Coastal Climate Resilience Initiative: Accelerating Implementation of 20 Years of Partnership Efforts
institutions: Washington State Coastal Climate Resilience Partnership
University of Washington Climate Impacts Group
records.summary: This NOAA project summary describes the Washington State Coastal Climate Resilience Initiative, a $73,587,134 award under the Climate Resilience Regional Challenge led by the Washington Coastal Zone Management Program. It moves a shared coastal resilience vision, developed over 20 years of partnership, from planning to the state's first coordinated coast-wide implementation. Funded work includes habitat restoration, nature-based shoreline improvements for coastal highways, stormwater drainage upgrades, a tribal resilience grant program, a fellowship, workforce pathways and topobathymetric data collection.
insights: Funding amount: $73,587,134, led by the Washington Coastal Zone Management Program.
Projected disasters in Washington's coastal areas stand at six per year against one predicted for 1990, with up to ten a year expected by 2040.
Projects include nature-based shoreline improvements for State Routes 112 and 105 and the setback of critical infrastructure.
The Climate Resilience Regional Challenge draws on approximately $575 million appropriated through the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022.
The University of Washington Climate Impacts Group will compile coastal risk information and adaptation case studies to guide continued coordination.

records.title: Stronger, Together: Expanding Climate Adaptation Technical Assistance for Frontline Alaska Native Communities
institutions: Alaska Tribal Conference on Environmental Management
records.summary: This NOAA Climate Resilience Regional Challenge project summary describes a $74,950,045 award to the Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium to expand climate adaptation capacity in nearly 100 Alaska Native communities. The project establishes a voluntary community climate risk assessment program to inform decisions on protection-in-place, managed retreat and relocation. It expands statewide tribal adaptation technical assistance and builds networking and knowledge sharing among practitioners.
insights: The Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium was awarded $74,950,045 to serve nearly 100 Alaska Native communities.
Lack of community-specific hazard data is identified as a major barrier, addressed by a voluntary risk assessment program supporting protection-in-place, managed retreat and relocation decisions.
The award supports approximately 49 new and existing full-time staff providing technical assistance in engineering, economics, planning, contracting and grant writing and management.
Networking will expand the capacity of the Alaska Tribal Conference on Environmental Management to focus on climate adaptation.
The Climate Resilience Regional Challenge draws on approximately $575 million appropriated by Congress in 2022 through the Inflation Reduction Act.

records.title: Building a Climate Ready New Jersey
institutions: New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection
Jacques Cousteau National Estuarine Research Reserve
records.summary: This NOAA project summary describes a $72,493,449 Climate Resilience Regional Challenge award to the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection covering 16 coastal counties. The award funds three implementation projects in Newark, Paterson, Perth Amboy, Sawmill Creek and Little Ferry that combine green and gray infrastructure against storm surge, sea level rise and precipitation flooding. It also builds a resilience planning and project design pipeline so plans are ready for future funding and financing, and an education and workforce initiative called EduCATE.
insights: The award to New Jersey DEP totals $72,493,449 across 16 coastal counties.

Three implementation projects: stormwater and neighborhood resilience in Newark, Paterson and Perth Amboy; coastal ecosystem restoration at Sawmill Creek Wildlife Management Area; and the Little Ferry Riverfront Park.
A planning and design pipeline aims to produce project designs ready for future funding and financing.
The Climate Resilience Regional Challenge draws on about $575 million appropriated by Congress through the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022.

records.title: Q&A: Can Debt-for-Nature 'Swaps' Help Tackle Biodiversity Loss and Climate Change?
records.summary: This Carbon Brief Q&A examines debt-for-nature swaps, financial agreements in which a conservation organisation or government reduces or restructures a developing country's debt in exchange for investment in local conservation, tracing their origins from 1987 to a current resurgence. Since the 1980s, 145 swaps worldwide have written off $3.7bn in face-value debt, with $2.4bn in Latin America and the Caribbean. The piece weighs proponents' claims that swaps can unlock $100bn+ for developing countries against critics who call them too small, sovereignty-undermining, and unproven for biodiversity outcomes, and examines governance, greenwashing, and human rights concerns through case studies in Ecuador, Seychelles, Gabon, and Bolivia.
insights: 145 debt-for-nature swaps since the 1980s have written off $3.7bn in face value globally, with $2.4bn concentrated in Latin America and the Caribbean, dwarfed by the $443.5bn that low- and middle-income countries paid to service foreign debt in 2022 alone.

A 2023 IIED analysis estimates debt-for-nature and debt-for-climate swaps could collectively free up more than $100bn of debt in developing countries, but critics note current deal sizes are far too small: the landmark Seychelles swap was only $23m and Ecuador's record 2023 swap wrote off $1.1bn against a $9tn total developing-country debt stock.

Ecuador's 2023 Galapagos swap, the largest by debt volume at $1.1bn cancelled, committed $450m to conservation but faced documented governance failures: lack of Indigenous consultation, limited monitoring, no additional international disbursements, and a 20% administration fee to a foreign-owned conservation entity that immediately reduced country savings.

Poland's 1992 swap allocated the highest absolute conservation investment of any swap on record at over $500m; Ecuador's 2023 swap ranks second at over $400m earmarked for conservation, illustrating how deal design, not just volume, determines conservation yield.

A 2023 study found 67 debt-distressed countries collectively host 22% of global biodiversity priority areas, and for 35 of them, all unprotected priority areas could be conserved for a fraction of national debt, establishing a theoretical economic case for swaps even if current execution falls short.

High transaction costs from multilateral negotiations, intermediary fees, and legal advisors erode conservation value; currency risk compounds losses, Zambia's 1989 swap funds were exhausted in one year due to rapid local currency devaluation.

records.title: Ten Years in, D.C.’s Stormwater Credit Market Is Thriving and Still Growing
records.summary: Washington D.C.'s Stormwater Retention Credit (SRC) market, established a decade ago, has become a model for innovative stormwater management, allowing developers to purchase credits from green infrastructure projects to meet runoff requirements. This program has significantly increased green spaces and improved water quality, drawing interest from cities globally as a potential solution to similar environmental challenges.
insights: The SRC market allows developers to buy credits to meet stormwater runoff obligations, promoting green infrastructure deployment.
Since 2014, over 1.7 million credits have been sold, capturing more than 40 million gallons of runoff annually.
The market incentivizes projects in under-resourced areas and supports ecological and social co-benefits.
D.C. is seen as a leader in stormwater credit markets, with cities like Grand Rapids and Cook County developing similar programs.
The Nature Conservancy's involvement highlights the potential for private investment in stormwater solutions.
The SRC market has influenced educational programs at major universities to teach its model to future practitioners.
Financial benefits from green infrastructure investments can yield substantial community returns, such as $7.80 per dollar invested.
The market continues to evolve, with policy updates planned to enhance local participation and support small businesses.

records.title: The Preparedness Payoff: The Economic Benefits of Investing in Climate Resilience
records.summary: The report titled 'The Preparedness Payoff: The Economic Benefits of Investing in Climate Resilience' outlines the substantial economic advantages of investing in disaster preparedness, revealing that every dollar spent yields significant savings in economic costs, job retention, and damage reduction. The findings highlight that proactive investments not only mitigate the impacts of natural disasters but also enhance community resilience and economic stability, providing a solid return on investment.
insights: Every $1 invested in disaster preparation saves $13 in total economic costs.
For every dollar invested in resilience, communities can save $7 in economic costs.
Preparedness investments can preserve jobs, with $10.8 billion potentially saving 184,000 jobs in Miami.
Smaller investments, like $83 million for tornado readiness in Nashville, can save over 5,300 jobs.
Investments lead to increased economic activity and workforce retention, even when disasters do not occur.
Disasters exceeding $1 billion in impacts highlight the need for significant preparedness investments.
High-severity disasters require larger upfront investments to mitigate potential damages.
Preparedness measures like early warning systems enhance overall community resilience.
Economic savings include reduced damage, cleanup costs, and less economic damage during disasters.

records.title: The Many Stories of Adaptation Finance
records.authors: Stéphane Hallegatte; Jia Li; Ferzina Banaji
institutions: United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction
records.summary: World Bank authors argue that tracked adaptation finance, $63 billion in 2021-22 against an estimated $212 billion needed per year by 2030 for developing countries, captures only part of what builds resilience. Drawing on Country Climate and Development Reports, they say resilience requires more rapid development, more resilient development and targeted adaptation interventions, and only the last is counted as adaptation finance. They stress that building new assets right is cheaper than retrofitting, and call for better climate risk information and stronger land-use and infrastructure regulation. They point to taxonomies, disclosure standards and rating systems as foundations for spending better, not only more.
insights: Adaptation finance was $63 billion in 2021-22, against an estimated $212 billion needed per year by 2030 for developing countries alone (CPI).
Adaptation finance declined in 2023 as a proportion of total climate finance.
Access to safely managed drinking water rose from 62% of the global population in 2000 to 74% in 2020, an example of development reducing vulnerability that is not counted as adaptation.
Every building, infrastructure asset or urban plan that accounts for climate risk is effectively adaptation investment not captured by any tracker.
Retrofitting is costly and often justified only for critical assets, so building new assets right matters most in low- and middle-income countries.
In Tunis, sharing planned infrastructure locations helped steer urban development to low-risk zones.

records.title: Navigating Climate Risks: Progress and Challenges in U.S. Insurance Sector Disclosures
institutions: Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures
records.summary: Ceres's second annual analysis, conducted with Manifest Climate, assesses major US insurers' climate risk strategies through their responses to the NAIC Climate Risk Disclosure Survey, which is aligned with the TCFD framework. It finds more groups reporting, and improvement in some risk management and emissions sub-areas, but significant gaps, especially in metrics and targets. It argues that the pace of improvement is too slow given the materiality of climate risk to insurer solvency.
insights: The analysis covers responses from 516 insurance groups, over 1,695 companies, representing 80% of the US insurance market and over $2 trillion in direct premiums written in 2022; 494 groups reported the year before.
94% of groups report on risk management, 86% on strategy, 81% on governance and only 29% on metrics and targets.
Just 26% of the 516 groups reported across all four TCFD categories, while 44% disclosed on three of the four.
Reporting declined in two sub-areas: management's role in assessing climate risks and opportunities, and the targets used to manage them.
Between 2017 and 2023, 137 separate billion-dollar disasters cost over $1 trillion in damage.
Adoption of climate scenario analysis by insurers is increasing, but transparency on greenhouse gas emissions reductions remains limited.

records.title: Housing Amenity and Affordability Shape Floodplain Development
records.authors: Christopher Samoray, Miyuki Hino, A.R. Siders, Armen Agopian, Katharine J. Mach
institutions: University of Miami Climate Resilience Institute
University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
records.summary: Samoray and colleagues analyse 87 million US residential parcels against FEMA Digital Flood Insurance Rate Maps to characterise floodplain housing stock by value and type and to measure how new development changes exposure. Of the 87.1 million parcels, 4.8 per cent, or 4.1 million, are in the Special Flood Hazard Area: 2,818,694 single-family homes, 963,043 multi-family and 261,186 mobile homes. Exposure follows a U-shaped distribution in housing value that deepens over time: 7 per cent of the most expensive quintile and 5.5 per cent of the most affordable quintile are in floodplains, against the middle range, and in the extreme 5 per cent tails the shares reach 9.3 and 6.2 per cent. The pattern splits by geography: in coastal communities the most expensive quintile holds 21.4 per cent of floodplain housing against 11.9 per cent in the middle, while inland the most affordable quintile is 1.6 percentage points above the middle. Using a floodplain price ratio comparing a community's median floodplain value to its county median, 5613 of 10,237 communities have affordable floodplains and 4616 expensive ones; coastal communities average a ratio of 2.13 against 1.06 inland. In the 112 communities with a ratio below 0.25, 38 per cent of floodplain housing stock is mobile homes, falling below 10 per cent as the ratio approaches 1. Between 2001 and 2019 communities with very expensive floodplains built an average of 105 new floodplain residences against 15 for communities with very affordable floodplains. Mobile home construction in floodplains peaked in the 1990s at 6374 a year and fell to 2787 a year after 2000, while single-family homes rose to about three-quarters of new floodplain housing in the 2010s.
insights: The U-shaped exposure curve is the finding that breaks the standard policy frame: both the richest and the poorest housing is over-represented in the floodplain, and a national policy designed for either one underserves the other.

The bifurcation in housing value is a bifurcation in the ability to self-finance, so the same physical hazard produces two entirely different financing problems, one of affordability and one of moral hazard around protecting expensive private property with public funds.

The floodplain price ratio is the paper's most usable instrument for policy design, because it shows that community-scale averages mask who is actually at risk: 112 communities have floodplain housing worth under a quarter of the local median, and 38 per cent of it is mobile homes.

Exposure is growing fastest where it is most expensive: 105 new floodplain homes per very expensive community against 15 per very affordable one over two decades, so the NFIP's future book is being written on the coast.

The authors name the NFIP pricing dilemma precisely, that premiums must signal risk to affluent coastal owners while staying affordable for inland residents, which is a single instrument being asked to do two opposite things.

Mobile homes in floodplains halved after 2000 while single-family construction rose to three-quarters of new floodplain housing, so the exposure is shifting toward higher-value, more insurable and more politically defended assets.

records.title: Firm Adaptation to Climate Risk in the Developing World
records.summary: The resource examines the adaptation of firms in the developing world to climate risks, emphasizing that while extreme weather events typically hinder competitiveness, effective recovery is possible under certain conditions. It highlights the influence of firm capabilities, access to information, and public infrastructure quality on resilience. Additionally, the impacts of gradual climate changes, particularly temperature increases, are analyzed, revealing adverse effects on productivity and labor supply, with a focus on the varying challenges faced by different sectors. The role of government in facilitating adaptation through infrastructure investment and policy support is also stressed.
insights: Firms' adaptation to climate changes significantly impacts national economic growth in developing countries.
The ability of firms to bounce back from weather events relies on internal capabilities and external conditions.
Real-time weather forecasting enhances risk assessments, influencing strategic decisions.
Market frictions and information asymmetries hinder adaptation speed, especially for smaller firms.
Government infrastructure investments can create moral hazards, leading firms to underestimate risks.

records.title: Climate Resilient Debt Clause — FAQ
records.summary: This World Bank FAQ document (last updated June 3, 2024) describes the Climate Resilient Debt Clause (CRDC), a no-cost option embedded in IBRD loans and IDA credits that allows eligible small state and Small Island Developing State borrowers to defer principal and/or interest payments for up to two years following a qualifying natural disaster (tropical cyclone at Category 3+ intensity or earthquake ≥ Mw 7.0, or damages ≥ 10% of GDP). The instrument is designed to free fiscal space for disaster recovery without triggering debt restructuring, and sits within the World Bank's broader crisis response toolkit.
insights: The clause is an option the borrower elects into, deferring principal, interest and other loan charges for up to two years after a natural disaster, so it converts a debt service obligation into contingent liquidity without new borrowing.

Eligibility is confined to IBRD and IDA Small State Economies, Small States Forum members and UN-defined Small Island Developing States, with subnational borrowers in those countries also eligible, which is a deliberately narrow perimeter.
The trigger perimeter is earthquakes and tropical cyclones for small islands and other small states, so the clause does not cover slow-onset or non-geophysical climate shocks.

A borrower must be current on debt service to the World Bank to have the clause included, and it will not be added to existing loans during a restructuring with other lenders, so the instrument is unavailable precisely to the most distressed.

It arrived in June 2023 as part of the World Bank's expanded crisis response toolkit approved by the Board, which locates it in a wider shift toward contingent instruments rather than as a standalone product.

records.title: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 2024-2027 Climate Adaptation Plan
records.summary: The US Environmental Protection Agency's Climate Adaptation Plan for 2024 to 2027, published June 2024 and opening with the Administrator's policy statement on climate change adaptation. The statement frames climate change as a direct threat to the agency's own mission of protecting human health and the environment: it exacerbates existing pollution problems and environmental stressors, and its impacts fall disproportionately on low-income communities and communities of colour, children, the elderly, Tribes and indigenous people. It records the May 2021 direction to assistant, associate and regional administrators and the general counsel to incorporate climate adaptation planning proactively into the agency's programmes, policies, rules and operations. The plan is an agency adaptation strategy rather than a financing document: across 192,654 characters the word grant appears seven times, funding six and financing once.
insights: The distinctive move is that the agency treats climate change as a threat to its regulatory capability rather than only to the public. Adaptation here means keeping the Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act workable under conditions they were not written for, which is a different object from protecting an asset.
It is federal policy rather than finance: financing language is measurably scarce in the text, so the document sets objectives rather than inventorying funding.
The May 2021 internal direction is the provenance that makes the plan auditable: it names who was told to do what, which is what lets a later reader check whether the plan was implemented.

records.title: Public Preferences for Coastal Adaptation: Economic Evidence from a Discrete Choice Experiment for Hard Structures and Nature-Based Solutions in Miami, Florida
records.authors: Carlie Dario, Renato Molina, David L. Kelly
institutions: University of Miami Climate Resilience Institute
records.summary: Dario, Molina and Kelly, all at the University of Miami, use a discrete choice experiment in Miami-Dade County to establish public preferences and trade-offs between hard structures and nature-based solutions for coastal risk reduction, specifically seawalls and mangroves. Respondents favour deploying any coastal measure over the status quo, and show a higher willingness to pay for nature-based solutions than for hard structures. Marginal willingness to pay, computed with representative values from the 2021 American Community Survey for Miami-Dade rather than from the non-representative sample, is $7.31 per month for mangrove rather than seawall type, $10.74 per mile per month for length of protected coastline, $0.42 per month per foot of height and $0.52 per month to avoid one flood day. On average respondents are willing to pay $18.05 a month for a mile of mangrove protection along Biscayne Bay, against $10.74 for a seawall with the same characteristics.
