Respondents under 65, in the labour force, with a college degree and income above $50,000 were less likely to pick the status quo, as were respondents who did not identify as White and those living within 15 km of the coastline. The authors place their values in range with Chen, Gao and Bi, who found $21.32 a month for seawalls, $18.99 for beach nourishment and $16.09 for stormwater pumps in the same county.
insights: The $7.31 monthly premium for mangrove over seawall is a directly measured public preference for nature-based solutions, which is the number a Miami-Dade special assessment or stormwater fee would need in order to justify the nature-based option on willingness to pay alone.

Length of protected coastline is worth more per month than height, $10.74 a mile against $0.42 a foot, so residents value extent of protection over depth of protection, which is the opposite of how a hard-structure engineering case is usually argued.
Willingness to pay for the nature-based option at $18.05 a month per mile makes a recurring revenue instrument, a fee or a district levy, arithmetically plausible rather than hypothetical.
Preference for action over the status quo held across the sample, so the political constraint in Miami-Dade is not public willingness but which measure and who pays.
The authors use census-representative values rather than sample means, which is the methodological choice that makes the figures usable for a real revenue estimate rather than only for a ranking.

records.title: Valuing Climate Adaptation Helps Us Orient Our Compass Toward Effective and Resilient Pathways: Climate Adaptation Costing in a Changing World
records.summary: The resource highlights the urgent need for effective climate adaptation investment strategies in Europe to address increasing climatic shocks and associated economic losses. It emphasizes the importance of valuing climate adaptation through comprehensive costing methodologies, case studies, and stakeholder engagement to guide policymakers in identifying viable investments, enhancing overall resilience, and ensuring that financial resources are allocated effectively across sectors. The report advocates for transformational adaptation strategies and improved collaboration among public and private stakeholders to close the adaptation finance gap.
insights: Proactive investments in climate adaptation can yield substantial socio-economic and environmental benefits, including cost savings and job creation.
Transformational adaptation is necessary to address long-term climate risks and requires a shift from incremental adjustments to systemic changes.
Effective climate adaptation costing requires comprehensive methodologies and engagement across sectors to enhance decision-making and resource allocation.
Public-private partnerships and innovative financing mechanisms are essential for mobilizing the necessary investments for climate adaptation.
Valuing climate adaptation helps prioritize actions, supports better budgeting, and addresses existing knowledge gaps in adaptation costs.

records.title: Tailwind Climate's A&R Taxonomy, World Bank Warns Europe on Resilience, & More
records.summary: An issue of the Climate Proof newsletter by Louie Woodall, dated 20 May 2024, whose lead item is the release of Tailwind Climate's Taxonomy for Adaptation and Resilience Investments. The taxonomy breaks potential adaptation and resilience investments across eight themes and 35 sectors, and for each sector gives examples across four categories: Intelligence, Products and Services, Finance and Insurance, and Enabling Interventions. It maps those investments onto the North American Industry Classification System, the Global Industry Classification system and OECD Development Assistance Committee markers, and links them to the 2023 Sharm-El-Sheikh Adaptation Agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals. Development partners included the Climate Bonds Initiative, whose own Resilience Taxonomy was then in progress, the Global Adaptation and Resilience Investor group, Climate Policy Initiative, ClimateWorks Foundation and Vibrant Data Labs. The issue also covers the World Bank and European Commission series on the economics of disaster prevention in Europe, which recommends an EU-level Disaster Risk Finance strategy, and a round-up of adaptation funding announcements.
insights: The author's own position shifts inside the piece, and the shift is the argument: he had been dismissive of the proliferation of adaptation taxonomies for classifying companies rather than encouraging investors, and concludes instead that they are interdependent components of one intellectual infrastructure that unblocks capital by making dedicated portfolios buildable and marketable.

Interoperability is the taxonomy's design choice rather than a feature list. Mapping to NAICS, GICS and OECD DAC markers means an investor can apply it inside existing processes, which is what separates an adopted classification from a published one.

Tailwind states that the taxonomy is a classification and exploration tool and must be used alongside impact assessment criteria to determine whether an investment is in fact adaptation, which keeps the burden of proof on the assessment rather than on the label.

The World Bank risk transfer paper's recommendation is an EU-level Disaster Risk Finance strategy setting out how much member states should have to pay to cover catastrophic events, which is sovereign risk retention stated as a policy target.

records.title: Pilot Climate Scenario Analysis Exercise: Summary of Participants' Risk-Management Practices and Estimates
records.summary: The Federal Reserve's summary of the pilot climate scenario analysis exercise it ran in 2023 with six large bank holding companies: Bank of America, Citigroup, Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan Chase, Morgan Stanley and Wells Fargo. The exercise was exploratory, with no consequences for bank capital or supervision, and was intended to learn about participants' climate risk-management practices and to build the ability of banks and supervisors to identify, estimate, monitor and manage climate-related financial risks. It ran a physical risk module and a transition risk module. Participants took different approaches to constructing the detailed scenarios and translating them into climate-adjusted credit risk parameters, driven by business model, views on risk, data access and prior participation in foreign climate scenario exercises. Most relied on existing credit risk models and assumed the historical relationships between model inputs and outputs continue to hold as the climate and the economy change. Participants reported significant data and modeling challenges, naming a lack of comprehensive and consistent data on building characteristics, insurance coverage and counterparties' own plans for managing climate risk, and in many cases relied on external vendors to fill those gaps. The report also covers governance, internal controls and internal audit arrangements.
insights: The assumption most participants made, that historical relationships between model inputs and outputs continue to hold as the climate changes, is the one that a climate scenario is designed to break, so the exercise mostly measured how banks stretch existing credit models rather than how they model climate.

Insurance coverage is named as a top data gap, which matters because a mortgage's credit risk under physical stress turns almost entirely on whether the property is insured and at what price, and the banks could not see it.
Reliance on external vendors to fill data gaps concentrates supervisory risk in a small number of model providers, which is the systemic consequence of a data gap rather than the gap itself.
The exercise carries no capital or supervisory consequence by design, which is what makes participation honest and also what limits what it can change.

That six of the largest US banks produced materially different estimates from the same prescribed scenarios is the finding a supervisor would act on, because it means the number is not yet comparable across institutions.

records.title: Resilience Monetization and Credits Initiative: A Background Paper
records.authors: Rania A. Al-Mashat, Marc Jeuland, Jyotsna Puri, Pablo A. Vieira, Mahinour Aboulatta, Saib Ahmad, Jahan-Zeb Chowdhury, Alejandro Diaz-Herrera, Mirna Elsharief, Farida Farghal, Jonathan Phillips, Nada Tawfik, Liilnna Teji, Drew von Glahn
institutions: James E. Rogers Energy Access Project
records.summary: This May 2024 working paper from Duke University's James E. Rogers Energy Access Project introduces the Resilience Monetization and Credits Initiative (RMCI), a proposed framework to bridge the climate adaptation finance gap in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). The paper proposes resilience credits as a novel asset class designed to mobilize and align public and private capital for climate adaptation in the most vulnerable communities, while ensuring equitable benefit sharing. Adaptation investment is estimated to fall 5–10 times short of actual need, motivating the RMCI design.
insights: Adaptation finance for LMICs falls 5–10 times short of actual need, representing one of the largest documented gaps in climate finance relative to risk exposure.
The RMCI proposes resilience credits as a novel asset class, a market-based mechanism intended to align public and private capital around measurable resilience outcomes in vulnerable communities.

The $100 billion annual climate finance target established at COP15 (2009) has not been met for LMICs, and adaptation finance lags mitigation finance disproportionately, signaling a structural allocation failure rather than a resources gap alone.

Equitable benefit sharing is embedded as a design principle of the RMCI, positioning distributional outcomes as a core feature of the credit instrument rather than an afterthought, relevant for ESG allocators and DFIs evaluating social co-benefits.

The RMCI represents an attempt to create a standardized, tradeable resilience credit that could function analogously to carbon credits, potentially opening adaptation to voluntary and compliance market participation by private capital.

By framing resilience as a monetizable asset class, the initiative signals a shift from grant-dependent adaptation toward balance-sheet-legible instruments, a prerequisite for institutional investor participation.

The initiative is authored by a multi-institutional team including academics and practitioners, suggesting an intent to ground the credit design in both empirical methods and real-world implementability.

records.title: Mayor Adams Celebrates Launch of New York City’s First Climate Budgeting Process
institutions: New York City Mayor's Office of Management and Budget
records.summary: New York City introduced its first climate budgeting publication through the Fiscal Year 2025 Executive Budget, becoming the first large city in the United States to adopt climate budgeting and joining London, Oslo and Mumbai in doing so. Climate budgeting incorporates science-based climate considerations into budget decision-making by evaluating how today's actions and spending contribute to longer-term climate targets and needs. The stated purposes are to let the city understand the climate impact of the dollars it spends, identify where more effort is needed, and champion forward-looking investments. The release is explicit that this formally integrates climate into city decision-making so that climate is weighed in all relevant investment decisions, and that it serves both the net-zero-by-2050 emissions goal and resiliency to extreme heat and flooding. Delivery sits with the Mayor's Office of Management and Budget, which has embedded new processes from that year, and Mayor Adams frames it as changing the calculus of government spending by weighing climate impacts at the critical early stages of the budget process.
insights: The instrument is the budget process itself rather than a fund: embedding climate assessment at the early stage of capital decisions changes what gets proposed, which reaches further than any single financing vehicle.

It covers both mitigation and resilience, assessing capital commitments for alignment with net-zero and separately for alignment with climate resiliency, so adaptation is not folded into an emissions frame.
Being the first large US city, and joining London, Oslo and Mumbai, makes this the reference precedent other US cities will cite, which matters for how quickly the practice spreads.
Placing delivery with the Office of Management and Budget rather than a sustainability office is the structural choice that gives the process authority over spending.

records.title: Climate Risk and Financial Stability: Evidence from Syndicated Lending
records.authors: Thomas Conlon, Rong Ding, Xing Huan, Zhifang Zhang
records.summary: This peer-reviewed study (European Journal of Finance, 2024) develops a bank-level climate risk measure using NOAA Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters data linked to Dealscan syndicated lending records, then tests whether unexpected physical climate shocks transmitted via cross-state lending increase US banks' individual and systemic risks. Across 12,142 lender-borrower-year observations (42 banks, 1,314 borrower firms, 1999–2019), a one-standard-deviation increase in the cross-state climate risk measure raises marginal expected shortfall by 14.7%, value-at-risk (1%) by 10.2%, and systemic risk contribution (1%) by 6.1%. Banks subsequently reduce lending and increase loan-loss provisions. Higher bank profitability partially offsets these effects.
insights: A one-standard-deviation increase in cross-state climate risk exposure raises banks' marginal expected shortfall (MES) by 14.7%, VaR at 1% by 10.2%, and systemic risk contribution (CoVaR at 1%) by 6.1%, all significant at the 1% level across 12,142 lender-borrower-year observations.

Banks reduce their loans-to-assets ratio and increase loan-loss provision ratios following unexpected climate shocks, indicating post-shock credit contraction and more conservative risk provisioning, both material signals for bank credit allocators and regulators.

The climate risk transmission mechanism operates through cross-state (not same-state) syndicated lending: exposure to borrowers in climate-stressed states raises lender-bank risk even when the bank itself is located in a lower-risk state, identifying a portfolio-level contagion channel.

Bank profitability acts as a partial buffer: for CoVaR1, the aggregate climate-risk coefficient is more than halved (from 0.117 to 0.052) during high-profitability periods, supporting the regulatory implication that maintaining robust bank earnings strengthens financial system resilience against climate risk.

Loans earmarked for operating and capital expenditures amplify the climate risk effect on bank systemic risk (interaction term significant for 5 of 6 risk measures), consistent with the mechanism that climate losses impair borrowers' physical assets and repayment capacity, whereas M&A- and capital-structure-purpose loans show no significant amplification.

The NOAA Billion-Dollar Disasters dataset covering 1980–2020 records 290 events, 14,492 deaths, and $1.98 trillion in total losses (CPI-adjusted to 2020); in 2020 alone, losses reached $99.5 billion (~0.5% of US GDP), underscoring the macro-financial scale of physical climate risk.

records.title: FEMA Policy 206-23-001: Benefit-Cost Analysis Discount Rate and Streamlined Cost-Effectiveness Approaches
records.summary: FEMA Policy 206-23-001 changes two things about how the agency decides whether a hazard mitigation project is cost effective, which is a minimum criterion for funding under the Stafford Act and the National Flood Insurance Act. First, it adopts the OMB Circular A-94 discount rate of 3.1 per cent for benefit-cost analyses of hazard mitigation projects, implementing the federal guidance in Appendix D of that circular. Second, it introduces streamlined cost-effectiveness determinations, allowing subapplicants to submit a cost-effectiveness narrative instead of a full benefit-cost analysis for projects costing less than $1 million. The policy states its principles as reducing complexity and promoting equity of grant programmes, especially for applicants proposing projects that benefit disadvantaged communities, promoting consistency in award decisions, simplifying requirements for Hazard Mitigation Assistance grants, and helping communities implement cost-effective projects that address future risk. FEMA says it will continue engaging with OMB to improve implementation in service of accelerating risk reduction and adaptation nationwide.
insights: The discount rate is the whole lever: at 3.1 per cent rather than a higher rate, long-dated avoided losses retain far more present value, so projects whose benefits accrue over decades become cost effective that previously were not.

Allowing a narrative instead of a full benefit-cost analysis below $1 million removes a fixed analytical cost that falls hardest on small and under-resourced applicants, which the policy names as an equity measure rather than a simplification.
Cost-effectiveness is a minimum eligibility criterion under statute, so the discount rate is not guidance but a gate: it determines which mitigation projects can be funded at all.
The policy explicitly aims at projects that address future risk, which is the category a backward-looking benefit-cost method tends to reject.

records.title: State and Trends in Climate Adaptation Finance 2024
records.authors: Global Center on Adaptation; Climate Policy Initiative
records.summary: State and Trends in Climate Adaptation Finance 2024, by the Global Center on Adaptation, an international organisation hosted by the Netherlands, with Climate Policy Initiative as analytical partner. It is structured as an assessment of the adaptation funding gap, then current trends in tracked adaptation finance flows, then an assessment of public and private finance institution adaptation commitments, then an analysis of the instruments deployed for adaptation finance, then challenges and recommendations, then the intersection of adaptation finance and humanitarian assistance. Two annexes cover building resilience to external shocks through the IMF's Resilience and Sustainability Trust, and the methodology behind the finance institution commitment assessment.
insights: Section 4 counts adaptation finance by INSTRUMENT rather than by source and sector, which is the cut that says what the money is actually doing rather than where it came from.

Separating tracked flows from institution commitments is the right structure and a quiet indictment: a commitment is an announcement and a flow is a disbursement, and the report keeps them in different chapters rather than adding them.

The humanitarian assistance chapter is unusual for a finance-flows report: adaptation finance and disaster relief draw on overlapping money, and the report treats that overlap as part of the accounting rather than as an aside.
Annex 1 describes the IMF's Resilience and Sustainability Trust, which gives the report a named concessional sovereign instrument rather than only aggregate flows.

records.title: When Climate Meets Real Estate: A Survey of the Literature
records.authors: Justin Contat, Carrie Hopkins, Luis Mejia, Matthew Suandi
records.summary: This article examines the intersection of climate change and the real estate market, outlining the significant risks posed by physical hazards like flooding and wildfires as well as transition risks related to decarbonization policies. The research highlights impacts on housing prices, mortgage performance, and community dynamics, particularly for disadvantaged groups, and calls for further investigation into the intricate relationship between climate risks and real estate.
insights: Climate change significantly impacts real estate, with increased natural disaster frequency leading to adverse effects on property values and mortgage performance.
Vulnerable communities face heightened challenges in housing affordability and access due to climate risks, particularly in flood-prone areas.
Factors such as energy efficiency and decarbonization policies can influence mortgage performance, exacerbating affordability issues for disadvantaged populations.
Post-disaster scenarios illustrate shifts in demographics and homeownership challenges, particularly for low- and middle-income individuals who may be priced out.
Empirical studies reveal that flood risk discounts and perceptions of climate risks play crucial roles in shaping real estate pricing and demand.

records.title: Guide for Adaptation and Resilience Finance
institutions: United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction
records.summary: The 'Guide for Adaptation and Resilience Finance' emphasizes the urgent need for enhanced private sector investment in climate adaptation and resilience, particularly in emerging markets and developing economies, highlighting significant economic returns from adaptation initiatives and the necessity for clarity in investment definitions. It presents strategies and frameworks to encourage investments in critical areas such as infrastructure and healthcare while addressing barriers to funding and the need for collaboration between public and private sectors.
insights: Investment in adaptation could yield returns of up to USD 12 for every dollar spent.
There is an annual financing gap of USD 194-366 billion for adaptation in developing countries.
Clear definitions of what constitutes adaptation investments are essential to attract private sector financing.
Public and philanthropic funding must be combined with private investments to effectively scale adaptation finance.
Nature-based solutions are crucial for enhancing resilience across various sectors and should be prioritized.
records.publisher: UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction

records.title: Infrastructure for a Climate‑Resilient Future
records.summary: The resource 'Infrastructure for a Climate‑Resilient Future' highlights the urgent need for integrating climate resilience into infrastructure planning and financing to address the escalating impacts of climate change. It underscores the significance of nature-based solutions and public-private partnerships in building sustainable infrastructure while advocating for innovative financing mechanisms and policy reforms to unlock global investments, particularly in developing countries. The report emphasizes the necessity of collaborations, community engagement, and long-term planning strategies to achieve infrastructure that aligns with both sustainable development and climate adaptation goals.
insights: An estimated annual investment of USD 6.9 trillion is needed by 2030 for infrastructure aligned with sustainable development and climate goals.
Nature-based solutions can enhance infrastructure resilience while providing additional environmental benefits, yet face challenges in regulatory frameworks and capacity building.
Delaying climate resilience measures can lead to substantial additional costs, estimated at USD 1 trillion over ten years in low- and middle-income countries.
Investment in climate-resilient infrastructure can significantly lower future repair costs and damages, with a potential return of USD 4 for every USD 1 invested in developing countries.
Collaboration between public and private sectors is crucial to mobilizing the necessary investments for climate-resilient infrastructure.
Effective stakeholder engagement throughout the infrastructure lifecycle is critical for aligning public interests and enhancing project success.
International cooperation and innovative financing tools are essential for addressing the unique challenges faced by developing countries regarding climate-resilient infrastructure.

records.title: Three Ways to Equitably Advance Local Climate Action and Economic Development
records.summary: Three ways cities can pursue local climate action and economic development together and equitably, drawn from a discussion with community organisations in Fresno and Rochester: align short and long term climate, economic development and equity goals inside planning documents; move from community engagement to community ownership of plans, property and infrastructure; and combine multiple funding streams. The framing is that Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act and Inflation Reduction Act money creates the opportunity, that work at the intersection of these goals is still nascent, and that equity has not been consistently operationalised in local climate action plans.
insights: A forthcoming Urban Institute finding is quoted as the premise: equity has not been consistently evaluated or operationalised in local climate action plans, and community and economic development plans have not consistently integrated climate action, so the two planning tracks are running separately.

Community ownership rather than consultation is the sharpest recommendation: community-based organisations and cooperatives owning planning processes and local assets, including climate resilient and perpetually affordable housing, energy systems and open space, so benefits accrue rather than merely reach.

The barrier named for federal money is capacity, not eligibility: tracking, applying for and meeting reporting requirements for federal funds takes capacity many local organisations lack, so the influx does not reach them.

One practical workaround offered is to seek funding with flexible uses, grants without an explicit climate or equitable development purpose whose parameters still allow climate activities, which is a route around programme-specific capacity requirements.

Vertical integration across state, county and jurisdictional planning bodies is presented as both an equity mechanism and a funding mechanism, because it governs whether money earmarked for states or counties is distributed equitably across jurisdictions.

records.title: Adaptation & Resilience Impact: A Measurement Framework for Investors
institutions: United Nations Environment Programme - Finance Initiative (UNEP FI)
records.summary: This April 2024 guidance, produced by the Adaptation and Resilience Investors Collaborative (ARIC) with UNEP FI support, presents a practical measurement framework for private investors to assess and report adaptation and resilience (A&R) impact. It applies the Impact Management Project's Five Dimensions of Impact (what, who, how much, contribution, risk) to A&R investment, proposes aggregable output- and outcome-level metrics across three impact aspects (people, planet, economy), and embeds impact management into the full investment cycle. The framework targets the emerging multi-trillion-dollar private climate adaptation market and aligns with GIIN IRIS+, GIZ, and Climate Bonds Initiative approaches.
insights: The World Economic Forum (2024) identified extreme weather as the most significant global risk over the next ten years, underpinning growing private investment in adaptation and resilience, projected to become a multi-trillion-dollar market (WEF, 2022).

The framework distinguishes two investment types with distinct impact pathways: 'enabling' investments (which make others more climate-resilient, e.g. distributing flood warning technology) and 'adapted' investments (which reduce the physical climate risk of the investee itself, e.g. hardening a port against sea level rise), with many investments exhibiting both characteristics.

Three dimensions of resilience capacity, absorptive, adaptive, and transformative, map to increasing intensity of structural change, from parametric insurance to wholesale shifts in agricultural systems, giving investors a clear typology for portfolio differentiation.

Metrics are organized across people (e.g., number of people supported to be more climate resilient), planet (e.g., hectares of habitat under climate-resilient management), and economy (e.g., USD value of assets made more climate resilient), with economy-based value metrics being the most readily aggregable across portfolios.

The framework highlights maladaptation risk, unintended increases in climate vulnerability, as a formal dimension of impact risk requiring due diligence; examples include riverside flood defences that shift flood risk to downstream communities and solar-powered irrigation pumps that deplete groundwater for others.

Counterfactual analysis (with-vs-without investment comparison) is prescribed as the basis for contribution assessment; a worked port infrastructure example shows how comparing 10 vs. 5 flood events per year quantifies the value of a coastal drainage upgrade over a 30-year horizon.

records.title: Supervisors Allocate $500,000 to Tackle Sea Level Rise
records.summary: On 19 March 2024 the Marin County Board of Supervisors committed $500,000 to a project that will recommend a unified approach and a countywide governance structure for responding to sea level rise, addressing how Marin's city, town, county, utility and transportation agencies might work together. Marin is surrounded on three sides by water and is among the San Francisco Bay Area counties most vulnerable to sea level rise, with over 70 miles of ocean coastline and 40 miles of bay shoreline, much of it low lying and exposed to tidal, creek and storm flooding; neighborhoods with a higher percentage of people of color are disproportionately affected. Assistant County Executive Ariel Espiritu Santo frames a multi-jurisdictional governance model as a way to address disparities and close race-equity gaps while handling long-term planning. The county's Community Development Agency already runs two longstanding programmes, C-SMART for oceanfront communities and BayWAVE for bayfront neighborhoods, plus the Stinson Beach Adaptation and Resilience Collaboration. The 2023 Marin County Community Survey found 77 per cent of respondents said addressing sea level rise was essential or very important, 76 per cent said the same of climate change generally and 90 per cent of improved disaster preparedness. Supervisor Katie Rice notes that significant federal funding is available and that the county is committed to working with towns, city councils, community leaders and special districts to access it collectively. AECOM Technical Services will be contracted to guide the project, funded from 2023-24 fiscal year General Fund balance set aside for climate resiliency.
insights: The $500,000 buys governance rather than infrastructure, and the stated reason is access to federal money: a fragmented set of cities, towns, utilities and special districts cannot apply collectively, so the county is paying to become an eligible applicant at scale.

Supervisor Rice's framing makes the sequence explicit, years of vulnerability data first and a governance structure second, which places institutional design after assessment and before capital in the local adaptation pipeline.

The money comes from General Fund balance set aside for climate resiliency rather than from a grant or a bond, so this is discretionary local revenue funding the preparatory work that grants will not cover.

Two existing programmes, C-SMART and BayWAVE, already split the county by oceanfront and bayfront, which is the fragmentation the new structure is meant to resolve and a reminder that hazard-specific programmes accrete their own boundaries.

records.title: Resilience Rating System: A Methodology for Building and Tracking Resilience to Climate Change - Synthesizing Key Lessons from IDA19 Piloting
records.summary: The Resilience Rating System (RRS), developed by the World Bank Group, is a comprehensive methodology designed to evaluate and enhance the resilience of investment projects against climate risks. This system, which rates projects from C to A+ based on their design and expected outcomes, promotes early integration of climate considerations and supports effective decision-making. Piloted across various sectors, it has shown potential for broader impacts, emphasizing the need for sector-specific guidance and robust data to improve project resilience outcomes.
insights: The RRS distinguishes between resilience of project design and resilience through project outcomes.
Successful application of the RRS relies on early integration of climate considerations in project design.
Robust data and tools are essential for project decision-making related to climate risks.
Collaboration with climate specialists enhances the integration of resilience measures into projects.
The simplicity of the RRS rating system aids decision-makers without deep technical expertise.
Flexibility in the application of RRS allows for adjustments to meet unique project objectives.
The methodology has evolved to include flexibility in rating projects that primarily operate within one resilience dimension.

records.title: NAIC Adopts First National Climate Resilience Strategy for Insurance to Close Coverage Gaps and Improve Recovery from Natural Disasters
records.summary: The National Association of Insurance Commissioners adopted its first National Climate Resilience Strategy for Insurance, developed by the NAIC's Climate and Resiliency Task Force co-chaired by Alaska's insurance director Lori K. Wing-Heier and California Insurance Commissioner Ricardo Lara. The strategy's stated goal is faster and more effective risk reduction by state insurance regulators so that insurance remains available and reliable for communities facing climate risk. Its action plan has four strands: advocating home hardening against wildfire, flood and storm; using catastrophe modelling information; better informing the public of risks; and updating solvency tools to incorporate further analysis of climate risk. The linchpin named is the states' Property and Casualty Market Intelligence data call, which collects and analyses data covering more than 80 per cent of the US property insurance market by premium volume. The release stresses that the strategy is nonpartisan and drew on regulators from large and small, coastal and inland, urban and rural jurisdictions, including island jurisdictions.
insights: The instrument is a regulator-led data call rather than a rule: the Property and Casualty Market Intelligence collection covering over 80 per cent of the market by premium is what gives state regulators a shared evidence base on availability and pricing.
Home hardening appears as something insurance regulators advocate, which puts a building-standard intervention inside the remit of the bodies that supervise solvency and rates.
Solvency tools are explicitly in scope for updating to incorporate climate analysis, so the strategy reaches capital adequacy and not only consumer protection.

It is the first national strategy of its kind from the NAIC and was reached across a deliberately heterogeneous membership, which is what makes it a coordinating document rather than one state's position.

records.title: Building for Resilience – My Safe Florida Home Program Offers Solutions
records.summary: An article of 5 March 2024 in the Citizens Property Insurance policyholder newsletter on the My Safe Florida Home program. It opens on Hurricane Ian in southwest Florida in September 2022, where engineers conducting preliminary assessments noted a bright red line separating the vulnerability of buildings constructed before and after Florida's modern building codes, and sets that alongside lessons from Charley in 2004 and Michael in 2018. My Safe Florida Home, administered by the Florida Department of Financial Services, offers free wind mitigation inspections to eligible homeowners statewide, identifying wind resistance features and recommending strengthening upgrades. Qualifying homeowners in windborne debris regions along the coast may also receive up to $10,000 in grants, when available, toward upgrades or retrofits, though the article notes the program was not accepting new grant applications at the time of writing. Retrofits focus on two areas: protecting openings, meaning windows, doors, garage doors, skylights and gable end vents, through hurricane shutters or impact-resistant windows and garage doors; and reinforcing the roof through additional metal connectors installed during replacement, increased roof deck nailing, a secondary water barrier, and hurricane clips and straps. The article states that annual insurance discounts and credits over time help offset the cost of the upgrades, and that a strengthened home is a more attractive and insurable risk.
insights: The whole loop is stated in three sentences by the insurer itself: a state grant of up to $10,000 pays for the retrofit, the retrofit earns annual insurance discounts, and the discounts offset the cost. It is a live consumer programme rather than a proposed structure.
The bright red line from Hurricane Ian is natural-experiment evidence rather than modelling: the damage boundary tracked the building standard.

The programme was not accepting new grant applications, which is the constraint worth recording: the instrument works and the appropriation is exhausted, so the binding limit is annual state funding rather than demand or efficacy.

Naming the specific retrofits, roof deck nailing, secondary water barrier, hurricane clips and straps, gives the intervention vocabulary that an insurance discount is actually written against, which is what makes a premium credit verifiable.
That a strengthened home is a more attractive and insurable risk is the underwriting consequence the insurer draws: the programme's own logic is that premiums fall because physical risk fell.

records.title: Municipal Finance Shapes Urban Climate Action and Justice
records.authors: Claudia V. Diezmartínez, Anne G. Short Gianotti
records.summary: This peer-reviewed article in Nature Climate Change (March 2024) uses 34 expert interviews with US municipal officials, consultants, and climate finance professionals to examine how urban climate finance tools (public revenues, grants, municipal bonds, loans, and public-private partnerships), shape the implementation of climate action and justice in US cities. The study demonstrates that financial logics tied to creditworthiness, debt affordability, and real estate markets systematically bias cities toward mitigation over adaptation, favor wealthier neighborhoods, and can entrench climate vulnerability and gentrification. It also identifies emerging innovations, such as Denver's Climate Protection Fund and Portland's Clean Energy Community Benefits Fund, that embed justice into climate budgeting.
insights: Adaptation is systematically disadvantaged in municipal finance: city officials and experts describe it as 'not bankable' or lacking a 'clear business model,' because its benefits appear as future avoided costs rather than present-value revenues, pushing cities toward mitigation over resilience.

Credit rating agency relationships constrain climate investment: cities are incentivized to protect creditworthiness by starving climate and maintenance budgets, one city official reported achieving AAA credit rating 'at the expense of maintaining parks and playgrounds.'

Smaller and under-resourced municipalities face disproportionate barriers to accessing federal climate grants due to administrative complexity, staff capacity shortfalls, and reimbursement-based structures that require upfront spending, creating unequal geographies of climate finance access.

Financial logics incentivize carbon-intensive and flood/wildfire-prone real estate development to protect property tax bases, with respondents noting cities see climate adaptation and insurance reforms as threatening 'the fundamental growth model of a region.'

Temporal mismatches between fiscal cycles and climate needs are a documented constraint: federal COVID-19 assistance grants used for climate action must be spent by December 2026, limiting long-term programme design and community engagement.

Funders (including Bloomberg Philanthropies, the Barr Foundation, and Justice40), are reshaping municipal climate finance by embedding justice requirements into grant programmes, though respondents warn this also shifts decision-making power away from city governments.

records.title: Climate Risk in Mortgage Markets: Evidence from Hurricanes Harvey and Irma
records.authors: Pedro Gete, Athena Tsouderou, Susan M. Wachter
institutions: University of Miami Climate Resilience Institute
records.summary: Gete, Tsouderou and Wachter use the Credit Risk Transfers issued by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to ask how mortgage markets would price hurricane risk in the absence of government intervention. Today that risk is priced equally across locations even though it is location-specific. The authors hand-collect a detailed database to exploit the heterogeneous exposure of CRTs to Hurricanes Harvey and Irma and estimate private investors' reaction to hurricane risk with a difference-in-differences specification. They use those estimates to calibrate a model of mortgage lending, simulate hurricane frequencies and mortgage default probabilities in every US county, and derive the market price of mortgage credit risk as implied guarantee fees. The central result is that market-implied guarantee fees in the counties most exposed to hurricanes would be 70 per cent higher than in inland counties.
insights: The 70 per cent figure is the size of the cross-subsidy: it is what hurricane-exposed counties would pay if the guarantee fee were risk-based, and the gap between that and the uniform fee is what inland borrowers currently fund.

Credit Risk Transfers are the instrument that makes the question answerable, because they are the one place where private capital actually prices agency mortgage credit risk and so reveal a market view the guarantee fee hides.

A uniform national guarantee fee is a resilience policy by omission: it removes the price signal that would otherwise make a borrower or a lender pay attention to hurricane exposure, and therefore removes the incentive to mitigate.
The method generalises: any risk with a CRT exposure and a discrete event can be priced this way, which makes this a template for measuring other climate cross-subsidies inside the agency system.

records.title: How Climate Risks Are Shaping Municipal Funding
records.summary: The excerpt discusses how climate risks are influencing municipal funding and financing strategies. It highlights the financial burden of climate change on municipalities, including increased insurance costs and reduced revenues during disaster recovery. The importance of municipal bonds and ESG principles for building resilient infrastructure is emphasized, along with federal responses to climate-related disasters and the necessary disclosure practices for municipalities dealing with climate risks.
insights: Climate change costs the U.S. $150 billion annually due to increasing weather-related disasters.
The financial market often underestimates climate risks, viewing them as long-term issues.
Strategic financing plans, including municipal bonds, are vital for building climate-resilient infrastructure.
High-risk states experience challenges in securing insurance, leading to higher premiums and reduced coverage.
The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act allocates significant funding for mitigating climate risks.
Municipal ESG bonds are emerging as a means to finance environmentally sustainable projects.
Climate-related disasters can severely strain municipal budgets, impacting their ability to recover.
Disclosure of climate risks is becoming increasingly crucial for municipal issuers to inform potential investors.
Rating agencies will adjust their criteria to account for climate risks in evaluating municipal credit.
The growing frequency of climate events necessitates innovative funding solutions to support resilient infrastructure.

records.title: Launch of Green Guarantee Company to Mobilise Billions in Climate Finance
records.summary: The Green Guarantee Company (GGC), the world's first climate-focused guarantee company, launched operations on 2 February 2024 with a Market Closing Ceremony at the London Stock Exchange. Backed by ~USD 100 million from GCF, FCDO (via MOBILIST), NSIA, USAID (Prosper Africa), and Norfund, GGC will provide up to USD 1 billion in investment-grade (BBB/Stable, Fitch) guarantees for green bonds listed on the LSE and private credit instruments issued by borrowers in developing countries across Africa, Asia, and Latin America, targeting USD 5 billion in guarantee capacity by 2035.
insights: GGC leverages USD 100 million in initial capital to provide up to USD 1 billion of guarantees, a 10:1 mobilization ratio, with a long-term target of USD 5 billion or more in guarantee capacity by 2035.

GGC holds a BBB/Stable investment-grade rating from Fitch Ratings, enabling institutional investors (pension funds, insurers) bound by investment-grade mandates to access climate debt from developing countries for the first time through standard capital market channels.

Credit enhancement via guarantees is the core mechanism: by lifting borrower credit ratings above investment grade, GGC reduces the cost of long-term hard-currency debt for green infrastructure, renewable energy, and clean transportation projects in ODA-eligible countries.

Priority geographies include India, Indonesia, Brazil, Bangladesh, Philippines, Egypt, Vietnam, and Kenya, countries facing both acute climate vulnerability and sovereign rating pressure post-pandemic that constrains private-sector capital market access.

GGC plans capacity-building support for issuers on climate impact reporting, aiming to establish green bonds and loans from developing countries as a credible, consistently-reported asset class attractive to global institutional portfolio allocators.

The capital structure blends public development finance (GCF, FCDO/MOBILIST, USAID, Norfund) with a sovereign wealth fund co-investor (Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority), demonstrating a South-South as well as North-South funding architecture.
GGC intends to expand beyond the LSE to other major exchanges and to raise additional private-sector capital as it scales, signaling a replicable platform model rather than a one-off transaction.

records.title: Measuring Resilience: Community-Informed and Evidence-Based Resilience Metrics in New York City
records.authors: Kate Boicourt; Anushi Garg; Theodore P. Toombs; Rob Freudenberg; Ravena Pernanand; Ellis Calvin
institutions: New York City Mayor's Office of Management and Budget
U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
University of Texas School of Public Affairs
records.summary: EDF and Regional Plan Association report a pilot to derive community-informed, evidence-based climate resilience indicators for New York City. From a review of 41 community-based plans with more than 500 goals, plus a literature review and four stakeholder workshops, they identify eight goal themes, 20 goals and 29 indicators, with candidate metrics and data sources. The report positions these system-level resilience indicators as a complement to existing social vulnerability and hazard exposure tools, and names four applications: tracking progress and inequity, prioritising resources, informing planning and advocacy. It notes the city's Climate Budgeting initiative and the need to set targets as the next step.
insights: 41 community-based plans encompassing more than 500 goals yielded eight core goal themes, 20 goals and 29 indicators.
Government-led plans showed a greater overall focus on infrastructure than community-organization-led plans, though alignment across the two was strong.

The eight themes are education and empowerment, economically and socially restorative, green and natural infrastructure, healthy communities, governance, built infrastructure, shelter, and emergency preparedness and response.
EDF's Climate Vulnerability Index draws on 184 data sets; the report argues few comprehensive indices measure the attributes of resilience itself rather than vulnerability.
NYC OMB's Environmental Sustainability and Resiliency Task Force was to publish the city's first Climate Budget report in April 2024, a potential user of such indicators.
Many proposed metrics lack data today and are marked as requiring data development.

records.title: Quantifying the Impact of Climate Change on Human Health
records.summary: The report assesses the profound health impacts and economic ramifications of climate change, projecting an additional 14.5 million deaths and $12.5 trillion in losses by 2050, primarily affecting vulnerable populations. It highlights the urgent need for resilient healthcare systems and comprehensive strategies to prepare for climate-related health crises, exacerbated by extreme weather events such as floods, droughts, and heatwaves, which pose significant risks to public health and equity.
insights: Climate change is projected to cause 14.5 million additional deaths and $12.5 trillion in economic losses by 2050.
Floods are expected to cause the highest acute mortality risk, leading to an estimated 8.5 million deaths.
Vulnerable populations, particularly in Africa and southern Asia, will bear the brunt of climate-related health impacts.
Heat waves and extreme weather events will significantly increase healthcare costs, with heat-related diseases costing an estimated $7.1 trillion globally.
Psychological impacts such as anxiety and PTSD are common in populations affected by climate-related disasters, indicating a need for mental health support.
Innovative healthcare solutions and governmental policies are necessary to build climate-resilient healthcare systems.

records.title: It's Not Easy Being Anti-Greenwashing
records.summary: A 2024 law review article by Caroline Bradley of the University of Miami School of Law, focused on greenwashing as a financial rather than a consumer-protection issue. The argument is that preventing greenwashing requires defining what is and is not green, and that no international agreement on that definition exists, nor in many cases any domestic one. Regulators including the SEC are working on climate-related disclosure rules, but those address the definitional problem only indirectly. The article compares the US and EU approaches and finds them substantially different, most sharply on materiality: the EU's double materiality covers both the impact of climate change on a business and the impact of the business on the climate, while the US focuses on simple materiality, the impact of climate change on the business. EU rules nonetheless reach some US-based enterprises. The two jurisdictions also differ in how politically contested the core concepts of sustainability and of the regulatory state are. The deeper claim is that greenness and sustainability have no inherent meaning, being a function of political processes and of actors seeking to influence how policymakers frame climate change and the role of law, so if regulatory concepts of green are inadequate then enforcement against greenwashing will be inadequate too, and the resulting confusion may itself discourage firms from mitigation. The article extends the charge to governments, which fail to disclose their own climate risks, issue green bonds with no binding commitment to use proceeds for sustainability, subsidise fossil fuels and present inadequate policies as promoting sustainability.
insights: The article extends the greenwashing charge to governments, which issue green bonds carrying no binding commitment to use the proceeds for sustainability, fail to disclose their own climate risks and subsidise fossil fuels while presenting inadequate policy as sustainable.

Single against double materiality is the sharpest difference the article draws: the EU covers both the impact of climate change on a business and of the business on the climate, while the US covers only the first, so a US filing and an EU filing are not answering the same question.

Definitional emptiness is the load-bearing argument: greenness and sustainability have no inherent meaning and are a function of political processes, so if the regulatory concept of green is inadequate then enforcement against greenwashing must be inadequate too.

The article is written from a law faculty and treats greenwashing as a financial-regulation problem rather than a consumer-protection one, which is why its remedies are disclosure rules rather than advertising standards.

records.title: Economics of Drought: Investing in Nature-Based Solutions for Drought Resilience
records.authors: Richard Thomas; Jonathan Davies; Caroline King; Johannes Kruse; Mark Schauer; Nina Bisom; Daniel Tsegai; Kaveh Madani
institutions: United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification
records.summary: A 2024 report published by the UN Convention to Combat Desertification with the Economics of Land Degradation Initiative and the UN University Institute for Water, Environment and Health, subtitled Proaction Pays, on the economics of investing in nature-based solutions for drought resilience. Eight lead authors across WREM, UNU-INWEH, the ELD Initiative and GIZ, and UNCCD. Drought is the subject throughout: the term appears 263 times across the 291,041-character extraction against 67 for resilience and 11 for adaptation. The argument the subtitle states is that acting before a drought costs less than responding to one, and the report assembles the economic case for nature-based rather than engineered responses.
insights: Proaction pays is the report's own subtitle and its central claim: acting before a drought costs less than responding to one, argued for drought specifically rather than for hazards in general.
The remedy the report costs is nature-based solutions and sustainable land management, so the intervention is land and water management rather than built infrastructure.
Financing nature-based solutions has a chapter of its own, separate from the chapter making the benefits case, so the report treats the money as a distinct problem from the economics.

records.title: Innovative Climate and Disaster Risk Finance Solutions: Resilience Building and Fiscal Strengthening
records.summary: The Inter-American Development Bank's guide to its Climate and Disaster Risk Finance products for borrowing member countries, aimed at strengthening resilience and fiscal sustainability. Three instruments are set out in turn, each with what it is, its value proposition, its terms and conditions and its current portfolio: the Contingent Credit Facility, the Climate Resilient Debt Clause, and risk transfer products. The case for them is fiscal: natural disasters in Latin America and the Caribbean have affected around 7 million people a year on average since 1980 and caused average annual economic losses of US$9.9 billion in real terms, on a clear upward trend driven by tropical cyclones, floods, droughts and wildfires.
insights: THE CLIMATE RESILIENT DEBT CLAUSE IS DOCUMENTED HERE WITH TERMS AND A PORTFOLIO, which is a lender's own specification of the instrument rather than a third-party description of it.

The Contingent Credit Facility is pre-arranged liquidity rather than post-disaster lending: the value proposition is that the money is committed before the event, which changes a sovereign's fiscal position at the moment of the shock rather than months afterwards.

All three instruments are presented as fiscal management rather than as project finance, which is the distinction that separates disaster risk finance from adaptation investment: they protect the balance sheet rather than reduce the hazard.

The loss baseline is specific and long: around 7 million people affected a year on average since 1980 and US$9.9 billion in average annual economic losses in real terms, calculated by the IDB from EM-DAT with inflation adjustment.

The guide explicitly frames the products as mobilising public AND private resources for disaster risk management, so the contingent and risk-transfer instruments are positioned as catalytic rather than purely sovereign.
Integrated Finance Solutions appears as a closing section, so the bank expects the three instruments to be combined rather than chosen between, which is a layered risk financing design.

records.title: New York City Climate Budgeting: The City of New York Executive Budget, Fiscal Year 2025
institutions: New York City Mayor's Office of Management and Budget
records.summary: The City of New York's first Climate Budgeting publication, issued with the Fiscal Year 2025 Executive Budget under Mayor Eric Adams and Budget Director Jacques Jiha. The document sets out the city's climate budgeting process and then applies it, which is what distinguishes it from the announcement. It explains the Office of Management and Budget's role in the city's climate challenge and the climate science, health and environmental justice context, describes the process itself, and then reports investments and findings: sustainability investment highlights, resiliency investment highlights, and an assessment of the climate alignment of city capital investments. That assessment carries its own stated methodology and is run twice, once for alignment of the FY2024 to FY2028 Capital Commitment Plan with net-zero emissions and once for alignment with climate resiliency, with additional analysis of co-benefits across air quality, circular economy, ecology and sustainable living. It closes with the city's anticipated progress on citywide and city government greenhouse gas emissions.
insights: Assessing the capital commitment plan for resiliency alignment separately from net-zero alignment is the methodologically important choice: a single climate score would let emissions performance mask adaptation gaps, and running two assessments makes the resilience shortfall visible.
The published methodology for assessing climate alignment is the transferable artefact, since any city adopting climate budgeting needs a defensible rule for classifying a capital project.
Applying the assessment to a five-year capital commitment plan rather than a single annual budget matches the horizon of infrastructure decisions, which is where climate alignment actually binds.
Co-benefit analysis across air quality, circular economy, ecology and sustainable living is how the document accounts for value that neither emissions nor hazard reduction captures.
This is the underlying publication behind the city's climate budgeting announcement, so it is the primary source for the process and the announcement is the secondary one.

records.title: Resilient Maine: Local Adaptation and Resilience Actions at a Coastwide Scale
records.summary: A NOAA Office for Coastal Management project summary for a $69,008,683 award to the Maine Governor's Office of Policy Innovation and the Future under the Climate Resilience Regional Challenge, funded from the roughly $575 million IRA appropriation of 2022. The stated ambition is for Maine to become a national leader in climate resilience among rural states by the end of the decade, supporting the goals of the state climate action plan Maine Won't Wait. Three strands: building enduring community resiliency, which expands the Community Resilience Partnership already reaching 225 communities and funds 20 to 30 subgrants for risk assessment and implementation; investing in nature-based solutions, including living shorelines, changes to state land-use and permitting regulation, and shore corps stewards trained to help communities implement adaptation; and strengthening working waterfronts along 3,500 miles of tidal coastline, where commercial fishing and aquaculture access is treated as economic resilience. The case for urgency is stated concretely: storms in December 2023 and January 2024 caused $90 million in damage to public infrastructure and four deaths.
insights: Capacity, expertise and funding are named together as the reasons municipalities cannot act, and the programme is structured to supply all three rather than money alone, with nearly 500 municipalities and tribal governments in scope.
Regulatory change is funded as a project component: updating land-use and permitting rules is treated as adaptation infrastructure alongside the physical work.

Working waterfronts are framed as economic resilience rather than as coastal protection, with fishing and aquaculture access, aggregation of facilities and energy efficiency conversions all inside the resilience award.
The damage figure cited as the trigger, $90 million to public infrastructure from two storms in a single winter, is public-asset loss, which is the balance sheet a state can act on directly.

records.title: How a Holistic Risk Approach Increases Resilience in the Face of a Changing Climate
records.authors: Lara Whitmore, Sandra Hansen, Katy Reyner, Swenja Surminski
records.summary: This Marsh McLennan white paper argues for a holistic risk management approach that integrates risk assessment, risk financing, and climate adaptation to close growing protection gaps. Drawing on Guy Carpenter reinsurance renewal surveys (January 2024) and Marsh's corporate adaptation survey, it finds that fewer than half of global respondents quantify their climate risk, and that the U.S. protection gap exceeds 40%. The paper highlights catastrophe model applications, parametric insurance, community-based catastrophe insurance (CBCI) pilots in New York City, and return-on-investment frameworks for adaptation interventions as practical tools for building resilience.
insights: Fewer than half of global (re)insurance clients quantify their climate risk, per Guy Carpenter's post-January 2024 reinsurance renewal survey; 48% of corporate risk managers assess climate risks only qualitatively (Marsh Corporate Adaptation Survey).
The U.S. insurance protection gap exceeds 40%, while UAE insurance penetration (all lines) is only 2.75%, illustrating severe underinsurance in both developed and developing markets.

Global average temperature from July 2023 to June 2024 reached a record 1.64°C above pre-industrial levels, with named storms (Beryl, Helene, Milton) and Italian hailstorms and floods in Brazil, UAE, and Spain driving insured loss increases.

Parametric insurance is identified as a versatile complement to traditional coverage, capable of extending protection to high-risk assets and supply chains and containing uninsurability risk where conventional underwriters are withdrawing.

Marsh McLennan's community-based catastrophe insurance (CBCI) pilot in New York City uses parametric triggers and group purchasing by local government or community organizations to reduce administrative and distribution costs, expanding flood coverage to lower-income residents.

Catastrophe models can quantify resilience interventions, such as building code improvements and flood defenses, by modifying vulnerability modules, enabling premium-saving estimates to be set against implementation costs and supporting ROI-based adaptation decisions.

Nature-based solutions such as mangroves remain difficult to incorporate into catastrophe models; the paper identifies this as an emerging area requiring industry-academia collaboration, citing The Nature Conservancy and Guy Carpenter's 2021 wildfire NbS quantification report.

records.title: The Changing Wealth of Nations: Adding Water to the Changing Wealth of Nations
records.summary: The excerpt introduces a technical report that adds a focus on water resources to the understanding of wealth dynamics in nations, emphasizing the importance of integrating water management into broader economic and environmental assessments.
insights: Water resources are critical to national wealth and economic stability.
Integrating water management into economic assessments can lead to more accurate evaluations of wealth.
Climate change impacts water availability, affecting both economies and ecosystems.
Sustainable water management is essential for long-term resilience and prosperity.
Countries must consider water resources when developing climate policies.
Investing in water infrastructure can yield significant economic benefits.
The relationship between water and wealth should be reflected in national accounts.
Water scarcity poses a risk to food security and public health.
There is a growing need for collaborative governance in water management.

records.title: The Changing Wealth of Nations: Estimating the Global Contribution of Aquaculture Towards the Changing Wealth of Nations
records.authors: Malcolm W. Dickson, Harrison Charo-Karisa, Stefanie Onder, Robert Smith
records.summary: The excerpt discusses a technical report titled 'The Changing Wealth of Nations', which focuses on assessing the global economic impact of aquaculture and its contribution to national wealth, underscoring its significance in the context of changing environmental and economic conditions.
insights: Aquaculture plays a critical role in global food security.
The report emphasizes the economic value generated by aquaculture.
It highlights the need for sustainable practices in aquaculture.
The assessment of aquaculture's contribution is crucial for policymaking.
Changing wealth dynamics require reevaluation of natural resource contributions.
Aquaculture can mitigate the impacts of climate change on fisheries.
Economic assessments must consider environmental sustainability.
The report aims to inform stakeholders about the benefits of aquaculture.

records.title: The Changing Wealth of Nations: Global Assessment of the Economic Value of Non-Wood Forest Ecosystem Services
records.authors: Juha Siikamäki, Matías Piaggio, Natalia da Silva, Ignacio Álvarez, Ziyan Chu
institutions: International Union for the Conservation of Nature
records.summary: The resource provides a comprehensive analysis of the economic value of non-wood forest ecosystem services, utilizing advanced statistical methods, including machine learning and meta-regression, to derive updated local and global estimations. It underscores the critical role these services play in global natural capital wealth, with a focus on biodiversity, recreation, and sustainable development. The findings advocate for informed decision-making regarding conservation, resource management, and policy development, emphasizing the need for localized studies to enhance valuation accuracy in underrepresented regions.
insights: Non-wood forest ecosystem services account for approximately 29% of the total global wealth from renewable natural resources.
The average marginal value per hectare for non-wood forest products is estimated at US$6.8, while recreation services reach up to US$48 per year.
Machine learning models, including Bayesian Additive Regression Trees, enhance the accuracy in predicting ecosystem service values compared to traditional regression models.
Protected areas contribute significantly to the economic value of non-wood forest services, accounting for about 16% of the total value associated with recreation, hunting, and water services.
The geographic coverage of value estimates is uneven, with notable gaps in developing regions, stressing the importance of localized studies for better conservation and resource management.

records.title: The Changing Wealth of Nations: Building Coastal Resilience with Mangroves: The Contribution of Natural Flood Defenses to the Changing Wealth of Nations
records.authors: Pelayo Menéndez, Michael W. Beck, Sheila Abad, Iñigo J. Losada
records.summary: The report 'Building Coastal Resilience with Mangroves' evaluates the vital role of mangroves as natural flood defenses from 1995 to 2020, revealing their increasing economic value in protecting coastal communities against rising flood risks attributed to climate change. It illustrates the significance of integrating high-resolution data and socioeconomic factors in understanding flood risks and emphasizes the urgent need for policies that support the conservation and restoration of mangrove ecosystems.
insights: Mangroves provide essential coastal protection services, significantly mitigating flooding and erosion during storms.
The flood reduction benefits from mangroves increased to a present value of $855 billion by 2020, despite global losses in mangrove cover.
Socioeconomic growth often leads to heightened flood risks, particularly affecting areas previously safeguarded by mangroves.
Data updates indicate a growing number of countries benefiting from mangrove ecosystems, with a rise from 92 to 97 nations.
Mangroves enhance local biodiversity and ecosystem services while promoting sustainable livelihoods for coastal communities.
Investing in mangrove restoration is crucial for enhancing resilience to climate variability and reducing vulnerability to flooding.
Natural flood defenses like mangroves are more cost-effective compared to traditional engineered solutions.
Accurate and high-resolution data on mangrove distribution, socioeconomic factors, and coastal elevation are critical for effective flood risk modeling and management.

records.title: What Did the UN Climate Talks at COP28 Achieve and What's Next?
institutions: United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR)
records.summary: A December 2023 blog post by Union of Concerned Scientists Policy Director Rachel Cleetus assessing the outcomes of COP28 in Dubai, where nations agreed to the UAE Consensus. The piece evaluates the Loss and Damage Fund operationalization (initial pledges of ~$800 million), the first Global Stocktake's fossil fuel transition language, adaptation finance shortfalls ($194–$366 billion annual gap for developing countries), and the process agreed for a new collective quantified goal (NCQG) for climate finance to be set at COP29. It flags loopholes in transition fuel and CCS language and criticizes insufficient adaptation finance commitments.
insights: The Loss and Damage Fund was operationalized at COP28 with initial pledges of just under $800 million, including Italy ($108M), France ($108M), UAE ($100M), Germany ($100M), and the US ($17.5M), far below what climate-vulnerable nations require.

The UN Adaptation Gap Report cited in the piece quantifies the annual adaptation finance shortfall for developing countries at $194–$366 billion per year, a benchmark that COP28 adaptation text failed to meaningfully address.

The UAE Consensus calls for globally tripling renewable energy and doubling the annual rate of energy efficiency improvements by 2030, but contains open-ended loopholes referencing 'transition fuels' and carbon capture and storage (CCS) that could extend fossil fuel use.

A process was agreed at COP28 to negotiate a new collective quantified goal (NCQG) for climate finance to be decided at COP29, representing the primary near-term vehicle for scaling public climate finance from wealthy nations.

The first Global Stocktake's energy package language ('transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems, in a just, orderly and equitable manner' to achieve net zero by 2050) marks the first global agreement to address fossil fuels but stops short of a phaseout mandate.

The US pledged $3 billion to the Green Climate Fund at COP28 but simultaneously was producing and exporting oil and fossil gas at record levels, illustrating the gap between international pledges and domestic policy.
Adaptation finance doubled-by-2025 commitments from developed countries remained aspirational, with the text only urging a report on doubling from 2019 levels rather than binding commitments.

NDCs (nationally determined contributions) due by 2025 and the NCQG represent the next concrete deadlines for translating COP28 commitments into investable policy signals that capital allocators can price.

records.title: Enabling Asset-Based Community Development Solutions: Pro-Poor Urban Climate Resilience in Kumasi, Ghana
records.authors: Pius Kwabena Appau; Michael Osei Asibey; Richard Grant
institutions: Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology
records.summary: An article in Cities, available online 14 December 2023, on asset-based community development as a route to pro-poor urban climate resilience in Kumasi, Ghana, by Pius Kwabena Appau of Miami University, Michael Osei Asibey of KNUST and Richard Grant of the University of Miami. The premise is that Ghanaian cities combine weak urban planning capacity with inadequate finance for climate risk, and that the urban poor are excluded from official climate interventions, so community-led approaches are what provide a minimum localised capacity. The authors surveyed 367 households and six governmental agencies and ran focus groups across two long-established informal settlements, investigating perceptions of climate change, knowledge of the asset-based community development approach, its influence on building resilience, and the obstacles to implementing it. Residents demonstrated good understanding of the most salient manifestations of climate change, naming flooding, heat and drought. Three things impede the approach: the absence of formally recognised associations, the difficulty of using community assets, and households' high expectations of government aid. The authors conclude that mainstreaming the approach within urban planning and governance can be improved by emphasising co-benefits and better alignment with a shared vision.
insights: Households' high expectation of government aid is named as an obstacle to community-led resilience, which is charity hazard operating on unpaid community effort rather than on insurance premiums.

The absence of formally recognised associations is a financing obstacle rather than a social one: without a recognised legal entity there is nothing for a grant, a loan or a guarantee to be made to, which is the constraint any pro-poor adaptation instrument hits first.

Community assets are proposed as a substitute for finance that is not arriving, so the paper describes what the urban poor do when adaptation finance does not reach them rather than designing an instrument.

Residents named flooding, heat and drought unprompted, which is a useful counterpoint to the Miami climate gentrification record where buyers were not reading the hazard at all. Awareness is not the binding constraint in Kumasi; capital and legal standing are.

records.title: ROI: The Economic Case for Resilient Design
records.summary: The resource discusses the economic implications of resilient design in architecture, emphasizing its importance in mitigating the effects of the climate crisis. It outlines the role architects play in creating adaptive built environments that contribute to economic resilience, emphasizing factors such as risk anticipation, system interconnections, and the significance of maintaining business continuity in the face of disasters.
insights: Resilient design enhances economic resilience, allowing communities to better withstand and recover from economic shocks.
Architects must integrate resilience measures into designs to improve the sustainability and value of the built environment.
The economic impacts of climate-related risks are interconnected across various socio-economic and financial realms.
Establishing economic resilience involves anticipating risks and developing flexibility to mitigate adverse economic incidents.
Direct economic benefits of resilient design can be easily quantified as avoided losses, such as reduced insurance costs.
Indirect benefits may include improved public relations and enhanced ecosystem services resulting from resilient infrastructure.
Investment in resilient retrofits often yields significant returns, as demonstrated by case studies like the Anheuser-Busch seismic retrofit.
Maintaining business continuity is crucial for economic recovery and can prevent high rates of business failure post-disaster.
Infrastructure systems are interrelated, meaning disruptions in one system can lead to cascading impacts on others.

records.title: Turning Science Into Solutions: IBHS's Strategy 2026
records.authors: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety
institutions: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety
records.summary: The Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety's Strategy 2026, adopted by its board in November 2023 and titled Turning Science into Solutions. It sets out how IBHS intends to convert building science into resilience practice: full-scale structural testing against high wind, wind-driven rain, hail and wildfire identifies the points of failure during those events, and that research then flows into building practices, retrofits and mitigation programmes for residential and commercial properties. IBHS has run its Research Center since 2010 and the strategy positions the institute as the body shaping the scientific knowledge and the solutions available across its core perils. The financing vocabulary is present rather than incidental: FORTIFIED appears 52 times, insurance 41 and insurers 8, so the strategy is written with the transmission from standard to underwriting in view even though it specifies no instrument.
insights: IBHS is an insurer-funded research body that tests full-scale structures against wind, wind-driven rain, hail and wildfire, so the document is the supply side of the standard that insurance discounts are written against.
The title names a target year that is not the publication date: Strategy 2026 was adopted by the board in November 2023.
records.publisher: Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety

records.title: 2023 Louisiana Statewide Resilience Annual Report
records.summary: The first Louisiana statewide resilience report required under Act 315 of the 2023 Regular Session, arriving at the end of one administration and the start of another. It is a status report on the new structures and processes designed to increase coordination and communication across levels and agencies of government, and a set of recommendations to drive early work in the incoming administration. It is explicitly written to supply language and ideas that local, state and non-governmental entities can use to strengthen federal grant applications under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act and the Inflation Reduction Act. The framing figure is that Louisiana has the third highest total costs from federally declared billion-dollar disasters in the United States at $290 billion. The report argues that Louisiana's existing strengths, the Coastal Protection and Restoration Authority and the Louisiana Watershed Initiative among them, are proactive resilience successes, but that building resilience requires more than disaster response and more than green or gray infrastructure: it must address the human consequences of disasters, and the state will need to adapt to hazards beyond the coast including extreme heat, excessive rainfall and drought.
insights: The report states its own instrumental purpose, to supply language for federal grant applications under the IIJA and IRA, which makes it a state capacity-building document as much as a plan and is a candid account of what a resilience report is for.
$290 billion in federally declared billion-dollar disaster costs, third highest in the country, is the exposure figure any Louisiana resilience revenue instrument would be sized against.

The argument that resilience is more than green or gray infrastructure, and must address the human consequences of disasters, is the opening for social and economic programmes in a state framework that has been built around coastal engineering.
