Extending the frame past the coast to heat, rainfall and drought is the same widening Brookings observes nationally, and it is what makes a coastal-only authority structurally insufficient.
Every page is marked DRAFT, so this is a working document rather than a final statutory report and should be read as such.

records.title: Climate Adaptation, Resilience, and Financial Inclusion: A New Agenda
institutions: Consultative Group to Assist the Poor (CGAP)
records.summary: The resource emphasizes the importance of financial inclusion in enhancing climate adaptation and resilience, particularly for low-income and vulnerable communities, including women who face disproportionate impacts from climate change. It highlights the persistent gaps in access to tailored financial products that specifically address the unique climate risks faced by these populations. A collaborative, coordinated approach is needed to integrate financial inclusion with climate adaptation strategies and develop innovative solutions that meet the diverse needs of affected communities.
insights: Financial inclusion is vital for empowering vulnerable populations to develop autonomous adaptation strategies against climate change.
Over 1.4 billion adults are financially excluded, with a significant concentration in climate-vulnerable countries.
There is a critical need for financial products specifically designed for climate adaptation and resilience.
Women are disproportionately affected by climate change, facing greater financial exclusion and vulnerabilities.
Current financial services often fail to serve the specific needs of low-income communities facing climate risks.
Collaboration among stakeholders is essential to align financial inclusion and climate adaptation efforts effectively.
Innovative solutions and deeper research are required to understand how financial services can better support climate resilience.

records.title: Adaptation Gap Report 2023: Underfinanced. Underprepared. Inadequate Investment and Planning on Climate Adaptation Leaves World Exposed
records.summary: The Adaptation Gap Report 2023 emphasizes the significant shortfall in climate adaptation financing, highlighting urgent needs for increased investment and planning to address the climate vulnerability faced by developing countries. With annual adaptation finance needs estimated to be between $215 billion and $387 billion, current flows fall drastically short at $21.3 billion. The report calls for enhanced international cooperation, innovative funding mechanisms, and comprehensive strategies to address structural inequities and foster resilience among vulnerable populations.
insights: The adaptation finance gap is estimated between $194 billion and $366 billion per year, indicating a significant shortage compared to financial needs.
Approximately 40% of the global population is located in highly climate-vulnerable regions, underscoring the urgency for scaled-up adaptation efforts.
Despite some increases in adaptation finance commitments from 2017 to 2020, there was a concerning 15% decline in 2021, reflecting a downward trend in financial support.
Only 24% of countries have established monitoring and evaluation systems for assessing adaptation efforts, highlighting a significant gap in effectiveness tracking.
Gender equity and social inclusion considerations are often neglected in adaptation finance, necessitating a focused approach to support marginalized groups.

records.title: Scaling Conservation Agriculture Practices Through the Soil and Water Outcomes Fund
records.summary: The Soil and Water Outcomes Fund, in partnership with the Iowa Soybean Association and Quantified Ventures, incentivizes farmers to adopt conservation agriculture practices that improve environmental outcomes such as water quality and carbon sequestration. The fund operates on a pay-for-performance model, enabling cost-effective solutions for addressing water quality challenges while supporting farmers' economic resilience. Since its launch, it has successfully enrolled 1.7 million acres, leading to significant environmental benefits.
insights: The Soil and Water Outcomes Fund employs a multi-payor financing model to support farmers in implementing conservation practices.
Financial incentives are tied to verifiable environmental outcomes like improved water quality and carbon sequestration.
The program provides greater per-acre payments compared to traditional conservation programs, enhancing farmers' participation.
Since 2020, the fund has enrolled 1.7 million acres across 21 states.
The initiative has resulted in the sequestration of 1.4 million metric tons of greenhouse gases.
It has successfully prevented significant amounts of nitrogen and phosphorus from leaving enrolled fields.
The program's innovative approach has the potential for replication in other U.S. watersheds.
Collaboration between private investors, farmers, and outcome purchasers is essential to the fund's model.
The Soil and Water Outcomes Fund addresses critical water quality challenges faced by agriculture-heavy regions.
The program strategically combines multiple environmental outcomes into a single transaction for cost efficiency.

records.title: New Study Finds Blue-Green Infrastructure in New York City Would Generate $2 Return on Every $1 Invested
records.summary: This October 2023 press release announces a joint report by Rebuild by Design and Ramboll, "Blue-Green Infrastructure: A Business Case for New York City," which finds that blue-green infrastructure designed to a 10-year storm standard generates $2.09 in return for every $1 invested. Using city-wide flood and climate-risk modeling across all five boroughs, the study performs a Benefit-Cost Analysis and finds that up to 82% of NYC has a positive business case for managing stormwater with blue-green solutions, and that DEP could save 20% on sewer upgrade costs. The report was released two weeks after the September 29, 2023 flooding event that shut down NYC schools and subways.
insights: Blue-green infrastructure designed to a 10-year storm standard generates a $2.09 return for every $1 invested in New York City, establishing a documented BCR of approximately 2.09:1.
Up to 82% of New York City's land area has a positive business case for managing stormwater with blue-green infrastructure, indicating broad citywide investability.

Implementing blue-green infrastructure citywide would save NYC's Department of Environmental Protection 20% on costs of upgrading existing sewers to future service levels, reducing gray infrastructure capital expenditure.
City-wide blue-green infrastructure is feasible up to a future 50-year design storm in NYC, meaning the solution scales to more severe future climate scenarios without losing its business case.
151,000 new trees could be planted in NYC within a positive blue-green infrastructure business case, quantifying the co-benefit potential of urban canopy expansion alongside stormwater management.

Co-benefits (including air quality improvement, biodiversity, urban cooling, recreational access, and mental health), are described as essential to closing the business case for blue-green infrastructure, meaning allocators must account for multi-benefit valuation rather than flood damage reduction alone.

Blue-green infrastructure is most feasible when implemented in parks, plazas, and public housing, suggesting that publicly owned land provides the highest-return deployment sites and that public housing residents are direct beneficiaries.

The New York City Panel on Climate Change projects up to 25% more annual rainfall and a 50% increase in days with more than one inch of rain by end of century, establishing the forward-looking risk context that underpins the investment case.

records.title: The Global Costs of Extreme Weather That Are Attributable to Climate Change
records.summary: The resource evaluates the global economic costs of extreme weather attributable to climate change, estimating approximately $143 billion in annual damages from 2000 to 2019. It utilizes Extreme Event Attribution methodology to highlight the significant mortality and economic impacts tied to such events, while calling for improved data collection and methodologies to accurately reflect these costs and inform effective policy and adaptation strategies.
insights: Approximately $143 billion per year in extreme weather costs is attributable to climate change.
63% of climate change-induced costs resulted from human loss of life, totaling over $430 billion in value.
High-income countries bear a significant share (47%) of climate change-related economic costs despite lower relative GDP impacts compared to low-income countries.
Floods and storms account for the majority of economic damages attributed to climate change.
The study estimates that climate change is responsible for two-thirds of the economic costs from certain extreme weather events.
Economic costs associated with extreme events are often underestimated, as indirect losses and psychological impacts are frequently excluded from data.
1.4 billion people were estimated to be affected by climate-related extreme weather events from 2000 to 2019, leading to significant but often unquantified economic costs.
Continued efforts to improve data collection and methodological precision in attribution studies are essential for effective climate change policy and planning.

records.title: Can Florida’s Coast Survive Its Reliance on Development?: Fiscal Vulnerability and Funding Woes Under Sea Level Rise
records.authors: Linda Shi, William Butler, Tisha Holmes, Ryan Thomas, Anthony Milordis, Jonathan Ignatowski, Yousuf Mahid, Austin M. Aldag
institutions: Journal of the American Planning Institute
records.summary: Florida’s coastal municipalities face substantial fiscal vulnerability due to sea level rise, which threatens their reliance on property taxes from coastal development. Over half of the state’s municipalities are projected to experience significant revenue losses, highlighting the need for innovative financial strategies and improved governance to address these challenges. Despite the looming financial risks, there is little correlation between municipalities' prioritization of climate adaptation and their fiscal exposure, complicating efforts to enhance resilience along the coast.
insights: More than half of Florida's 410 municipalities will be impacted by sea level rise, with significant revenue losses anticipated.
Fiscal exposure is disproportionately concentrated in smaller, wealthier, and less diverse municipalities, complicating equitable adaptation efforts.
There is no correlation between local governments' prioritization of climate adaptation and their fiscal exposure to sea level rise.
Rising flood insurance rates are placing a financial burden on residents and local governments.
Public funding for coastal adaptation projects is crucial for sustaining Florida's economy.
Emerging climate finance strategies could help local governments diversify funding sources to adapt to sea level rise.
Insurance markets are adjusting to the risks posed by climate change, affecting homeowners financially.
Collaboration between state and local governments is necessary to address climate challenges effectively.
records.publisher: Journal of the American Planning Association

records.title: A Generalized Framework for Designing Open-Source Natural Hazard Parametric Insurance
records.authors: Carmen B. Steinmann; Benoit P. Guillod; Christopher Fairless; David N. Bresch
records.summary: An article in Environment Systems and Decisions, volume 43 pages 555 to 568, accepted 5 August 2023 and published online 2 September 2023, by Carmen B. Steinmann, Benoit P. Guillod, Christopher Fairless and David N. Bresch. Parametric insurance lets payouts be triggered by real-time hydrological and meteorological parameters rather than waiting for a damage assessment, so claims settle swiftly and people get funds right after the event. The authors propose a framework for designing parametric schemes and for systematically quantifying the basis risk, the difference between the parameter-based payout and the actual damage, and implement it in CLIMADA, the open-source global risk assessment platform. They illustrate it with two stylised case studies, tropical cyclones in Mozambique and winter storms in France. The data used and the code base provided are globally consistent, open source and readily available, so the methods are applicable in data-scarce areas and accessible to public and private stakeholders, and the approach adapts to other hazards and exposures worldwide.
insights: Open source is the point, not a detail. Parametric scheme design has been the preserve of reinsurers and modelling firms, and a globally consistent open code base lets a municipality, a ministry or a trust design and price its own trigger. That changes who can be a sponsor, which is the constraint the Cayman record states as a cost question.

Choosing Mozambique and France as the two cases is deliberate: one data-scarce and one data-rich, which is how the authors demonstrate the claim about applicability in data-scarce areas rather than asserting it.
CLIMADA is the platform, a documented and auditable open-source risk model rather than a proprietary one, so the hazard assumptions behind any result are inspectable.

records.title: Integrating Climate Risk into an Insurer’s Strategic Asset Allocation
records.authors: Tully Cheng, Sarah Peasey, Gilles Drukier, Oliver Little, Flora Xu, Zhengyang Su
records.summary: This September 2023 Neuberger Berman white paper presents a proprietary "Climate SAA" framework that integrates climate-adjusted capital market assumptions, built on Climate Value at Risk (Climate VaR) and a sovereign bond equivalent, into strategic asset allocation (SAA) optimizations for European insurance portfolios. Applied to illustrative UK general insurer and Continental European life insurer portfolios under a 2°C warming scenario, the framework recovers 21 bps and 16 bps of estimated return respectively versus ex-post climate adjustment, while simultaneously lowering solvency capital requirements (SCR) and reducing financed emissions by up to ~40%, with further reductions possible via emissions constraints.
insights: Climate SAA recovers 21 bps of estimated return (from 4.94% to 5.15%) for a UK general insurer relative to standard ex-post climate adjustment at ~3% surplus volatility, while also reducing total SCR from 6.1% to 5.4%, a simultaneous improvement in both return and solvency capital efficiency.

For a Continental European life insurer, Climate SAA recovers 16 of 20 basis points of estimated return lost to ex-post climate adjustment (from 3.59% to 3.75%), reducing SCR from 13.6% to 13.4%, at ~4% surplus volatility.

Ex-ante climate integration reduces financed emissions substantially without adding volatility: the UK insurer portfolio's carbon intensity falls from 96 to 61 (–35) and carbon footprint from 52 to 31 (–21) tons CO₂e per $M, purely as a byproduct of optimization.

Adding financed emissions as explicit constraints in the Continental European life insurer's Climate SAA reduces carbon intensity by a further 28–34 and carbon footprint by a further 13–15, cutting total portfolio emissions roughly 50% versus the standard portfolio, with estimated return declining by only 1–2 bps.

The mechanism behind return recovery is counterintuitive: traditionally higher-return asset classes (equities, high yield, EM debt) receive the largest climate-cost penalties (e.g., US HY BB: –163 bps/yr, UK equity: –77 bps/yr), so ex-ante optimization shifts allocations toward core fixed income that is penalized less, raising net expected return.

SAA drives up to 90% of variation in portfolio returns over time per the paper's framing, meaning climate risk left unaddressed at this level represents a structurally significant unmanaged exposure for insurers and other institutional allocators.

records.title: Climate Risk Management in the U.S. Insurance Sector: Detailed Analysis of 15 Companies
institutions: Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures
records.summary: This Ceres/Manifest Climate report (July 2023) provides a detailed TCFD-alignment analysis of 15 U.S. insurance companies selected for high disclosure quality, covering governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets across more than 200 climate risk action items. The 15 companies (spanning P&C, life, health, and reinsurance), range from $230M to $75B in direct premiums written. The report finds widespread but shallow disclosure: while most companies integrate climate into ERM and disclose Scope 1/2 metrics, critical gaps remain in board decision-making processes, Scope 3 materiality, scenario analysis breadth, carbon pricing, and climate-linked executive compensation.
insights: Only 5 of 15 companies disclosed scenario analyses covering all three temperature bands (<2°C, 1.5°C, and >2°C), and only 2 of those also addressed physical risk, transition risk, and time horizons, a critical gap for capital allocators trying to stress-test insurer balance sheets.

None of the 15 companies disclosed the percentage of assets aligned with climate opportunities; only Prudential and Swiss Re disclosed the percentage of assets materially exposed to climate risks, leaving a core portfolio-level data point missing for investors.

Swiss Re adopted an internal carbon price of $100/tonne as of 2021, rising to $200/tonne by 2030, covering Scope 1, 2, and significant upstream Scope 3 emissions, one of only two companies disclosing voluntary carbon pricing and the only one disclosing its trajectory.

Only 1 of 15 companies (Munich Re) disclosed board-level climate-linked pay; only 1 (AFLAC) disclosed executive climate-linked incentives, limiting accountability mechanisms that ratings agencies and institutional investors increasingly require.
Six of 15 companies provided no Scope 3 disclosures at all, and none provided a clear materiality assessment for Scope 3, undermining comparability across the sector for financed-emissions analysis.

Five companies (Swiss Re, Molina, Munich Re, Travelers, John Hancock/Manulife) indicated transition plans; none included detail on resource allocation impacts, annual updates, or processes to review goals, the content most relevant to transition-risk pricing.

Prudential linked a $4 billion five-year credit facility to sustainability targets including GHG reduction and leadership diversity, one of the only examples in the sample of a direct financial instrument tied to climate performance metrics.

records.title: NOAA Announces $2.6 Billion to Strengthen Resiliency of Coastal Communities
records.summary: A National Association of Counties explainer on NOAA's announcement of $2.6 billion through the Climate-Ready Coasts and Communities programme, funded from the $3.3 billion the Inflation Reduction Act provided to NOAA, with counties directly eligible to apply. The programme comprises five initiatives, of which the post details those most relevant to counties. The Climate Resilience Regional Challenge is a $575 million competitive grant programme split into two tracks: Track One for regional collaborative building and strategy development, with 20 to 25 anticipated grants of $500,000 to $2 million, and Track Two for implementation of resilience adaptation actions, with anticipated awards from $15 million to $75 million. Neither track carries a match requirement. The Climate Ready Workforce initiative offers $60 million in competitive grants and technical assistance for workforce development programmes focused on climate resiliency, with 10 to 20 anticipated grants of $500,000 to $10 million and no local match. The stated focus of the Regional Challenge is reducing climate risk, building local capacity to address extreme weather, and promoting equity and inclusion.
insights: No match requirement on either track is the detail that matters for under-resourced applicants, since a match is the usual reason a small county cannot pursue a large federal award.

The two-track design funds strategy development separately from implementation, at $500,000 to $2 million and $15 million to $75 million respectively, which is an explicit attempt to pay for the pre-development stage that normally goes unfunded.
Counties being directly eligible rather than passing through a state changes who controls the project, and is the reason a county association is explaining the programme.
A separate $60 million workforce initiative treats delivery capacity as a fundable object, which is the same enduring-capacity concern the programme page names.

records.title: The Social Value of Hurricane Forecasts
records.summary: Molina and Rudik build a county-level dataset of hurricane wind and precipitation forecasts and outcomes for all major US hurricanes from 2005 to 2020, covering 90 percent of hurricane property damage and deaths on the mainland, and estimate what forecasts are worth. Federal emergency protective funding follows forecast wind speeds before landfall, and under-forecasting wind speed raises damages and post-landfall recovery spending. Their main contribution is a method that values a forecast improvement without observing protective actions, by regressing damages plus recovery spending on the squared forecast error. Forecast improvements from 2007 to 2020 cut total hurricane costs by 19 percent, about $5 billion per hurricane, more than the annual federal weather forecasting budget.
insights: Counties forecast to receive hurricane-force winds receive more federal protective funding before landfall than counties forecast sub-hurricane winds, equivalent to 0.5 percent more of GDP or $200 more per person.

Under-forecasting wind speed by 10 m/s, up to two Saffir-Simpson categories, raises county damages by $500 million and post-landfall federal recovery spending by $30 million, about 40 percent of county GDP in damages.

A one standard deviation forecast improvement lowers protective, damage and recovery costs by $30 million per county per hurricane, about 3 percent of local GDP, and the value comes entirely from counties that experience hurricane-force winds.
The average annual forecast improvement reduced total per-hurricane costs by $700,000 per county, including unobserved protective spending.
Improvements in forecasting from 2007 to 2020 reduced total hurricane costs by 19 percent, averaging $5 billion per hurricane, which exceeds the budget for all US federal weather forecasting in 2015.

records.title: Insurance Supervision and Regulation of Climate-Related Risks
records.summary: The resource outlines the regulatory landscape governing the insurance industry in relation to climate-related risks, emphasizing the crucial role of effective supervision and adaptive frameworks in enhancing resilience and financial stability. It discusses the integration of climate considerations into insurance practices and the need for collaboration among stakeholders to mitigate potential risks, highlighting the ongoing efforts by regulators and the insurance sector to address evolving challenges posed by climate change.
insights: Effective insurance regulation is essential for managing climate-related risks and enhancing resilience in the insurance sector.
Regulatory frameworks must adapt to the evolving nature of climate risks to ensure financial stability and sustainable practices among insurers.
Collaboration between regulators, insurers, and stakeholders is vital for developing comprehensive climate risk management strategies.
Transparency and disclosure of climate-related risks are critical for improving accountability and stakeholder understanding within the insurance industry.
Consumer education regarding climate risks and insurance coverage is necessary to alleviate misconceptions and enhance engagement with appropriate products.

records.title: Designing a Climate Resilience Classification Framework to Facilitate Investment in Climate Resilience Through Capital Markets
institutions: United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction
records.summary: The resource presents a comprehensive blueprint for a climate resilience classification framework designed to enhance investment flows through capital markets, addressing the urgent financing needs for climate resilience, especially in developing countries. It proposes structured definitions and criteria based on established global frameworks to categorize resilience investments across various sectors, aiming to mobilize substantial capital towards sustainable development and effective adaptation strategies.
insights: Investment needs for climate resilience are estimated at US$ 1.8 trillion by 2030, necessitating new mechanisms for capital access.
Seven climate resilience themes have been identified to ensure investments contribute effectively to resilience against climate impacts.
Only 19% of labeled green bonds currently finance resilience-related projects, indicating a significant gap in investment focus.
The classification framework aims to provide consistent standards and clear pathways for assessing and categorizing climate resilience investments.
Stakeholder consultations and evidence-based definitions will ensure robust investment eligibility criteria and enhance investor clarity.
Mobilizing $1.5 trillion towards resilience investments by 2025 through the thematic bond market is a key initiative goal.
Collaboration and systematic engagement with diverse stakeholders are essential for refining and implementing the classification framework.
The framework emphasizes avoiding maladaptation and ensuring alignment with sustainability objectives in investment choices.
records.publisher: UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction

records.title: How Much Bilateral and Multilateral Climate Adaptation Finance Is Targeting the Health Sector? A Scoping Review of Official Development Assistance Data Between 2009–2019
records.authors: Tilly Alcayna; Devin O'Donnell; Sarina Chandaria
institutions: Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre
London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine
records.summary: A scoping review in PLOS Global Public Health establishing a baseline for how much bilateral and multilateral climate adaptation finance reached the health sector over the decade 2009 to 2019. Searching international financial reporting databases, the authors estimate that USD 1,431 million, or 4.9 per cent of total multilateral and bilateral adaptation finance, was committed to health activities across the decade, and say that is likely an overestimate of the true figure. Health was largely a co-benefit of projects rather than their principal objective. Most health adaptation projects were in Sub-Saharan Africa, with average project funding comparable to East Asia and the Pacific and to the Middle East and North Africa. Fragile and conflict affected countries received 25.7 per cent of total health adaptation financing. The authors single out the paucity of health indicators in project monitoring and evaluation criteria and the lack of emphasis on local adaptation.
insights: The finding that health is a co-benefit rather than a principal objective is what makes the 4.9 per cent figure an overestimate rather than an understatement: the money counted was largely committed for something else and credited to health afterwards.
The baseline is decade-scale and database-derived, measuring adaptation finance actually received by sector, which is the backward-looking denominator rather than a forward-looking estimate of need.

The absence of health indicators in project monitoring is a measurement gap with a financing consequence: a sector whose outcomes are not tracked cannot demonstrate the returns that would justify a larger share of the flow.

records.title: Inflation Reduction Act: A Historic Investment in America’s Climate Resilience
records.summary: On 6 June 2023 the U.S. Secretary of Commerce announced $3.3 billion in Inflation Reduction Act investments for NOAA, directed at making American communities and the economy ready for and resilient to climate change. NOAA Fisheries receives a share to strengthen science-based management and conservation of marine resources, building on Bipartisan Infrastructure Act investments. The money funds research, observations, modeling, predictions and service delivery against wildfire, flood, drought and extreme heat risks, plus facilities, hurricane hunter aircraft, supercomputing capacity and permitting efficiency. Climate-Ready Fisheries, one of four new NOAA initiatives, supports the nation's $370 billion fishing industry and the states, communities and tribes that depend on it, modernising the stock assessment enterprise to incorporate climate and ecosystem data for real-time advice and long-range projections. NOAA prioritised North Atlantic right whales, red snapper and Pacific salmon on urgency, impact on dependent coastal communities, and where investment would most advance climate resilience. Implementation plans were to be executed between the announcement and 2026.
insights: The investment is framed as buying predictive capacity rather than physical protection: supercomputing, observations, modeling and stock assessments, which is adaptation spending on the information layer rather than on assets.

NOAA states the exposure it is protecting in economic terms, 1.7 million jobs and $244 billion in annual activity from fisheries and a $370 billion fishing industry, which is the benefit denominator any return-on-resilience calculation for this spending would use.
Prioritisation was explicit and published, on urgency, community dependence and marginal resilience gain, which is a rare public statement of how a federal agency rationed a lump-sum appropriation.
The funding is a one-time appropriation with an implementation window to 2026, so the recurring cost of the capacity it builds is not addressed in the announcement.

records.title: Using Return on Investment and Resiliency Return on Investment for Preparedness
records.summary: The paper discusses the importance of using Return on Investment (ROI) and Resiliency Return on Investment (RROI) as tools for decision-making in capital investments aimed at enhancing preparedness and resiliency. It highlights the challenges associated with quantifying benefits, particularly soft benefits, and emphasizes the need for a methodical approach to measure both the hard and soft benefits of investments in law enforcement and airport security. The author argues that computing ROI and RROI, despite their complexities, is crucial for justifying investments against future risks and uncertainties.
insights: ROI is a fundamental decision-making tool in capital investments but challenging to apply to resiliency measures.
Resiliency Return on Investment (RROI) accounts for benefits associated with enhancing the resiliency of operations and facilities.
Quantifying soft benefits, such as improved public safety and reassurance, is essential but often underrepresented in ROI calculations.
The paper emphasizes that a culture of resiliency is increasingly necessary in the face of frequent disruptions and risks.
Clear communication of ROI and RROI is critical for gaining approval from senior management and stakeholders.
The need for backup power and operational redundancy in airports highlights the complexities involved in calculating RROI.
Investments in training and emergency management personnel are often justified more by soft benefits than by hard benefits.
The document posits that the true value of resiliency investments may not be realized until after a significant incident.
Efforts to capture soft benefits can provide a more comprehensive understanding of the true impacts of resiliency investments.
Decision-makers must be prepared to invest time and resources to compute ROI and RROI effectively.

records.title: Green Banks: An Overview for Governors
institutions: New York State Energy Research and Development Authority
records.summary: An NGA issue brief explaining state green banks to governors: the actions a governor can take to create or support one, the financing tools green banks use with large private investors and with consumers, and profiles of seven existing state institutions. It describes direct lending, co-lending, loan guarantees, credit enhancement, warehousing and securitization, green bonds, C-PACE, on-bill repayment and PPAs. It closes with the Inflation Reduction Act's $27 billion Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund and its three grant competitions.
insights: More than ten states and territories have established green banks since the Connecticut Green Bank was created in 2011 under Public Act 11-80.
NY Green Bank enhanced its liquidity by $314 million through a 2021 portfolio monetization with Bank of America, described as the largest by a green bank in the United States.

Hawai'i's Act 211 (2013) authorized $150.0 million of Green Energy Market Securitization bonds to capitalize the Hawai'i Green Infrastructure Authority, which later took on C-PACER financing for resiliency projects.
Connecticut Green Bank green notes let individuals invest as little as $100, and its Green Liberty Bonds program raised $25 million.
38 states have enacted PACE-enabling legislation, many without a green bank.
EPA's April 19, 2023 plan split the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund into $14 billion, $6 billion and $7 billion (Solar for All) competitions.

records.title: Sea-Level Rise Exposure and Municipal Bond Yields
records.authors: Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham; Matthew T. Gustafson; Ryan C. Lewis; Michael Schwert
records.summary: The published version of the paper establishing that municipal bond markets began pricing sea-level rise exposure in 2013, a date the authors tie to upward revisions in worst-case sea-level rise projections and to the uncertainty accompanying those revisions. The effect is larger for long-maturity bonds and is not solely driven by near-term flood risk, which is the result that separates a climate-uncertainty story from a flood-exposure story. The authors use a structural model of credit risk to quantify the implied economic impact and to distinguish the effect of underlying asset values from the effect of uncertainty itself. Two robustness findings carry the argument: the sea-level rise exposure premium follows a different trend from house prices, and it is unaffected by house price controls, so it is not a housing market effect transmitted to bonds. Their conclusion is that climate uncertainty, rather than expected damage alone, is an important driver of municipal bond prices.
insights: The premium is attributed to uncertainty rather than to expected loss: it appears in 2013 alongside upward revisions to worst-case projections, is concentrated in long maturities, and survives house price controls, so what the market prices is the width of the distribution.
A 2013 onset is a dateable market response to a change in scientific projections rather than to a disaster, which is unusual evidence that climate information alone moves the cost of public capital.
The maturity structure of the effect means the cost falls on exactly the long-dated borrowing that resilience infrastructure requires, so climate uncertainty raises the price of adapting.
A structural credit risk model is used to separate asset value effects from uncertainty effects, which is what lets the authors put an implied economic magnitude on a yield spread.
The premium trending differently from house prices rules out the simplest alternative explanation, that bond investors are merely tracking local property markets.

records.title: Florida SB 302: Statewide Framework for Nature-Based Coastal Resilience
records.summary: Florida Governor DeSantis signed SB 302 into law, establishing a statewide framework and permitting process for nature-based and hybrid coastal resilience projects, and directing the Florida DEP to develop design guidelines for green and hybrid infrastructure. Builds on multi-year stakeholder collaboration since 2022 and strengthens state-local coordination on sea-level rise adaptation.
insights: The load-bearing provision is the enabling legislation making Florida eligible for FEMA's Safeguarding Tomorrow Revolving Loan Fund, which supplies direct low-interest loans to local governments for hazard risk reduction and is described as reducing the burden of grant applications.

HB 111 expands Sea-Level Impact Projection study requirements from publicly funded projects in the coastal construction zone to projects in all areas threatened by current and projected sea level rise, which widens a study mandate from a coastal strip to a risk footprint.
The revolving loan structure is presented as a route to nature-based infrastructure and to addressing multiple flood risks at once, rather than as generic hazard money.
The bill passed the House unanimously and moved through the Senate, which the release frames as bipartisan support for the framework.
EDF's own recommendation is to continue by prioritising nature-based solutions and science-based decisions, so the organisational position and the legislative fact should not be conflated.

records.title: Federal Resilience Funding
institutions: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality
records.summary: An NCSL Snapshot for state legislators on the federal programs that fund disaster mitigation and resilience. It covers FEMA's BRIC program, the new Safeguarding Tomorrow Revolving Loan Fund, the Department of Defense REPI program, and how federal funds can be layered and used as match. It gives state examples from New York, Kentucky, Sonoma County and North Carolina and notes that some mitigation money requires a presidential major disaster declaration.
insights: NOAA counted 18 disasters costing more than $1 billion each in 2022, against an annual average of eight from 1980 to 2022.
Mitigation investment by FEMA, EDA and HUD over 25 years saved $6 per $1 spent, totaling $160 billion.
The Safeguarding Tomorrow Revolving Loan Fund, funded by the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, is the first federal revolving loan fund for hazard mitigation.
REPI has leveraged over $1.18 billion, $1.05 billion of it from non-DoD partners, to preserve 830,000 acres, and its funds can serve as match for any federal conservation or resilience program.
New York created a Storm Mitigation Loan Program within its Clean Water SRF after Hurricane Sandy.
In 2021 every jurisdiction with a COVID-19 major disaster declaration was eligible for 4% of disaster costs for mitigation projects.

records.title: Enhancing the Insurance Sector’s Contribution to Climate Adaptation
records.summary: The resource highlights the insurance sector's pivotal role in climate adaptation by providing coverage against climate-related disasters and promoting risk reduction measures. However, increasing climate-related risks and existing regulatory and market constraints pose challenges to insurers, limiting their ability to facilitate resilient rebuilding and invest in long-term risk management. The document suggests necessary regulatory and communication changes to enhance the sector's contribution to climate adaptation and improve overall community resilience.
insights: Climate change is predicted to increase the frequency and intensity of climate-related disasters, impacting insurance availability.
Adequate insurance coverage can facilitate quicker recovery and limit economic disruption following disasters.
Challenges in providing adequate climate risk assessments hinder the insurance sector's ability to price premiums effectively.
Regulatory and business challenges may impede the integration of climate risk analytics in the insurance sector.
Collective community-based insurance approaches may improve broader resilience against climate-related risks.
Encouraging multi-year insurance contracts may foster an environment where policyholders are more likely to invest in risk reduction.

records.title: Debt-for-Adaptation Swaps: A Financial Tool to Help Climate Vulnerable Nations
institutions: Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies (SAIS)
records.summary: The authors propose debt-for-adaptation swaps, in which bilateral and multilateral creditors forgive sovereign debt on condition that the savings fund climate adaptation and resilience. They argue adaptation is neglected because it generates little revenue, with about $50 billion tracked for adaptation in 2019-2020 against $571 billion for mitigation. Using ND-GAIN vulnerability, IMF and World Bank debt sustainability data and GCF allocations, they identify 11 priority countries holding $32 billion in bilateral and multilateral external debt. They set out five steps for the United States to lead, including convening Paris Club creditors.
insights: About 90% of climate finance went to mitigation; roughly $50 billion in adaptation finance was tracked in 2019-2020 versus $571 billion for mitigation.
Grants account for only 6% of climate finance, and 61% of climate finance is delivered through debt instruments.
Climate vulnerability raised the average cost of borrowing by 1.17%, about $40 billion in additional interest over 10 years.
Priority countries are Chad, Sudan and Zimbabwe, then Guinea-Bissau, Liberia, Tonga, Mauritania, Sierra Leone, Burundi, Ethiopia and Afghanistan, holding $32 billion of external non-private debt.
Precedents cited: the 1987 Bolivia swap, the 2018 Seychelles ocean swap ($21 million) and Belize's 2021 repurchase of $553 million of debt.
Caribbean small island states spend 30-70% of public revenue on debt repayment.

records.title: Adaptation Infrastructure and Its Effects on Property Values in the Face of Climate Risk
records.summary: Kelly and Molina measure what adaptation infrastructure does to property prices, using over 400,000 property transactions and 162 infrastructure projects in Miami-Dade County, an area highly exposed to flooding and sea level rise. By exploiting the timing and siting of different adaptation projects they identify significant gains in property values after project completion, concentrated in areas close to the project and in projects that are visually identifiable. Their central estimate is an aggregate mean benefit, net of adaptation cost, of about $0.68 million per project, and almost $300 million in aggregate net benefits across all projects in the sample. They also report that most projects generated positive net benefits, which they read as indicating that the vast majority of adaptation effort in the county is being placed in areas that pass a benefit-cost test. The authors are both at the University of Miami and the work was supported by the university's Laboratory of Integrative Knowledge.
insights: The benefit is capitalised into property value and is therefore measurable and, in principle, capturable: a mean net benefit of about $0.68 million per project and nearly $300 million in aggregate is exactly the value a tax increment or special assessment district could monetise.

The effect is concentrated in projects that are visually identifiable, which means the market is pricing perceived protection as much as engineered protection, and has a direct implication for how adaptation projects should be designed and communicated if value capture is the funding route.

Finding that most projects pass a benefit-cost test is a validation of existing siting decisions rather than a critique, which is an unusual and useful result for a county already spending on adaptation.
The identification comes from the timing and siting of 162 separate projects against 400,000 transactions, which is a strong design for a question usually answered with hedonic cross-sections.
records.publisher: Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists

records.title: Safeguarding Tomorrow Revolving Loan Fund: Florida Public Notice
records.summary: A public notice from the Florida Division of Emergency Management's Bureau of Mitigation seeking proposals from communities interested in low interest loans for hazard mitigation projects under the Safeguarding Tomorrow Revolving Loan Fund. The Safeguarding Tomorrow through Ongoing Risk Mitigation Act, the STORM Act, became law on 1 January 2021 and authorises FEMA to provide capitalization grants to eligible entities, meaning states, eligible federally recognized tribes, territories and the District of Columbia, which then make their own funding decisions and award loans directly to local communities. The Division is gathering information with the intent of applying for a capitalization grant under the Fiscal Year 2023 notice of funding opportunity published on 20 December 2022, funding opportunity number DHS-23-STORM-139-00-01, and must solicit projects from local governments for a minimum of six weeks to build a project proposal list to accompany its application; a well-developed list lets the state focus limited loan funds on the local governments most in need and prioritise projects ready for financing. Local governments may apply to the state for a loan and must have adopted their county Local Mitigation Strategy plan; individuals are not eligible. FEMA's four stated priorities are to empower entities through engagement and technical assistance, to create innovative funding solutions by letting applicants leverage loans for the non-federal cost share of other FEMA hazard mitigation assistance programs so underserved communities can access additional resources, to deliver equitable investments with a goal that 40 per cent of the overall benefits of the loan funds flow to underserved communities, and to reduce grant application complexity.
insights: The revolving structure is the point: repayments recapitalise the fund, so a single federal capitalization grant finances successive rounds of local mitigation rather than one round of it.

The leverage mechanism is the sharpest detail. A STORM loan may be used as the non-federal cost share for another FEMA hazard mitigation grant, which converts borrowed money into match money and multiplies a community's access to federal grants. That is a genuinely different use of debt from financing the works directly.
The eligibility gate is an adopted county Local Mitigation Strategy plan, so the capital is conditioned on a completed plan rather than on an application.

The 40 per cent equitable-benefit goal is a distributional target attached to a LOAN rather than a grant, and that carries a built-in tension: underserved communities are the least able to carry debt.

records.title: More than Checking a Box: Delivering Real-World, Validated Forward-Looking Financial Metrics for Physical Climate Risks
records.summary: Claire Souch of Moody's RMS argues that anyone estimating physical climate risk, whether for a lending portfolio, for the disruption of critical facilities or for a TCFD report, needs to know how the estimate is derived and how its outputs are validated, because those choices drive financial management decisions made under high uncertainty. The post describes how Moody's models these numbers using Climate on Demand version 2, which integrates physical climate risk modeling from Moody's RMS. It sets out the credibility case: Moody's RMS has worked in physical risk modeling for three decades and maintains 400 risk models covering countries and regions worldwide; those models underpin the highly regulated US$2.5 trillion global insurance industry and are now applied to asset management, investments, credit risk and lending decisions; they are developed and supported by over 1,200 staff including hundreds with doctorates, with sustained research and development investment. The physical risk financial model has evolved to assess compounding hazard impacts and physical damage at a highly granular level.
insights: The argument is that validation, not resolution, is what makes a climate risk number usable, which is the right emphasis and also the hardest thing for a buyer of these products to check independently.

The provenance claim is the interesting one commercially: the same models that underwrite a $2.5 trillion insurance industry are now being sold into credit and lending, so the insurance sector's risk view is quietly becoming the banking sector's.
That migration is what gives insurance pricing leverage over mortgage and corporate credit decisions, so the paper names the transmission channel rather than assuming it.
The post is vendor marketing and should be read as such: the capability claims are the company's own and the validation method is described rather than shown.
It is nonetheless a useful dated record of when physical risk catastrophe models crossed from insurance into mainstream credit analytics, which is early 2023 on this account.

records.title: Exemplary Forestry Investment Fund: A Blended Capital Model to Mitigate Climate Change and Secure the Future of the Maine Woods
records.summary: The Exemplary Forestry Investment Fund (EFIF) aims to address both ecological and financial challenges in Maine's North Woods by combining over $90 million of public, private, and philanthropic capital to acquire and manage over 100,000 acres of forest. This fund promotes Exemplary Forestry practices, enhancing long-term forest health, carbon sequestration, and biodiversity, while also providing sustainable financial returns. The initiative recognizes the necessity of a new financial model to support long-term forest stewardship and addresses the urgent climate and biodiversity crises.
insights: The EFIF is an impact-first investment vehicle blending over $90 million to manage Maine's forests.
Exemplary Forestry practices aim to improve ecological and financial outcomes in the forest sector.
40% of Maine's North Woods are understocked, affecting timber quality and ecosystem services.
80% of Maine's forests have changed ownership in the past 40 years, increasing fragmentation risks.
The fund focuses on long-term conservation management to ensure timber productivity and biodiversity.
Initial acquisitions of 10,000-15,000 acres are planned for 2023-24, with a goal of 100,000 acres by 2029.
The EFIF is self-sufficient at managing 35,000 acres, expected to be reached by 2026.
The fund seeks to monetize ecosystem services like carbon credits to enhance long-term viability.
Community engagement is vital for the fund's success, emphasizing local partnerships and support.

records.title: Unpriced Climate Risk and the Potential Consequences of Overvaluation in US Housing Markets
records.authors: Jesse D. Gourevitch, Carolyn Kousky, Yanjun (Penny) Liao, Christoph Nolte, Adam B. Pollack, Jeremy R. Porter, Joakim A. Weill
records.summary: The analysis reveals significant overvaluation of residential properties in the U.S. housing market, specifically those at risk of flooding, estimated between $121 to $237 billion. This overvaluation is mostly prevalent in coastal areas with inadequate flood risk disclosure laws, disproportionately affecting low-income households and municipalities dependent on property tax revenues. The findings emphasize the need for improved flood risk communication and policy changes to address the financial vulnerabilities imposed by climate change and flooding.
insights: Residential properties exposed to flood risk are overvalued by $121 to $237 billion.
Overvaluation is particularly evident in coastal counties with lenient or absent flood risk disclosure laws.
Low-income households face heightened risk of losing home equity due to potential property price deflation.
The cumulative annual losses from flooding are projected to rise significantly by 2050, increasing economic strain on property owners.
Properties outside the Special Flood Hazard Areas (SFHAs) are significantly overvalued, highlighting systemic issues in flood risk communication.
The inadequacies of the National Flood Insurance Program's pricing methodology may exacerbate the mispricing of flood risks.
Policy changes regarding flood risk disclosure and housing could lead to either gradual price adjustments or abrupt market corrections.
Improved access to flood risk data for homebuyers may enhance purchasing decisions and market pricing accuracy.
Local governments heavily reliant on property taxes may encounter fiscal shortfalls if property values decline.

records.title: Miami-Dade County and Municipalities Receive over $39 Million for Resilience Projects from the State of Florida
records.summary: Miami-Dade County and its Resilient305 partners, the cities of Miami and Miami Beach, received over $39 million from the Resilient Florida Grant Program on 6 February 2023, out of 75 grants awarded statewide. Seven of those grants went to Miami-Dade County, with $16,975,000 going directly to county-led projects. The four county projects are raising the banks of secondary canals feeding the C-8 Canal and Biscayne Canal, restoration of Environmentally Endangered Lands at Matheson Hammock, stormwater improvements at the Regional West Waste Transfer Station, and protecting the Virginia Key Wastewater Treatment Plant from sea level rise and storm surge. Miami Beach received funds to adapt the West Avenue neighborhood to sea level rise and to build a retention lake in Bayshore Park; Miami received money for flood improvements in Auburndale. The county frames the awards against the flood risks identified in its Sea Level Rise Strategy and says it continues to seek support for water and sewer protection, land acquisition and natural area restoration.
insights: Of the $39 million awarded across the Resilient305 partnership, $16.975 million went to county-led projects, so most of the money reached municipal rather than county applicants, which is the distribution a state competitive programme produces when cities apply separately.

Two of the four county projects protect single pieces of water infrastructure, the Virginia Key Wastewater Treatment Plant and the Regional West Waste Transfer Station, which is where a utility's own capital plan and a state resilience grant meet.
The county names its Sea Level Rise Strategy as the document that identified the risk the grants address, so the state grant is buying implementation of a plan the county had already paid to write.
The release lists water and sewer protection, land acquisition and natural area restoration as still-unfunded needs, which is a public statement of the gap the state programme did not close.

records.title: Goldman Sachs 2023 TCFD Report
institutions: Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures
records.summary: Goldman Sachs' 2023 firmwide TCFD report, its first since 2021, structured on the four TCFD pillars: Governance, Strategy, Risk Management, and Metrics and Targets. The sustainability strategy rests on three pillars, work with clients, management of the firm, and partnerships that address market gaps. On strategy it sets out the Sustainable Finance Framework, the client-facing groups carrying climate expertise, and the firmwide $750 billion sustainable finance commitment. On risk it describes a three lines of defence model, climate risk identification and assessment, and the integration of climate risk into financing and portfolio management alongside other environmental considerations. On metrics it reports progress against 2030 sectoral targets, the operational and supply chain commitment and GHG emissions, and is candid about data challenges. Named execution examples include bookrunning General Motors' first green bond, the Horizon platform, and the Climate Innovation and Development Fund, a blended finance facility with Bloomberg Philanthropies and the Asian Development Bank that financed an 88 megawatt Vietnamese wind farm and bus electrification in Vietnam and India. The report is a transition document throughout: it addresses the impact of climate change on the business and of the business on the climate, and contains no adaptation or physical-resilience programme.
insights: It is a transition document throughout, with no adaptation or physical-resilience programme in it: resilience, adaptation, catastrophe and insurance each appear zero times across 178,428 characters. What it discloses is exposure to the transition, not to the hazard.
It is a worked example of what a large US bank actually discloses under TCFD, filed against the four pillars, so it shows the level of specificity a firm chooses when the framework is voluntary.

The Climate Innovation and Development Fund is the one blended-finance structure here with named deals: a bank, a philanthropy and a development bank sharing risk to move capital into markets that had priced it out, financing an 88 megawatt Vietnamese wind farm and bus electrification in Vietnam and India.
The report says plainly that data availability and quality still limit what can be measured, which is a disclosure about the limits of its own metrics rather than a claim about performance.

records.title: Sustainable and Resilient Cities of Tomorrow
records.summary: An impact story from the infrastructure investor Meridiam describing The Urban Resilience Fund, launched in 2021 with the Rockefeller Foundation and the United Nations Capital Development Fund to help large and emerging cities in Europe and Africa respond to urbanisation and climate vulnerability. The fund is structured in three parts: a EUR 20 million catalytic capital fund for project preparation, a EUR 150 million investment fund for OECD countries and a EUR 350 million investment fund for non-OECD countries, specifically Africa. The framing is that project preparation, not capital, is the binding constraint: cities lack both infrastructure expertise and the financial resources to scope potential projects. Worked examples span nature-based coastal defences in Nouakchott, Mauritania, protecting some 75,000 people in low-lying areas from flooding caused by rising sea levels, fibre connections in Indiana and Montabaur, school and childcare spaces in Espoo, Finland, and bus rapid transit in Dakar.
insights: The EUR 20 million catalytic tranche sits ahead of the two investment funds and pays for project preparation, which is the explicit answer to the stated constraint: cities are not short of capital so much as short of bankable projects, and the fund structure puts money where that gap is.

Splitting the investment funds by OECD and non-OECD membership, EUR 150 million and EUR 350 million, allocates more than twice as much to the non-OECD side, which inverts the usual pattern of adaptation capital concentrating where risk is best priced.
In the Nouakchott case the nature-based coastal defence is delivered through a public-private company with an institutional investor on the equity side rather than through a public works budget.
The document states no publication date. The record carries a January seed date that the document does not confirm.

records.title: The Cascading and Compounding Impacts of Drought
institutions: United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction
United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification
records.summary: This policy brief from the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD), the International Drought Resilience Alliance, and the National Drought Mitigation Center (University of Nebraska) synthesizes the cascading and compounding socioeconomic, ecological, and financial impacts of drought globally. It frames drought as systemic risk (affecting agriculture, energy, transportation, and ecosystems), and outlines a three-pillar resilience framework (early warning, vulnerability assessment, risk mitigation) with sector-specific and whole-of-society recommendations, including blended finance, gender-responsive planning, nature-based solutions, and land degradation neutrality as investment priorities.
insights: Drought is one of the most expensive natural disasters globally, causing widespread crop loss, land degradation, reduced hydropower production, and broad socioeconomic losses across large areas over time, without leaving the defined destruction path of hurricanes or earthquakes, making financial quantification harder and advocacy weaker.

The Horn of Africa case study illustrates compounding systemic risk: five consecutive drought seasons (2020–2022), record UN FAO Food Price Index in 2022 (driven partly by the Ukraine war), and drought-induced food insecurity affecting 23 million people, demonstrating how remote geopolitical events can amplify local drought impacts for the most financially vulnerable populations.

Women spend a collective 200 million hours per day collecting water globally (UNICEF), representing an enormous hidden productivity and health cost that is rarely captured in drought damage assessments or investment cases, creating a measurable equity and economic efficiency argument for water infrastructure in underserved areas.

Vulnerability to drought is framed as substantially a function of social and political resource-allocation decisions, including investments in human capital, environmental systems, and infrastructure, meaning resilience investments can be designed and targeted, not merely reactive.

Nature-based solutions (forest and watershed protection/restoration, land degradation neutrality, riparian buffers) are identified as cost-effective multi-benefit interventions that simultaneously reduce climate risk, improve soil water retention, and deliver ecosystem co-benefits, key attributes for blended finance structuring.

records.title: California Wildfire Innovation Fund
records.summary: The California Wildfire Innovation Fund (CWIF) aims to mitigate wildfire risks in California by providing flexible financing to companies and entrepreneurs focused on forest restoration and wildfire prevention. It represents a commitment to industry innovation that protects communities and the environment while also generating financial returns.
insights: The CWIF is designed to reduce wildfire risks across California.
It offers flexible financing targeted at forest restoration and wildfire mitigation.
The initiative is seen as a responsibility to minimize the impact of climate-induced disasters.
Investments in the CWIF are expected to yield competitive financial returns.
The fund aligns economic viability with environmental and social goals.
Significant investments from organizations like CSAA Insurance Group underline its importance.
The fund represents a sustainable approach to addressing critical environmental challenges.
The initiative highlights the growing trend of financing solutions in climate-related sectors.

records.title: FRB Catalyst Facility
records.summary: The FRB Catalyst Facility is an investment initiative aimed at accelerating funding for various forest restoration projects across the Western U.S., with a focus on preventing catastrophic wildfires and addressing climate challenges. By pooling investments, it plans to finance over $50 million in restoration work while offering returns to investors.
insights: The FRB Catalyst Facility aims to expedite financing for multiple landscape restoration projects.
It is designed to mitigate the risks of wildfires exacerbated by climate change.
The initiative will potentially finance over $50 million in restoration efforts.
Projects are being implemented in multiple states, including Oregon, California, and Washington.
The facility operates on a pooled investment model that allows for broader financing capabilities.
Active restoration efforts are highlighted in forests like Eldorado, Tahoe, and Rogue River-Siskiyou.
The facility's structure is intended to attract and provide returns for diverse investors.
The approach emphasizes both community safety and environmental sustainability.

records.title: Decoupled Net Present Value: Protecting Assets Against Climate Change Risk by Consistently Capturing the Value of Resilient and Adaptable Investments
records.authors: David Espinoza; Javier Rojo; William Phillips; Andrew Eil
records.summary: An open access article in Sustainable and Resilient Infrastructure, volume 8 supplement 1 pages 323 to 336 for 2023, published online 9 December 2022, by David Espinoza, Javier Rojo, William Phillips and Andrew Eil, on decoupled net present value as a way of protecting assets against climate change risk by consistently capturing the value of resilient and adaptable investments. The method addresses a defect in conventional appraisal: a single risk-adjusted discount rate conflates the time value of money with compensation for risk, and because resilience benefits arrive late and reduce variance rather than raise expected return, standard net present value systematically undervalues them. Decoupling the two components allows the value of resilience and of adaptability, meaning the option to adjust later, to be carried through the calculation rather than discounted away.
insights: Decoupling the discount rate is the technical move. A conventional net present value applies one rate to every year of a project's life, which drives the value of avoided losses in distant years to nearly nothing; the method separates the discounting of protection benefits from the discounting of ordinary cash flows so that a long-horizon benefit survives appraisal.

Treating adaptability as an option with value is the second half of the argument and the more radical one. Conventional appraisal penalises a design that can be changed later, because flexibility costs money up front and shows no return; an option-aware valuation pays for it.
A consulting engineering firm rather than an academic economics department produced this, so the method was built to be used inside project appraisal rather than to be argued in a journal.

It bears directly on the co-benefit gap the Miami-Dade plan network record and the CRA guidebook both identify. A park that is also a stormwater asset has a benefit stream that a single discount rate flattens, and decoupled discounting is a way to keep it.

records.title: The Impact of Climate Risk on Corporate Credit Risk
records.summary: This 2022 peer-reviewed article from Cogent Economics & Finance develops a quantitative framework for translating climate physical and transition risk shocks into corporate probabilities of default (PD). Using Geometric Brownian Motion (GBM) to simulate 10,000 equity price paths and the KMV/Merton distance-to-default model, the authors construct a scaling factor matrix showing how climate shocks of varying severity (20%–80% equity price drops) amplify PDs across credit grades (AAA through CCC/C). The paper focuses on Africa as the most climate-exposed region and produces calibration outputs directly applicable to IFRS-9 provisioning and Basel regulatory capital calculations.
insights: A 60% climate shock applied to an A-rated corporate produces a ~4x spike in implied PD; the PD recovers roughly exponentially to pre-shock levels within five years absent further shocks, providing a concrete time-decay profile for credit loss provisioning.

Multiple mild shocks (≥20% equity price drop) arriving at annual or sub-annual frequency cause inevitable corporate default regardless of price drift or post-shock volatility, illustrating that shock frequency matters as much as severity for credit quality.

The scaling factor matrix quantifies PD amplification as a function of both shock size and initial (unshocked) PD: impacts on AAA-rated credits are negligible but scaling factors reach ~4x for CCC/C-rated credits under an 80% physical shock, with transition shocks producing slightly lower but comparable multipliers.

Physical climate shocks increase post-event equity volatility, compounding PD deterioration, while transition shocks (e.g., carbon tax announcements) do not increase volatility because they are anticipated, a distinction with direct implications for how banks should model each risk type under BCBS/EBA frameworks.

Africa faces the most severe climate-driven credit deterioration: Eastern and Western African GDP per capita growth is forecast to fall 15% below baseline by 2050 under a high-warming scenario (+4°C by 2100), with losses in high-warming scenarios 50%–85% higher than low-warming scenarios by 2050 for Central and Western Africa respectively.

EBA Pillar III ESG disclosure standards (mandatory for Basel-compliant banks from 1 January 2024, including Green Asset Ratio reporting) create a regulatory deadline that makes this calibration framework operationally relevant for near-term compliance.

records.title: Towards a Climate-Risk Data Architecture: Common and Open Risk Metrics to Align Finance with Climate-Resilient Development Goals
records.authors: Jenty Kirsch Wood, Nicola Ranger, Benedikt Signer
institutions: United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction
UK Centre for Greening Finance and Investment (CGFI)
records.summary: The document discusses the urgent need for a global climate-risk data architecture that provides open and standardized risk metrics to enhance climate adaptation finance. It underscores initiatives like the Global Resilience Index Initiative (GRII) and the UNDRR's Risk Information Exchange (RiX), which aim to facilitate effective financial decision-making aligned with climate-resilient development goals. By promoting common metrics, the resource advocates for improved fiscal resilience, investment strategies, and better integration of climate-related data across sectors.
insights: A new climate-risk data architecture is crucial for mobilizing finance for climate adaptation and resilience.
Common metrics facilitate the integration of physical climate risks into financial decision-making.
The GRII and RiX initiatives aim to create a shared, open architecture that consolidates risk data.
Standardized climate-risk metrics help assess and compare the resilience benefits of different investments.
Climate stress testing is vital for understanding the resilience of financial institutions to climate impacts.
Data gaps exist in the availability, reliability, and comparability of climate-related financial metrics.
Collaborative efforts among global stakeholders are necessary to close data gaps and enhance climate-risk analytics.
records.publisher: UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction

records.title: New York Voters Pass Historic 2022 Environmental Bond Act
records.summary: An Environmental Defense Fund press release of 9 November 2022 on New York voters' passage of the Clean Water, Clean Air and Green Jobs Environmental Bond Act the previous day. At $4.2 billion it is the largest environmental bond act in New York State history and was the largest measure on any ballot anywhere in the nation in 2022, and it is expected to support environmental improvements preserving, enhancing and restoring the state's natural resources while creating more than 84,000 local jobs. The release credits a coalition of more than three hundred environmental organisations, unions and business groups, and carries a statement from Kate Boicourt, EDF's Director of Climate Resilient Coasts and Watersheds for New York and New Jersey, framing the vote as New Yorkers saying yes to clean water, clean air, reduced flooding, environmental justice and jobs.
insights: A $4.2 billion voter-approved general obligation bond, authorised by referendum rather than raised in a market, which makes the instrument accountable to the people who will service it.

Reduced flooding is one of five stated purposes alongside clean water, clean air, environmental justice and jobs, so the resilience share of the $4.2 billion is undetermined here. That multi-purpose structure is what gets an environmental bond passed and what makes its resilience benefit hard to attribute.

This is a stakeholder statement rather than the instrument's own documentation. The Environmental Defense Fund was part of the coalition that campaigned for the act, so the framing of the result is an advocate's.

records.title: Toward Holistic Coastal Resilience: A Cross-Government Assessment of Louisiana’s Resilience Challenges and Opportunities
records.summary: A cross-government assessment of Louisiana's resilience challenges and opportunities, produced after Governor Edwards joined ten other states in 2020 by naming a Chief Resilience Officer to advance a cross-agency approach to environmental hazards in the coastal area. After two years of engagement, vulnerability assessments and exploration of adaptation options, the report finds that environmental change in coastal Louisiana is producing direct and indirect consequences for the core missions and functions of every agency in state government, and that the challenges ahead will not be limited to the coastal region. Its central recommendation is that addressing these needs requires a formal and continued emphasis on resilience-building across all hazards and the entire state through permanent positions, structures and processes, with a single focal point for statewide effort, in order to avoid damage to infrastructure and assets, preserve economic and workforce development, sustain the natural environment, protect vulnerable people and cultures, and secure funding to implement adaptation. On vulnerability, the most common exposure across agencies is to buildings and assets such as transportation infrastructure, facilities, vehicles and equipment, which affects both budgets and service delivery; service-providing agencies additionally face scattered clients, damage to their own employees' homes, and new post-disaster demands for programming with no additional staff, while disasters damage the state's attractiveness to business and its workforce retention.
insights: The finding that matters for finance is indirect: disasters damage a state's attractiveness to business and its workforce retention, which is a revenue effect on the state's own tax base rather than a repair cost, and it does not appear in a damage estimate.

Naming a single focal point and permanent positions is a request for institutional capacity rather than money, which is the same diagnosis Marin County acted on and the same one the Brookings report finds explains why some states plan and others do not.

Service-providing agencies face a compounding failure the asset inventory misses: their clients scatter, their own staff lose homes, and demand rises with no new staff, so the delivery capacity falls exactly when it is needed.

A Chief Resilience Officer appointed in 2020 puts Louisiana among the earliest states to create the role, which is the institutional precondition a statewide adaptation funding strategy needs before it can be written.

records.title: Massachusetts Municipal Vulnerability Preparedness (MVP) Program: State Case Study
records.summary: A November 2022 case study of the Massachusetts Municipal Vulnerability Preparedness programme, created in 2017 under Executive Order 569 issued by Governor Charlie Baker in 2016, which provides technical assistance to help communities assess climate and natural hazard vulnerabilities and develop strategies to address them. The programme has expanded to cover 97 per cent of Massachusetts municipalities and is frequently used as a template by other states, including Rhode Island. The problem it addresses is stated with numbers: over 50 per cent of the state's residents live along the coast and face a projected one to three feet of sea level rise by 2050, and inland flooding from extreme precipitation, ice jams and dam failure is among the most common hazards. The design has two parts in sequence. Communities first apply for planning grants to run workshops that assess vulnerabilities, gather community input and identify adaptation strategies. Having completed those workshops they are designated MVP Communities and may then apply for action grants to fund the strategies identified, typically one to two year projects covering infrastructure redesign and retrofits or local bylaw updates that use nature-based solutions such as stormwater parks, with an emphasis on equity, forward-looking data and natural systems.
insights: The sequencing is the instrument. A planning grant is the gate to an action grant, and designation is the token that passes it, so the state buys a pipeline of appraised projects rather than fielding unprepared applications. That is how a public funder manufactures bankability, and it is transferable to any concessional lender facing the same problem.

97 per cent municipal coverage is the number that makes this more than a programme description: near-universal take-up means the planning stage is not self-selecting toward already-capable communities, which is the usual failure of a competitive planning grant.

The programme runs in two stages, a planning grant that produces a municipal vulnerability assessment followed by an action grant that funds what the assessment identifies, so the money is released against a plan the municipality has already made rather than against an application.

Action grants explicitly exclude studies and plans, so the second stage buys construction rather than more analysis. Combined with the planning-grant gate, the programme separates the two kinds of spending that public resilience funding usually conflates.

records.title: Southeast Florida Regional Climate Action Plan 3.0
institutions: Southeast Florida Regional Climate Change Compact
records.summary: Regional Climate Action Plan 3.0 is the Southeast Florida Regional Climate Change Compact's five-year update, setting goals, recommendations and supporting strategies across 11 focal areas: agriculture, energy, equity, informed and engaged communities, natural systems, public health, public policy advocacy, regional economic resilience, risk reduction and emergency management, sustainable communities and transportation, and water. It serves Broward, Miami-Dade, Monroe and Palm Beach counties, 109 municipal governments, the Seminole Tribe of Florida and the Miccosukee Tribe of Indians of Florida, a regional population of more than 6.2 million. The twin objectives are net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 against a 2005 baseline and strengthened adaptive capacity and climate resilience for the region's communities, institutions and economy.
insights: The plan serves four counties, 109 municipal governments and two sovereign tribal nations across a regional population of more than 6.2 million, which is the governance unit that makes it a regional plan rather than a county one.

It was developed with more than 150 named subject matter experts drawn from county staff, universities, utilities, chambers of commerce, federal agencies and community organisations, and each of the 11 focal areas carries a named chapter lead from a member county.

Regional Economic Resilience is a focal area in its own right alongside Risk Reduction and Emergency Management, which separates the economic continuity question from the emergency management one rather than folding the first into the second.

The plan is explicitly iterative, on a five-year update cycle, and positions itself as a springboard for harmonised regional action while leaving implementation to local conditions, so its recommendations are not binding on member governments.
records.publisher: Southeast Florida Regional Climate Change Compact

records.title: Marsh McLennan Report: Mobilizing Insurance Sector Capabilities to Advance Community-Level Climate Risk Reduction and Adaptation
institutions: United Nations Climate Change High-Level Champions
