records.summary: A joint report of the UN Climate Change High-Level Champions, the UN Race to Resilience, the Adrienne Arsht-Rockefeller Foundation Resilience Center and Marsh McLennan, presented at COP27 as the Sharm el-Sheikh Resolution on Insurance Sector Leadership on Climate Risk Reduction and Adaptation. Its argument is that the insurance sector should expand its role beyond risk transfer into actively advancing community-level climate risk reduction and adaptation. The High-Level Champions' statement of purpose frames the sector as uniquely positioned because it is built on the mathematics of risk, and calls on it to assemble the tools, networks and capabilities to de-risk, finance and accelerate community-level risk reduction, invoking the industry's legacy of enhancing societal resilience against new and complex risks. The operative phrase is that insurers should help communities cope with climate change not just through innovative risk transfer mechanisms but by actively deploying their capabilities to flatten the climate risk curve. The report carries a capabilities framework and a set of pioneer projects as supporting materials, and sits within the Champions' 2030 Adaptation Outcomes for Finance.
insights: The ask is explicitly beyond risk transfer: insurers are called on to deploy their analytical and network capabilities to reduce risk, not only to price and carry it, which reframes the sector as an adaptation actor rather than a counterparty.
Flattening the climate risk curve is the framing metaphor, and it makes the sector's commercial interest and the public interest point the same way, since a lower loss curve preserves insurability.
A capabilities framework plus pioneer projects is the structure of the report, so it is a template and a set of precedents rather than an argument, which is what makes it usable.
Presenting this as a COP27 resolution gives it standing as a sector commitment rather than a consultancy view, though the commitments are voluntary.
Marsh McLennan is the publisher, so the delivery-model proposal comes from a broker with a commercial position in the market it is describing.

records.title: Climate Gentrification in Miami: A Real Climate Change-Minded Investment Practice?
records.summary: A paper in Cities by Han Li and Richard J. Grant of the University of Miami, published online 10 October 2022, testing whether climate gentrification in Miami is genuinely a climate-change-minded investment practice. Their answer is that it is not. Homebuyers' awareness of sea level rise is not the major factor pushing buyers to higher ground: climate gentrification in Miami is better explained as a rational economic response to expensive flood insurance than to sea level rise itself. Buyers are steered by the flood insurance FEMA requires and by the historical record of flooding, rather than by elevation or by scientific projections of storm surge. Unlike other global cities, Miami's wealthy and well-educated homebuyers show fewer concerns about rising seas. The authors also find that climate gentrification is being used by some developers and both interpreted and misinterpreted by local policymakers to facilitate neoliberal redevelopment and place marketing, while the real estate industry fails buyers by not providing accurate sea level rise information. They propose two policy instruments: include sea level rise risk assessment in homebuyer contracts, and improve FEMA insurance maps to incorporate sea level rise scenarios.
insights: The finding inverts the usual causal story: the transmission from climate risk to housing markets runs through insurance pricing, not through risk perception. Buyers are not pricing the hazard, they are pricing the premium, which means the instrument is doing the work the information was supposed to do.

That has a direct consequence for adaptation finance. If premiums are the signal, then anything that suppresses premiums, subsidy, rate caps, or a map that omits future risk, also suppresses the adaptation response, and the record names the specific artifact: FEMA maps that do not incorporate sea level rise scenarios.
Historical flooding beats projected flooding in buyer behaviour. A model that prices 2050 exposure is not what the market is reading.
The two remedies the paper proposes are both disclosure rather than financing: a risk assessment in the purchase contract, and better maps. Neither moves capital; both change what the price means.

records.title: Developing Adaptive Resilience in Infrastructure Systems: An Approach to Quantify Long-Term Benefits
records.authors: Prerna Singh; Adjo Amekudzi-Kennedy; Baabak Ashuri; Mikhail Chester; Samuel Labi; Thomas A. Wall
records.summary: An open access article in Sustainable and Resilient Infrastructure, volume 8 supplement 1 pages 26 to 47 for 2023, published online 29 September 2022, by Prerna Singh, Adjo Amekudzi-Kennedy and Baabak Ashuri with Mikhail Chester, Samuel Labi and Thomas A. Wall, on developing adaptive resilience in infrastructure systems and an approach to quantifying its long-term benefits. The treatment is hazard-specific rather than abstract, with hurricane the recurring case. The paper has been viewed 4,036 times and cited 10 times.
insights: Adaptive resilience is a distinct concept from resilience as robustness, and the distinction has a financing consequence: a system designed to change as conditions change has a benefit stream that only appears over a long horizon, which is exactly the stream a single discount rate destroys.

The paper's target is the quantification of long-term benefit, and it is explicit that what counts as a benefit is itself contested rather than given, which is why the method spends its effort on defining the benefit stream before discounting it.

The author list spans civil engineering, transport and a national laboratory, which places the work in infrastructure asset management rather than in finance, so its units are engineering ones rather than financial.

records.title: Data-Driven Parametric Insurance Framework Using Bayesian Neural Networks
records.summary: An arXiv preprint, by Subeen Pang and Chanyeol Choi of MIT and Wecover Platforms, proposing a data-driven parametric insurance framework built on Bayesian neural networks. Their argument is that traditional insurance risk models rest on statistical analyses that are inaccurate and becoming more flawed as climate change makes weather more erratic and extreme, and that data-driven parametric insurance can supplement traditional cover. They use the deep sigma point process, a Bayesian neural network approach, for the data analysis part of parametric insurance, with residential internet connectivity dropout in the United States as the case study.
insights: The case study is the interesting choice: residential internet connectivity dropout as the index. It is a continuously measured, nationally available proxy for infrastructure disruption that needs no weather station and no damage survey.

A Bayesian approach gives calibrated uncertainty rather than a point estimate, which matters for a parametric trigger specifically: the quantity an underwriter needs is the distribution of basis risk, not its expected value.

The authors' framing is that traditional statistical risk models are becoming more flawed as weather grows more erratic, and the Bayesian approach is offered as an answer to that non-stationarity rather than as a refinement of fit.
It is a preprint and should be cited as one: the contribution to take from it is the trigger idea and the method rather than a peer-reviewed result.

records.title: Homebuyers with Access to Flood-Risk Data Bid on Lower-Risk Homes
records.authors: Lily Katz, Daryl Fairweather, Sebastian Sandoval-Olascoaga
records.summary: A study by Redfin revealed that access to flood-risk data significantly influences homebuyers' decisions, leading them to bid on homes with 54% lower flood risk. The randomized controlled trial demonstrated that users who were initially interested in homes with severe flood risks shifted toward lower-risk options once they were informed about the risks involved, with particular trends observed in flood-prone areas like Cape Coral, FL, and Houston, TX.
insights: Homebuyers with access to flood-risk data are more likely to consider lower-risk properties.
Redfin users who initially viewed homes with high flood-risk scores shifted to bidding on homes with significantly lower risk after accessing relevant data.
The study involved a randomized controlled trial of 17.5 million users, half of whom had access to flood-risk scores.
There is a growing awareness among homebuyers of the impact of climate risk on property values.
Users in flood-prone areas were more likely to engage with flood-risk information when searching for homes.
Home values in flood-prone regions could decline as awareness of flooding risks increases.
Areas with lower flood risk may experience rising home values as buyers seek safer options.
Online search behaviors shifted, with homebuyers becoming more selective in their housing searches when provided with flood-risk data.
The experiment's findings suggest stronger buyer demand for homes with minimal flood risk, especially as the market cools.

records.title: California Senate Bill 852
records.summary: The text of California Senate Bill 852, Chapter 266, introduced by Senator Dodd and approved by the Governor and filed with the Secretary of State on 9 September 2022, adding Division 6 commencing with Section 62300 to Title 6 of the Government Code and titled Climate resilience districts: formation: funding mechanisms. It authorises a city, a county, a city and county, a special district, or any combination of those entities to form a climate resilience district for the purpose of raising and allocating funding for eligible projects and the operating expenses of eligible projects. Each district is deemed to be an enhanced infrastructure financing district and must comply with the existing law governing those districts except as specified, and a district may finance only projects meeting the bill's definition of an eligible project. The digest sets that against existing law, under which a legislative body may establish an enhanced infrastructure financing district to finance public capital facilities or other projects of communitywide significance including projects that enable communities to adapt to the impacts of climate change, financed among other ways by the issuance of bonds serviced by property tax increment revenues, with a public financing authority established as the district's governing board before the district is formed and an infrastructure financing plan adopted.
insights: The statute invents no new instrument. By deeming a climate resilience district to be an enhanced infrastructure financing district, it borrows an existing financing machinery, bonds serviced by property tax increment revenue, and points it at adaptation. That reuse is why it was passable.

The mechanism has an uncomfortable logic: tax increment financing is repaid out of rising property values inside the district, so a resilience project funds itself by making the protected area more valuable, and the repayment structure therefore depends on the displacement pressure it creates.

Allowing a combination of entities to form a single district is a deliberate answer to jurisdictional mismatch: flood risk does not respect municipal boundaries, and under this statute the financing district does not have to either.

Funding operating expenses as well as capital projects is unusual and important. Most public resilience money buys construction and leaves maintenance unfunded, which is how a green stormwater asset degrades into a liability.

records.title: Sinking Tax Base: Land & Property at Risk from Rising Seas
records.summary: The report 'Sinking Tax Base' by Climate Central assesses the impact of sea level rise on the tax base of coastal U.S. counties, highlighting the potential loss of taxable properties as rising waters alter boundary lines between public and private land. This shift threatens local tax revenues, which are crucial for funding schools and services, with projections indicating that over 648,000 tax parcels could be affected by mid-century, resulting in significant financial implications.
insights: Over 648,000 tax parcels in coastal U.S. counties could be partly below tidal boundaries by mid-century.
Approximately 4.4 million acres of land are at risk from rising sea levels.
More than 48,000 properties may be entirely submerged below tidal boundaries.
Florida, Louisiana, and Texas are the most affected states in terms of the number of impacted properties.
Rising sea levels may cause significant shifts in property values and local tax revenues.
At least $108 billion in assessed property value is at risk by 2100 due to sea level rise.
Densely-developed areas along the coast are reaching a tipping point as sea levels rise.
The report includes over 250 individual county-level analyses to assess risks more accurately.

records.title: Pragmatic Cost–Benefit Analysis for Infrastructure Resilience
records.authors: Russell M. Wise, Tim Capon, Brenda B. Lin, Mark Stafford-Smith
institutions: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
records.summary: Wise and colleagues argue that infrastructure investment must account for climate change, but that most day-to-day projects are small and poorly served by economic assessment processes, and propose four simple adjustments to cost-benefit practice. They note strong convergence between the World Bank, the OECD, the UK National Infrastructure Commission and Infrastructure Australia on two points: that resilient infrastructure is robust, profitable and urgent, with the extra cost as little as 3 per cent of overall investment against at least a fourfold return, and that technical and institutional capacity to manage climate risk must be developed alongside access to information and tools, specifically cost-benefit analyses that properly value resilience and consider risk and uncertainty. The scale problem is the core of the argument: investment plans are large in aggregate, the US Bipartisan Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act committed $1.2 trillion and low- and middle-income countries spend around $1 trillion a year, but they are implemented through many small projects run by local planners who often lack the capability for complex appraisal. The US bill included $110 billion for aging roads and bridges, with more than 43,500 of about 620,000 bridges considered structurally deficient; Frankston City, one of 537 Australian local councils, spends nearly half its annual budget on 706 km of roads, 996 km of pathways, 950 km of pipes and drains, 160 bridges, 331 buildings and 525 parks. The paper names the well-known limitations of how cost-benefit analysis is normally deployed, how discount rates are applied, how residual values are treated, the timeframe of analysis and the inclusion of social and environmental benefits, and observes that comprehensive solutions exist but are complicated for practitioners in real institutional settings.
insights: The argument is about the unit of decision rather than about the method: a $1.2 trillion programme is spent through thousands of small projects appraised by local planners, so improving national guidance does nothing unless the fix is simple enough for a council to apply.
3 per cent extra cost for a fourfold return is the resilience premium stated plainly, and it is why the authors treat the binding barrier as appraisal capability rather than economics.

The four named limitations, discount rate, residual value, timeframe and omitted social and environmental benefits, all bias the same way, against long-lived resilience investment, so the errors compound rather than cancel.

Framing this as needing four SIMPLE adjustments rather than a better method is the practical contribution: the sophisticated approaches already exist and are not being used, which makes adoption the problem.
The Frankston City inventory is a useful reminder of what a resilience capital plan is actually made of at the local level: pipes, pathways and small bridges, not headline megaprojects.

records.title: Global Finance and Urban Adaptation: Governing Climate Risk in Miami, Florida
records.summary: The resource 'Global Finance and Urban Adaptation: Governing Climate Risk in Miami, Florida' explores the complex interplay between global finance and urban adaptation strategies to address climate risks in Miami. It emphasizes the necessity of effective governance, public-private partnerships, and community engagement in developing sustainable urban infrastructure. The document highlights the importance of innovative financial mechanisms, adaptive governance structures, and collaborative frameworks to enhance resilience against climate impacts such as rising sea levels and extreme weather events.
insights: Financial mechanisms are critical for funding urban adaptation projects to mitigate climate risks.
Effective governance structures must be adaptive and inclusive to tackle climate-related challenges.
Public-private partnerships are essential for mobilizing resources and expertise in urban adaptation efforts.
Community engagement is crucial for developing sustainable urban policies that address local needs.
Innovative financial instruments are needed to fund urban adaptation initiatives sustainably.
Data-driven decision-making enhances the effectiveness of adaptation strategies in urban environments.
Collaborative governance involving local communities and stakeholders increases adaptation efforts' success.
Investment in climate-resilient infrastructure is vital, particularly in coastal cities like Miami.

records.title: Resilience in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act: What Funding Opportunities Does IIJA Provide for Regional Networks?
records.summary: A Georgetown Climate Center toolkit page inventorying the resilience and adaptation programmes created by the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, Public Law 117-58, and asking specifically which of them are open to regional collaboratives rather than to single jurisdictions. Each entry carries the public law section number and page, the administering agency, the total appropriation with its year-by-year split, the list of eligible entities, whether Justice40 applies, and what the page calls the programme's collaborative feature. The largest is PROTECT, Promoting Resilient Operations for Transformative, Efficient, and Cost-saving Transportation, at $8.7 billion split $7.3 billion formula and $1.4 billion competitive. Others include the Electric Grid Reliability and Resilience Research, Development and Demonstration Program at $1 billion over fiscal years 2022 to 2026, the Healthy Streets programme at $500 million for cool and porous pavements and tree cover, and Transportation Resilience and Adaptation Centers of Excellence at $250 million in planning grants and $750 million in capital construction grants.
insights: The page's organising question is not how much money exists but who may apply together. It sorts programmes by whether the collaborative feature sits in the eligible-entity list or in the programme's own stated purpose, which is the distinction a regional collaborative with no legal authority of its own actually needs.

PROTECT's $7.3 billion formula share dwarfs its $1.4 billion competitive share, so most of the largest federal transportation resilience programme reaches states without a competition, and the collaborative route runs through multi-state or multijurisdictional joint applications.

Georgetown's framing of regional climate collaboratives, drawn from its own Lessons in Regional Resilience, is that they are loose membership networks with no legal authority that build capacity and make recommendations, which is why eligibility language decides whether they can touch this money at all.

records.title: Climate-Related Risks in Financial Assets
records.authors: Emanuele Campiglio, Louis Daumas, Pierre Monnin, Adrian von Jagow
institutions: RFF-CMCC European Institute on Economics and the Environment
records.summary: This 2023 Journal of Economic Surveys article by Campiglio, Daumas, Monnin, and von Jagow provides a comprehensive critical review of empirical and theoretical literature on how climate-related risks (physical, transition, and liability), affect the pricing of financial assets across equities, bonds, loans, and real estate. The paper develops a four-channel transmission framework (assets, investment, production network, credit), reviews backward-looking evidence showing predominantly negative asset price effects, and surveys forward-looking stress tests that find share price declines up to 60% and earnings at risk up to 140% under disorderly transition scenarios. Appendix tables catalog study-level findings on carbon intensity, EU-ETS compliance premia, and policy-driven cost-of-capital shifts. The authors conclude that financial markets currently underprice climate risks and call for expanded network-effect modeling and improved disclosures.
insights: Financial markets systematically underprice climate-related risks: backward-looking studies show that new climate information predominantly leads to negative asset price effects across equities, bonds, loans, and real estate, yet most papers find these effects are smaller than efficient pricing would require.

Four transmission channels carry climate costs to asset prices: (1) physical/transition destruction of capital assets (stranding); (2) forced infrastructure investment (CapEx increases); (3) supply chain and demand disruptions (revenue/opex impacts); and (4) credit channel repricing (higher interest rates and insurance premia).

Forward-looking stress tests report starker losses than long-term scenario models: share price declines of 20–60% under 'too late, too sudden' transition scenarios (Ralite & Thomä 2019), earnings at risk up to 140% for utilities (Trucost 2019), and equity losses amplified 2–3× when interbank network second-round effects are included (Battiston et al. 2017).

Physical risk drivers predominantly reduce real estate prices: SLR exposure discounts properties by 7% (Bernstein et al. 2019), hurricane inundation areas show 36–48% markdowns (Atreya & Ferreira 2015), and a one-standard-deviation increase in SLR exposure raises municipal bond issuance costs by 23.4 basis points (Painter 2020).

A 'carbon premium' is documented empirically: higher corporate carbon emissions are associated with higher stock returns across sectors and continents (Bolton & Kacperczyk 2021), while scope-1 emissions increase cost of debt by 38–62 basis points per standard deviation (Jung et al. 2018); investors demand compensation rather than penalizing emitters through lower valuations.

records.title: Climate‑resilient Finance and Investment: Framing Paper
records.summary: The 'Climate-resilient finance and investment: Framing paper' emphasizes the urgent need to align financial flows with climate resilience goals amidst growing climate challenges. It highlights the necessity for increased funding for adaptation, the redirection of current investments away from vulnerabilities, and the development of frameworks like the EU Taxonomy to assess adaptation-aligned finance. The paper underscores the importance of public and private collaboration, robust risk management, and the establishment of metrics for evaluation, all essential for fostering sustainable financial practices that contribute to climate-resilient development.
insights: Aligning financial flows with climate resilience is critical for adapting to climate change impacts.
Public and private finance currently involves significant investments that must be redirected to support climate-resilient activities.
Strong inter-sectoral collaboration is essential for effective adaptation and resilience planning.
Investors increasingly demand adaptation-aligned finance, focusing on both financial returns and positive climate outcomes.
Metrics for adaptation alignment are still underdeveloped and require further methodological advancement.

records.title: Return on Investment for Mangrove and Reef Flood Protection
records.authors: Michael W. Beck, Nadine Heck, Siddharth Narayan, Pelayo Menéndez, Borja G. Reguero, Stephan Bitterwolf, Saul Torres-Ortega, Glenn-Marie Lange, Kerstin Pfliegner, Valerie Pietsch McNulty, Iñigo J. Losada
records.summary: The article discusses the economic feasibility of restoring coral reefs and mangroves for flood protection in over 20 Caribbean countries, emphasizing the strong Return on Investment (ROI) these ecosystems can provide for coastal adaptation. Despite the challenges of insufficient environmental funding and high restoration costs, the study finds that investing in these natural defenses could yield substantial long-term benefits and identifies potential funding sources to support such initiatives.
insights: Coral reefs and mangroves provide significant flood protection benefits and can yield strong ROI for restoration projects.
Restoration costs for mangroves in the Caribbean can vary significantly, with the median cost being $23,000 per hectare, while Florida has much higher costs at $45,000 per hectare.
Tax districts and federal disaster recovery funds are underutilized sources for financing habitat restoration projects.
The study indicates robust potential for immediate flood risk reduction benefits from mangrove and coral reef restoration, affecting plans for disaster risk management.
Sensitivity analyses reveal that ROI remains largely positive across various discount rates and restoration benefit timelines.
Investment opportunities exist in regions such as Cuba, Bahamas, and Jamaica, where cost-effective restoration of coastal habitats can significantly reduce flood risk.
The article highlights a funding gap in ocean conservation, with only $4 to $10 billion annually being spent compared to an estimated $100 billion needed.
Restoration projects could lead to exponential benefits over time, which may enhance future funding opportunities for natural infrastructure.
Combining reef and mangrove restoration can maximize flood risk reduction, enabling better coastal resilience.

records.title: The Challenge of Financial Recovery from Disasters: The Case of Florida Homeowners after Hurricane Michael
records.authors: Kyle Sweeney; Helen Wiley; Carolyn Kousky
institutions: Wharton Risk Management and Decision Processes Center
records.summary: This report presents a 2021 survey of Bay County, Florida homeowners who lived through Hurricane Michael in October 2018, documenting the full range of costs a hurricane imposes and how households financed recovery. It finds costs extending well beyond property damage, including evacuation, debris removal, generators, fuel, temporary housing and higher insurance prices, and that rebuilding took 18 months on average. Homeowners insurance was the most common recovery source and insured households were less likely to fall behind on bills or sell belongings, while federal aid was small. The authors conclude that current disaster finance leaves many needs unmet and that household financial preparedness needs wider options and policy support.
insights: Hurricane Michael caused an estimated $25 billion in damage, of which only $7.4 billion was insured; Florida bore $18.4 billion.
Respondents took 18 months on average to repair their homes; uninsured owners with severe damage took the longest, at 34 months.
66% of respondents drew on savings, about 20% took on credit card debt, 14% received an SBA disaster loan and only 10% used FEMA grants.
The average FEMA Individuals and Households Program award after Michael was $4,771 across more than 30,000 homeowners.
Almost 40% of respondents reported homeowners insurance price increases, and about three quarters said external funds were insufficient to cover their costs.
About 73% undertook some mitigation while rebuilding, most often a roof upgrade (53%).

records.title: The Hidden Value of Trees: Quantifying the Ecosystem Services of Tree Lineages and Their Major Threats Across the Contiguous US
records.authors: Jeannine M. Cavender-Bares; Erik Nelson; Jose Eduardo Meireles; Jesse R. Lasky; Daniela A. Miteva; David J. Nowak; William D. Pearse; Matthew R. Helmus; Amy E. Zanne; William F. Fagan; Christopher Mihiar; Nicholas Z. Muller; Nathan J. B. Kraft; Stephen Polasky
records.summary: An article in PLOS Sustainability and Transformation, published 5 April 2022, quantifying the ecosystem services of US tree lineages and the threats those services face, by fourteen authors across the University of Minnesota, Bowdoin, Maine, Penn State, Ohio State, the USDA Forest Service, Imperial College, Temple, the University of Miami, Maryland, the US Forest Service, Carnegie Mellon and UCLA. Combining macroevolutionary and economic valuation approaches with spatially explicit species and lineage data, the authors find that five key ecosystem services generated by US trees are worth $114 billion a year, with a low of $85 billion and a high of $137 billion in 2010 dollars. The non-market value from carbon storage and air pollution removal far exceeds the commercial value from wood products and food crops. Two lineages, pines and oaks, account for 42 per cent of that value. On threats, the majority of species face climate change pressure, many face increasing fire risk, and known pests and pathogens threaten 40 per cent of total woody biomass, with the most valuable species among the most threatened: the species most valuable for carbon storage are the ones most at risk from increasing fire threat.
insights: The correlation between value and threat is the finding that matters, and it is the opposite of a diversified portfolio: the species carrying the most carbon value are the ones most exposed to fire, so the asset and its risk are concentrated in the same lineages.

Non-market value exceeding commercial value by a wide margin is the structural reason this asset class is underfinanced. The revenue a landowner can capture is the small part, which is the gap a payment-for-ecosystem-services instrument exists to close.
Forty per cent of total woody biomass threatened by known pests and pathogens is a biological exposure rather than a climate hazard in the usual sense: slow, chronic, and driven by a living agent.

Two lineages at 42 per cent of value is a concentration figure an underwriter would recognise immediately, and it makes a national tree-service valuation behave like a portfolio with two dominant positions.
The $114 billion is a per annum flow covering only the five services with adequate data, so it is a floor on the benefit rather than a total.

records.title: National Flood Insurance Program: The Current Rating Structure and Risk Rating 2.0
records.summary: This Congressional Research Service report (R45999, updated April 2022) explains the National Flood Insurance Program's legacy rating structure and documents FEMA's Risk Rating 2.0 overhaul, the most significant premium methodology change since 1968. The NFIP covers more than 5 million policies across 22,500 communities, collecting ~$4.6 billion in annual premiums against $1.3 trillion in coverage. Risk Rating 2.0, effective October 2021 for new policies and April 2022 for renewals, shifts from zone-based group pricing to property-specific actuarial rates incorporating replacement cost value, distance to water, and multiple flood types, with statutory caps of 5–18% annual increases for primary residences.
insights: Risk Rating 2.0 projects premium increases for 77% of NFIP policyholders and immediate decreases for 23%, with FEMA estimating 50% of policies will reach full risk-based rates within 5 years and 90% within 10 years, signaling a decade-long repricing of U.S. residential flood risk.

The current national average NFIP premium is $818.70, but properties subject to 25% annual increases (non-primary residences, severe repetitive loss, etc.) carry an average premium of $5,878.15, a 7x gap that illustrates the cross-subsidy embedded in the program.

FEMA set a first-year premium cap of $12,125 for single-family primary residences under Risk Rating 2.0, down from a prior maximum of $45,925, a structural affordability floor with no parallel funding mechanism, creating a fiscal exposure FEMA lacks authority to remedy.

75% of primary residences would face increases greater than 18% annually if statutory caps did not exist, underscoring that actuarial risk far exceeds what statute currently permits to be charged, and that the program remains structurally under-reserved.

As of September 2018, approximately 13% of NFIP policies received a pre-FIRM subsidy, ~9% were grandfathered, and ~4% received a newly-mapped subsidy, together roughly 26% of the portfolio is cross-subsidized, representing a material pricing distortion for capital allocators assessing flood-exposed assets.

Risk Rating 2.0 expands flood risk sources modeled from two (fluvial and coastal) to include pluvial, tsunami, Great Lakes, coastal erosion, and leveed-area flooding, broadening the actuarial basis and potentially reclassifying millions of properties currently outside Special Flood Hazard Areas.

records.title: Incorporating Climate Risk in to Strategic Asset Allocation
records.summary: This April 2022 Moody's Analytics whitepaper outlines a five-step framework for climate-aware Strategic Asset Allocation (SAA) for insurance companies and institutional investors: target setting, asset universe definition, scenario analysis, portfolio optimization, and metric analysis. It describes how climate scenario analysis (using NGFS-aligned orderly, disorderly, and hot-house pathways), can be embedded into SAA and ALM processes, and introduces Moody's Climate Pathway Scenario Service and temperature alignment data covering ~4,400 publicly listed companies as tools to translate climate pathways into financial risk variables.
insights: Insurance companies face a dual challenge: aligning investment portfolios with net-zero commitments while managing climate physical and transition risks that affect GDP, inflation, interest rates, and equity risk premium simultaneously.

The UK Prudential Regulatory Authority found 'significant variation between firms in translating climate science into targets and scenarios, on modeling climate-related market risk and capital modeling,' signaling that methodological standardization is still nascent and creates differentiated risk for allocators.

UK pension schemes (large) were required as of 1 October 2021 to report on at least three climate metrics: an absolute emissions metric, an emissions intensity metric, and one additional metric such as portfolio alignment or Climate Value-at-Risk, establishing a regulatory precedent that is likely to spread to insurers.

Moody's temperature alignment data assesses forward-looking emissions trajectories for approximately 4,400 large publicly listed companies, providing a quantifiable metric for comparing portfolio warming potential against established climate pathway indices.

A combined top-down (macroeconomic) and bottom-up (sector/company) climate scenario approach is recommended over top-down alone, as purely top-down analysis can net out regional and sectoral impacts, particularly in diversified portfolios, a methodological nuance material to allocators pricing physical and transition risk.

Three NGFS-derived scenarios (Orderly, Disorderly, and Hot House), anchor the Bank of England's biennial climate stress testing exercise (launched June 2021), and the same scenarios are available through Moody's Climate Pathway Scenario Service for insurer use in SAA and ALM.

records.title: Resilience Leaders Highlight Climate Adaptation Pathways for Affordable Housing
records.authors: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety
institutions: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety
Federal Home Loan Bank of Dallas
records.summary: A news release from the Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety on its first Making Affordable Housing Climate Ready roundtable, held 31 March 2022, which brought public and private participants together on how to encourage, support, incentivise and finance resilient construction in affordable housing. IBHS president Roy Wright frames the problem as a financing one: the science to build homes that withstand severe weather exists, but individual homeowners often cannot act on it, so the financial avenues have to be found to bring resilience into every construction and re-roofing project. Pat Forbes of the Louisiana Office of Community Development describes the state's use of resilient standards including FORTIFIED in state-funded affordable housing, naming the Audubon Estates, The New Isle and Les Maisons de Bayou Lafourche resettlements, and argues that publicly funded rebuilding must incorporate standards like FORTIFIED. The panel included the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority multifamily division, Fannie Mae's multifamily green financing business, Enterprise Community Partners and Habitat for Humanity Mississippi Gulf Coast.
insights: The document is thin but its map is specific: it names the institutions that sit between a building standard and the capital that would pay for it, a state community development office, a state housing finance authority, a GSE multifamily green financing desk and a CDFI-adjacent nonprofit.

Louisiana's position is that disaster-prone geography and vulnerable population overlap, so the state applies resilient standards in publicly funded affordable housing rather than leaving the standard to the individual homeowner. That is a procurement answer to an insurance problem.
FORTIFIED appears here as a condition on public rebuilding money rather than as an insurance discount, which is a different transmission mechanism for the same standard.
records.publisher: Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety

records.title: Ready-to-Fund Resilience Toolkit
records.summary: A practitioner toolkit built by the American Society of Adaptation Professionals with Climate Resilience Consulting, funded by the Climate Resilience Fund, aimed squarely at small and mid-sized local government staff and the organisations that support them. Its subject is not what to build but how to make a resilience project fundable: the toolkit is organised around ten characteristics of ready-to-fund projects, and argues that projects which secure funding are those benefiting from collaborative partnerships, intentional processes, comprehensive accounting practices, and enabling regulatory and policy frameworks. Alongside a funding and finance primer it carries quick reference sections on policy incentives, risk management mechanisms, financing mechanisms, discounting alternatives, US federal resilience funding sources and the characteristics of potential partners. The framing is deliberately operational: it teaches local government leads to work within the finance and policy systems that exist, by pulling policy levers, seeking partnerships, using innovative accounting practices, inverting power structures and redesigning internal processes.
insights: The toolkit's premise is that fundability is a property of the project's preparation rather than of the hazard it addresses, which relocates the bottleneck from capital availability to project design.
Discounting alternatives get their own reference section, which is unusual and consequential: the discount rate is what decides whether a long-dated avoided-loss benefit can justify present spending.

The audience is explicitly small and mid-sized local governments, the jurisdictions least able to fund a dedicated resilience finance function, so the toolkit is a substitute for capacity rather than a supplement to it.

Comprehensive accounting practices are named as one of the four traits of a fundable project, which is the same point PRE Collective and others make: the benefit has to appear on somebody's balance sheet before it can be financed.

records.title: Paying for the Paris Agreement: A Primer on Government Options for Financing Nationally Determined Contributions
records.authors: Molly Caldwell, Natalia Alayza, Gaia Larsen
records.summary: The report explores financing options for Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) needed to meet global climate goals outlined in the Paris Agreement. It emphasizes the urgent need for governments to increase financial flows, utilize different financing instruments, and monitor their success in implementing climate commitments, especially in developing countries where the financial need is significant.
insights: Substantial financial shifts are necessary for implementing NDCs effectively.
Global mitigation investment must increase 36 times by 2030 to limit warming to 2 C.
Developing countries have an urgent financial need totaling $4.3 trillion for climate action.
Governments should create financing strategies that outline funding requirements and governance structures.
A mosaic of actions, rather than a single solution, is needed to meet climate targets.
The process of financing NDCs varies greatly between high- and low-income countries.
Establishing systems to track financial flows is crucial for monitoring progress towards climate goals.
There is a challenge in aligning public finance with climate commitments across different contexts.
Various financial instruments need to be mobilized to channel funds towards climate objectives.

records.title: This Changes Everything: Climate Shocks and Sovereign Bonds
institutions: Nova School of Business and Economics
records.summary: This Changes Everything: Climate Shocks and Sovereign Bonds, by Serhan Cevik of the IMF and Joao Tovar Jalles of Lisbon, in Energy Economics volume 107, article 105856, available online 3 February 2022 and copyright the International Monetary Fund. The paper's starting observation is that there is a large literature on the economic consequences of climate change and scarce research on the link between climate change and sovereign risk. It investigates the impact of climate change vulnerability and resilience on sovereign bond yields and spreads across 98 advanced and developing countries over 1995 to 2017, and finds that both have a significant effect on the cost of government borrowing after controlling for the conventional determinants of sovereign risk: countries more resilient to climate change have lower bond yields and spreads than countries with greater vulnerability. Partitioning the sample shows the magnitude and statistical significance of the effect are much greater in developing countries, which have weaker capacity to adapt to and mitigate the consequences of climate change.
insights: Resilience lowers the cost of sovereign borrowing, measured across 98 countries over 22 years. The benefit of resilience is not only avoided loss, it is a cheaper yield curve, which means a government can in principle finance adaptation out of the spread it saves.

The effect being larger in developing countries cuts against the usual pattern of climate finance. The places with least access to capital are the places where resilience does most for the cost of it, which is the strongest available argument that concessional support for adaptation pays for itself in market terms.
The authors are explicit that the gap they fill is the sovereign one: physical risk had been priced at asset and company level, and this is the same exercise at the level of the state.

records.title: Lightsmith Group Closes Inaugural $186M Growth Equity Fund — First Focused on Climate Resilience and Adaptation
records.authors: The Lightsmith Group (founding partners Jay Koh, Sanjay Wagle)
records.summary: Lightsmith Group announced the final close of Lightsmith Climate Resilience Partners at $186 million of commitments, the first private equity fund focused on climate resilience and adaptation, investing in growth-stage technology companies that address the physical effects of climate change. Investors include PNC Insurance Group, the Rockefeller Foundation, Kinneret Group, Caprock Impact Partners, the Green Climate Fund, the European Investment Bank, the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, KfW on behalf of the German development ministry, the Nordic Development Fund and the Government of Luxembourg. The Green Climate Fund committed $46 million to become the largest investor, with Pegasus Capital Advisors as its accredited entity. Climate Policy Initiative concluded the fund is the first private equity fund focused on climate resilience and reported that less than $500 million a year of private investment had targeted adaptation. The fund targets six technology areas: water efficiency and smart water management, resilient food systems, agricultural analytics, geospatial intelligence, supply chain analytics, and catastrophe risk modeling and risk transfer, against an estimated addressable market above $170 billion. Initial investments are SOURCE Global, an off-grid water harvesting company, and WayCool Foods, an Indian agriculture and food supply chain services company. The strategy derives from CRAFT, the Climate Resilience and Adaptation Finance and Technology-transfer facility, developed with the Global Innovation Lab for Climate Finance and others.
insights: The capital stack is the point: a $186 million commercial private equity fund anchored by $46 million from the Green Climate Fund plus four other development finance institutions and a sovereign, which is blended finance used to establish an asset class rather than to subsidise a project.
CPI's finding that under $500 million a year of private capital targeted adaptation makes this single $186 million fund a material share of the entire private adaptation market at the time of close.

Two of the six target areas, catastrophe risk modeling and risk transfer and geospatial intelligence, are the infrastructure other resilience instruments depend on, so the fund is partly investing in the measurement layer that would let adaptation be priced.
The GCF's stated rationale is technology transfer to developing countries, which is a different objective from the fund's commercial return thesis, and the fund has to satisfy both.

The fund was assembled through a public facility, CRAFT, developed with the Global Innovation Lab for Climate Finance, so the design cost was carried by concessional money before any commercial capital was raised.

records.title: Unlocking Clean Water State Revolving Funds to Finance Resilience Projects Across the Great Lakes Region
records.authors: Katy Hansen; Shaun Roberts; Sanjiv K. Sinha
records.summary: A report on redirecting Clean Water State Revolving Fund money toward resilience and green stormwater infrastructure across the Great Lakes states. It sets out the scale of the programme: established by Congress in 1987, CWSRFs have provided more than $145 billion to finance more than 42,800 projects nationwide, and in FY2021 Congress appropriated a further $11.7 billion under the $1.2 trillion infrastructure law, an amount the authors note is well short of need but significant in catalysing public and private investment. Their starting premise is that water infrastructure, grey or green, is expensive and mostly financed through the municipal bond market, with intergovernmental aid an important additional source of capital. The report reviews how CWSRF dollars have actually been spent across the Great Lakes states and proposes greener priorities intended to shift environmental, economic, public health and social outcomes. The hazard case is made concretely: per NOAA Atlas 14, the 100-year rainfall in the Detroit area rose by nearly 0.8 inches, from 4.4 to 5.2 inches, between 1992 and 2019.
insights: The lever is allocation rather than appropriation: the CWSRF already exists at $145 billion cumulative and $11.7 billion in a single year, so the report's proposition is to change what the existing revolving fund prioritises rather than to ask for new money.

Green stormwater infrastructure is positioned as the eligible use that delivers environmental, economic, public health and social outcomes together, which is the argument for preferring it inside a programme designed for water quality.

The municipal bond market is named as the primary financing route with the revolving fund as intergovernmental aid layered on it, so the two instruments are complements and the SRF's role is to lower the cost of the bond-financed project.

The rainfall change is given as a design-standard change, the 100-year Detroit event rising from 4.4 to 5.2 inches between 1992 and 2019, which is what makes existing systems undersized rather than merely old.

records.title: The Inflation Reduction Act’s Climate Investments and What They Mean for Community Development
institutions: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
records.summary: LISC's senior policy director reads the Inflation Reduction Act for what it offers community development and affordable housing. Of close to $370 billion in climate spending and tax incentives, about $60 billion targets disadvantaged communities and an estimated $25 billion can support affordable housing. He singles out HUD's nearly $1 billion for efficiency and climate resilience in assisted housing, rebate programs for retrofits and electrification, the $27 billion Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund, and a new Environmental and Climate Justice Block Grant. CDFIs, green banks and credit unions are expected to deploy much of the capital.
insights: The IRA provides close to $370 billion in new climate spending and tax incentives, including about $60 billion targeted to disadvantaged communities, of which an estimated $25 billion can support affordable housing.

HUD receives nearly $1 billion to improve energy efficiency, water efficiency and climate resilience in assisted properties, an expanded Green Retrofit Program that can fund resilience work as well as retrofits.

The EPA Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund provides $27 billion, $15 billion of it for underserved communities, expected to flow through green banks, CDFIs and credit unions as loans and technical assistance.
An Environmental and Climate Justice Block Grant funds community-based organizations for resiliency and adaptation, urban heat island risk, air monitoring and indoor air pollution.
Affordable rental projects serving lower-income households can receive rebates of up to 100 percent of retrofit or electrification cost.

records.title: Innovative Financing for Natural Infrastructure and Climate Adaptation in Mississippi River Basin
records.summary: A joint press release of 3 November 2022 from Environmental Defense Fund and Quantified Ventures announcing their report 'Generating revenue to finance natural infrastructure projects in the Mississippi River Basin'. The framing is that the basin supplies drinking water to 20 million people, supports 65 per cent of US harvested cropland and more than a million jobs, and is imperilled by two linked problems, poor water quality and lengthening periods of drought and flood, both worsened by climate change. Restoring wetlands and floodplains and deploying other natural infrastructure can protect drinking water and reduce flood risk, but such projects have historically been hard to finance through public loan programmes such as the Clean Water State Revolving Fund because they lack a dependable revenue source. The report gives states, cities, towns and watershed groups five replicable ways to generate revenue and so make natural infrastructure financeable.
insights: The stated blocker is the absence of a revenue stream, not the absence of capital. The Clean Water State Revolving Fund is a loan programme and a loan needs something to repay it; grey infrastructure has a rate base and a restored floodplain does not.

It is the press release, not the report. The five revenue mechanisms are named in the report rather than enumerated here, so this document carries the framing and the citation rather than the mechanisms themselves.

The scale framing, 20 million people's drinking water and 65 per cent of harvested cropland, is the argument for treating the Mississippi basin as infrastructure of national consequence, which is how a federal funding case would have to be made.

records.title: The SEC’s Climate Disclosure Rule: Critiquing the Critics
records.summary: An article by George S. Georgiev of Emory University School of Law, published at 50 Rutgers Law Record 101 in 2022, analysing the principal legal challenges to the SEC's March 2022 proposed climate disclosure rule and finding them unpersuasive. The framing is that climate change entails a wide variety of physical risks as well as sizeable but underappreciated economic risks, and that the proposed rule addresses information gaps about how those risks affect firms. The article records that the proposal met opposition unusual in its intensity and consistency, with critics disputing the SEC's statutory authority and motivations, questioning the materiality of information about the economic impacts of climate change, and advancing administrative and constitutional law theories drawn from unrelated contexts. Reviewing the features of the traditional disclosure regime and of the rule itself, the author concludes that the SEC has the statutory authority to act, that its motivations are neither improper nor novel, that materiality properly understood presents no obstacle, and that the major questions and compelled speech theories are misplaced here. The author notes he co-authored a June 2022 comment letter to the SEC with Jill Fisch, Donna Nagy and Cynthia Williams on behalf of 30 corporate and securities law scholars.
insights: The rule's core function as the author states it is to put in place an information-generating framework for capital markets, which is the upstream condition for pricing physical risk at all.

Materiality is the pivot. If information about the economic impacts of climate change is not material, the whole physical-risk disclosure project has no statutory hook, and the article's argument that materiality properly understood presents no obstacle is the legal load-bearing claim.

The article rebuts three constitutional challenges to the rule, two of them the major questions doctrine and a compelled-speech theory, so the obstacle it treats as binding is constitutional rather than technical or economic.

The author's disclosed role as a comment-letter co-author is provenance worth recording: this is advocacy scholarship by a participant in the rulemaking, which does not weaken the analysis but does place it.

records.title: USDA Departmental Offices Climate Adaptation Plan 2022
records.summary: The 2022 climate adaptation plan of four United States Department of Agriculture departmental offices, produced under Executive Order 14008 and USDA Departmental Regulation 1070-001, which directs the Office of the Chief Economist to require Mission Areas, agencies and staff offices to complete their own adaptation plans. The four offices covered are the Office of the Chief Economist, the Office of Budget and Program Analysis, the Office of Homeland Security, and the Office of Property and Environmental Management. Each assesses how climate change affects its own mission delivery and sets adaptation actions integrating those risks into planning, programmes, operations and management, alongside staff professional development needs, engagement with the USDA Climate Hubs, and alignment with departmental environmental justice initiatives.
insights: Adaptation planning here is cascaded by regulation rather than by initiative: Departmental Regulation 1070-001 directs the Office of the Chief Economist to issue guidance requiring each contributing organisation to produce its own plan, which is the mechanism that turns one department-wide plan into many office-level ones.

The unit of analysis is mission delivery rather than estate or emissions, so each office asks how climate change affects the function it performs for the department rather than how to reduce its own footprint.

The Climate Change Program Office is responsible for ensuring agencies monitor and evaluate progress against their own plans and for reporting to the White House Council on Environmental Quality, which supplies the accountability loop the individual plans lack.

This is the departmental offices' plan and not the USDA-wide Action Plan for Climate Adaptation and Resilience released in October 2021, which it implements; a reader wanting the department-wide commitments needs that separate document.

records.title: Increasing Investment in Affordable Housing, Climate Resilience, and Small Business in Underserved Communities
records.summary: The Robert Wood Johnson Foundation provided a guarantee of up to $10 million to the Community Investment Guarantee Pool, a vehicle created by the Kresge Foundation that pools more than $42 million of unfunded guarantee commitments from 14 investors, 12 philanthropies, the health system Common Spirit and LOCUS's parent company Virginia Community Capital, with the intention of growing past $50 million. By aggregating unfunded guarantee commitments, CIGP uses the strength of philanthropic balance sheets, a relatively untapped resource, to unlock capital for affordable housing, small business and climate resilience in low-income communities and communities of color. The stated aims are to accelerate investment, give guarantee users more efficient access, demonstrate that a pooled model lets foundations better manage financial risk and gives intermediaries a one-stop shop for credit enhancement, and put foundation balance sheets to work. In its first full year of operation in 2020 CIGP deployed $1.5 million to Genesis LA for publicly supported supportive housing and naturally occurring affordable housing in Los Angeles County, $2 million to the Low Income Investment Fund backing a $20 million fund for affordable housing developers affected by COVID-19, and $3.6 million to the Local Initiatives Support Corporation for its $36 million Diverse Developer Loan Fund lending to minority-owned or led developers with limited balance sheets. Cumulative investments total $15.1 million in affordable housing and $1.5 million in small business. Other guarantors include the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, the Annie E. Casey Foundation and CommonSpirit Health, with grant support from the Rockefeller, Hewlett and Wells Fargo foundations. CIGP is an LLC operated by the nonprofit consultancy LOCUS and a subsidiary of Virginia Community Capital, which has issued close to 800 loans totaling close to $1 billion.
insights: The instrument is an unfunded guarantee, which is the point: a foundation pledges its balance sheet rather than moving cash, so a philanthropic commitment does credit enhancement work without leaving the endowment.

The leverage is visible in the deployments: $3.6 million of guarantee supports a $36 million loan fund and $2 million supports a $20 million fund, so the pool is operating at roughly ten to one on the guaranteed tranches.

Pooling is what makes it usable: an intermediary gets a one-stop shop for credit enhancement instead of negotiating with twelve foundations separately, and the transaction cost saved is the reason the vehicle exists rather than the subsidy.

Climate resilience is one of three mandates alongside affordable housing and small business, and the reported cumulative totals, $15.1 million in housing and $1.5 million in small business, name no climate deployment, so the resilience leg is authorised rather than exercised.

The vehicle is structured around the social determinants of health rather than around climate, which is how a health funder reaches resilience investment, and is a route into adaptation capital that does not run through climate finance at all.

records.title: Equitable Green Infrastructure in Buffalo, NY
records.summary: The Equitable Green Infrastructure initiative in Buffalo, NY, involves a $54 million Environmental Impact Bond aimed at enhancing green stormwater infrastructure to manage over 200 acres of impervious surfaces. By partnering with the Buffalo Sewer Authority, the project seeks to improve water quality, create jobs, and address environmental justice, while significantly increasing the pace of infrastructure installation to mitigate flooding risks and enhance community vitality.
insights: The $54 million Environmental Impact Bond is the largest of its kind to date.
Green stormwater infrastructure (GSI) includes features like rain gardens and permeable pavement.
The project aims to increase the installation of green infrastructure from 9.5 acres to over 28 acres per year.
Buffalo's combined sewer system is vulnerable to combined sewer overflow events, especially during heavy rainfall.
The initiative is designed to create approximately 700 sustainable jobs in the community.
The focus areas for GSI projects are chosen based on both environmental needs and social equity considerations.
The Buffalo Sewer Authority is the first in the U.S. to link investment incentives to performance outcomes in such a bond.
The project also includes an option for early bond refinancing based on successful outcomes.
This initiative promotes the greening of the city while reducing stormwater fees for residents.
The EIB was recognized as the U.S. municipal green bond of the year.

records.title: Blue Forest Asset Management (BFAM)
records.summary: Blue Forest Asset Management (BFAM) focuses on accelerating forest restoration through sustainable, community-based economic initiatives. The organization connects investors to diverse mission-aligned opportunities, while engaging in investments across the entire forestry value chain to enhance capacity for restoration and wildfire risk reduction, fostering workforce development in rural areas.
insights: BFAM prioritizes sustainable forest restoration and community-based economic development.
The organization connects investors with mission-aligned investment opportunities beyond traditional projects.
Investments are made across the entire forestry value chain, from harvesting to utilization.
BFAM aims to build system capacity for achieving forest restoration and wildfire risk reduction goals.
The initiative promotes regenerative natural resource stewardship.
Workforce development and sustainable employment for rural communities are key components of BFAM's strategy.
BFAM highlights the importance of both scaling restoration work and developing a supportive economic framework.
The California Wildfire Innovation Fund (CWIF) is one of BFAM's related investment strategies.

records.title: Finance for Developing Country Climate Action
records.summary: The 'Finance for Developing Country Climate Action' project aims to promote financial support for climate initiatives in developing countries by addressing key capacity bottlenecks and facilitating access to multilateral climate funds. It works closely with national institutions to enhance coordination, decision-making, and alignment of climate-compatible projects with finance flows, which is essential for meeting Paris Agreement goals.
insights: Developing countries often lack sufficient finance for climate action.
Identifying capacity bottlenecks at the national level is crucial for mobilizing finance.
Accessing multilateral climate funds is a key focus of the project.
Effective institutional coordination and decision-making is vital for climate finance.
The project aims to match climate-compatible projects with available finance flows.
Support is provided to finance and environment ministries in developing countries.
International finance mobilization is essential for enabling low-carbon pathways.
Knowledge products and tools are developed to help overcome financial constraints.
Collaboration with specialized climate funds enhances project implementation.
Past initiatives include analyzing funding strategies and the impacts of global events on climate finances.

records.title: Quantifying Insurance Benefits of a Nature-Based Approach to Reducing Risk: Wildfire Risk Reduction Buffers
records.summary: Using Paradise, California (devastated by the 2018 Camp Fire) as a case study, this Guy Carpenter report quantifies the insurance and property-loss benefits of nature-based wildfire risk reduction buffers. The authors apply a U.S. wildfire catastrophe model to assess how wildland buffer strategies, including ignition reduction and ember spotting mitigation, can lower expected insurance premiums and reduce property loss, with the goal of restoring insurability in communities currently deemed uninsurable. The framework is presented as replicable across other fire-dependent forest ecosystems in California and the broader western U.S.
insights: The quantified result is a return-period shift rather than a percentage saving: fire buffer strategies combined with updated code enforcement would have cut value-at-risk across most probabilities by 42 percent, converting a one-in-100-year loss level into a one-in-350-year level.

A fire buffer along a single corridor in Paradise is found to be as effective at reducing fire risk as enforcing updated fire-resilient building codes, which puts a land-use intervention on a par with a building-standard intervention in the same catastrophe model.

The explicit purpose is to enable the risk transfer chain: the framework is offered as a way to make fire insurance accessible and affordable in areas currently viewed as uninsurable, so the benefit is expressed as avoided loss and lower expected premium.

Community-Based Catastrophe Insurance is named as the instrument that captures the benefit, with coverage arranged by the community for homes in its jurisdiction, so that community-scale mitigation can be reflected in pricing for insureds. Linking insurance to mitigation is what creates the incentive to invest.

The land-use corollary is that buffers doubling as urban growth boundaries could replace WUI sprawl with clustered development, which would in turn allow controlled burning to expand in fire-dependent ecosystems, restoring habitat while further reducing catastrophic fire risk.

The scale of the underlying loss is stated: the Camp Fire caused 86 deaths, destroyed 95 percent of the town's structures including 11,000 homes, and produced USD 12.5 billion insured and USD 16.5 billion total property loss, with only 500 homes rebuilt by the end of 2020.

records.title: A System for Resilience Learning: Developing a Community-Driven, Multi-Sector Research Approach for Greater Preparedness and Resilience to Long-Term Climate Stressors and Extreme Events in the Miami Metropolitan Region
records.authors: Tiffany G. Troxler, Amy C. Clement, Katharine J. Mach, Jayantha Obeysekera, Shimon Wdowinski, and 25 others
institutions: University of Miami Climate Resilience Institute
records.summary: A thirty-author collaboration spanning Florida International University, the University of Miami, Miami-Dade County, the cities of Miami and Miami Beach, and Miami civic organisations describes the design of a Resilience Learning System to support research on and implementation of the Resilient305 Strategy for Greater Miami and the Beaches. The strategy, developed over three years with support from the Rockefeller Foundation's 100 Resilient Cities programme, sets out 59 actions across resilient places, resilient people and resilient pathways. The system rests on three foundations: strong partnerships among community members, government and non-government leaders and researchers from multiple academic institutions; subject matter expertise and local knowledge to identify information and translational gaps, formulate metrics and evaluate outcomes from the community perspective; and a comprehensive understanding of civic engagement activities, technological tools and resilience-building capacities including policy and financial innovations. The paper reports initial co-produced metrics, mapping the strategy's forty intended outcomes to Core Area metrics and then reviewing them a second time to map metrics for unintended co-benefit outcomes, so triple dividends and unintended consequences can both be evaluated. On the funding context, nearly $1 billion in general obligation bond funding was approved in fiscal year 2018-19 by voters in Miami and Miami Beach, two of Miami-Dade County's thirty-four municipalities; in fiscal year 2020-21 the county's operating budget included nearly $705 million targeted at resilience and $3.285 billion of the $3.335 billion capital plan was dedicated to community resiliency. The Global Commission on Adaptation projects a 4:1 return from resilience investments over the next decade through triple dividends.
insights: The system's purpose is measurement rather than money: it exists to establish whether $3.285 billion of dedicated capital spending is producing the resilience outcomes it was authorised for.

Mapping metrics twice, once for intended outcomes and once for unintended co-benefits, is the methodological move that makes triple dividends measurable rather than asserted, and it is what would let a co-benefit be pledged to an instrument.

The Miami Forever Bond and its Miami Beach counterpart, nearly $1 billion of general obligation borrowing approved by voters in two of thirty-four municipalities, is the concrete demonstration that a municipal balance sheet can carry adaptation when the electorate authorises it.

The paper insists that resilience trade-offs are as important as dividends and are anticipatable with better knowledge, which is the counterweight to a literature that reports only the upside of adaptation.

The author list itself is the finding about capacity: thirty authors across two universities, a county, two cities and six civic organisations were required to co-produce one metric set, which is the true cost of the community-driven approach.
Three co-authors write from the University of Miami and one from the Miami-Dade Office of Resilience, so the design is a joint academic and municipal product rather than an external evaluation.

records.title: Accelerating Climate-Resilient Infrastructure Investment in China
records.authors: Helen Ding; Tian Yu; Wenyi Xi; Lu Lu; Wee Kean Fong; Ying Cao; Shuya Kuang; Ying Cui; Jieyu Zhou; Huixin Liu; Yinlong Xu; Kuo Li
institutions: National Center for Climate Change Strategy and International Cooperation
Central University of Finance and Economics
Institute of Environment and Sustainable Development in Agriculture
China Banking and Insurance Regulatory Commission
Royal Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs
records.summary: This WRI executive summary models climate risks to infrastructure in three Chinese locations and applies a Triple Dividend cost-benefit framework (avoided losses, economic benefits, social and environmental benefits) to three types of climate-resilient infrastructure: water-saving irrigation in Ningxia, sponge city construction in Wuhan and green-grey sea dikes in Shenzhen. It finds that every RMB 1 invested returns RMB 2 to 20 over 30 years, with benefit-cost ratios from 2.1 to 20.3. It estimates an annual funding gap of nearly RMB 500 billion over the next five years and finds that financing remains dominated by public money. Drawing on the Saiss project in Morocco, New York City's Green Infrastructure Grant Program and the Louisiana Environmental Impact Bond, it recommends Resilience Bonds, PPPs, trust funds and Resilience Impact Bonds tailored to each case.
insights: Every RMB 1 invested in climate-resilient infrastructure across the three cases generates RMB 2 to 20 of returns over 30 years; benefit-cost ratios range from 2.1 to 20.3.
China faces an annual climate-resilient infrastructure funding gap of nearly RMB 500 billion (RMB 480 billion, citing Chai et al. 2019) over the next five years.
The July 2021 '7.20' Henan rainstorm caused 302 deaths and destroyed RMB 114.269 billion of economic value.

For Ningxia irrigation, the report recommends Resilience Bonds issued with development and commercial banks plus a blended investment fund with repeated bond issuances to cover operation and maintenance.
Wuhan sponge city benefits come mainly from added real estate value and stormwater recycling, so the report proposes a blended public-private trust fund and developer subsidies.
The Shenzhen Dapeng sea dikes (RMB 8.21 billion cost) are fully funded by the municipal government and Water Affairs Bureau; the report suggests Resilient Impact Bonds to bring in private capital.

records.title: Connecticut Public Law 21–115: An Act Concerning Climate Change Adaptation
records.summary: Connecticut Public Law 21-115, signed by Governor Ned Lamont on 6 July 2021, expands local resilience planning options, legal authorities and financing for adaptation projects through three components. It authorises municipal stormwater authorities, which develop stormwater management programmes, run public outreach, and may recommend property taxes to their municipal legislative bodies as a revenue source for green infrastructure and resiliency investment. It expands the purview of municipal flood and erosion control boards to include flood prevention and climate resilience, renaming them flood prevention, climate resilience and erosion control boards. And it expands the Connecticut Green Bank, established in 2011 for clean energy, by creating an Environmental Infrastructure Fund covering water, waste and recycling, climate adaptation and resilience, agriculture, land conservation, parks and recreation, and environmental markets, and usable to leverage state and federal infrastructure funding. The entry notes this last provision is significant because it lets a state infrastructure bank invest in climate adaptation rather than only clean energy and hard infrastructure. Across all provisions the law directs prioritised financing to frontline communities and areas of historical underinvestment.
insights: The green bank expansion is the transferable piece: creating an Environmental Infrastructure Fund lets a state green bank capitalised for clean energy invest in adaptation, which is the same move Montgomery County made and a route available to any jurisdiction with an existing green bank.
Municipal stormwater authorities are given the power to recommend property taxes as a dedicated revenue source, so the law creates both the institution and its funding mechanism.
Renaming flood and erosion control boards to include climate resilience is not cosmetic: it extends existing legal authorities to a new purpose without creating a new body.
Prioritising frontline communities and areas of historical underinvestment is written into the financing provisions rather than added as guidance, which makes distribution a term of the instrument.

records.title: Catastrophe Bonds (A Primer)
records.summary: A July 2021 primer in the Wharton Risk Management and Decision Processes Center's primer series, by Alexander Braun and Carolyn Kousky, on catastrophe bonds. It places the instrument inside the wider category of insurance-linked securities, the route by which risk is placed directly in the capital markets rather than transferred to an insurer or reinsurer, and dates the ILS market's emergence to the aftermath of Hurricane Andrew in 1992, which was the costliest US natural disaster until Katrina in 2005 and left an insufficient supply of reinsurance for coastal catastrophe risk. Catastrophe bonds are the best-known type of ILS and the second-largest by volume, the first were issued in the mid-1990s and the market has grown steadily since. The primer explains the general mechanics, gives examples of use and outlines future opportunities. A footnote records that since 2012 the largest ILS instrument by volume has been collateralized reinsurance rather than catastrophe bonds, citing Aon Securities' 2020 ILS annual report.
insights: A footnote carries the most consequential fact in the primer: collateralized reinsurance has been the largest instrument in the insurance-linked securities market by volume since 2012, so the catastrophe bond is the famous instrument rather than the dominant one.

The primer treats catastrophe bonds as one member of the insurance-linked securities family rather than as a standalone instrument, which is the level at which a new risk-linked security would enter and inherit conventions.
Carolyn Kousky is the author, and the document is a primer rather than a deal description, so it states the conventions that deal documentation assumes.

It pairs with the Chicago Fed letter in the same batch: two primers on one instrument, three years apart, one from a central bank and one from a business school, with no textual overlap. The pair is a usefully independent check on the shared account of the market's history.

records.title: Understanding the Improbable: A Survey of Fat Tails in Environmental Economics
records.authors: Marc N. Conte; David L. Kelly
records.summary: A survey in the Annual Review of Resource Economics, volume 13 pages 289 to 310, first published as a Review in Advance on 25 June 2021, by Marc N. Conte of Fordham and David L. Kelly of the University of Miami. It reviews the growing literature on fat-tailed distributions in environmental economics, examines their theoretical and statistical properties, and asks when those properties are likely to arise in environmental problems. The authors find that a number of variables in the field are fat tailed, including climate sensitivity, natural disaster impacts, the spread of infectious diseases, and stated willingness to pay, and argue that different fat-tailed distributions arise from common pathways. They review the policy implications and the controversies over interpretation, concluding that the literature has established when fat tails matter for optimal environmental policy but that much remains unclear: how alternative policies affect fat-tailed distributions, what the optimal policy is in a computational economy containing many fat-tailed problems, and how to account for imprecision in empirical tests for fat tails. The opening example is Hurricane Harvey, where 39.23 inches of rain fell on Beaumont, Texas in 48 hours against a late-August daily average of about 0.2 inches, causing $125 billion in damages.
insights: The survey's honest residual is its most useful statement: it is not known how alternative policies affect a fat-tailed distribution. That is precisely what an instrument is for, since an instrument exists to change the distribution rather than to describe it.

Stated willingness to pay being fat tailed is a warning about the benefit layer specifically. If the valuations feeding a benefit estimate are drawn from a fat-tailed distribution, sample means are unstable and a benefit-cost ratio computed from them is less informative than it looks.

Grouping climate sensitivity, disaster impacts, disease spread and willingness to pay as arising from common pathways is the survey's organising move, and it is what makes the treatment general rather than specific to hazard modelling.
It is the general treatment by the same authors whose 2016 work established the hurricane-specific result, so the survey states the theory the applied paper instantiates.

records.title: Buffalo Sewer Authority Issues Largest-Ever U.S. Environmental Impact Bond
