records.summary: A Quantified Ventures press release of 22 June 2021 announcing that the Buffalo Sewer Authority closed a $54 million Environmental Impact Bond, the largest in the United States at the time, to finance green infrastructure and stormwater mitigation under its Rain Check 2.0 initiative. The proceeds fund green infrastructure that captures stormwater, reduces combined sewer overflows and delivers community benefits including jobs. The transaction was assembled after The Ralph C. Wilson, Jr. Foundation and the Community Foundation for Greater Buffalo funded Environmental Consulting & Technology to bring newer delivery models, including alternative financing, to the Greater Buffalo region. Morgan Stanley and Quantified Ventures provided the underwriting and the outcomes-based financing structure. The release names the stated objectives as water quality, job creation and environmental justice, and points to the bond's issue details on MSRB EMMA and to the Rain Check 2.0 opportunity report.
insights: An environmental impact bond ties repayment terms to measured environmental performance, so the resilience benefit is connected to a financial term by contract rather than by argument.

The route in is worth recording: a philanthropic pair funded the technical assistance that made the deal structurable at all. The binding constraint was capacity, not capital, and two foundations paid for the capacity.

At $54 million and billed as the largest US EIB at the time, this is a scale data point for a class usually described in pilot terms, and it sits in a municipal sewer authority rather than a special-purpose vehicle.
Stormwater and combined sewer overflow is a regulatory-compliance driver as much as a resilience one, which is part of why this deal had a sewer rate base to pledge against the bond.

records.title: The Economics of Climate Change
records.summary: Swiss Re Institute's landing page for The Economics of Climate Change. The headline finding is that by mid-century the world stands to lose around 10 per cent of total economic value from climate change if temperature increases stay on the current trajectory and neither the Paris Agreement nor 2050 net-zero targets are met. The Climate Economics Index stress-tests how climate risks will affect 48 countries representing 90 per cent of the world economy and ranks their overall climate resilience across four dimensions: total index, adaptive capacity, GDP impact and extreme weather risk. All countries are affected but some are more vulnerable: economies in south and southeast Asia are most exposed to physical risks and have the most to gain from limiting temperature increases, while many advanced northern hemisphere economies are both less exposed and better resourced to cope. Transition risks may also fall hardest on Asia, showing up as large shifts in asset values and higher costs of doing business as the world moves to a low-carbon economy. Group Chief Economist Jérôme Haegeli frames climate risk as systemic and addressable only globally. The page positions reinsurers as providers of risk transfer capacity, risk knowledge and long-term investment, using their understanding of risk to help households, companies and societies mitigate and adapt.
insights: Ranking 48 countries on adaptive capacity as a separate axis from GDP impact is the analytically useful move: it separates how hard a country is hit from what it can do about it, which is the distinction an adaptation finance allocation needs.

A 10 per cent loss of global economic value by mid-century is the headline figure, and it is a gross loss estimate rather than a net-of-adaptation one, which is why it is larger than most sectoral numbers.
Placing the greatest physical exposure and the greatest transition exposure on the same region, south and southeast Asia, is a compounding finding rather than two separate ones.

The reinsurer describes its own role in three parts, risk transfer capacity, risk knowledge and long-term investment, which is the sector arguing it is an information provider and an investor as well as a bearer of risk.
This is the landing page rather than the report: the substantive text runs to about 1,500 characters and the sigma publication behind it is a separate document.

records.title: Striving for Improvement: The Perceived Value of Improving Hurricane Forecast Accuracy
records.authors: Renato Molina, David Letson, Brian McNoldy, Pallab Mozumder, Matthew Varkony
institutions: University of Miami Climate Resilience Institute
records.summary: Molina and colleagues, four of them at the University of Miami, estimate the public's willingness to pay for further improvement in hurricane forecast accuracy, combining atmospheric modeling with a double-bounded dichotomous choice contingent valuation experiment. The survey covers 4,650 respondents in the FEMA-defined regions affected by Hurricanes Florence and Michael in 2018, 3,150 and 1,500 respectively, with a mean respondent aged 43, earning $65,176 and living 87 km from the coast. The Hurricane Forecast Improvement Project, established in 2008, had cut track and wind speed forecast error by more than 40 per cent each over the following decade, and respondents are asked to value maintaining that rate for another ten years. Average willingness to pay is $26.07 per household per year for storm track, $28.89 for wind speed and $21.63 for precipitation, so wind speed is valued most across both samples. Extrapolated to the Florence and Michael regions, annual totals are $60 million, $67 million and $50 million respectively. Extended to the most exposed US areas, those with historical hurricane wind speeds above 50 mph, the totals are $376 million, $428 million and $327 million; extending to less exposed areas raises them to $1.4 billion, $1.6 billion and $1.3 billion, with per capita values between $9.85 and $13.30 a year. Projected over ten years and discounted at 2 per cent, the present value of continued improvement is between $90.25 and $121.86 per person. For comparison, total federal meteorological funding in 2018 was $5.3 billion, 0.081 per cent of federal obligations, so a median income household's share of meteorological services and research was about $3.49, only a fraction of which goes to hurricane forecasting. The authors attribute the primacy of wind speed to the Saffir-Simpson scale being single-dimensional, familiar from media coverage and quick to assess.
insights: The tax comparison is the argument: a household's share of all federal meteorological spending is about $3.49 a year while its stated willingness to pay for continued hurricane forecast improvement alone is $21 to $29 per attribute, so the perceived value exceeds the entire programme cost by an order of magnitude.
This is adaptation spending on information rather than on assets, and the benefit of the information product is quantified in dollars, which is what lets a public budget be sized against it.

Wind speed is valued most because the Saffir-Simpson scale is one-dimensional and familiar, which the authors call an availability effect, so the public pays most for the forecast attribute it can act on rather than the one that causes most harm.

The attributes are physically coupled, so research improving one improves the others, which means the sum of the three willingness-to-pay figures is an upper bound and the true joint value sits between the largest single estimate and that sum.

The estimates are six to eight times the earlier Lazo and Waldman figure of $15 per household per year, which the authors attribute to method and timing, and that gap is itself the reason a public funding decision based on contingent valuation remains contestable.
records.publisher: Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society

records.title: Climate Change and Financial Stability
records.authors: Celso Brunetti, Benjamin Dennis, Dylan Gates, Diana Hancock, David Ignell, Elizabeth K. Kiser, Gurubala Kotta, Anna Kovner, Richard J. Rosen, Nicholas K. Tabor
records.summary: A Federal Reserve staff note describing how risks arising from climate change may affect financial stability, and connecting that to the Federal Reserve's existing financial stability monitoring framework. It reaches three conclusions: the monitoring framework is flexible enough to broadly incorporate many key elements of climate-related risks; climate change increases financial stability risks but substantial improvements in data and models are needed to incorporate them fully; and domestic and international transparency efforts around climate-related financial exposures may help clarify the nature and scope of those risks.
insights: The central analytical move is to insist that climate-related economic or financial losses are not by themselves a financial stability problem: the economy can lose output and investors can lose money without the financial system amplifying it. Stability is at issue only when losses reach levered intermediaries, disrupt market functioning, or trigger sudden repricing of large asset classes.

Climate risk is mapped into the existing framework in two distinct ways, as SHOCKS and as VULNERABILITIES, which is what lets the Fed use machinery it already has rather than building a parallel regime.

Acute hazards such as storms, floods and wildfires are treated as information events as much as damage events: they can quickly change or reveal new information about future economic conditions or asset values, which is the channel by which a physical event becomes a repricing.

The note is explicit that the work is early: analysis and research on climate-related financial risk is at an early stage and substantial improvements in data and models are needed, which is a central bank declining to claim more than it has.
Transparency and disclosure are offered as the third lever alongside monitoring and research, on the argument that clarity about exposures is what makes the scope of the risk knowable at all.

records.title: Enabling Private Investment in Climate Adaptation and Resilience: Current Status, Barriers to Investment and Blueprint for Action
records.authors: Arame Tall, Sarah Lynagh, Candela Blanco Vecchi, Pepukaye Bardouille, Felipe Montoya Pino, Elham Shabahat, Vladimir Stenek, Fiona Stewart, Samantha Power, Cindy Paladines, Philippe Neves, Lori Kerr
institutions: Global Facility for Disaster Reduction and Recovery (GFDRR)
records.summary: The report 'Enabling Private Investment in Climate Adaptation and Resilience' emphasizes the critical need to mobilize private sector investment to bridge the significant adaptation finance gap, particularly in developing countries. While public funding has increased, it remains inadequate to meet urgent climate adaptation needs. The document identifies barriers to private investment and presents a structured Blueprint for Action with five key entry points to facilitate private engagement, supported by case studies demonstrating successful strategies in nations like Bangladesh.
insights: Private sector investment in climate adaptation is currently minimal, accounting for only 1.6% of total adaptation finance.
Barriers to private investment include lack of localized climate risk data, unclear investment gaps, and insufficient financial incentives.

The Blueprint for Action outlines five critical entry points to mobilize private capital: long-term adaptation planning, national investment plans, market assessment, project preparation, and transaction coordination.
Adaptation strategies can yield significant economic returns, with benefits estimated at $4 for every $1 invested.
Governments play a crucial role in creating an enabling environment through clear policies, legal frameworks, and innovative financial instruments.

records.title: Resilience Rating System: A Methodology for Building and Tracking Resilience to Climate Change
records.authors: Stephane Hallegatte; Viviane Clement; Sundus Siddiqi; Michelle Winglee
records.summary: The Resilience Rating System (RRS), developed by the World Bank Group, offers a structured methodology to assess and enhance climate resilience in projects across various sectors and countries. By evaluating both the resilience of projects and their capacity to foster resilience in outcomes, the RRS aims to improve disaster risk management and facilitate better decision-making regarding investments in climate-resilient initiatives. The methodology incorporates rigorous risk assessments, sensitivity analyses, and stakeholder engagement, guiding project developers to implement effective adaptation measures throughout the project lifecycle while promoting transparency and best practices.
insights: The RRS evaluates projects based on their design and outcomes related to climate resilience, with ratings ranging from C to A+.
A primary goal of the RRS is to inform decision-makers and create incentives for better climate adaptation investments.
The methodology emphasizes integrating risk assessments and adaptation options into all phases of project development.
It incorporates stakeholder engagement and contingent planning to address uncertainties and enhance project resilience.
Higher project ratings indicate greater confidence in achieving expected outcomes despite climate risks.
The RRS adapts to various contexts and is applicable to both public and private sector projects.
Regular monitoring and updates are essential for adaptive management as new climate data becomes available.
Best practices identified by the RRS can be scaled across sectors and countries to improve resiliency efforts.

records.title: Climate Finance Policy in Practice: A Review of the Evidence
records.authors: Rishikesh Ram Bhandary, Kelly Sims Gallagher, Fang Zhang
records.summary: This resource evaluates the effectiveness of various climate finance policies through empirical performance analysis, highlighting strengths and weaknesses while identifying critical knowledge gaps. It assesses nine policy types based on criteria such as mobilization effectiveness, economic efficiency, environmental integrity, and equity, emphasizing the importance of policy design features and the role of innovative financial instruments in enhancing climate action.
insights: Different climate finance policies have varying strengths and weaknesses that affect their effectiveness.
Feed-in tariffs and tax credits effectively mobilize private finance, while the impact of national climate funds remains unclear.
Significant data and research gaps exist regarding the empirical effectiveness of many climate finance policies.
Balancing mobilization effectiveness with economic efficiency, environmental integrity, and equity is crucial for policy selection.
Investment barriers for renewable energy are significant and require targeted policy interventions.
Green bonds are emerging as a viable financing tool for low-carbon projects.
State investment banks play a crucial role in mobilizing private finance for climate innovation.

records.title: Investing in Blue Natural Capital to Secure a Future for the Red Sea Ecosystems
records.authors: Maha J. Cziesielski; Carlos M. Duarte; Manuel Aranda; Andrew C. Baker; and others
institutions: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology
records.summary: A policy and practice review in Frontiers in Marine Science, published 15 January 2021, on investing in blue natural capital to secure a future for Red Sea ecosystems. Led from KAUST by Maha J. Cziesielski with Carlos M. Duarte and Manuel Aranda and a large multi-institution author list that includes Andrew C. Baker of the University of Miami, it makes the case for treating Red Sea marine ecosystems, coral reefs, mangroves and seagrass among them, as natural capital worth investing in rather than as a conservation cost, at a moment of rapid coastal development on the Saudi Arabian coast.
insights: The Red Sea is an unusually clean test case for blue natural capital: its reefs are among the most heat-tolerant in the world, so the investment case rests on development pressure rather than on thermal risk.

The author list spans some twenty institutions across the Red Sea states, Europe, North America and Australia, which makes the paper a consensus policy and practice review rather than a single group's position.

records.title: Inter-American Development Bank Group Climate Change Action Plan 2021-2025
records.authors: Amy Lewis, Claudio Alatorre, Adrien Vogt-Schilb
records.summary: The IDB Group's climate change action plan for 2021 to 2025, covering the IDB, IDB Invest and IDB Lab. It reviews progress and lessons from the previous 2016 to 2020 plan, then sets out actions organised against the MDB building blocks with sector-specific considerations, a monitoring framework, and a treatment of risks, resources and next steps. Its instruments of implementation are institutional rather than financial: climate risk assessment, disaster and climate change risk assessment, country strategies, the corporate results framework and development effectiveness tracking.
insights: The plan is organised against the shared MDB BUILDING BLOCKS rather than against IDB's own structure, which is what makes it directly comparable with other development banks' climate plans.

It covers three entities with different instruments, the sovereign IDB, the private-sector IDB Invest and the innovation arm IDB Lab, so the plan has to reconcile concessional, commercial and grant capital in one framework.

Climate Risk Assessment and Disaster and Climate Change Risk Assessment appear as named institutional processes with abbreviations, which means climate screening is embedded in project appraisal rather than added as a review.

Monitoring is given its own section and its own tooling, the Corporate Results Framework and the DELTA development effectiveness instrument, so the plan commits to measurement in a way most institutional strategy documents do not.

Lessons learned from the 2016 to 2020 plan are carried in an electronic appendix rather than the main text, which is worth knowing: the operational review that would explain what did not work is a separate document.

records.title: Community-Based Catastrophe Insurance: A Model for Closing the Disaster Protection Gap
records.authors: Alex Bernhardt; Carolyn Kousky; Andy Read; Christopher Sykes
records.summary: The foundational description of community-based catastrophe insurance, a disaster insurance programme arranged by a local government, a quasi-governmental body such as a special-purpose district, or a community group, covering individual properties within that community. The report starts from the persistent US protection gap: many households and small businesses lack sufficient coverage to fund repair and rebuilding, for reasons the authors separate into affordability constraints, limited risk awareness, poor understanding of insurance, and behavioural biases in decision making. CBCI is offered as a delivery model rather than a product, with the potential to enhance community financial resilience, provide affordable and reliably available disaster insurance, and create incentives for risk reduction at both community and individual level. The authors are explicit that it can occupy several positions in the existing ecosystem: complementing traditional catastrophe markets with supplemental protection, acting as full-limit single-peril property protection in high-risk areas, or giving a community a way to work with carriers or private capital providers to rebuild and sustain insurance uptake in the face of loss volatility. The report covers possible CBCI structures and a roadmap to implementation, drawing on interviews with leaders and stakeholders.
insights: The innovation is in who arranges the cover rather than in what it pays: a local government, special-purpose district or community group buying for individual properties changes the unit of purchase and therefore the risk pool, without requiring a new product.

Creating incentives for community-level and individual risk reduction is named as a purpose of the structure, so mitigation is intended to be internalised by the same body that buys the cover, which is the alignment most insurance arrangements lack.

The authors identify four distinct causes of the protection gap, affordability, risk awareness, comprehension and behavioural bias, and only the first is a price problem, which is why a delivery-model change can reach households a cheaper premium would not.

CBCI is presented as flexible enough to be supplemental, to be full-limit single-peril cover where risk is high, or to be a vehicle for working with carriers to sustain uptake through loss volatility, so it is three different instruments depending on the market it enters.
A special-purpose district as the purchasing entity is the structural move: the same body can both levy and insure, so the premium has a compulsory revenue source behind it.

records.title: The National Flood Insurance Program and the Need for Reform
records.summary: A research paper examining the National Flood Insurance Program and arguing for reform through a market-based risk scheme. It organises the programme's problems into four: debt, inaccurate risk pricing, repetitive loss properties, and the unintended consequences of the programme itself. The paper traces the NFIP's emergence and the root causes of each issue, on the premise that the programme was created to give communities access to primary flood insurance and to mitigate flood risk by regulating floodplain development. Its proposed solution is deliberately two-part rather than a straight privatisation: integrating private insurance with federal grants and subsidies, with private insurance described as half of the solution and subsidies and grants as the other half. The context given is that floods are the most common natural disaster in the United States, with every state and nearly every city having experienced flood damage, and with rising sea levels, shoreline erosion and warmer seas increasing both the frequency and magnitude of storms.
insights: The four problems are treated as connected rather than separate: debt follows from inaccurate risk pricing, repetitive loss properties follow from both, and the unintended consequences follow from the programme's own floodplain development role.

The proposed structure is explicitly hybrid, private insurance plus federal grants and subsidies, with the author naming each as half the solution, which rejects both the status quo and pure privatisation.
Regulating floodplain development was part of the NFIP's original purpose, so the paper's unintended-consequences argument is that the insurance arm undermined the land-use arm.

Affordability is the reason subsidies remain in the proposal: a market-based risk price is the fix for the pricing problem and the cause of an access problem, which is why the author keeps a public half.

records.title: The Value of US Coral Reefs for Flood Risk Reduction
institutions: Center for Coastal Climate Resilience at UC Santa Cruz
United States Army Corps of Engineers
records.summary: A Nature Sustainability paper valuing the flood protection that US coral reefs provide. The authors set the physical stakes: coral reefs line more than 3,100 kilometres of the most at-risk US coastlines across Florida, Hawaii and the US Trust Territories, and recent measurements in Hawaii, Florida and the US Virgin Islands show reefs have eroded more than a metre vertically over recent decades, a trend expected to worsen with climate change and other stressors. The paper's argument is that ecosystem loss can escalate flood risk within years to levels sea-level rise would not reach for decades or a century, and that while the World Bank, the US Army Corps of Engineers and the insurance industry increasingly acknowledge the role of ecosystems in reducing loss, hazard mitigation and environmental management remain largely unaligned. The funding asymmetry is the sharpest point: in 2018 the United States provided about $15 billion to the Army Corps for flood and storm damage reduction, of which more than $10 billion went to states and territories hit by hurricanes Harvey, Irma and Maria, while the most ambitious US reef restoration project, Iconic Reefs in the Florida Keys, proposes roughly $5 million a year.
insights: The funding asymmetry is the finding that matters for instrument design: about $15 billion in one year for Army Corps flood and storm damage reduction against roughly $5 million a year for the most ambitious US reef restoration project, a ratio of three thousand to one for interventions addressing the same hazard.

Ecosystem degradation is argued to advance flood risk faster than sea-level rise does, reaching in years levels not otherwise expected for decades or a century, which reframes reef loss as an acceleration of exposure rather than a conservation loss.
Reefs have eroded more than a metre vertically in recent decades in Hawaii, Florida and the US Virgin Islands, which is a measured loss of protective structure rather than a projection.

The paper names the institutional gap precisely: multilateral agencies, the Army Corps and insurers all acknowledge the protective role of ecosystems, and hazard mitigation and environmental management budgets remain unaligned, which is the gap a payment mechanism would have to bridge.

records.title: Hampton, VA: An Environmental Impact Bond to Fight Flooding
records.summary: Hampton, VA has launched Virginia's first Environmental Impact Bond (EIB) to address flooding through nature-based projects. The $12 million bond will finance three initiatives aimed at enhancing stormwater management in underserved communities, while providing measurable outcomes for investors and improving water equity.
insights: The EIB aims to develop innovative solutions for flooding challenges in Hampton, VA.
The City of Hampton's projects are designed to improve stormwater storage capacity and water quality.
Public engagement and regional partnerships played a critical role in the EIB's development.
Low- to moderate-income communities will benefit from improved flood resilience and environmental conditions.
The structure of the EIB allows for enhanced impact measurement compared to traditional green bonds.
Hampton's EIB was oversubscribed, indicating strong demand from ESG-focused investors.
Investments from the EIB are expected to contribute to the city’s long-term resilience strategy.
Nature-based projects include converting drainage ditches into bioswales and elevating key transportation corridors.
The bond is part of a multi-stage resilience pipeline to address chronic environmental stresses.

records.title: The Implications of Climate Change for Financial Stability
records.summary: The document examines the implications of climate change for financial stability, identifying physical and transition risks that can impact the financial system. It highlights the potential for these risks to interact and amplify, causing uncertainty and volatility in markets. While current estimates suggest that overall risks are manageable, concentrated exposures and data gaps pose challenges for financial institutions in risk management. The report calls for stronger regulatory measures and improved data availability to enhance resilience against climate-related risks, particularly in vulnerable economies.
insights: Climate-related risks include physical risks from climate impacts and transition risks from moving to a low-carbon economy.
A disorderly transition could destabilize financial systems, amplifying both physical and transition risks.
Emerging markets are more vulnerable to climate-related risks due to their weaker financial defenses.
Self-reinforcing feedback loops may occur, decreasing lending and harming economic prospects.
A lack of consistent disclosures about climate risks contributes to market uncertainties and mispriced risks.

records.title: Adaptation Principles: A Guide for Designing Strategies for Climate Change Adaptation and Resilience
records.authors: Stephane Hallegatte, Jun Rentschler, Julie Rozenberg
records.summary: The 'Adaptation Principles' resource outlines a comprehensive framework to assist countries in developing effective strategies for enhancing climate change adaptability and resilience. It emphasizes the integration of proactive, inclusive development strategies, robust institutional frameworks, cross-sectoral coordination, and financial planning to manage climate risks while addressing the needs of vulnerable populations. The guide underscores the importance of continuous monitoring, evaluation, and adaptation of strategies to ensure effective implementation and long-term economic stability amidst increasing climate-related challenges.
insights: Proactive adaptation strategies can effectively reduce climate risks and promote sustainable development.
Governments play a crucial role in enhancing resilience by minimizing barriers for private actors and ensuring the accessibility of information.
Integrating climate considerations into economic recovery plans, particularly following crises like COVID-19, is essential for building long-term resilience.
Stakeholder participation is vital at every stage of the climate adaptation process to enhance ownership and accountability.
Monitoring and evaluating adaptation strategies is imperative for adapting to ongoing changes in climate uncertainty.
A layered approach to disaster risk financing combining various financial tools is recommended for effective risk management.
Investment in adaptive social protection systems can improve resource management in post-disaster situations.

records.title: Building Codes Save: A Nationwide Study
records.summary: The 'Building Codes Save: A Nationwide Study' analyzes the financial benefits of adopting hazard-resistant building codes in the U.S. since 1980, revealing that such codes significantly reduce losses from natural disasters, which have amounted to over $1.6 trillion during this period. The study highlights the importance of modern building codes, particularly the International Codes (I-Codes), in minimizing risks from floods, hurricanes, and earthquakes. It emphasizes that communities with updated codes see substantial economic savings and that ongoing advocacy for these standards is crucial for enhancing resilience against future disasters.
insights: Natural disasters in the U.S. have caused over $1.6 trillion in losses since 1980, with significant savings achievable through the adoption of hazard-resistant building codes.
The study identifies an average annualized loss avoided (AALA) of $1.6 billion due to building codes, showing that approximately 51% of analyzed post-2000 buildings benefit from these codes.
Adopting and enforcing updated International Codes (I-Codes) can result in savings of $11 for every $1 invested in hazard-resistant construction.
Flooding remains the most common hazard, contributing to 90% of all natural disaster events, while improved building codes significantly lower potential losses from these events.
The study projects future savings of $132 billion if the adoption of I-Codes continues and expands, especially in communities prone to seismic, flooding, and hurricane risks.

records.title: What Are Resilience Bonds and How Can They Protect Us Against Climate Crises?
records.authors: Felipe Larrain Bascunan, Dominic Molloy, Berend Sauer
records.summary: Resilience bonds are innovative financial instruments designed to enhance climate resilience by raising capital specifically for adaptation projects. Despite the growing need for adaptation finance, current investments are significantly lower than required. Resilience bonds can unlock funding for countries to improve their climate readiness, while offering potential economic returns due to their ability to raise capital on favorable terms.
insights: There is an increasing need for adaptation funding, estimated to reach $300 billion per year by 2030 for developing countries.
Investment in climate resilience offers significant economic benefits with potential returns of up to $7.1 trillion from a $1.8 trillion investment by 2030.
Resilience bonds are a subset of green bonds, aimed specifically at funding climate-resilient projects.
The market for green bonds has rapidly expanded, highlighting the potential for resilience bonds to grow if defined properly.
The first dedicated resilience bond was launched by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, raising $700 million.
Resilience bonds can help countries and regions leverage finances for climate resilience, although they may not be suitable for all countries facing debt issues.
Green bonds have experienced high demand, particularly for projects focused on sustainability and resilience initiatives.
California is planning to launch a resilience bond aimed at preparing for drought and wildfire risks.
Continued research and development into resilience bonds is essential for scaling their use in vulnerable countries.

records.title: Stocktake of Financial Authorities’ Experience in Including Physical and Transition Climate Risks as Part of Their Financial Stability Monitoring
records.summary: The stocktake report evaluates how financial authorities incorporate physical and transition climate risks into their stability monitoring, revealing that while a significant majority are engaged, approaches vary widely. Challenges in data consistency, risk quantification, and the integration of these risks into supervisory practices persist, highlighting the need for improved disclosures, collaborative approaches, and international coordination.
insights: Approximately 75% of financial authorities consider or plan to consider climate-related risks in their monitoring.
Quantifying climate-related risks remains challenging due to inconsistent data and the complex translation of climate outcomes into financial exposures.
Pension funds have reduced exposure to climate-risk affected securities, while banks and insurers maintained constant exposure levels.
The European Systemic Risk Board reports that economic costs of climate risk are not fully reflected in asset prices due to insufficient disclosures.
Current modeling techniques provide limited insight into long-term climate risks and physical risks are not adequately reflected in asset prices.
A unified set of scenarios is needed to compare impacts across firms, and significant collaboration is necessary to enhance data quality and sharing.
International coordination among regulators is vital to avoid market fragmentation and improve overall climate risk assessments.

records.title: Flood Risk Management in the United States – Building Flood Resilience in a Changing Climate
institutions: Wharton Risk Management and Decision Processes Center
Department of Housing and Urban Development
records.summary: Part of a Geneva Association study of flood risk management in mature insurance markets, this report reviews the US system: governance, risk information, early warning, insurance, mitigation and post-flood recovery. It finds US flood risk rising with heavier precipitation, sea level rise, development in high-risk areas and ageing infrastructure, and management shared across many agencies with duplication and gaps. The NFIP is the primary non-structural tool but is billions of dollars in debt, has limited take-up and has turned to catastrophe bonds for reinsurance. The report concludes the system remains reactive and needs a forward-looking, climate-informed approach with stronger incentives for risk reduction.
insights: Over 90% of federal flood risk reduction dollars are appropriated in off-budget supplemental legislation tied to particular disasters, with much less appropriated pre-disaster.
From FY2005 to FY2018 Congress appropriated USD 23 billion in standard annual appropriations but USD 45 billion in disaster supplemental bills.
The NFIP secured reinsurance from capital markets through catastrophe bond issuances in 2018 and 2019 and sought a third in January 2020, and began buying private reinsurance in 2017.
Generous federal disaster aid to local governments may create perverse incentives, since localities gain from lax floodplain land use while federal taxpayers pay most flood costs.

North Carolina, after Hurricane Floyd in 1999, became a Cooperating Technical Partner in 2000 and built structure-level flood risk profiles with premium estimates and mitigation options on Flood.NC.gov.

records.title: The Belt Line Center: The Michigan PACE Market's First Green Roof Project
records.summary: This case study documents the Belt Line Center PACE project in Detroit, Michigan, the first green roof financed via PACE in Michigan. Located in Wayne County, the $1,035,185 project combines a 16,800 sq. ft. vegetated green roof with a rain garden to manage stormwater runoff and reduce energy use at a historic Albert Kahn building. Over a 20-year term, the project generates $1,079,375 in total savings, exceeding project cost, and eliminates an estimated 462 metric tons of CO2 annually. The project is administered through Lean & Green Michigan's public-private PACE program.
insights: Total savings of $1,079,375 exceed the $1,035,185 financed amount over 20 years, demonstrating a positive net return and validating the economic case for green roofs as a PACE-eligible investment.

The project finances 100% of upfront costs via a property tax special assessment, allowing a 20-year repayment term that aligns repayment with energy savings, resolving the mismatch between typical 3–5 year commercial loan tenors and longer payback periods for efficiency projects.
The 16,800 sq. ft. green roof paired with a rain garden provides a layered stormwater management system, with the rain garden capturing infiltration overflow not retained by the green roof.
The project is estimated to eliminate 462 metric tons of CO2 per year, equivalent to removing 100 cars from the road annually, providing a quantified GHG co-benefit alongside energy savings.

Wayne County established a countywide PACE district in December 2013 under Lean & Green Michigan, using the county's property tax enforcement authority to provide lenders security equivalent to a tax lien, enabling fixed-rate, long-term private financing without public credit risk.
This is the first green roof project in Michigan financed through PACE, establishing a replicable proof point for green infrastructure financing via special assessment in Midwest urban markets.

PACE's structure shifts energy project financing from a capital expenditure requiring short-term debt repayment to a long-term obligation tied to the property, making projects cash-flow positive from year one, a model relevant to commercial building owners facing deferred capital reinvestment decisions.

records.title: Flood Your Neighbors: Spillover Effects of Levee Building
records.summary: A selected paper by Haoluan Wang of the University of Maryland, prepared for the 2020 Agricultural and Applied Economics Association annual meeting and dated 31 May 2020, on the spillover effects of levee building along the Mississippi River. The starting point is that measures taken to protect against natural catastrophes can raise the risk of damage by incentivising economic activity in catastrophe-prone areas, and the less analysed half of the problem is that one agent's self-protection can worsen catastrophic risk for others or force them to protect themselves in turn. Using the Great Mississippi Flood of 2011 as a plausibly exogenous shock and a difference-in-differences strategy on newly digitised data covering every levee along the Mississippi and its tributaries across eight states, the paper finds that levees in flooded counties were heightened by 0.7 to 1 per cent after the flood, and that a 1 per cent increase in upstream levee elevation increased downstream levee elevation by 0.7 to 1.3 per cent. The conclusion is that inter-jurisdictional cooperation on levee building matters for managing flood damage while limiting negative externalities across jurisdictions.
insights: A downstream elasticity of 0.7 to 1.3 against a 1 per cent upstream increase means protective investment is very nearly self-propagating: one jurisdiction's levee obliges its neighbour's, so the aggregate capital requirement is set by the arms race rather than by the hazard.
This is maladaptation with a measured coefficient: the paper prices the externality a levee imposes on a neighbour rather than treating protective investment as unambiguously beneficial.

It has a direct financing implication the paper does not draw: a lender or insurer appraising a levee project on its own protective benefit is systematically overstating the net benefit, because the induced downstream response is a cost the project causes and does not bear.
The 2011 flood as an exogenous shock is what makes the estimate credible, and it also dates the evidence: this is a decade-old response pattern in a basin that has kept building since.

records.title: Forest Resilience Bond (FRB)
records.summary: The Forest Resilience Bond (FRB) is a conservation finance model aimed at generating new revenue streams for forest restoration projects. By blending public and private funds, the FRB provides upfront capital for faster project implementation, alleviating cash flow constraints while supporting local restoration economies through long-term contracts and partnerships.
insights: The FRB creates new revenue streams by quantifying ecosystem benefits.
It is a public-private partnership that alleviates financial burdens on restoration projects.
The FRB allows implementation partners to pay contractors quickly, enhancing cash flow.
It provides critical upfront capital for restoration efforts, enabling projects to scale effectively.
The initiative develops long-term contracts to support local economies involved in restoration.
It brings multiple stakeholders together, including land managers, governments, and non-profits.
Investment returns for private investors are modest, emphasizing a balance between profit and ecological benefits.
The FRB addresses the problem of overstocked forests that become susceptible to severe wildfires.
The FRB Catalyst Facility accelerates the development and launch of multiple FRB projects.

records.title: Natural Hazard Mitigation Saves: 2019 Report
records.summary: The 'Natural Hazard Mitigation Saves: 2019 Report' provides a thorough analysis of the economic advantages of pre-disaster mitigation strategies, emphasizing the necessity for improved building codes and practices to enhance community resilience against escalating natural disasters. The report showcases extensive research on the benefit-cost ratios of various mitigation measures, highlighting their effectiveness in reducing losses, enhancing safety, and promoting economic stability.
insights: Investments in natural hazard mitigation strategies produce significant societal benefits, with benefit-cost ratios (BCRs) demonstrating that for every dollar spent, major future losses can be avoided.
Effective building codes and compliance with updated standards lead to substantial reductions in disaster-related losses and improved community safety.
Collaboration among federal, state, and local entities is crucial for successful implementation and funding of hazard mitigation measures.
Understanding local risk profiles and tailoring mitigation strategies is essential for achieving optimal cost-effectiveness and resilience.
Economic analyses show a strong correlation between pre-disaster investments in infrastructure and post-disaster recovery speed and cost reductions.
Mental health impacts and social vulnerabilities are critical considerations in disaster preparedness and recovery planning.
Flood mitigation and retrofitting measures yield high returns on investment, particularly in vulnerable areas, preventing extensive property damages and loss of life.

records.title: Mitigation Saves: Mitigation Saves Up to $13 per $1 Invested
records.summary: The resource 'Mitigation Saves: Mitigation Saves up to $13 per $1 Invested' highlights the substantial financial benefits of investing in climate mitigation strategies, claiming that every dollar spent can result in savings of up to $13 through avoided climate-related costs and damages. It emphasizes the economic viability and necessity of proactive investments in mitigation measures to enhance community resilience, create jobs, and reduce the fiscal burden of future climate impacts.
insights: Investing in mitigation can yield savings of up to $13 for every $1 spent.
Mitigation strategies significantly reduce future climate-related costs and health impacts.
Proactive climate measures generate substantial economic returns and job creation.
Early investments in mitigation can prevent larger expenditures associated with disaster response.
Policy frameworks that support mitigation enhance community resilience and financial benefits.

records.title: The Role of Insurance in Coastal Adaptation: Workshop Findings
records.summary: Findings from a Wharton Risk Center workshop on what insurance can and cannot do for coastal adaptation, organised around four problems the participants treated as distinct. The recovery of low-income families, where federal disaster aid is limited and delayed and the flood insurance gap is widest, and where standard flood policies do not cover temporary living expenses and other recovery costs. The protection of coastal ecosystems, which provide protection against some disaster risks but are under-funded for conservation and for restoration after the very storms they buffer. Meeting community fiscal needs, which is the municipal side of the same exposure. And homeowners policies and mitigation, where the workshop examined how standard cover interacts with risk reduction. The overview also names gaps beyond flood, including high deductibles for wind damage, and barriers to using insurance to relocate out of high-risk areas, a strategy the authors expect to matter more as the sea rises.
insights: Standard flood insurance not covering temporary living expenses is a specific, fixable product gap that falls hardest on low-income households, and it is separate from the affordability problem usually discussed.

Coastal ecosystems are identified as under-funded for restoration precisely after the storms for which they provide protection, which is the same asymmetry the coral reef paper quantifies and points at a mechanism gap rather than a knowledge gap.
Barriers to using insurance proceeds to relocate rather than rebuild are named as a design problem, and the authors expect managed retreat to become more important as sea level rises.
High wind deductibles are flagged alongside the flood gap, so a coastal household can hold cover for both perils and still be materially unprotected.
The workshop format means these are participant findings rather than original analysis, which is worth noting before grounding a claim in them.

records.title: Florida Climate Outlook: Assessing Physical and Economic Impacts Through 2040
records.authors: Daniel Raimi, Amelia Keyes, Cora Kingdon
records.summary: The 'Florida Climate Outlook: Assessing Physical and Economic Impacts through 2040' report evaluates the expected physical and economic consequences of climate change on Florida, highlighting rising temperatures, sea level rise, and increased storm intensity. The assessment underscores the urgent need for adaptation strategies as climate-related risks escalate, particularly for coastal cities like Miami, with potential impacts on health, agriculture, and infrastructure.
insights: Florida is projected to experience summer temperatures exceeding 83°F and significant sea level rise by 2040, increasing flooding risks.
The state's agricultural sector faces substantial threats, particularly citrus crops affected by diseases linked to climate change.
Major urban areas like Miami are at risk of flood-related damages, with significant economic assets threatened.
Health risks are expected to escalate due to extreme heat, particularly among vulnerable populations such as the elderly.
Environmental factors will decrease outdoor labor productivity by up to 17%, complicating agricultural operations.
The need for anticipatory adaptation measures could lead to the abandonment of certain areas due to unsustainable living conditions.
Low-income households may bear an increased burden from climate impacts due to higher relative energy expenditures.
Carbon taxation discussions are becoming more pertinent as they relate to economic modeling and emissions reduction.

records.title: Can Parametric Microinsurance Improve the Financial Resilience of Low-Income Households in the United States?
records.authors: Carolyn Kousky; Helen Wiley; Len Shabman
institutions: Wharton Risk Management and Decision Processes Center
records.summary: This proof-of-concept examination from the Wharton Risk Center asks whether parametric microinsurance, long used in developing countries, can improve the post-disaster financial resilience of low-income US households. It reviews evidence that poorer households are disproportionately harmed by disasters and lack savings, credit, insurance and timely government aid. It explains how parametric triggers cut loss-adjustment costs enough to make low-limit, low-premium policies viable, and sets out the market challenges. It proposes five US delivery models and identifies research, regulatory and public-support steps needed for adoption.
insights: Five delivery models are proposed: an aggregator, a mobile-based application, a joint product or joint sale, a community captive, and a public-sector disaster insurance program.

In July 2020 Puerto Rico introduced regulations enabling parametric microinsurance for low-income families, and the firm Raincoat was ready to offer a product; no microinsurance had previously been offered in the US.
Parametric policies pay a set amount when an observable parameter such as wind speed is reached, removing costly loss adjusting and making lower-limit policies economical.
The US poverty rate for 2020 was roughly 12%, and indemnity-based disaster policies are generally unaffordable for lower-income households, who are usually uninsured.
The authors find no research documenting in detail the specific financial costs households face by peril and the post-disaster financing gap, which they identify as a precondition for product design.
They argue the product would benefit from public support, such as premium subsidies or funding for development and piloting.

records.title: Climate Risk Solutions
records.authors: Mark Alan Hughes; Ioana Marinescu; Steven O. Kimbrough; Jean Galbraith; Howard Kunreuther; Bob Meyer; Benjamin J. Keys; Frederick Steiner; Anna Mikulska; Erick Guerra; Julie Keenahan; Mark P. Nevitt; Sarah Light; Carolyn Kousky; Howard F. Chang; William W. Braham; Daniel E. Walters; Allison Lassiter; Trevor M. Penning; Marilyn Howarth; Alexander Braun; Regina Austin; Brett Lingle; Michael Jones-Correa; Nicholas Pevzner; Witold Henisz; Matthijs Bouw; Eric Orts; Billy Fleming; Charles Howard; Daniel Aldana Cohen; Cary Coglianese
institutions: Wharton Risk Management and Decision Processes Center
records.summary: This University of Pennsylvania collection compiles 30 short policy ideas from a summer 2019 ideation session on mitigation, adaptation and transition risk, hosted by the Wharton Risk Management and Decision Processes Center, the Kleinman Center for Energy Policy, the Penn Program on Regulation and the Faculty Senate. The ideas range from carbon taxes and border adjustments to insuring ecosystems, redirecting insurance capital flows, a resilience policy score for communities, and climate risk disclosure. Idea 6 argues that the federal mortgage finance system, through Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and FHA/VA programs, bears unpriced flood and sea level rise risk and could help manage it. The coda argues that solving climate risk ultimately requires normative change.
insights: Thirty solutions were proposed by Penn researchers across schools, covering mitigation, adaptation and transition risk.
Agency MBS guaranteed through Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac or FHA/VA account for over 60 percent of outstanding US residential mortgage debt, yet these agencies do not price heightened flood risk.

Idea 6 proposes that FHFA and FHA/VA study their exposure to storm surge, nuisance flooding and sea level rise, and enforce the NFIP mandatory purchase requirement by linking flood policy data to mortgage data.
Kunreuther and Meyer suggest tying home resilience improvements to long-term loans on the mortgage so annual premium savings offset the cost.
Other ideas include insuring ecosystems (Light and Kousky), a community resilience policy score (Kousky) and mandatory disclosure of material climate risks (Henisz).

records.title: The Business Case for Resilience in Southeast Florida: Regional Economic Benefits of Climate Adaptation
institutions: Southeast Florida Regional Climate Change Compact
records.summary: An economic analysis of the regional benefits of climate adaptation in Southeast Florida, produced by ULI with AECOM's Sustainable Economics practice, the Southeast Florida Regional Climate Change Compact and a stakeholder group drawn from chambers of commerce, community foundations, developers and design firms. It was reviewed for consistency and accuracy of the original economic analysis. The framing is the business case: what the region gains economically from adapting, addressed to the private sector actors whose investment decisions determine whether adaptation is funded.
insights: The project is structured to reach the private sector rather than only local government: the stakeholder group is chambers of commerce, a beacon council, developers, architects and a roofing contractor, alongside the four Compact counties.
The analysis values the actions rather than proposing them: it takes a regional climate action plan as given and asks what the plan is worth.

AECOM's Sustainable Economics practice carried the analysis and ULI states it was independently reviewed for consistency and accuracy, which is a stronger provenance claim than most grey literature makes for itself.
Brizaga, a local engineering firm, supplied both the local project manager and the design team, so the report is regionally authored rather than a national template applied to Florida.

The Compact is described as more than a decade of collaboration across Broward, Miami-Dade, Monroe and Palm Beach counties with bipartisan support, which is the institutional precondition the economic case depends on.

records.title: Climate Risk and Real Estate: Emerging Practices for Market Assessment
records.summary: ULI and Heitman's second collaboration on climate risk in real estate, following their 2019 report on investment decision-making, turning from asset-level to MARKET-level risk. It finds that leading investment managers and institutional investors now treat market-scale climate risk assessment as something that will shape future investment decisions, mirroring advances already made at the asset level. The report covers the climate-risk context, how investors assess risk at market scale, how markets respond through infrastructure and policy, and an actuarial perspective on measuring real estate risk contributed by Milliman, with Arup and academic collaborators on city fiscal health. It is written from interviews with ULI members, reconnecting with the investors interviewed for the 2019 report.
insights: The unit of analysis moves from the building to the city: investors are beginning to judge a market by its resilience strategy and its infrastructure and policy response, which makes municipal resilience investment an input to private capital allocation rather than only a public good.

The report pairs two capabilities that rarely appear in one document: an actuarial view of measuring real estate risk from three Milliman consulting actuaries, and city fiscal health analysis from Arup with academics at Nebraska-Omaha and North Carolina State. Fiscal capacity and catastrophe modelling are treated as two halves of one market judgement.

It was published into the COVID-19 period and says so: chief resilience officers had shifted focus to pandemic resilience and cities had cut funding for infrastructure and sustainability, which the preface treats as evidence that behaviour can change quickly rather than as a reason to defer.

Heitman is described as managing approximately $43 billion and as among the investment managers furthest along in quantifying climate risk, so the practices reported are from a participant rather than an observer.

The stated purpose is symmetrical: better market-level understanding is meant to inform city efforts to address risk through policy and infrastructure, not only to inform investors deciding whether to enter a market.

records.title: Managing Climate Risk in the U.S. Financial System
records.authors: Leonardo Martinez Diaz, J. M. Keenan
records.summary: 'Managing Climate Risk in the U.S. Financial System' outlines the urgent need for enhanced regulatory frameworks and collaboration between public and private sectors to address the systemic risks posed by climate change to the U.S. financial system. It discusses the inadequacies of traditional risk modeling, emphasizing the importance of climate risk management, improved data transparency, and standardized disclosures as crucial components for maintaining financial stability and supporting sustainable investments.
insights: Climate change poses significant risks to the stability of the U.S. financial system.
Effective climate risk management requires improved data, tools, and communication between regulators and financial institutions.
The lack of common definitions and standards for climate-related data hinders effective risk management.
Financial regulators must enhance institutional capacity and knowledge around climate risk management through research and engagement.
Investments in climate adaptation and resilience technologies are crucial for mitigating potential losses across economic sectors.
Regulators should support the creation of consistent climate risk data and classification systems to facilitate better risk assessment.
Collaborative efforts between government and private sectors are crucial for innovative finance solutions.
There is a growing demand for transparent climate-related disclosures from companies to assess long-term risks.
Understanding both physical and transition risks is essential for banks and investors to make informed decisions.

records.title: Atlanta: First Publicly Offered Environmental Impact Bond
records.summary: The Atlanta Environmental Impact Bond (EIB), structured by Quantified Ventures and Atlanta's Department of Watershed Management, is a pioneering $14 million bond designed to fund six green infrastructure projects aimed at improving stormwater management in historically underserved neighborhoods. Closed on January 31, 2019, this bond represents a significant shift towards outcomes-based financing in public municipal markets, showcasing potential benefits such as flood risk reduction, enhanced water quality, job creation, and increased access to green spaces.
insights: The EIB closed on January 31, 2019, marking it as the first publicly offered Environmental Impact Bond.
The $14 million bond finances six green infrastructure projects in economically distressed neighborhoods along Proctor Creek.
The bond uses a two-tiered performance structure that incentivizes higher performance in stormwater capture.
Atlanta's Department of Watershed Management anticipates the projects will absorb 55 million gallons of stormwater annually.
The projects are expected to protect nearly 500 homes from future flooding and create dozens of local jobs.
The EIB is linked to measurable environmental outcomes, such as flood risk reduction and water quality improvement.
Public issuance of the EIB opens avenues for mainstream municipal bond investors to participate in outcomes-based financing.
Innovations in the EIB include using aerial imagery for project evaluation instead of continuous sensor monitoring.
The financing approach highlights the importance of social equity and community engagement in environmental project planning.
The bond serves as a proof case for mobilizing future funding for green infrastructure initiatives in other cities.

records.title: CLIMAFIN Handbook: Pricing Forward-Looking Climate Risks Under Uncertainty
records.authors: Stefano Battiston, Antoine Mandel, Irene Monasterolo
institutions: Vienna University of Economics and Business
records.summary: The CLIMAFIN Handbook (Part 1) presents a science-based framework for pricing forward-looking climate transition risks in financial contracts under deep uncertainty. Developed by researchers at University of Zurich, Vienna University of Economics and Business, and Paris School of Economics, it introduces climate-scenario-adjusted valuation models for equity holdings, corporate bonds, and sovereign bonds, alongside novel risk metrics, the Climate Spread and Climate Value-at-Risk (Climate VaR). The framework addresses structural limitations of traditional financial pricing models when applied to non-linear, path-dependent, fat-tailed climate risks, and is designed to support both investors managing portfolio exposure and financial supervisors designing prudential measures for systemic risk.
insights: Traditional financial pricing models (assuming normally distributed shocks, complete markets, backward-looking metrics) are structurally inadequate for climate risk, which exhibits deep uncertainty, non-linearity, fat tails, path-dependency, and endogeneity, requiring entirely new frameworks.

The CLIMAFIN tool introduces two new risk metrics: the Climate Spread (change in bond spread conditional on a climate policy shock scenario) and the Climate Value-at-Risk (worst-case portfolio loss conditional on forward-looking climate policy shock scenarios), providing actionable signals for portfolio risk management.

Climate policy shocks are modeled as transitions from Business-as-Usual to IPCC-aligned scenarios (450 ppm and 500 ppm targets), with shocks calculated at the sector, country, and regional level using LIMITS IAM database trajectories, quantifying GVA impacts on fossil fuel, electricity fossil, and electricity renewable sectors.

For sovereign bonds, the framework links climate policy shocks to sovereign default probability via changes in net fiscal assets (tax revenues minus subsidies from climate-relevant sectors), with the elasticity of profitability to market share assumed at 1 (empirical range: 0.2–0.6), providing an upper-bound estimate of shock magnitude.

The investor risk management strategy is formulated as a minimax problem: minimize the worst-case Climate VaR across all feasible forward-looking climate policy shock scenarios, explicitly accounting for incomplete information and the absence of prior probabilities on scenario occurrence.

Recent empirical research cited in the handbook finds that investors are not yet pricing climate-related risks in portfolios, and that market benchmarks are carbon-intensive, creating a systematic mispricing gap with potential implications for price volatility, portfolio performance, and financial stability.

records.title: Texas Flood Infrastructure Fund
records.summary: Texas established the Flood Infrastructure Fund in 2019 to finance drainage, flood mitigation and flood control projects for political subdivisions, administered by the Texas Water Development Board and offering both grants and zero-interest loans. Eligible activities fall into four categories: flood protection planning for watersheds; planning, acquisition, design, construction and rehabilitation; federal award matching funds; and measures immediately effective in protecting life and property. Funding covers structural and non-structural work, explicitly including nature-based approaches, property acquisition, natural system restoration and permeable pavements. The grant-to-loan mix is set by a means test: a community with annual median household income below 50 per cent of the statewide figure that has had a federally declared flood disaster in the last five years can receive 100 per cent grant funding for flood protection planning, and the grant share falls as income rises. The grant share can be raised again for high unemployment, declining population, rural status, or where at least 30 per cent of project costs are green or nature based. Applicants must show benefits exceed costs, and the project area must have floodplain ordinances enforced to at least National Flood Insurance Program standards. The fund was authorised by Senate Bill 7 in 2019, approved by voters through Proposition 8 as a constitutional amendment, and initially capitalised with $793 million.
insights: The grant-to-loan ratio is set by a formula rather than by discretion, sliding with median household income and adjusted upward for unemployment, population decline, rural status and green content, which makes affordability an explicit term of the instrument.
A 30 per cent green or nature-based share of project cost earns a larger grant share, which prices nature-based solutions into the subsidy rather than merely permitting them.
Voter approval of a constitutional amendment lets the Water Development Board administer the money without further appropriations, which insulates the fund from the annual budget cycle.

Two conditions tie the money to regulation: benefits must exceed costs, and the project area must enforce floodplain standards consistent with the NFIP, so the fund buys land-use compliance as well as infrastructure.

records.title: Climate Risks in Financial Assets
records.authors: Emanuele Campiglio, Pierre Monnin, Adrian von Jagow
records.summary: This 2019 Council on Economic Policies discussion note by Campiglio, Monnin, and von Jagow reviews academic evidence on how climate-related physical and transition risks affect equity and debt instrument prices. It finds that hurricanes, droughts, and extreme temperatures already reduce firm cash flows and increase non-performing loans; conservative stress tests estimate portfolio losses of up to 10% within five years from transition shocks, rising to 40% under sudden expectation revisions in a no-transition physical-risk scenario. The paper concludes that financial markets do not adequately price in future climate costs and recommends mandatory climate stress tests incorporating expectation revisions and second-round network effects.
insights: Conservative transition-risk stress tests (Vermeulen et al., 2018) find Dutch insurer and pension fund portfolios (holding equities, bonds, and loans), could lose up to 10% of value within 5 years under a combined policy and technology shock, without accounting for second-round effects or expectation revisions.

CISL (2015) estimates that a sudden investor expectation revision pricing in a no-transition (high physical risk) scenario could produce a 40% correction in a balanced portfolio within one year; a transition to a 2°C world reduces this to a 10% correction.

Battiston et al. (2017) find that second-round contagion through bank cross-exposures can more than double the initial loss from a transition shock: first-round equity losses of ~13% across fossil fuel, utilities, and energy-intensive sectors rise to ~28% once second-round effects are included.

Empirical evidence of market under-pricing: Hong et al. (2019) show drought trends forecast food-sector stock returns across 31 countries (1985–2014), and Kumar et al. (2019) show firm temperature sensitivity predicts future returns, both consistent with markets underreacting to climate risk.

Addoum et al. (2019) find analysts make no forecast revisions after 8,584 identified extreme temperature events in the US, indicating analysts do not integrate physical climate impacts into earnings expectations.

Chinese Clean Air Action (2013) caused default rates of high-polluting firms to rise ~50%, yet Chinese banks' loan spread increase of only 5.5% to high-polluting firms was insufficient to match the observed default risk, illustrating systematic under-pricing of transition risk in credit markets.

records.title: Introduction to Climate Value-at-Risk: Methodologies and Tools to Evaluate the Financial Impact of Climate-Related Risks and Opportunities
records.summary: This November 2019 MSCI/Carbon Delta document introduces the Climate Value-at-Risk (CVaR) methodology, a framework for quantifying the net-present-value financial impact of climate-related risks and opportunities on companies and portfolios. It covers three components, policy (transition) risk, technology opportunities, and physical risk, across 1.5°C, 2°C, and 3°C warming scenarios, applied to listed equities, fixed income, and real estate. The tool draws on facility-level emissions data, 90 million patents across 400+ low-carbon technology groups, and probabilistic hazard models to produce aggregated CVaR metrics for regulatory compliance, risk management, and portfolio construction.
insights: Carbon Delta's CVaR methodology decomposes climate financial impact into three components: policy/transition risk (emission compliance costs), technology opportunity (low-carbon patent valuation), and physical risk (facility-level hazard exposure), each projected 15 years forward to 2100.

Company-level scenario analysis illustrates stark divergence in compliance costs: a sample company with 34.1 MtCO2e emissions faces annual costs of -$140M under a 3°C/NDC scenario, -$551M under 2°C, and -$2.0B under a 1.5°C scenario, a 14x cost range across scenarios.

Physical risk is calculated as Expected Cost = Vulnerability × Hazard × Exposure, applied across seven hazard types (extreme heat/cold, heavy precipitation/snowfall, wind gusts, wildfires, coastal flooding, tropical cyclones, and fluvial flooding) using facility-level asset location data covering 500,000+ enterprise assets globally.

Technology opportunity is proxied through patent analysis, 90 million patents across 10,000+ companies and 400+ low-carbon technology groups, allowing CVaR to capture upside from R&D investment in sectors such as e-vehicles, wind, photovoltaic, and smart grids.

CVaR outputs are designed for multiple capital-markets use cases: regulatory compliance (TCFD reporting), 2°C alignment assessment, new financial product development, portfolio optimization, shareholder engagement, and alpha generation through green technology overweights.

The methodology uses Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) as the basis for the 3°C policy scenario, integrating country-level emission trajectories into facility- and company-level cost calculations, directly linking sovereign climate commitments to corporate financial valuation.

records.title: EBRD Issues World's First Dedicated Climate Resilience Bond (US$700m)
institutions: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development
United Nations Environment Programme Finance Initiative
records.summary: The EBRD announces the first dedicated climate resilience bond, a five-year issue raising US$ 700 million from about 40 investors in 15 countries. Proceeds finance existing and new climate resilience projects in resilient infrastructure, resilient business and commercial operations, and resilient agriculture and ecological systems. The bond follows the four core Green Bond Principles, with use-of-proceeds projects selected under the Climate Bonds Initiative's Climate Resilience Principles, published 17 September 2019. The EBRD holds some EUR 7 billion of climate resilient projects.
insights: The five-year bond raised US$ 700 million from approximately 40 investors in 15 countries.
It is the first bond aligned with the CBI Climate Resilience Principles, published 17 September 2019.
Eligible uses fall in three categories: climate resilient infrastructure, climate-resilient business and commercial operations, and climate-resilient agriculture and ecological systems.
The EBRD's climate resilient portfolio is some EUR 7 billion, including the Qairokkum hydropower upgrade in Tajikistan and the Saiss water conservation project in Morocco.
Since 2010 the EBRD has issued over EUR 4.5 billion of green bonds in 14 currencies.
records.publisher: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development

records.title: Adapt Now: A Global Call for Leadership on Climate Resilience
records.summary: The flagship report of the Global Commission on Adaptation makes the human, environmental and economic case for accelerating climate adaptation. It finds that returns on resilience investment are high, with benefit-cost ratios of 2:1 to 10:1, and frames adaptation as delivering a triple dividend of avoided losses, economic gains and social and environmental benefits. It calls for three revolutions, in understanding, planning and finance, and applies them to food, the natural environment, water, cities, infrastructure, disaster risk management and finance. It closes by launching a Year of Action from September 2019 to December 2020 driven by eight Action Tracks.
insights: Investing $1.8 trillion globally from 2020 to 2030 in five areas (early warning systems, climate-resilient infrastructure, dryland agriculture, mangrove protection and water resources) could generate $7.1 trillion in total net benefits.
Benefit-cost ratios for improved resilience range from 2:1 to 10:1, and climate-proofing infrastructure returns about 4:1 on average.
Mangroves provide more than $80 billion per year in avoided coastal flood losses and protect 18 million people, plus $40 to $50 billion per year in non-market benefits.

Without adaptation, rising seas and storm surge could cost coastal urban areas more than $1 trillion each year by 2050, and climate change could push more than 100 million people in developing countries below the poverty line by 2030.

The public sector is cast as both a direct funder and an enabler of private finance through disclosure requirements, metrics and incentives, with the private sector sharing the costs of infrastructure, contingency finance and insurance.
In coastal cities the cost of good adaptation is put at one-tenth the cost of no action.

records.title: The Mandatory Purchase Requirement: Origins and Effectiveness in Achieving NFIP Goals
records.authors: Wharton Risk Management and Decision Processes Center (no author name in the extracted text; the cover is an image)
institutions: Wharton Risk Management and Decision Processes Center
US Department of Homeland Security Science and Technology Directorate
Department of Housing and Urban Development
records.summary: The report explains how the NFIP mandatory purchase requirement (MPR), legislated in December 1973, works today and whether it still meets Congress's three original goals for the program. The MPR requires federally regulated or backed lenders to require flood insurance on mortgaged property in the mapped 1% annual chance floodplain, and applies to federal assistance for construction or repair there. It finds the MPR succeeded in driving community enrollment and floodplain regulation, but that expanding residential take-up will do little to cut federal disaster aid, since most aid does not go to individuals. Because the MPR covers only about 35% of households in the SFHA and none outside it, closing the insurance gap needs changes to the MPR or new voluntary-purchase programs.
insights: Before the MPR, only about 10% of flood-prone communities had joined the NFIP and there were only 95,000 policies.
As of 2019 there were 22,384 participating communities and roughly 5.02 million policies in force.
The MPR applies to roughly 35% of households living in the SFHA, based on shares of 41% mortgaged owners, 23% owners without a mortgage and 36% renters.
FEMA assistance to households is only about 20 to 25% of the agency's disaster relief spending, and the average recipient receives about $5,000 against an FY 2019 cap of $34,900.

Required coverage is the lesser of the loan balance, the NFIP maximum ($250,000 for one-to-four-unit residences) or the structure's insurable value, and NFIP limits have not risen as home values grew (median $302,700 in March 2019).

records.title: Parametric Loss and Damage Insurance Schemes as a Means to Enhance Climate Change Resilience in Developing Countries
records.summary: A synthesis article in Climate Policy, volume 20 issue 6 pages 693 to 703, published online 15 July 2019, by Morten Broberg of the Faculty of Law at the University of Copenhagen, on parametric loss and damage insurance schemes as a means of enhancing climate change resilience in developing countries. It takes its starting point from Article 8 of the 2015 Paris Agreement, which calls on the parties to cooperate to address loss and damage, and examines what parametric schemes can and cannot do against that mandate. The article has been viewed 8,361 times and cited 15 times.
insights: A law faculty rather than an economics or insurance one is the useful provenance. Article 8 of the Paris Agreement is a legal instrument, and the question of whether a parametric payout discharges a loss and damage obligation is a legal question before it is an actuarial one.

Loss and damage is the one part of climate finance where the instrument is asked to do compensation as well as risk transfer, and parametric cover is poorly suited to compensation because the payout is keyed to a trigger rather than to a loss. That tension is what the article exists to examine.
Eight thousand views and fifteen citations for a 2019 synthesis article make this a reference point in the literature rather than a primary result, and it should be cited as a synthesis.

records.title: California Wildfire Fund (Assembly Bill 1054)
records.summary: The text of California Assembly Bill 1054, approved by the Governor on 12 July 2019, which restructured how catastrophic wildfire costs are paid for in California. It establishes the Wildfire Fund to pay eligible claims arising from a covered wildfire, continuously appropriating the money to a Wildfire Fund Administrator, and requires the Public Utilities Commission to open a rulemaking on using its existing authority to make electrical corporations collect a nonbypassable charge from ratepayers to support the fund, with funding coming from utility contributions and that charge. It authorises an electrical corporation to apply for a financing order allowing recovery of catastrophic wildfire costs through bonds secured by a rate component. It creates a safety certification that changes the burden of proof in a cost-recovery proceeding: ordinarily the utility must show by a preponderance of the evidence that its conduct was reasonable, but a utility holding a valid safety certification for the period in which the covered wildfire ignited has its conduct deemed reasonable unless a party raises serious doubt, at which point the burden returns. Reasonableness is defined against what a reasonable utility would have done in good faith at the time on the information then available. It also establishes a seven-member California Wildfire Safety Advisory Board, requires wildfire mitigation plans to cover at least three years from 2020, and authorises a penalty of up to three times the normal amount where a utility seeks recovery of costs already authorised.
insights: The safety certification is a resilience-linked incentive written into liability law rather than into a price.
