Mitigation investment buys a presumption of reasonableness, which is worth real money in a cost-recovery proceeding, so the statute converts hardening expenditure into a reduction in regulatory risk. That is the resilience-bond logic in a regulatory instrument.

Three distinct financing mechanisms sit in one statute: a mutualised catastrophe fund, a ratepayer charge to capitalise it, and rate-secured securitisation of past costs. Combining all three in one jurisdiction is what makes the design unusual.

A nonbypassable charge is the design detail that makes the fund work and also makes it regressive: every ratepayer pays, whether or not they are in a fire zone, which is the cross-subsidy question any pooled resilience fund has to answer.
This is primary legislation rather than commentary on it, so its provisions can be read from the statutory text rather than from a description of them.

records.title: An Inconvenient Cost: The Effects of Climate Change on Municipal Bonds
records.summary: This peer-reviewed Journal of Financial Economics study (2020) provides the first empirical evidence that municipal bond markets price physical climate change risk. Using a sample of 327,152 U.S. municipal bond issues from 2004–2017, the author finds that counties with higher sea-level-rise exposure, measured as mean annual loss as a percentage of GDP from Hallegatte et al. (2013), pay 23.4 basis points more in annualized issuance costs for long-term bonds (≥25-year maturity) but no premium for short-term bonds. The effect is concentrated in bonds rated below AA−/Aa3, and a difference-in-differences test around the 2006 Stern Review release confirms investor attention as a causal mechanism.
insights: A 1% increase in county-level climate risk (sea-level-rise expected annual loss as % of GDP) raises long-term municipal bond annualized issuance costs by 23.4 basis points, translating to an average additional $1.7 million in annualized issuance costs per affected county over the sample period.

The climate risk premium is entirely absent for short-term bonds (<25-year maturity) across all specifications, confirming the market prices the temporal horizon of physical risk, a key signal for allocators structuring long vs. short duration exposure in climate-exposed jurisdictions.

The premium is driven by bonds rated below AA−/Aa3: a 1% increase in climate risk raises issuance costs by 52.7 basis points for sub-AA− long-term bonds, versus an insignificant effect for high-grade bonds, evidence that market pricing already differentiates credit quality in relation to climate risk, which has direct implications for Moody's proposed climate-driven downgrades.

Before the 2006 Stern Review, the issuance cost difference between climate and non-climate long-term bonds was an insignificant −15.9 basis points; after the Stern Review, the interaction term rises to 60.7 basis points (significant at 5%), demonstrating that investor attention, not just underlying risk, is a prerequisite for physical risk to be priced into fixed income.

New Orleans (Orleans Parish) carries the highest climate risk at 1.479% mean annual GDP loss; New York/Newark is lower in percentage terms (0.089%) but carries the largest absolute expected annual loss at over $2.1 billion, illustrating that percentage-based risk metrics can obscure enormous dollar exposures in dense urban markets.

records.title: Uncertainty of Climate Policies and Implications for Economics and Finance: An Evolutionary Economics Approach
records.authors: Irene Monasterolo, Andrea Roventini, Tim J. Foxon
institutions: Vienna University of Economics and Business
records.summary: This 2019 special issue introduction in Ecological Economics argues that traditional climate economics and financial risk models (constrained by equilibrium conditions, linearity, and representative agents), are inadequate for capturing the complexity of climate risks and policy uncertainty. The authors survey nine papers applying evolutionary economics, agent-based models, Stock-Flow Consistent models, and network models to assess climate-aligned policies and financial instruments, identifying a USD 2.5 trillion annual investment gap through 2050 and highlighting systemic risks such as pension funds holding up to 45% of equity portfolios in carbon-intensive sectors.
insights: A USD 2.5 trillion per year investment gap in climate mitigation and adaptation persists through 2050, requiring ambitious fiscal policies, development banks, and central bank engagement beyond market forces alone.

Pension funds hold up to 45% of their equity portfolios in carbon-intensive sectors; financial network reverberation can amplify these direct exposures into systemic risk, as shown by Battiston et al.'s (2017) climate stress-test.
Financial markets were not yet pricing climate risks into asset valuations as of 2018, despite evidence of higher risk associated with high-carbon indices emerging after the Paris Agreement.

Climate policy uncertainty creates a self-reinforcing barrier: investors unable to anticipate policies face abrupt asset price volatility and carbon stranded-asset losses once policies are introduced, which in turn discourages pre-emptive green investment.

Agent-based integrated assessment models (e.g., the DSK model by Lamperti et al.) generate larger climate damages than standard IAMs under comparable scenarios, and endogenously produce tipping points that shift growth from self-sustained to stagnation, findings with direct implications for physical risk pricing.
A mix of market-based carbon taxes and centralized public R&D spending on resource-saving technologies outperforms either policy alone for achieving low-carbon transition under hysteresis conditions.

Climate change causes long-term negative impacts on GDP growth, bank leverage, and asset prices in global simulations (2016–2120); central bank green QE programmes can partially mitigate climate-induced financial instability.

Voluntary TCFD-style climate disclosure is assessed as insufficient to scale up green private capital investment to the levels required by the Paris Agreement, pointing toward mandatory disclosure and taxonomy standards.

records.title: Quintana Roo Coral Reef Parametric Insurance (Coastal Zone Management Trust)
records.summary: Swiss Re's case study of the parametric hurricane cover on the Mesoamerican coral reef off Quintana Roo, Mexico, the first insurance policy written on a natural asset. It opens with the scale: the total economic value of the world's reefs is estimated at USD 9.9 trillion, a healthy reef is connected to a region's ability to sustain itself economically, and reefs provide protection against disasters and erosion. Quintana Roo's economy depends heavily on the reef and the tourism income tied to it, and both the public and private sectors wanted a more reliable source of funding for repair work after regular storm damage. Swiss Re developed the initial solution, insuring a stretch of reef and the adjacent beaches along the Yucatan Peninsula, with The Nature Conservancy and the State Government of Quintana Roo. As part of a public-private partnership the Coastal Zone Management Trust was established to take out the policy and to maintain the reef continuously. The cover is triggered by wind speed within a pre-defined area, and a payout is used by the Trust to fund the Reef Brigades, a team of local divers, marine biologists and others who collect and mend broken coral. The Swiss Re Foundation provided the grant that created the Reef Brigades. In 2020, Hurricane Delta triggered the insurance.
insights: The insured is a trust, not an owner. Nobody owns a coral reef, so the structure had to manufacture an insurable interest: the Coastal Zone Management Trust holds the policy and the maintenance obligation together, which is what makes the payout usable. That device is the transferable part of this deal.

The payout funds labour, not repair contracts. The Reef Brigades are a standing team of divers and biologists, so the instrument pays for a capability that exists before the storm rather than for reconstruction afterwards, and the Swiss Re Foundation grant that created them is the concessional layer under the commercial one.
Hurricane Delta triggered the policy in 2020, so this is an instrument that has actually paid out rather than one announced or designed.
Wind speed in a pre-defined area is a cheap and fast trigger and a crude proxy for reef damage, which is the basis risk this structure accepts in exchange for speed of payout.

records.title: High Tide Tax: The Price to Protect Coastal Communities from Rising Seas
records.summary: This 2019 study by the Center for Climate Integrity and Resilient Analytics provides the first contiguous U.S. estimate of seawall construction costs needed to protect public coastal infrastructure from sea-level rise under moderate emissions scenarios (RCP4.5) by 2040. The headline finding: $416 billion in seawall costs across 22 states by 2040, rising to $518 billion by 2100, covering 50,145 miles of barriers. Florida faces the largest state-level bill at ~$76 billion. The study explicitly frames these costs as a fraction (10–15%) of total adaptation needs and positions fossil fuel industry liability as the central policy question.
insights: The contiguous U.S. faces an estimated $416 billion in seawall construction costs by 2040 under a moderate emissions scenario (RCP4.5, 50th percentile), rising to $518 billion by 2100, representing only 10–15% of estimated total coastal adaptation costs over the same period.

Florida alone accounts for ~$76 billion in seawall costs by 2040 across 9,243 miles of coastline, with 23 counties each facing at least $1 billion in expenses, making it the single most financially exposed state in the analysis.

More than 130 counties face at least $1 billion in seawall costs by 2040; in 19 small communities the per-capita cost exceeds $1,000,000, and in 178 communities it exceeds $100,000, thresholds that signal managed retreat as the only financially viable option for many.

The study covers 137 congressional districts across 22 states; Republican districts collectively face $224 billion in costs vs. $192 billion for Democratic districts, but Republicans hold a disproportionate share of the highest-cost districts, with 24 of the top 40 most-expensive districts represented by Republicans.

Seawall costs are modeled only for 1-year storm surge protection against public infrastructure, not private property or broader resilience line items (utilities, healthcare, transportation, etc.); New York City's own comprehensive plan shows coastal protection is just 16–20% of total city-level resilience costs.

The study uses geographically specific, locally calibrated per-linear-foot cost estimates differentiated between coastal seawalls and inland bulkheads, with 150 m² grid resolution tied to NOAA Medium Resolution Shoreline data, providing a replicable, scalable methodology for planning-level financial exposure assessment.

records.title: The Economic and Health Consequences of Climate Change: Testimony of Roy E. Wright to the House Committee on Ways and Means
institutions: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety
records.summary: Congressional testimony arguing that adaptation is a sound fiscal strategy as well as a public health and humanitarian one, and that much severe weather damage is avoidable if the whole building performance chain is addressed: where you build, how you design and construct, and how well you maintain and repair. IBHS is a 501(c)(3) funded by the property insurance industry to produce building safety science, and the testimony sets out three priorities: lead with the roof, solve with research on vulnerability and loss, and prevent avoidable damage. It presses for cost-effective provisions such as the sealed roof deck to be written into model building codes.
insights: The headline return figure cited is the National Institute of Building Sciences finding that federal grants from FEMA, the Economic Development Administration and Housing and Urban Development returned a national benefit of $6 for every $1 invested.

Roof failure is identified as the dominant loss pathway: when roofs fail they trigger water infiltration, projectile damage and destruction of rooftop equipment, accounting for as much as 70 to 90 percent of insured residential losses in some disasters.

The sealed roof deck is offered as the worked example of asymmetric cost and benefit: taping horizontal and vertical joints before underlayment adds several hundred dollars to a roofing installation and can save tens of thousands if the roof cover is blown off.

IBHS's FORTIFIED standard is positioned as a voluntary specification for owners who want resilience beyond the mandatory levels in state and local building codes, and the testimony argues the sealed roof deck requirement should move from voluntary into the codes themselves.

The testimony connects adaptation to emissions without conflating them: the same actions reduce post-disaster debris that overwhelms landfills and the carbon dioxide released when buildings burn, which is offered as a co-benefit rather than a purpose.
records.publisher: Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety

records.title: DC Water: First Ever Environmental Impact Bond
records.summary: The DC Water Environmental Impact Bond represents the first instance of using this innovative financing mechanism to support green infrastructure projects aimed at mitigating combined sewer overflows in Washington, DC. By engaging private investors and linking returns to environmental performance, DC Water sought to improve water management, reduce pollution, and generate community benefits while minimizing taxpayer risk. The successful implementation of the bond led to significant reductions in stormwater runoff and the creation of green spaces, setting a precedent for similar initiatives in other cities.
insights: DC Water implemented the first-ever Environmental Impact Bond to finance green infrastructure.
The bond was issued for $25 million, focusing on projects like permeable pavements and green roofs to address stormwater management.
The bond structure shifted performance risk from the government to private investors, reinforcing a pay-for-success model.
The project aimed to reduce combined sewer overflows significantly, improving water quality in local rivers and the Chesapeake Bay.
The bond's success resulted in the creation of new green spaces, enhancing community health and providing workforce development opportunities.
Upon achieving targeted metrics, the bond facilitated scaling up green infrastructure investments, potentially avoiding costly gray infrastructure solutions.
The Environmental Impact Bond not only tackled environmental goals but also engaged community stakeholders by creating visible benefits.
The National Green Infrastructure Certification Program emerged as part of workforce development efforts linked to the green infrastructure projects.
The success of the DC Water EIB has encouraged other cities to explore similar outcomes-based financing models for various infrastructure challenges.
The project demonstrated the potential of integrating financial innovation with environmental stewardship to deliver broad societal benefits.

records.title: Forecast-Based Financing: A New Era for the Humanitarian System
institutions: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC)
Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre
records.summary: The brochure explains Forecast-based Financing (FbF), the Red Cross Red Crescent approach that releases humanitarian funding for pre-agreed early actions when a weather or climate forecast crosses a defined trigger threshold. Each national society sets out its triggers, actions and responsibilities in an Early Action Protocol, and a dedicated fund, Forecast-based Action, allocates money automatically once a trigger activates. A Bangladesh case study shows cash transfers delivered before the July 2017 Bogra flood. It reports that 16 national societies are piloting FbF and invites donors to contribute to the fund.
insights: FbF releases funding automatically when a forecast reaches a pre-defined threshold, solving the problem that humanitarian money is generally available only after a disaster.
The German Red Cross began the first FbF pilots in 2013; the Movement has worked on the approach since 2007 and 16 national societies are now involved.
In Bogra, Bangladesh, the Early Action Protocol activated seven days before the July 2017 flood and 20 staff and 100 volunteers distributed cash to 1,039 families in four communities.
One recipient received approximately EUR 50, used it to evacuate and feed her cows, and avoided a high-interest loan; FbF households took new loans less often than comparison households.
The Forecast-based Action fund sits alongside the IFRC Disaster Relief Emergency Fund, established in 1985, which can release funds within 24 hours.

records.title: State of California Tackles Drought with IoT & Blockchain
records.summary: The State of California is addressing groundwater sustainability challenges through a collaboration involving The Freshwater Trust, IBM Research, and SweetSense Inc. This initiative utilizes blockchain technology and IoT sensors to monitor and manage groundwater use in real-time, enabling transparent tracking and trading of water usage shares. The project aims to support farmers and other stakeholders in achieving sustainable groundwater practices while responding to the requirements of the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act.
insights: The project is a partnership between The Freshwater Trust, IBM Research, and SweetSense Inc.
IoT sensors will be used to monitor groundwater usage and transmit data to satellites.
Blockchain technology will provide a transparent and immutable record of groundwater transactions.
Water consumers can trade groundwater shares as needed, helping to optimize resource allocation.
The initiative is aligned with California's Sustainable Groundwater Management Act, aiming for sustainable practices by 2040.
The pilot program will be implemented in the Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta, a crucial water system for the state.
The project leverages previous research and technologies developed for water management in Kenya.
Data from the sensors will aid in decision-making and improve access to sustainable water supplies.
The Freshwater Trust has developed various programs in the basin since 2016 for groundwater and surface water management.

records.title: Assessing the Feasibility of Conducting Social Return on Investment Analyses for “Whole Community” Engagement Activities
records.authors: Liesel Ritchie; Carolyn Kousky; Simone Domingue; Nnenia Campbell; Kathleen Tierney; Jamie Vickery; Brett Lingle
institutions: Wharton Risk Management and Decision Processes Center
Center for the Study of Disasters and Extreme Events
Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety
records.summary: This FEMA-funded study tests whether social return on investment (SROI) methods can value 'whole community' preparedness and resilience-building activities, using Tulsa's Disaster Resilience Network as the case. Through document analysis and interviews with more than three dozen informants in late 2016 and early 2017, it maps inputs, outputs and outcomes for the network's cross-cultural, business and housing councils. It concludes that a true SROI analysis is not feasible in Tulsa at this time, because programs did not collect or retain the needed data and preparedness benefits are hard to value. It recommends funded, independent studies that set data needs in advance, and provides a fourteen-step SROI process for preparedness programs.
insights: A credible SROI study of Tulsa's whole-community activities was judged not feasible because agencies had not collected or retained input and outcome data.
Interviewees identified increased social capital and higher trust as the two key outcomes of whole-community activities, but these could not be quantified.
The report cites Natural Hazards Mitigation Saves: $4 saved per federal dollar (2005), updated to $6 per dollar spent on mitigation (NIBS 2017).
After the 1984 flood, which killed 14, Tulsa relocated 300 homes, created a stormwater department and a stormwater utility fee, and has acquired 1,000 flood-prone properties.
Tulsa holds a Class 2 rating in FEMA's Community Rating System, which significantly lowers residents' flood insurance rates.
Methods for valuing preparedness benefits are less developed than those for mitigation and will require new market valuation studies.

records.title: Financing Third Party Wildfire Damages: Options for Electric Utilities
records.authors: Carolyn Kousky; Katherine Greig; Brett Lingle
records.summary: A Wharton Risk Management and Decision Processes Center report setting out how California's electric utilities could finance third party wildfire damages, written in February 2019 in the aftermath of utility-ignited fires. The report is organised as an options analysis rather than a recommendation. It reviews the financing mechanisms utilities currently use, then examines six disaster risk financing strategies in turn: funded self-insurance, commercial insurance, catastrophe bonds, an industry captive, a risk pool, and recovery bonds. It then addresses layering, that is how those instruments combine into a structure covering different tranches of loss, before turning to the separate question of funding, which it treats as a distinct choice among ratepayers, taxpayers and shareholders. That separation of financing mechanism from funding source is the report's organising distinction: the instruments determine when and how money is available, while the funding question determines who ultimately bears the cost.
insights: The report's structure carries its argument: six financing mechanisms are analysed separately from three funding sources, so the instrument choice and the question of who pays are treated as independent decisions rather than one.

Layering is given its own section, which is the practical point for a risk this large: no single mechanism covers the full loss distribution, so self-insurance, commercial cover, catastrophe bonds, a captive, a pool and recovery bonds occupy different tranches.
An industry captive and a risk pool are both considered, which are the two ways multiple utilities could mutualise a risk none can carry alone.
Recovery bonds appear as a financing mechanism, which is the securitisation of a future ratepayer charge and therefore the instrument that most directly puts the cost on ratepayers.

Third party damages, rather than a utility's own asset losses, is the exposure being financed, which is a liability rather than a property risk and is why conventional catastrophe cover is only part of the answer.

records.title: Catastrophe Bonds: A Primer and Retrospective (Chicago Fed Letter No. 405)
records.summary: Chicago Fed Letter number 405 of 2018, by senior research analyst Andy Polacek, a primer and twenty-year retrospective on the catastrophe bond market. It dates the market's origin to the aftermath of Hurricane Andrew, which struck Florida and the Gulf Coast in 1992 causing $27 billion in damages of which $15.5 billion was insured, was the costliest hurricane to make US landfall at the time, and led to the failure of eight insurance companies while pushing others toward insolvency. Insurers re-evaluated coastal exposure, homeowners' premiums in coastal communities rose markedly, and large insurers and reinsurers initially cut catastrophe exposure, so new capital had to be brought into reinsurance and the industry created the catastrophe bond. The first were issued in 1997, giving insurers access to broader financial markets and offering hedge funds, pension funds and mutual funds a return uncorrelated with other financial instruments in exchange for assuming catastrophe risk. The mechanics are explained through Mariah Re Ltd., issued in November 2010 for American Family Mutual Insurance Co.: a special purpose vehicle sat between investors and the insurer, transferring severe thunderstorm and tornado risk across the US off AFMI's balance sheet, providing up to $100 million of compensation once estimated industry losses exceeded an $825 million attachment point, paying $1 for each additional $1 of covered losses to the limit, with investors receiving a 6.25 per cent annual coupon over a three-year term and their $100 million of principal held in a US Treasury money market fund.
insights: The market's origin story is a capacity story rather than a pricing story: after Hurricane Andrew there was not enough reinsurance capital at any price, so the instrument exists to widen the pool of capital rather than to lower the cost of the existing pool.

Uncorrelated return is the investor-side reason the instrument works, and it is also its fragility: the appeal depends on catastrophe risk staying uncorrelated with financial markets, which is exactly what a systemic climate repricing would break.

Mariah Re is a usefully honest example because the deal failed in practice. Naming the attachment point, the industry-loss trigger and the coupon lets a reader see how an industry-index trigger separates the sponsor's recovery from its own losses.

A Federal Reserve bank publishing a catastrophe bond primer in 2018 is itself evidence about where the instrument sat in official thinking: explained to a policy audience rather than confined to the reinsurance trade.

records.title: RELEASE: Forest Resilience Bond to Help Fund $4.6 Million Restoration Project to Mitigate Wildfire Risk in Tahoe National Forest
records.summary: The Forest Resilience Bond, developed by Blue Forest Conservation with the World Resources Institute, reached its first deployment: a $4.6 million restoration project across 15,000 acres of the North Yuba River watershed in Tahoe National Forest. The structure is the point. Private capital funds the upfront cost of forest restoration today, and multiple beneficiaries share the cost of reimbursing investors over time, on the logic that everyone who gains from forest health contributes a portion. Financing came from The Rockefeller Foundation, the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation, Calvert Impact Capital and CSAA Insurance Group, a mix of philanthropic, impact and insurance capital. The restoration itself uses ecologically based tree thinning, meadow restoration, prescribed burning and invasive species management, all prescribed by the Forest Service, subject to public comment and carried out by existing restoration crews, and designed to reduce severe fire risk, improve watershed health and protect water resources. WRI's Todd Gartner frames the rationale as everyone contributing a little toward forest health so that ecological and economic benefit is realised by all.
insights: This is a worked Benefit to Instrument structure: the diffuse benefits of forest restoration, reduced fire risk, watershed health and water security, are converted into a repayment stream by having multiple beneficiaries share the cost of reimbursing investors.
The capital stack mixes philanthropic, impact and insurance money, and the presence of an insurer among the investors is notable because the insurer is also a beneficiary of reduced wildfire loss.

The restoration is prescribed by the Forest Service and delivered by existing crews, so the instrument finances the timing of public land management rather than substituting for it, which is what makes it replicable.
The bond moved from idea to deployment at $4.6 million over 15,000 acres, which is small enough to be a demonstration and specific enough to price.

records.title: Climate Adaptation Finance and Investment in California
institutions: Harvard University Graduate School of Design
CA Governor's Office of Land Use and Climate Innovation
records.summary: The resource 'Climate Adaptation Finance and Investment in California' discusses innovative financial strategies and investment opportunities to enhance climate resilience in California. It reviews the current landscape of climate adaptation financing, highlights the importance of integrating public and private funding, and stresses community engagement to effectively address climate vulnerabilities. The document outlines various funding mechanisms and frameworks aimed at systematically supporting adaptation initiatives to promote sustainable development while addressing specific climate risks across the state.
insights: California is actively seeking innovative financial solutions to address climate adaptation challenges.
Public-private partnerships play a crucial role in mobilizing funds for climate adaptation projects.
Investment in green infrastructure and technology is critical for enhancing urban resilience.
Community engagement is essential for ensuring that climate adaptation efforts meet local needs and priorities.
Monitoring and evaluation frameworks are necessary to assess the effectiveness of climate adaptation investments.
There is a need for clear policies and guidelines to streamline financing processes for adaptation initiatives.
Data-driven approaches are vital for informing investment decisions and prioritizing adaptation projects.
Equity considerations must be integrated into climate finance strategies to ensure vulnerable communities benefit.

records.title: Flood Risk and the U.S. Housing Market
records.authors: Howard Kunreuther; Susan Wachter; Carolyn Kousky; Michael LaCour-Little
institutions: Wharton Risk Management and Decision Processes Center
University of Pennsylvania (Institute for Urban Research)
records.summary: This working paper describes the US housing market's exposure to flood risk and sets a research agenda. It characterizes flood types and trends, how FEMA maps and catastrophe models assess risk, why homeowners underinsure against floods, and the federal programs that manage flood risk. It then examines how flood risk interacts with mortgage origination, house prices, neighborhood effects and the secondary mortgage market, warning that repetitive flooding could erode loan-to-value ratios and that flood-driven foreclosure risk may come to exceed other sources. It proposes property-specific risk scores, better maps and study of sea level rise effects on credit risk.
insights: Only about 20 percent of homes in areas hit by Hurricane Harvey, and 12 percent in East Baton Rouge Parish in August 2016, had flood insurance.
The NFIP paid $17.7 billion in 2005, more than in its entire prior history, and 2017 was projected at about $20 billion in claims.
More than 80 percent of the 1,743 presidential disaster declarations through 2017 were tied to floods and flood-related events.

A RAND study of New York City found that adopting the 2015 preliminary FIRMs could raise median pre-FIRM premiums from $3,000 to $5,600 (87 percent), cut property values by $10,000 to $100,000 and raise mortgage default rates by 50 percent in some neighborhoods.
Coastal flooding may inundate 2 percent of US homes by 2100, and the authors argue that flood-related foreclosure risk could then exceed other sources of foreclosure risk.
The authors propose structure-specific flood risk scores that could feed risk-based premiums, building codes, land use rules and buyout targeting.

records.title: Innovative Finance for Resilient Infrastructure
records.authors: Trevor Maynard; Lucy Stanbrough; Rebekah Clement; Flemmich Webb; Daniel Stander; Charlotte Acton; Conor Meenan; Jed Scanlon; John Ward; Irena Sekulska; Luke Kemp; David Ren
records.summary: Lloyd's and the UK Centre for Global Disaster Protection, with RMS and Vivid Economics, outline four financial instruments designed to monetise the resilience dividend and so draw investment into resilient infrastructure, chiefly in developing countries. The instruments came out of the Centre's first Innovation Lab, which worked hypothetical case studies with modelled resilience benefits. Two of them, the insurance-linked loan package and the resilience impact bond, are developed further with risk and cash flow modelling. The report argues that insurance premium reductions and donor payments are the cash flows through which resilience benefits can be returned to investors, and that policymakers and donors must fund pilots.
insights: Four instruments are proposed: insurance-linked loan packages, resilience impact bonds, resilience bonds (cat bonds with reduced coupons when resilience measures are implemented) and resilience service companies (ReSCos).
An insurance-linked loan package uses insurance premium savings from risk reduction to offset the loan's interest repayments, and needs only small changes from existing practice.

A resilience impact bond is a pay-for-performance contract in which a donor repays investors according to physical, operational and financial resilience measures delivered, suited to widely spread community benefits such as schools and hospitals.
The ReSCo is modelled on Energy Service Companies: an agent pays upfront for resilience on an insured asset in return for a share of future premium savings, and is untrialled in insurance.
Some studies cited show resilience investment benefits exceeding costs by a ratio of four to one, and the 2017 hurricane season left Dominica with losses of 224% of GDP.
The mechanisms other than the resilience impact bond depend on insurance pricing that fully reflects risk reduction, so insurers must price resilience into premiums for the products to work.

records.title: Procuring Resilience
records.summary: A toolkit treating procurement as an entry point for resilience innovation rather than an obstacle to it, produced by re:focus partners and The Atlas Marketplace from the Procuring Resilience Opportunities project launched in January 2018. Seven cities and eight private sector implementing partners applied three procurement tools already used in large cities to water infrastructure problems in smaller ones: the Request for Ideas, the Competition or Challenge, and the Performance Contract. Its deliberate scope is working inside existing procurement systems rather than reforming procurement law, and its three elements are problem framing, tool selection, and procurement definition.
insights: The performance contract is the financing instrument in the set: a form of agreement where payments are linked to achieving specific pre-stated measurable benchmarks or verified outcomes, which is outcomes-based finance arriving through the procurement door rather than the capital markets door.

The design constraint is what makes this usable: it explicitly declines to reform procurement processes or change state or federal legislative rules, and instead finds what cities can do immediately within their current systems, which is why capacity rather than authority is the selection variable.

Problem framing is treated as the step that determines whether innovation is possible at all: being too prescriptive limits innovation and discourages solutions with wider benefits, so the toolkit works backward from target outcomes, using the Ansari X-Prize as the model.

Tool selection is scored rather than chosen, by questionnaire and scorecard, and assigns a degree of difficulty matched to the problem and to the city's available resources and local implementation capacity.

The seven pilot cities are Anchorage, Camden, El Paso, Gary, Imperial Beach, Norfolk and Providence, which is a deliberate small and mid-sized city cohort rather than the large cities the tools came from.

The implementing partner list is named in full, Quantified Ventures with SCAPE, OptiRTC, Infrashares, RePipe, Meridiam North America, RISE and 120WaterAudit, so the delivery chain for the procurement model is specified rather than implied.

records.title: Financing the Response to Climate Change: The Pricing and Ownership of U.S. Green Bonds
records.authors: Malcolm Baker, Daniel Bergstresser, George Serafeim, Jeffrey Wurgler
records.summary: A study of the United States green bond market, defining green bonds as bonds whose proceeds fund an environmentally sensitive purpose, and testing pricing and ownership predictions from a framework in which some investors derive nonpecuniary utility from holding a security. The sample is 2,083 green US municipal bonds issued 2010 to 2016 and 19 green US corporate bonds issued 2014 to 2016, about $12 billion of par outstanding each at the end of 2016. The findings are that green municipal bonds are issued at a premium to otherwise similar ordinary bonds, that green bonds are more closely held than ordinary bonds, particularly small or nearly riskless ones, and that both effects are strongest for bonds externally certified as green. The subject is mitigation finance rather than resilience or adaptation.
insights: Green municipal bonds are issued at after-tax yields roughly 6 basis points below otherwise equivalent ordinary bonds, controlling for ratings, maturity, the yield curve, tax status and issuer fixed effects. Investors accept a lower return, so the premium is paid by the issuer's benefit rather than earned by the buyer.

CERTIFICATION IS PRICED, AND MORE THAN THE GREEN LABEL IS. Bonds registered with the Climate Bonds Initiative yield 26 basis points below comparable ordinary bonds in the first specification, which the authors note is the yield reduction equivalent to climbing two ratings notches, and still 15 basis points per year with issuer fixed effects and the full control set.

Certification was rare and new in this sample: 11.7 per cent of green municipal bonds carried any third-party certification, most often from Sustainalytics, and only 6.6 per cent of the green sample was registered with the Climate Bonds Initiative. The first third-party certified bonds were issued at the end of 2014 and every CBI-registered bond in the sample was issued in 2016.

The market was small in relative terms: about 2 per cent of new municipal issuance was green in 2016 and about 0.3 per cent of corporate issuance, despite the two segments carrying similar total par outstanding of roughly $12 billion each.

Green is a use-of-proceeds label and not a credit structure, and the data shows the difference: only 14.7 per cent of green municipals are general obligation bonds against 46.8 per cent of ordinary municipals, so a green bond is far more likely to be secured on a specific project's revenue than on the issuer's tax base.

records.title: Adaptation Finance Challenges: Characteristic Patterns Facing California Local Governments and Ways to Overcome Them
records.authors: Susanne C. Moser, Julia A. Ekstrom, Julia Kim, Samantha Heitsch
records.summary: The resource outlines the significant challenges California local governments face in accessing adaptation finance for climate resilience initiatives. It identifies barriers such as limited funding, bureaucratic hurdles, insufficient technical capacity, and governance complexities, while suggesting strategies like collaboration, community engagement, innovative financing mechanisms, and capacity building to enhance local resilience against climate impacts.
insights: Local governments struggle with securing adequate funding for climate adaptation due to bureaucratic complexities and inconsistent resource availability.
Community engagement and stakeholder inclusivity are critical for the success of adaptation initiatives and for garnering public support.
Collaboration among different governmental levels and sectors can enhance resource mobilization and improve access to adaptation finance.
Capacity building within local governments is essential for effectively managing adaptation projects and navigating funding landscapes.
Innovative financing mechanisms, including public-private partnerships, can unlock additional resources for climate adaptation efforts.

records.title: The Emerging Private Residential Flood Insurance Market in the United States
records.authors: Carolyn Kousky; Howard Kunreuther; Brett Lingle; Leonard Shabman
records.summary: A Wharton Risk Center report on the emerging private residential flood insurance market in the United States, written when private flood cover was beginning to grow alongside the National Flood Insurance Program. The report maps residential flood insurance as it then stood: an overview of private flood insurance, background on the NFIP, the size and shape of the flood insurance gap, and the market's structure. Its structural analysis is the substantive contribution, distinguishing admitted carriers from the excess and surplus lines market, examining how policies are distributed, and treating reinsurance as a determinant of how much private capacity exists. The framing question throughout is what role private capital can play in a market where a federal programme has been the dominant writer for decades, and what the growth of private cover implies for the NFIP, for policyholders and for the gap between those who hold flood insurance and those exposed to flood risk.
insights: The admitted versus excess and surplus distinction is the analytical core, because a surplus lines policy is not subject to the same rate and form regulation, which is what allows private carriers to price flood risk where admitted carriers will not.
Reinsurance is treated as the determinant of private capacity, so the availability of residential flood cover depends on a market most policyholders never see.
The report is a 2018 baseline of a market that has since changed substantially, which makes it most useful as the reference point for measuring how far private flood cover has actually grown.
Distribution is analysed separately from underwriting, which matters because a flood policy that exists but is not offered through the channels homeowners use does not close the gap.

records.title: Natural Hazard Mitigation Saves Interim Report
records.summary: The 'Natural Hazard Mitigation Saves Interim Report' emphasizes the critical benefits of investing in natural hazard mitigation, demonstrating how proactive measures significantly reduce disaster-related damages and costs. By showcasing compelling data and case studies, the report argues for early investments in mitigation as a strategic approach to enhancing community resilience and achieving substantial long-term savings, with every federal dollar spent on mitigation reportedly saving an average of $6 in avoided losses.
insights: Natural hazard mitigation leads to significant long-term cost savings, with every dollar spent saving multiple dollars in avoided damages.
Investments in mitigation enhance community resilience and improve public safety, contributing to fewer disaster-related fatalities.
Historical data supports that proactive investments in hazard mitigation yield economic benefits that exceed their costs.
Mitigation strategies tailored to local conditions improve the effectiveness of resilience efforts and community engagement.
Data-driven decision-making is essential for maximizing the impact of hazard mitigation projects and ensuring sustained investment.

records.title: Climate Resilience 2018 Handbook
records.authors: David Batchelor, Joel Makower, Lucy Nottingham, Jaclyn Yeo, Michael Lierow, Sirko Siemssem, Cornelia Neumann, Andreea Achimescu, Bob Orr, Eric Nelsen, Geoff Murray, Bjoern Maul, John Davies, Jane Ambachtsheer, John Colas, Ilya Khaykin, Alban Pyanet, Peter Reynolds, Gaurav Kwatra, Alex Bernhardt, Charles Whitmore, Thomas London, Robert Wykoff, Amal-Lee Amin, Benjamin Chee, Chantale LaCasse, Tom Markovic, Ellen Charnley, Melita Simic, Bev Adams, Duncan Ellis
institutions: Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures
records.summary: The inaugural Marsh & McLennan Companies Climate Resilience Handbook collects twenty short articles from Marsh, Guy Carpenter, Mercer and Oliver Wyman in three sections: strategies for climate resilience, financing for climate resilience, and risk management for climate resilience. The financing section is the substantive core, covering TCFD scenario analysis for banks, the mitigation skew of a green bond market of nearly $900 billion set against the adaptation financing deficit, public private flood pools such as Flood Re, sovereign and corporate disaster risk financing, credit enhancement to close a green financing gap estimated at $2.5 trillion to $4.8 trillion, and the World Bank Pilot Auction Facility's pay for performance price guarantees. The risk management section adds captive insurers used to fund climate exposures, gaps in Director and Officer cover as climate litigation begins, and satellite and drone imagery for post event loss assessment. The financing section reprints a 2017 standalone collection.
insights: UNEP puts the annual climate adaptation investment requirement at $56 to $76 billion in 2015, rising to $140 to $300 billion by 2030, roughly $1.5 to $3 trillion over fifteen years, yet only 3 to 5 percent of green bond issuance has been tied to an adaptation project and all of it sits in the water sector.

Labelled green bonds stood at $221 billion outstanding in 2017, with a further $674 billion identified as climate aligned by the Climate Bonds Initiative for a market of nearly $900 billion, and the vast majority of the projects financed pursue mitigation rather than adaptation.

The green financing gap is estimated at $2.5 trillion to $4.8 trillion and is attributed largely to inadequate risk adjusted returns rather than to a shortage of capital, which is why credit enhancement and de risking instruments are offered as the remedy.

The UK's Flood Re pool is backed by a GBP 2.1 billion multi-year reinsurance programme and is expected to benefit an estimated 350,000 high flood risk homeowners, and is presented as the worked example of a public private risk transfer mechanism.

Sovereign catastrophe risk transfer is established rather than experimental: Mexico's cat bond covered US$160 million across three regions, and CCRIF operates as a regional catastrophe fund letting Caribbean governments limit fiscal exposure.

A one percent rise in insurance penetration is associated with a 13 percent reduction in total uninsured losses, a 22 percent reduction in taxpayer contribution following a disaster, and additional investment equivalent to one percent of national GDP.

Insurance covers an estimated 40 percent of catastrophic losses in developed countries, and of the record 2017 catastrophe year US$133 billion was insured, with the remainder falling on public and private balance sheets.

records.title: Using Simulations to Forecast Homeowner Response to Sea Level Rise in South Florida: Will They Stay or Will They Go?
records.authors: Galen Treuer; Kenneth Broad; Robert Meyer
records.summary: A paper in Global Environmental Change by Galen Treuer and Kenneth Broad of the University of Miami with Robert Meyer of the University of Pennsylvania, using simulations to forecast how South Florida homeowners will respond to sea level rise, and asking whether they stay or go. It is a behavioural study of the decision that sits underneath every property-market projection in a subsiding coastal market: what an owner actually does as flooding becomes more frequent, rather than what a discounted-cash-flow model says the property is worth.
insights: The homeowner decision is the link the paper models rather than assumes: it simulates how owners respond to risk information instead of inferring the response from property market outcomes.

Stay or go is not a binary in financing terms: an owner who stays but stops maintaining, or who cannot sell, produces a different credit outcome from one who leaves, and the simulation approach is what lets those paths be separated before the data exists.
South Florida is the test bed, chosen because the exposure is severe and the market is liquid enough for the simulated responses to be observable.
The article is paywalled, so the version of record for any quotation is the cached text rather than the publisher's page.

records.title: Miami Forever Bond
institutions: City of Miami Office of Capital Improvements
records.summary: The Miami Forever Bond is a $400 million general obligation bond approved in 2017 to fund citywide infrastructure and resilience projects over 30 years. It finances stormwater system upgrades, seawall repairs, wetland restoration, park improvements, affordable housing, urban tree canopy expansion, road and sidewalk elevations, water quality enhancements and equitable community initiatives to address sea-level rise and flooding.
insights: The bond is executed in three phases, Immediate Impact, Gain Momentum and Long Term Solutions, with a first tranche of $58.7 million across more than 100 ready projects, so the programme is structured around deployment capacity rather than around a single capital raise.

Tranche one is split into Series A for infrastructure, including sea-level rise and flood prevention, and Series B for affordable housing, which puts resilience and housing inside one general obligation instrument.

The Gain Momentum phase is explicitly a capacity assessment, addressing whether the city can deliver 100 projects in three years, and names alternative procurement methods and a risk management plan as the response.

The long-term phase commits to refining the project selection model from lessons learned and to updating zoning, planning and building standards so new development maximises resilience benefits, which is a regulatory output funded by a bond.
A city commission appointed civilian oversight board is named as part of the financial monitoring and reporting, which is the accountability structure attached to the instrument.

records.title: A Guide for Public-Sector Resilience Bond Sponsorship: Insuring for Resilience
records.summary: A practical guide for public-sector sponsors of resilience bonds, the second phase of the RE.bound Program, which in its first phase assembled insurance industry collaborators to validate the concept of a new class of bonds built on catastrophe bond structures. It sets out the building blocks of resilience bonds, the bond structure, why governments should look to insurance for resilience finance, and a sample bond design, then gives guidance on whether a resilience bond is a good fit and three entry points to insuring for resilience. Five worked opportunities follow, organised by structure: re:issue for wind and earthquake, re:balance for transit systems and flood protections, and re:align for small islands and urban slums.
insights: THE CORE MECHANISM IS THE REBATE: a resilience bond is a catastrophe bond whose pricing reflects the risk reduction delivered by a resilience project, so the premium saving becomes a funding source for the project itself.

The report names three distinct structures rather than one product, and the names describe the mechanism: re:issue where an existing cat bond is reissued at a lower price after a project, re:balance where risk transfer and risk reduction are traded off in one portfolio, and re:align where the sponsor and the beneficiary are different parties.

The framing argument is fiscal: governments are insurers of last resort and bear disaster costs whether or not they buy cover, so insurance pricing is already implicitly on the public balance sheet and a resilience bond makes it explicit.

The five opportunities are deliberately unlike each other, spanning wind, earthquake, transit systems, flood protections and small islands with urban slums, which is how the report tests whether the structure generalises beyond coastal flood.

The report is careful to state what it is not: it contemplates no specific financial transaction and endorses no specific instrument, a disclaimer that travels with any claim taken from the sample bond design.
This is phase 2 of a two-phase programme; the phase 1 output, Leveraging Catastrophe Bonds as a Mechanism for Resilient Infrastructure Finance of December 2015, is a separate document.

records.title: Resilience Dividend Valuation Model: Framework Development and Initial Case Studies
records.authors: Craig A. Bond; Aaron Strong; Nicholas Burger; Sarah Weilant; Uzaib Saya; Anita Chandra
records.summary: A 2017 RAND Corporation report, developing the Resilience Dividend Valuation Model in partnership with the Rockefeller Foundation, with six case studies selected jointly by the two organisations. Its starting complaint is precise: policymakers, practitioners and investors who want the greatest benefit from the resilience projects they support lack effective tools to estimate net benefits, and quantification has instead relied on indices and scorecards in which indicators assumed to correlate with resilience are measured and aggregated. Those indices, the authors argue, may be useful once validated but say nothing about the value of a resilience investment, which is what a decision-maker needs to make an evidence-based choice consistent with maximising social welfare. The report defines the resilience dividend as the difference in net benefits between the outcome of a resilience project and business as usual, meaning no project at all, and presents a conceptual modelling framework for evaluating that difference in a decision-analysis setting. It is written for practitioners, analysts and researchers to use in conceptualising systems and interventions in a structural economic framework and in planning the data collection and modelling needed to estimate parts of the dividend.
insights: The distinction between an index and a valuation is the whole argument: a resilience score cannot be financed, a net benefit can, and the model exists to produce the second rather than the first.

Defining the dividend against business as usual rather than against a counterfactual project is a strong and contestable choice. It makes the dividend large and it makes it hard to attribute, because the comparison is with doing nothing rather than with the next best use of the money.
The authors are explicit that the framework lets a user estimate parts of the dividend, not the whole, which is an honest boundary and the reason the model has not displaced scorecards in practice.
The report is a RAND and Rockefeller Foundation product and is the first-party statement of the resilience-dividend framework, rather than a description of it.

records.title: Financing for Climate Resilience
records.authors: Jane Ambachtsheer, John Colas, Ilya Khaykin, Alban Pyanet, Peter Reynolds, Gaurav Kwatra, Alex Bernhardt, Charles Whitmore, Jaclyn Yeo, Thomas London, Robert Wykoff, Amal-Lee Amin
records.summary: The excerpt highlights the critical need for green financing, which is essential for building resilient organizations and societies against climate change. With a significant financing gap estimated between $2.5 trillion to $4.8 trillion, greater collaboration between public and private sectors is required to close this gap and effectively support sustainable investment and climate resilience initiatives following the 2015 Paris Climate Agreement.
insights: The global green financing gap is estimated at $2.5 trillion to $4.8 trillion.
Sustainable investment increased by 25% from 2014 to 2016, reaching $23 trillion.
Closing the green financing gap is crucial for meeting sustainable development goals.
Collaboration between public and private sectors is necessary to mobilize private capital.
Efficient fund transmission to green projects is key to addressing climate challenges.
Organizations face challenges in financing climate resilience and sustainable growth.
Expert insights from Marsh & McLennan Companies highlight barriers to financing flows.
The 2018 Climate Resilience Handbook aims to provide strategies for financing resilience.

records.title: Does Federal Disaster Assistance Crowd out Flood Insurance?
records.authors: Carolyn Kousky, Erwann O. Michel-Kerjan, Paul A. Raschky
records.summary: This peer-reviewed empirical study (Journal of Environmental Economics and Management, 2018) provides the first causal estimates of whether U.S. federal disaster aid crowds out household flood insurance purchases. Using a ZIP-code-level panel of NFIP policies (2000–2011) combined with FEMA Individual Assistance grant and SBA disaster loan data, the authors employ fixed-effects and instrumental variable models, instrumenting for aid using politically motivated variation in disaster declarations tied to swing counties and presidential election years. They find that receiving IA grants reduces average flood insurance coverage per policy by $4,000–$5,000 (roughly 3% of mean coverage), while SBA loans have no crowding-out effect. The insurance purchase requirement attached to IA grants prevents declines in take-up rates.
insights: Receiving FEMA Individual Assistance grants reduces average flood insurance coverage per policy by $4,000–$5,000 in IV models, equivalent to roughly 3% of mean policy-level coverage ($151,716), and exceeds the average IA grant size of $2,984, implying the behavioral response to aid outweighs its dollar value.

Crowding out occurs on the intensive margin (coverage amounts) but not the extensive margin (take-up rates); the federal requirement that IA recipients purchase flood insurance appears effective at maintaining take-up levels, a policy lever directly relevant to NFIP solvency.

A $1,000 increase in the average IA grant reduces average coverage by approximately $1,600 per policy (IV model), suggesting a non-linear, amplified behavioral response, coverage reduction exceeds the grant increment received.

SBA low-interest disaster loans (up to $200,000 for homeowners) show no systematic crowding-out effect and may have a small crowding-in effect, likely because loans must be repaid, preserving the incentive to insure.

Presidential disaster declarations increased from 15–20/year in the 1950s to ~60/year in the 2000s, peaking at 99 in 2011; two-thirds are flood-related, and federal relief for the 2005 hurricane season covered roughly 70% of total estimated damages, illustrating the fiscal exposure dynamic the paper quantifies.

The IV strategy exploits politically motivated aid variation: Garrett and Sobel (2003) found federal disaster relief averages $140 million higher in election years; this exogenous variation isolates causal effects on insurance demand and is applicable to future research on public-private risk transfer.

NFIP covered $1.278 trillion in assets and collected $3.2 billion in premiums in 2011; any systematic crowding-out of coverage by federal aid directly undermines program revenue and increases taxpayer exposure to uninsured flood losses.
records.publisher: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

records.title: Small Cities with Big-City Infrastructure Problems: Three Case Studies in Stormwater Infrastructure Innovation
institutions: New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection
records.summary: This report documents Build it Green, a 2016 to 2017 technical assistance program that helped three New Jersey cities (Gloucester, Perth Amboy and Jersey City) design and fund integrated infrastructure projects addressing combined sewer overflows alongside other local priorities. It argues that small cities face big-city infrastructure problems without big-city capacity, and that integrated projects unlock nontraditional funding and financing, create near-term political wins and foster cross-sector collaboration. Each case study sets out the design, funding and implementation route recommended, from EDA predevelopment grants in Gloucester to NJEIT low-interest loans with principal forgiveness in Perth Amboy and catastrophe modeling to attract private finance for coastal protection in Jersey City.
insights: More than 800 US communities have combined sewer systems, and New Jersey has 21, whose 2015 NJDEP permits require significant and largely unfunded CSO reductions.

For Perth Amboy's 2nd Street Greenway the team recommended NJEIT as the primary funder, using its low-interest loans and the maximum principal forgiveness available for green infrastructure, plus NJDOT TAP grants of up to $1 million per project.
In Gloucester, the federal EDA was identified as a predevelopment and later construction funder, with its usual 50% local match met by assembling cash and in-kind commitments from local redevelopers.

For Mill Creek in Jersey City, a Hurricane Sandy storm surge path, the team concluded that financial catastrophe modeling is a prerequisite to attracting private capital for integrated coastal protection and CSO mitigation.
The report recommends best-value rather than least-cost bid evaluation that counts lifetime operations and maintenance costs, so green infrastructure is not disadvantaged by higher capital cost.

records.title: Coastal Wetlands and Flood Damage Reduction: Using Risk Industry-Based Models to Assess Natural Defenses in the Northeastern USA
records.authors: Siddharth Narayan, Michael W. Beck, Paul Wilson, Christopher Thomas, Alexandra Guerrero, Christine Shepard, Borja G. Reguero, Guillermo Franco, Jane Carter Ingram, Dania Trespalacios
institutions: Center for Coastal Climate Resilience at UC Santa Cruz
records.summary: The study highlights the economic benefits of coastal wetlands in reducing flood damage during Hurricane Sandy, estimating that these natural defenses saved over $625 million in property damages across the northeastern USA. It emphasizes the crucial role that wetland conservation and restoration can play in managing flood risks, particularly as coastal areas become increasingly vulnerable to severe weather events due to climate change.
insights: Coastal wetlands reduced Hurricane Sandy-related property damages by an estimated $625 million.
In New Jersey alone, wetlands prevented approximately $425 million in flooding damages.
Coastal wetlands can reduce average annual flood losses by over 20% for properties located behind them.
The benefits of wetlands in reducing damage vary significantly by state, with Maryland experiencing up to a 29% reduction.
Wetlands were found to have cumulative benefits across different townships, providing flood protection even in areas with few remaining wetlands.
During Hurricane Sandy, coastal wetlands contributed to more than a 10% reduction in property damages in census tracts where they existed.
Wetlands can sometimes increase flooding in areas directly in front of them by blocking water flow, similar to the effects of man-made barriers.
The study underscores the importance of integrating natural defenses like wetlands into risk management and insurance industry models.
Loss of wetlands due to urban development significantly heightens flood risks for surrounding communities.
Incorporating the protective value of wetlands into financial models can promote conservation and enhance coastal resilience strategies.

records.title: ‘Climate Value at Risk’ of Global Financial Assets
records.authors: Simon Dietz, Alex Bowen, Charlie Dixon, Philip Gradwell
records.summary: This 2016 Nature Climate Change letter by Dietz, Bowen, Dixon, and Gradwell introduces "climate value at risk" (climate VaR) as a framework for estimating the impact of 21st-century climate change on the present market value of global financial assets. Using a Monte Carlo simulation of an extended DICE integrated assessment model, the authors find an expected climate VaR of 1.8% (US$2.5 trillion) under business-as-usual emissions, rising to 16.9% (US$24.2 trillion) at the 99th percentile. Limiting warming to 2°C reduces expected climate VaR by 0.6 percentage points and makes financial assets worth an expected 0.2% more in present value terms including mitigation costs.
insights: Expected climate VaR of global financial assets under business-as-usual is 1.8% (US$2.5 trillion based on a US$143.3 trillion asset base); the 99th percentile risk is 16.9% or US$24.2 trillion, a tail risk exceeding the estimated US$5 trillion total market cap of fossil-fuel companies.

Limiting warming to 2°C reduces expected climate VaR by 0.6 percentage points and the 99th percentile by 7.7 percentage points, demonstrating that mitigation is disproportionately valuable for tail-risk reduction rather than mean-loss reduction.

Including mitigation costs, global financial assets have an expected present value 0.2% higher under a 2°C scenario than BAU, but ~65% of the simulated distribution shows BAU outperforming in PV terms, reflecting near-term drag from abatement costs (including stranded fossil-fuel assets).

Most climate VaR accrues in the second half of the century; applying a high 7% discount rate cuts expected climate VaR to 1.0% (99th percentile 7.7%), illustrating how discount rate choice is a first-order lever for whether institutional investors price long-dated climate risk.

Climate sensitivity is the single most important parameter driving expected climate VaR, followed by TFP growth rate, with the curvature of the damage function least important, guidance for risk modelers on where to focus uncertainty reduction efforts.

The framework assumes current financial asset prices do not incorporate climate forecasts, making these estimates a measure of potential asset-price corrections rather than additional losses on top of already-repriced assets, relevant for ratings agencies and stress-testers.

Tail climate risk is structurally unhedgeable: global incidence of impacts, long required holding periods, and irreversibility (no reversion to prior trend growth path) mean standard portfolio diversification cannot eliminate the exposure.

records.title: An Imperfect Storm: Fat-Tailed Hurricane Damages, Insurance, and Climate Policy
records.authors: Marc N. Conte; David L. Kelly
records.summary: A working paper by Marc N. Conte of Fordham and David L. Kelly of the University of Miami, dated 2 February 2016, on whether aggregate US hurricane damages are fat tailed and what that means for insurance and climate policy. Two tests reject the hypothesis that the damage distribution is thin tailed at the 95 per cent confidence level, even after correcting for inflation, population and per capita income growth, and the point estimates of the shape parameter indicate a distribution with finite mean but infinite variance. The second half develops a microfoundations model of insurance and storm size that generates the fat tail, and identifies its source: the distribution of the number of properties within a random geographical area lying in a hurricane's path. The authors confirm that the distribution of US coastal city population is itself fat tailed, and show both empirically and theoretically that other random variation, including the distribution of hurricane strength and the distribution of damages across individual properties, does not generate fat tails. They then consider climate mitigation, policies encouraging adaptation, reducing subsidies for coastal development, and disaster relief policies that distort insurance markets.
insights: The policy conclusion is the sharpest thing in the paper and it is uncomfortable: such policies can reduce the thickness of the tail but do not affect the shape parameter or the existence of the fat tail. Adaptation and subsidy reform change the scale of catastrophe, not its character, so an instrument that needs a finite variance to price will never get one.

Locating the fat tail in the spatial distribution of exposed properties rather than in hurricane intensity is a structural finding with an obvious corollary: the tail is a land-use artifact, so the lever is where building happens rather than how strong storms get.
Infinite variance is the technical reason catastrophe risk resists ordinary insurance pricing, and the paper establishes it for US hurricanes specifically rather than in the abstract.
The same two authors published a 2021 Annual Review survey of fat tails in environmental economics; this working paper is the hurricane-specific result rather than the general treatment.
Disaster relief is named as a distortion of insurance markets rather than as a backstop, so public post-event spending is modelled here as part of the pricing problem rather than as its remedy.

records.title: Lessons from U.S. Coastal Wind Pools About Climate Finance and Politics
institutions: Boston College Environmental Affairs Law Review
University of North Carolina School of Law
records.summary: This resource discusses the experiences and insights gained from U.S. Coastal Wind Pools to inform better practices in climate finance and the associated political landscape. Through analysis, it highlights the interplay between financial strategies and political actions in addressing climate-related challenges.
insights: U.S. Coastal Wind Pools provide a framework for understanding localized climate finance mechanisms.
Political dynamics play a crucial role in the success of climate finance initiatives.
Collaboration among stakeholders is essential for effective climate action.
Financial strategies must be adaptable to changing environmental conditions.
Lessons learned from wind pools can inform future resilience financing approaches.
Public policy can significantly influence investment in climate-resilient projects.
Evaluating stakeholder interests helps identify potential barriers to effective financing.
Transparency in funding allocations enhances trust and engagement among communities.
records.publisher: University of North Carolina School of Law

records.title: NDC Partnership
records.summary: The NDC Partnership is a global coalition aimed at accelerating climate action by supporting countries in implementing their Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement. With over 260 members, including countries and institutions, it mobilizes tailored support for developing countries to enhance their climate and development efforts. The partnership emphasizes coordinated resources, collective impact, and the integration of climate ambitions into national agendas.
insights: The NDC Partnership was established in 2016 to address the implementation of the Paris Agreement.
It has more than 260 members, including developed and developing countries as well as various institutions.
The partnership has mobilized over USD 1.8 billion in technical assistance and capacity building support.
Countries define their needs, and the partnership coordinates tailored support from its members.
The NDC Partnership focuses on supporting three key pathways: implementation, finance, and ambition.
The partnership serves as a neutral broker to facilitate resource deployment and best practice sharing.
It recognizes the diverse needs of its members and tailors support accordingly.
The governance structure includes Co-Chairs and a Steering Committee for strategic guidance.
The aim is to ensure that support aligns with national priorities to improve efficiency and effectiveness.
The NDC Partnership plays a crucial role in linking climate action with sustainable development goals.

records.title: Leveraging Catastrophe Bonds as a Mechanism for Resilient Infrastructure Project Finance
records.summary: Leveraging Catastrophe Bonds as a Mechanism for Resilient Infrastructure Project Finance, the December 2015 report of the RE.bound Program, an initiative of re:focus partners led by Shalini Vajjhala and James Rhodes as principal investigators and lead authors and funded by the Rockefeller Foundation, with RMS and Swiss Re as collaborating organisations. It runs under the programme's standing header, Insuring for Resilience. re:focus partners describes itself as a design firm developing integrated resilience solutions and innovative public-private partnerships for vulnerable communities, and identifying systemic opportunities to create both public value and new private investment potential through projects with sound financial returns and economic, social and environmental integrity. The report is the concept paper for using catastrophe bond structures to finance resilient infrastructure rather than only to transfer post-event loss.
insights: The move the report makes is to run a catastrophe bond backwards: instead of paying out after a loss, the structure prices the loss the project will prevent, so the premium saving becomes the project's revenue.

The collaborator list is the argument's credibility: a risk modeller and a reinsurer alongside a design firm and a foundation, which is the exact set of parties needed to price avoided loss and then sell it.

records.title: RE.invest Initiative
records.summary: This page describes the RE.invest Initiative, launched by re:focus partners in January 2013 with a $3 million Rockefeller Foundation grant, which worked for two years (to March 2015) with eight US partner cities to develop design and finance strategies for resilient infrastructure. The team, with Bechtel, Akin Gump and Wall Street Without Walls, aimed to aggregate cross-sector priority projects in water, communications, energy and transportation into portfolios that could attract large-scale, long-term private investment through public-private partnerships. It sets out six solution concepts that combine project elements to capture multiple revenue streams, and points to the Rockefeller and RAND Resilience Dividend Valuation Model as applied in Hoboken.
insights: The initiative was funded by a $3 million Rockefeller Foundation grant awarded in January 2013 and concluded in March 2015.
Eight partner cities were chosen by national competition: El Paso, Hoboken, Honolulu, Miami Beach, Milwaukee, New Orleans, Norfolk and San Francisco.
re:park combines stormwater retention with underground parking so that water rates and parking fees form two linked revenue streams.
re:pave repays private investors who provide upfront capital for street-level green infrastructure out of street parking revenues.
re:inforce proposes collective seawall and natural infrastructure upgrades by private owners, repaid over time through property value increases and insurance savings.
The Rockefeller Foundation defines the resilience dividend as the difference in value between a resilience approach and business as usual.

records.title: The Triple Dividend of Resilience: Realising Development Goals Through the Multiple Benefits of Disaster Risk Management
records.authors: Thomas Tanner; Swenja Surminski; Emily Wilkinson; Robert Reid; Jun Rentschler; Sumati Rajput
institutions: Global Facility for Disaster Reduction and Recovery
records.summary: The Triple Dividend of Resilience, subtitled Realising development goals through the multiple benefits of disaster risk management, a 2015 report produced jointly by the Overseas Development Institute and the World Bank through GFDRR, by Thomas Tanner, Swenja Surminski, Emily Wilkinson, Robert Reid, Jun Rentschler and Sumati Rajput. It is the source document for the triple dividend framing: that disaster risk management delivers avoided losses when a hazard strikes, unlocked economic potential from reduced background risk even when no hazard strikes, and development co-benefits from the investment itself. The argument reframes disaster risk management from a cost incurred against a probability into an investment with returns that accrue whether or not the disaster happens, which is what makes the second and third dividends the important ones.
insights: The second dividend is the one that matters for financing and the one most often dropped when the phrase is quoted: reduced background risk unlocks economic activity that would not otherwise happen, so the return does not depend on the hazard occurring. An instrument that only pays on a trigger captures the first dividend and leaves the second on the table.
Swenja Surminski is among the co-authors, which places the framework in the same body of insurance and resilience work as her later writing on risk transfer.
records.publisher: Global Facility for Disaster Reduction and Recovery

records.title: Floodplain Conservation as a Flood Mitigation Strategy: Examining Costs and Benefits
records.summary: This 2014 peer-reviewed study by Resources for the Future evaluates the costs and benefits of floodplain conservation as a flood damage reduction strategy, using the Meramec Greenway in St. Louis County, Missouri as a case study. Using FEMA's Hazus-MH model at the parcel level and a hedonic property value model, the authors estimate annual avoided flood damages of $7.7 million, an annual opportunity cost of $17.2 million, and annual proximity benefits capitalized in home prices of ~$23 million for ~9,000 acres of protected floodplain. The proximity benefits alone exceed opportunity costs, and are more than three times the avoided flood damages.
insights: Average annual avoided flood damages from the Meramec Greenway (9,000 acres protected) are estimated at $7.7 million/year using parcel-level Hazus-MH modeling; without the Greenway, annual flood damages in St. Louis County's Meramec floodplain would be ~59% higher.

Annual opportunity cost of the conserved floodplain lands is $17.2 million (based on $344M total present value annualized at 5% in perpetuity), meaning avoided flood damages alone offset only ~45% of opportunity costs, flood risk reduction alone does not justify the investment.

Hedonic model finds every 1,000 ft closer to a protected area raises home sale price by ~1% (~$2,156 for a median-priced home); aggregated across 36,000+ proximate parcels, this yields ~$352.6M in total capitalized value, or ~$22.9M/year, more than three times the avoided flood damage estimate and exceeding opportunity costs.

Spatial distribution of flood risk is highly skewed: 50% of protected parcels have an average annual loss per acre below $6,407, while the top 10% exceed $52,583/acre, demonstrating that targeted parcel selection could substantially improve the cost-effectiveness of floodplain conservation for flood mitigation specifically.

100-year flood damages to counterfactual development (2,075 hypothetical single-family homes on 2,178 protected acres) are estimated at $103.6 million in a single event, providing a tangible worst-case exposure figure for capital allocators evaluating floodplain development risk.

The analysis illustrates that floodplain conservation co-benefits (recreation, aesthetics, proximity value) are substantially larger than pure flood-risk-reduction benefits in this setting, suggesting that flood mitigation framing alone understates the full return and that multi-benefit funding coalitions (FEMA grants + parks + water quality funds) could unlock greater combined value.

records.title: Building Resilience : Integrating Climate and Disaster Risk into Development
records.summary: The World Bank's resource on integrating climate and disaster risk into development underscores the urgent need for building climate resilience to mitigate poverty and foster prosperity. It argues for proactive investments and effective strategies that interconnect climate change and development challenges, emphasizing the importance of financial frameworks, stakeholder engagement, and institutional coordination. The resource supports its arguments with case studies and stresses the necessity of collaboration among various stakeholders to enhance resilience and manage risks effectively.
insights: Investments in climate resilience can yield long-term benefits, despite higher initial costs.
Vulnerable populations face the greatest risks from climate-related disasters, exacerbating poverty and inequality.
Proactive measures such as early warning systems have proven effective in saving lives and reducing disaster impacts.
