Collaboration among stakeholders, including government, communities, and the private sector, is essential for effective climate resilience planning.
Predictable financing over extended periods is required to build effective resilience programs.

records.title: MetroCat Re Ltd. (Series 2013-1): The First Storm Surge Catastrophe Bond
records.summary: The Artemis deal directory entry for MetroCat Re Ltd. (Series 2013-1), the first catastrophe bond written purely on storm surge. The cedent is First Mutual Transportation Assurance Co., the New York State-licensed captive insurer and subsidiary of the New York Metropolitan Transportation Authority; MetroCat Re Ltd. is a Bermuda special purpose insurer issuing a single tranche that collateralises a reinsurance agreement with FMTAC. Size $200 million against a preliminary $125 million, issued July 2013, three years of per-occurrence cover, parametric trigger, rated BB minus by S&P, with GC Securities as lead manager, joint structuring agent and sole bookrunner and Goldman Sachs as co-senior manager and joint structuring agent, and RMS as risk modeller. The trigger is recorded storm surge height: an event index of 8.5 feet or more for Area A, the tidal gauges at The Battery, Sandy Hook and Rockaway Inlet, or 15.5 feet or more for Area B, East Creek and Kings Point. S&P reports that RMS data make The Battery and Kings Point the gauges most correlated with MTA exposure, and those were the two areas whose flooding entered subway and transit tunnels under Sandy, so they carry the highest weighting. On trigger the payment is 100 per cent of outstanding principal with no sliding scale. Cover is limited to named storms that were tropical cyclones, tropical storms or hurricanes at some point, so extra-tropical systems such as the Great Nor'easter of 1992 are excluded. RMS found no non-hurricane has ever breached the trigger, and historically only Hurricane Donna in 1960 at a modelled 9.52 feet in Area A and Superstorm Sandy in 2012 at 10.93 feet would have. Surge data comes from NOAA and USGS gauges, with mobile backup gauges to be deployed at all five locations and high-water marks as a final fallback.
insights: The MTA's stated motivation is the benefit itself: expand and diversify its sources of reinsurance, and obtain parametric cover that should pay out more quickly than indemnity coverage. Liquidity timing, not loss compensation, is what the instrument delivers, and the sponsor says so in its own words.

A 100 per cent principal payment with no sliding scale is a deliberate simplification that buys speed at the cost of basis risk, and the entry states the consequence plainly: the payout may not necessarily correlate with the sponsor's actual losses.

The sponsor is a captive insurer: a public transit authority using its own captive to reach the capital markets directly, rather than buying cover from a commercial insurer that would then reinsure it.

Two design details are worth carrying: the exclusion of extra-tropical cyclones means a 1992-type nor'easter is uncovered even though it can produce surge, and the mobile backup gauges plus high-water-mark fallback are an answer to the data-failure risk every parametric trigger carries.

records.title: Financing the Resilient City
records.summary: The paper 'Financing the Resilient City' advocates for a paradigm shift in urban risk reduction towards enhancing the performance and resilience of urban assets and systems. By positioning disaster risk reduction as an investment opportunity, the paper emphasizes the need for innovative financing mechanisms, comprehensive planning, and multi-sector collaboration to address the financial risks of climate-related disasters in rapidly urbanizing areas.
insights: The strategy reframes the adaptation problem from risk reduction as an end in itself to financing the performance of urban assets, areas and systems, which is what lets conventional private investment flows recognise it.

Resilience is proposed as an urban design and investment metric measuring the ability of assets to perform for users and investors across a wide range of conditions, so the metric is performance rather than hazard.
The explicit premise is that international adaptation funds will not mobilise enough capital, so the paper is about capital above and beyond those funds.
Mainstreaming is the stated objective: a performance-oriented approach supplies a business logic that attracts conventional investment into climate and disaster risk reduction.

records.title: A Methodological Approach for Pricing Flood Insurance and Evaluating Loss Reduction Measures: Application to Texas
records.authors: Jeffrey Czajkowski; Howard Kunreuther; Erwann Michel-Kerjan
records.summary: A Wharton Risk Management and Decision Processes Center white paper from January 2012 presenting a methodological approach for pricing flood insurance and evaluating loss reduction measures, applied to Texas. The paper's contribution is the method rather than the state: it sets out how a risk-based flood premium can be constructed and how the effect of loss reduction measures on that premium can be evaluated, then demonstrates the approach on Texas data. The authors are the Travelers and Willis Re research fellow Jeffrey Czajkowski, and Howard Kunreuther and Erwann Michel-Kerjan, the centre's co-directors, whose long-standing subject is how society manages low-probability high-consequence events. The work sits at the point where catastrophe modelling, insurance pricing and mitigation evaluation meet, which is the analytical foundation any mitigation-discount scheme requires: without a defensible link from a physical loss reduction measure to a premium, an insurer cannot price the mitigation and a homeowner cannot be rewarded for it.
insights: The contribution is methodological: it sets out how to price a flood premium and how to evaluate what a loss reduction measure does to that premium, which is the analytical step a mitigation-discount scheme needs in order to be priced rather than asserted.
Applying the method to Texas makes it a worked example rather than a framework, so the approach can be checked against a real exposure set.

It dates from 2012 and predates both the NFIP's Risk Rating 2.0 and the current private flood market, so it should be read as the methodological ancestor of those rather than as a description of current practice.
The authors' affiliations include insurer-funded research fellowships, which is context for a paper about how insurers should price.
